text:
The writer, a Los Angeles freelancer and former Detroit News business reporter, writes a blog, Starkman Approved.

By Eric Starkman

No joke: Ford CEO Jim Farley has been named Automotive News Industry Leader of the Year.

Yes, that Jim Farley—under whose watch Ford has led the entire U.S. auto industry in safety recalls for years running.

The Jim Farley whose company was dubbed the most iconically American by Time, yet sits in imminent danger of losing its historic No. 3 U.S. sales podium to South Korea’s Hyundai Motor Group.

The Jim Farley who just conceded it will take "a heck of an effort" just to launch Ford’s much-hyped, sub-$30,000 electric truck "at scale, at cost, on time."

On cue, Ford underscored the honor by recalling 40,000 late-model, high-margin vehicles over a contaminated LED chip. Individual components can't be serviced, so dealers will have to rip out and replace entire headlight assemblies—another margin-chewing hit to Ford’s multibillion-dollar warranty tab.

According to Ford Authority, Farley bested 16 other automotive executives to garner the accolade. Automotive News cited several factors, chief among them Farley’s vocal push to raise alarms about the "existential threat" China poses to domestic automakers, along with his strategy to counter it.

It seems to me that the executive actually responsible for building that competitive pressure might be a touch more deserving. That would be BYD’s Stella Li. Based in Southern California, Li oversees BYD’s Americas division and established the company's commercial and manufacturing footprint in California. She then spearheaded passenger vehicle market entry across Latin America and Europe.

While Farley and GM’s Mary Barra talk about affordable EVs, Li’s teams are actually delivering high-volume, cost-competitive hybrid and electric architectures to global markets at scale.

Li was named World Car Person of the Year in 2025 by a jury of roughly 100 automotive journalists across more than 30 countries. Her acceptance speech offered a telling contrast in executive perspective: “This award is the result of the highly appreciated 110,000 BYD engineers who continue to make EVs and Super Hybrid DM-i technology available for all of us,” she said. “I am glad to play my part in putting these sustainable technologies in the hands of as many consumers as possible around the world.”

Farley’s takeaway: “For me this is a really special full-circle moment... I really am so deeply appreciative of this recognition.”

One leader credits 110,000 engineers for operational execution; the other takes a victory lap for his efforts.

The folks at The Onion must be kicking themselves for getting scooped by Automotive News.

Starkman can be reached at eric@starkmanapproved.com. Confidentially is assured.

title: Arizona, Hopi may regain $181M in solar grants after courts reverse Trump EPA
authors: ellis preston cronkite news, Brandon Quester, Cronkite News Service
description:
Arizona and the Hopi Tribe could regain $181 million for solar projects in low-income communities after two federal judges ruled the Trump administration unlawfully rescinded the Biden-era grants.
The Environmental Protection Agency awarded nearly $7 billion in April 2024 under the Solar For All program, part of the Inflation Reduction Act.
Arizona received $42,000 of its $156.1 million grant, according to federal records on USASpending.gov.
The Hopi Tribe received $421,000 out of $25.1 million.
In September, federal judges in the District of Columbia and Rhode Island issued rulings days apart striking down EPA’s termination.
text:
Arizona and the Hopi Tribe could regain $181 million for solar projects in low-income communities after two federal judges ruled the Trump administration unlawfully rescinded the Biden-era grants.

The Environmental Protection Agency awarded nearly $7 billion in April 2024 under the Solar For All program, part of the Inflation Reduction Act.

The Trump EPA terminated the program in August 2025. Only about $71 million had been disbursed at the time, according to an agency audit, though all of it had already been promised to the 60 or so grantees.

Arizona received $42,000 of its $156.1 million grant, according to federal records on USASpending.gov. The Hopi Tribe received $421,000 out of $25.1 million.

In September, federal judges in the District of Columbia and Rhode Island issued rulings days apart striking down EPA’s termination. The rulings could clear the way for restoration of the grants, though neither judge directly ordered they be reinstated.

The EPA said in a statement that it is reviewing the rulings and considering whether to appeal.

The One Big Beautiful Bill, signed in July 2025, repealed the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund created by the Inflation Reduction Act and rescinded all unobligated money. The Trump administration argued that the provision covered the unspent Solar for All money.

“EPA no longer has the authority to administer the program or the appropriated funds,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in August 2025, asserting that Congress has provided “clear language and intent” to eliminate the funding.

Both the Rhode Island and D.C. judges disagreed, ruling that because the Biden EPA had promised the $7 billion and issued grant agreements, the funds were “obligated” and not subject to being rescinded under the One Big Beautiful Bill.

The governor’s office projected that the grant would reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 96,000 tons per year. Mahoney told the court it would create thousands of green jobs and allow the state to provide $33 million in loans for rooftop solar.

Nick Torrey, a lawyer at the Southern Environmental Law Center – which represented plaintiffs in the Rhode Island case – said the EPA misinterpreted the law.

“EPA just really got it wrong here,” he said. “EPA did the opposite of what Congress was telling it to do. It acted unlawfully.”

“They’ve got the money sitting right there,” Torrey added. “It’s time to get busy. … It’s a real opportunity to provide relief to working families.”

Adrianna Amato, spokeswoman for the Governor’s Office of Resiliency, said the office was “cautiously optimistic” that the state will receive the funds the EPA promised it in 2024.

In addition to Arizona’s $156 million allocation, the EPA granted $25 million to the Hopi Utilities Corporation to provide electricity for about 600 homes on the reservation, 35% of which lack access to electricity, according to a 2023 Department of Energy report.

Mahoney said in her declaration that 15,000 tribal households in Arizona lack any access to electricity.

Fletcher Wilkinson, the energy manager at Hopi Utilities Corporation, said he sees “a long road ahead” before the program can resume.

The corporation had finished planning and was ready to move to execution when the EPA cut off funding, he said.

“It was crushing,” Wilkinson said, adding the tribe “has experienced for so long this severe, egregious lack of access to utilities that we take for granted elsewhere.”

text:
Supra Elemental Recovery, an Austin-based firm, has received the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) contract to improve scandium extraction from industrial byproducts.

The U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) is backing the new technology to strengthen domestic supplies of the critical mineral.

According to Supra’s announcement, the Defense Logistics Agency awarded the critical minerals technology startup a Phase I Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) contract to evaluate the feasibility of applying its separation platform to scandium-bearing feedstocks and assess its potential for future scalability.

“The U.S. has scandium resources onshore,” said Katie Durham, co-founder and CEO of Supra, in the company’s release. She further stated that their technology can recover scandium at high purity and at scale to meet domestic demand.

The contract is significant due to the continued reliance of the United States on foreign scandium sources, a vulnerability the Pentagon is now working to address.

Scandium’s role in aerospace and advanced technology

Rare earth separation involves converting mixed material into individual oxides used across advanced manufacturing and other strategic industries. They are essential to electric vehicles, wind turbines, robotics, semiconductors, and military systems. But building a reliable supply chain still remains a challenge for the United States.

Scandium, a rare-earth element, is used in lightweight aluminum-scandium alloys, including in aerospace components, and in solid oxide fuel cells.

More from Energy

See All

Unlike minerals produced primarily from dedicated mines, scandium is often recovered alongside other materials, such as titanium, zirconium, cobalt, nickel, and aluminum, according to Metal Tech News.

Its proprietary platform uses advanced chemical separation technology to recover targeted elements from industrial feedstocks selectively.

Supra said peer-reviewed research has validated its underlying separation technology, which can apply to different minerals and feedstocks. The company says it is developing technology for low-cost, high-purity critical mineral production at mining and industrial sites.

U.S. projects target domestic scandium supplies

The Defense Logistics Agency (DLA)-backed research will evaluate separation and processing technologies that could contribute to a more diverse domestic supply chain.

But Supra’s work joins several projects pursuing scandium production and processing in North America, including USA Rare Earth and Texas Mineral Resources’ Round Top project in Texas and NioCorp Developments in Nebraska.

Rio Tinto in Canada extracts high-purity scandium oxide from titanium dioxide waste streams produced from its Lac Tio mine operations in Quebec. Similarly, Supra is pursuing recovery from existing industrial materials rather than relying solely on new primary scandium mining, as per Metal Tech News.

Supra further said that its platform can be adapted across different minerals and material sources. The Phase I contract will determine the feasibility of Supra’s approach with regard to the project.

The company will now evaluate its separation platform against relevant scandium-bearing feedstocks, with the initial research focused on determining whether the technology can support high-purity scandium recovery at larger scales. The Austin-based company recovers and refines critical minerals at mining and industrial sites and is also a member of the Defense Industrial Base Consortium.

title: Toyota's patient hybrid strategy pays off massively as global oil markets burn | Dagens.com
description:
While rival automakers spent the last three years abandoning hybrids to bet their entire futures on fully electric vehicles, Toyota quietly stayed the course.
Robust sales growth across the rest of the lineup, including the Camry, Sienna Hybrid, and Grand Highlander Hybrid, easily absorbed the difference.
While Toyota’s pure EV numbers remain a fraction of its hybrid volume, they are showing signs of life.
For the luxury Lexus division, the RX crossover remains the undisputed sales king, with hybrids heavily dominating the mix.
Just three years ago, legacy American automakers like General Motors and Ford were highly critical of Toyota’s reluctance to go “all-in” on battery electric vehicles.
text:
While rival automakers spent the last three years abandoning hybrids to bet their entire futures on fully electric vehicles, Toyota quietly stayed the course. Now, as geopolitical instability sends fuel prices skyrocketing, that conservative strategy is yielding historic dividends.

According to InsideEVs, electrified vehicles—the vast majority of them standard hybrids—accounted for a staggering 61% of Toyota and Lexus’s total sales mix in the third quarter of 2026.

The primary catalyst for this surge is not environmentalism, but basic economics. The ongoing U.S. war in Iran, which began in late February, has severely strained global oil supply chains and kept domestic gas prices elevated for months. Faced with sustained pain at the pump, American consumers are flocking to fuel-efficient hybrids in record numbers.

The Q3 breakdown

Overall, Toyota and Lexus sold 633,223 vehicles in the U.S. between July and September, representing a virtually flat 0.6% year-over-year increase. However, the internal mix of what buyers actually drove off the lot shifted radically.

The company moved 363,367 electrified models in Q3—a massive 28.5% jump from the same period last year. Through the first nine months of the year, Toyota has sold nearly a million hybrids. That volume was achieved even as overall sales of the flagship RAV4 temporarily dipped 6.6% in September while the automaker retooled its factories for the launch of the new, hybrid-only sixth-generation model. Robust sales growth across the rest of the lineup, including the Camry, Sienna Hybrid, and Grand Highlander Hybrid, easily absorbed the difference.

While Toyota’s pure EV numbers remain a fraction of its hybrid volume, they are showing signs of life. Sales of the refreshed bZ EV doubled compared to last year, reaching roughly 25,000 units year-to-date—surpassing domestic competitors like the Chevy Equinox EV, though still trailing Hyundai’s popular Ioniq 5. For the luxury Lexus division, the RX crossover remains the undisputed sales king, with hybrids heavily dominating the mix.

Detroit’s multi-billion dollar miscalculation

Toyota’s Q3 dominance highlights a brutal strategic miscalculation by the rest of the automotive industry.

Just three years ago, legacy American automakers like General Motors and Ford were highly critical of Toyota’s reluctance to go “all-in” on battery electric vehicles. Detroit largely abandoned hybrid development to pour tens of billions of dollars into pure EVs.

That bet failed to account for consumer hesitation and global supply shocks. As EV adoption cooled and gas prices spiked this year, consumers overwhelmingly signaled they wanted the middle ground: the fuel savings of a battery without the charging anxiety of a pure EV.

The resulting whiplash has been financially devastating for Toyota’s rivals. Earlier this year, GM was forced to take a $6 billion writedown to unwind its overly ambitious EV investments, while Ford has publicly scaled back its electric production to hastily pivot resources back toward hybrid development.

Toyota, meanwhile, never left the hybrid market. By maintaining a highly diversified lineup of standard and plug-in hybrids, the Japanese automaker was perfectly positioned to capture the panicked consumer demand that Detroit essentially abandoned.

title: Repeal of Roadless Rule would harm national forests like Shawnee - Chicago Tribune
description:

text:
For 73-year-old Harold “Cricket” Simons, a major appeal of the Shawnee National Forest is what isn’t there.

No motorized vehicles. No traffic passing on most trails. No horns or engines breaking the quiet.

Simons travels through the forest on horseback. The former Bloomington, Illinois, rodeo rider spends much of his retirement leading the Illinois chapter of the Back Country Horsemen of America, a national organization of horse-riding volunteers who help maintain trails and public lands.

His five horses are accustomed to the sounds of trail work: the occasional chainsaw or falling tree.

But he said his workhorses, like him, prefer silence.

That’s at risk as the Trump administration’s Department of Agriculture proposed in August to repeal a 2001 federal rule restricting road construction on national forest lands.

“We stand to lose our solitude in our roadless areas,” Simons said.

The repeal of the conservation regulation commonly known as the Roadless Rule, would affect nearly 45 million acres of national forests across the country, including about 10,666 acres in Shawnee.

Across the Midwest, more than 170,000 acres of public lands are protected under the Roadless Rule, including portions of Indiana’s Hoosier National Forest, Minnesota’s Superior and Chippewa national forests and Michigan’s Ottawa and Huron-Manistee national forests.

The proposal is drawing concern from horseback riders like Simons and hunters, hikers and other outdoor recreationists, as well as tribal groups with treaty rights across the Great Lakes region. Conservationists worry that numerous threatened and endangered species will be adversely affected.

“There’s a lot to lose here, and everybody needs to be made aware of it,” said Kelly Thayer, senior policy advocate with the Environmental Law & Policy Center.

The proposed repeal comes as the U.S. Forest Service is also contending with other changes to federal forest management policy, Thayer said, creating what he described as a “perfect storm” for public lands.

Along with a proposal to eliminate the Roadless Rule, the USDA and Forest Service revised the agency’s Travel Management Rule to allow increased access for motor vehicles on national forest lands. This applies to 193 million acres nationwide, including the Shawnee.

Together with staffing cuts and a Trump executive order to boost timber production in national forests by 25%, these actions have raised questions about how the Forest Service will manage its existing roads and trails — much less additional roads that could be built — and who will benefit.

“In order to mine or in order to log a national forest, roads are required,” Thayer said. “So this effort to roll back the Roadless Rule is very much intended to provide access to the timber industry and the mining industry. That’s the big national play here.”

The Forest Service says repealing the Roadless Rule would not immediately authorize roads, logging or mining in the Shawnee’s roadless areas.

“The intent to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule is to return to local decision making as part of individual national forest and grassland plans, which include robust public involvement and focus on land management decisions at the right scale,” said a U.S. Forest Service spokesperson in a Sept. 25 email to the Tribune.

In Illinois, where relatively few undisturbed forests remain, residents and environmentalists say saving these spaces is urgent.

“They’re just unbelievable beauty, and you see things you don’t see anywhere else,” Simons said. “To cut through them is like a crime, in my opinion.”

A ‘fragmented’ forest

Glaciers smoothed out most of Illinois millions of years ago, creating fertile, flat farmland. But on the edge of that glaciated area is the Shawnee, where a mixture of distinctly rugged geology and ecosystems converge. Hugging the Mississippi and Ohio rivers, it’s home to biological diversity unlike anywhere else in Illinois.

From the limestone bluffs and swamps of Larue Pine Hills to “Snake Road,” where thousands of reptiles and amphibians migrate across the gravel road every spring and fall, the forest contains some of the state’s most distinct landscapes.

“There’s more biodiversity in the couple thousand acres of Larue Pine Hills than there is in Smoky Mountain National Park,” said Matt Lechner, a retired Shawnee Forest Service employee. “It’s outstanding.”

But the Shawnee is not one continuous block of public land. The nearly 289,000-acre forest is interspersed with private property, farms, communities and roads, creating a patchwork of public and private lands across southern Illinois.

That makes the remaining relatively intact tracts especially important to preserve, according to conservation groups, particularly in a state like Illinois that has lost much of its native forests.

“At one point, forests covered 40% of Illinois’ landscape. And today that number is about 14%,” said Amanda Pankau, director of energy and community resiliency at Prairie Rivers Network.

“We don’t have very many remaining, and what we do have is highly fragmented,” she said. “It’s very important that we have very few of these contiguous tracts left, that they are protected.”

The Roadless Rule was adopted in 2001 after years of public debate over how much of the country’s remaining undeveloped national forest land should be protected from roads and commercial development.

Today, the rule covers tens of millions of acres of National Forest System land.

The Shawnee’s roadless areas are scattered across that landscape. The six areas — Bay Creek, Burden Falls, Burke Branch, Clear Springs, Eagle Creek and Ripple Hollow — cover more than 10,000 acres.

They are also part of a larger habitat supporting wildlife, wetlands, waterways and other ecological resources, including endangered species like the Indiana bat and state-threatened species like the timber rattlesnake.

In its announcement of the repeal proposal on Aug. 18, the Trump administration’s USDA said the policy has become an obstacle for active forest management.

The USDA argues the repeal would allow for more wildfire-risk reduction work, timber production, jobs and economic development and would return decisions to local forest managers to respond to environmental and economic conditions.

But the USDA’s own 300-page environmental impact analysis of the proposed repeal found that eliminating the national rule is “likely to adversely affect” 327 threatened or endangered species and 71 designated critical habitats nationwide.

In the Shawnee, conservationists point to threatened wildlife such as the Indiana bat and timber snake that depend on an intact forest habitat.

“There are two kinds of endangered bats in the Shawnee that are very important to agriculture because they’re insect-eating machines,” Thayer said. “They do hard work for us.”

The proposed repeal also comes as the Trump administration has narrowed the Endangered Species Act and as climate change puts additional pressure on Shawnee’s ecosystems.

Lechner said Shawnee’s Forest Service faces an even more basic problem: It doesn’t have the resources to fully assess the number of species already in the forest.

“The truth of the matter is we don’t even really know what we have,” he said. “We don’t have money to do basic inventory. … There is just a ton of biodiversity to protect, and you go opening up roads, you’re going to change the amount of sediment that’s coming down the creek and change the creek.”

Lechner echoed American ecologist Aldo Leopold’s famous warning about conservation, that society often stands guard over famous works of art while species representing “the work of aeons are stolen from under our noses.”

“The ‘Mona Lisa’ paints a pretty picture,” Lechner said. “But the Indiana bat and its ecological role deserves our protection.”

The costs of repeal

If the Roadless Rule is repealed, decisions about future road construction and management would return to individual national forests through their forest plans, subject to public involvement and existing environmental laws, according to the Forest Service spokesperson.

This would give local managers greater flexibility to address wildfire risk, forest health, watersheds, timber production and local economic conditions.

Timber production is a core part of the Trump administration’s argument for repealing the Roadless Rule, and the Forest Service says removing restrictions would potentially increase the amount of federal forestland available and generate additional revenue.

That argument is particularly relevant in rural communities where the timber industry remains an important source of employment and revenue.

The agency’s analysis projects up to $11 million in additional timber revenue from the repeal.

But the same August analysis also projects economic losses tied to the loss of roadless areas. The Forest Service estimates about $9 million in annual losses to outdoor recreation and tourism, along with up to $6 million in lost economic benefits from businesses and wildlife recreation in areas that are no longer roadless.

“So $5 (million) to $11 million in new timber revenue, maybe,” Thayer said. “And $15 million in negative economic harm to outdoor recreation and tourism, and another additional $5 (million) to $11 million in economic losses related to the ecosystem benefits that will be lost to cleaning our water, cleaning our air, and securing our climate.”

“So the federal government runs the numbers on its own proposal and finds out that we will be far worse off economically each and every year that the Roadless Rule is not in place,” Thayer said. “That’s their conclusion.”

Beyond aiding timber production, repealing the national rule could expand access for mining and other extractive operations, opponents say.

That possibility is particularly relevant in parts of the Shawnee.

Eagle Creek, one of the forest’s six roadless areas, sits near southern Illinois landscapes with a long history of coal mining, including active and historic mining areas outside the Shawnee’s boundaries.

“Illinois is the fourth-largest coal-producing state. We are still mining a lot of coal,” Pankau said.

Ripple Hollow, another roadless area, contains silica deposits.

Pankau emphasized that repeal itself would not mean mining or logging would immediately begin.

“It’s not like this is repealed, and all of a sudden they’re logging and mining silica at Ripple Hollow, but that would be a possibility,” she said.

Forests with fewer hands

For Simons, the Shawnee is both home and workplace.

He and his wife, Vicki, live with their five horses on property near roadless areas and trail systems. As chair of the Illinois chapter of the Back Country Horsemen of America, Simons works with the Forest Service and leads a team of volunteers who spend thousands of hours maintaining public lands.

His volunteers use horses to haul rocks, clear fallen trees and repair damaged trails — work that can be done without bringing motorized equipment into some of the forest’s more remote areas.

“The Back Country horsemen are great,” Lechner said. “They haul rocks for us and really help out with trail maintenance, and they understand one of the things about wilderness is you’re not supposed to change it.”

This support has been especially necessary as Lechner said Shawnee’s Forest Service has faced staffing and budget cuts, like the rest of the nation’s public lands workforce. When he started in 2003, Lechner said Shawnee’s Forest Service had 120 staff members — when he retired in 2020, he said the agency’s staff was down to around 50 or 60 employees doing the same amount of work.

Nationally, the Back Country Horsemen of America reported more than 200,000 volunteer service hours last year, with an estimated economic value of about $12 million. Simons said the Illinois chapter contributed roughly $97,000 worth of volunteer labor.

The staffing reductions extend beyond Shawnee. According to reporting from The New York Times, the Trump administration has cut nearly 6,000 Forest Service employees, responsible for managing millions of public lands across the country.

“There’s just fewer people to safeguard our forests, and there are fewer protections for the forests,” Thayer said. “It’s the citizens and it’s organizations that are filling the gap where the federal government should really be in the business of protecting our public lands, not selling them off.”

The work extends beyond trail maintenance. Simons said his team regularly picks up trash and has removed hundreds of illegally dumped tires from the forest.

He worries that additional roads and access could bring more of that work.

“If you build a road, all those things will increase,” Simons said. “All the bad influences that roads bring will increase.”

The Forest Service also has a substantial backlog of deferred road maintenance, with the agency estimating that cost at more than $9 billion.

“There’s far more roads in our national forest than there are miles of interstate highway system in the United States,” Thayer said. “It’s gotten away from us.”

According to the Forest Service, it maintains over 265,000 miles of roads. The interstate system is just under 47,000 miles, the Federal Highway Administration says.

“The bottom line is we can’t take care of the roads we have,” Lechner said. “So opening up more forest for more roads that they’re not going to be able to maintain doesn’t make any sense.”

‘Whiplash of administrations’

The debate over the Roadless Rule is also part of a decades-long cycle over how much control the federal government should have over undeveloped national forest lands.

The Roadless Rule was adopted in 2001 after receiving overwhelming public support, Thayer said.

“So many people commented on it that it set a record for the most comments ever on a federal rule,” he said.

But since then, the Roadless Rule has been on the chopping block with each administration. A proposed repeal was issued during the Bush years, and then again last June.

“There have been attempts to scrap the roadless rules since the very beginning,” Thayer said. “It’s really a saga of one administration that could come in and lift it up, and the next administration could come in and seek to overturn everything. And that seesaw battle has continued across the entire 25 years of the existence of the Roadless Rule.”

Indigenous people have also had to navigate the “whiplash of administrations,” according to Jenny Van Sickle, an outreach specialist with the Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission, an advocacy organization that works with the Ojibwe tribes in Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota.

“Tribal nations have been here since time immemorial,” she said. “We can be a helpful force in land stewardship, and we will work with any administration.”

Among the affected roadless areas, 196,000 acres are within Ojibwe territory. Van Sickle said 11 member tribes rely on treaty rights to harvest resources such as maple sap, cedar boughs and other forest products, essential for guaranteeing traditional ways of life on indigenous lands.

“Treaty rights are not optional,” Van Sickle said. “And it’s not a special privilege that anybody granted.”

She said changes to public lands can have implications beyond the boundaries of an individual forest because development, pollution or habitat loss can affect the resources tribes depend on.

“Shifting that responsibility to have it piecemeal in the states risks the integrity of a forest that is crossing boundaries it doesn’t know exists,” Van Sickle said. “It’s really difficult to treat that as a segmented system when it’s all very connected, like rivers and oceans.”

Because of these risks, many conservation groups and lawmakers are anxious to see permanent protections.

In 2025, Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois co-sponsored the Roadless Area Conservation Act, which would codify the rule’s protections in federal law. The legislation, which was reintroduced after earlier attempts, has not advanced out of committee.

“Shawnee National Forest, one of Illinois’ most beautiful landscapes, welcomes thousands of visitors each year who come to enjoy the view and hiking trails,” Durbin said in a Sept. 18 statement to the Tribune. “The Roadless Rule, which has overwhelming public support, has protected portions of Shawnee National Forest for more than two decades, and the Trump Administration’s attempts to strip the rule is shameful.”

Durbin also introduced legislation last year specifically addressing the Shawnee, including a proposal to establish 12,700 protected areas within the forest, called special management areas. Ripple Hollow and Burke Branch, two areas that are currently at risk of losing Roadless Rule protections would be within those special areas.

Public push

The USDA first announced a deadline of Sept. 21 for public input, but environmentalists pushed back to get it extended to Tuesday. Thayer said he still believes the process has been too rushed.

“One has to wonder why, when the federal government proposes something that it believes is a good idea, it would minimize public comment and hold no public meetings at all,” he said. “It’s very much a rush job to do something that the Trump administration absolutely knows is wildly at odds with what the public wants.”

ELPC has asked the public to sign a petition opposing the repeal. Last month, 164 members of Congress also signed a letter opposing the proposal.

Simons hopes people speak up.

“Once they change these things, you can’t just go and put them back,” he said. “To say we’re going to take this road out and plant trees back where the road is, it just doesn’t work that way. It takes 50 to 60 years.”

Christiana Freitag is a freelancer.

text:
Houston’s oil and gas industry is asking the Supreme Court to decide whether it can be on the hook for damages caused by global warming-causing emissions in a case that will be heard on Monday.

In 2018, Boulder, Co., sued Houston-based Exxon Mobil and Suncor, a Canadian energy company with refineries in Colorado. The city argued that as a result of climate change – sped up by fossil fuel companies – and their “misleading” marketing, Boulder residents were facing undue financial and environmental burdens.

The hearing marks the latest evolution in dozens of cases brought by city and state jurisdictions against fossil fuel companies over the last few years.

Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, causing more heat from the sun to be trapped in the atmosphere which, over time, leads to rising temperatures across the globe. Global warming has been linked to rising ocean levels, more severe weather and food and water supply issues.

The oil and gas industry has acknowledged they play a role in climate change, but maintains the global need for production while seeking cleaner energy options.

“The Suncor case will be transformational either way the Supreme Court rules,” said Ramanan Krishnamoorti, vice president for energy and innovation at the University of Houston.

Oral arguments start Monday, but a ruling isn’t expected until next year. Here’s what you should know:

What is the case about?

Boulder’s lawsuit against Exxon and Suncor seeks millions in damages for past and future costs associated with public health issues and environmental damages stemming from climate change. The companies misled the public about their role in climate change and continued to opaquely market their products, the city said in its lawsuit.

Exxon and Suncor have tried, and failed, to get the case thrown out or moved to federal court, saying state courts don’t have the right to try such claims. These issues fall under federal law and the Clean Air Act, the companies say.

The Colorado Supreme Court ruled last year that the case could go forward under state law. The companies then asked for the Supreme Court to step in.

Representatives for Exxon and Suncor declined to comment. Both companies have denied any wrongdoing in past statements and court documents.

RAILROAD COMMISSION: 'You better show up': Texas regulator blasts Exxon for going silent on residents near carbon project

"Local communities are living with the mounting costs of climate change," said Aaron Brockett, mayor of the city ⁠of Boulder, ​in a statement after the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case in February. "The Supreme Court should affirm Colorado's right to hold these companies accountable for ​the harm they have caused in Colorado."

Geoff Dembicki, managing editor at global climate investigations outlet DeSmog and author of The Petroleum Papers, said the heart of this case is about who can be held accountable for the costs of climate change.

“Whether that’s wildfire, a hurricane, drought, or extreme weather, up until this point, the cost of all of that has mainly been picked up by taxpayers,” Dembicki said. “What's really at stake with this U.S. Supreme Court decision is whether companies that have contributed to the warming of the atmosphere should also pay their share of disasters.”

Which Houston companies could be impacted?

This case names Suncor Energy, which operates two refineries in Colorado, and Exxon as petitioners.

But the Supreme Court’s ruling could impact more than 60 lawsuits across the country involving other major Houston oil companies, including Chevron, Occidental Petroleum, ConocoPhillips, Phillips 66, Shell and BP, accordingto the Center for Climate Integrity. Most of the cases assert that fossil fuel companies knowingly polluted the planet while ignoring their own internal research proving their role in global warming, referred to as climate deception.

In Washington state, the Shoalwater Bay Indian Tribe sued ExxonMobil, BP, Chevron, Shell, ConocoPhillips and P66 in 2023 for the hundred of millions of dollars the tribe says it will cost to relocate and protect their people and heritage from the rising sea level and flooding resulting from the energy companies’ practices.

Billions of dollars are on the line for Houston’s oil giants, research shows.

What are the likely possible outcomes?

The Supreme Court typically reviews final decisions made by state courts. But in this case, the state court hasn’t decided the substance of the case as Exxon and Suncor have litigated the proper jurisdiction for the lawsuit.

The energy companies have argued that since greenhouse gas emissions are a global phenomenon and supersede state and national boundaries, only federal courts and entities have the right to bring claims forward or regulate them.

A favorable Supreme Court decision for the companies, combined with recent environmental policy changes under the Trump administration, would likely change how energy companies address decarbonization issues, said Krishnamoorti from the University of Houston.

“It will free up many of the hydrocarbon companies to pursue their activities without fear of local or regional decision making,” he said.

VENEZUELA: Chevron, SLB signed Venezuela oil deals. Can smaller Houston firms do the same?

Boulder argues that courts have long applied state law to address environmental issues that cross state lines, adding that the federal government’s stance on global issues does not mean state or local claims should be dismissed.

Agreeing with Boulder’s arguments would cause “a significant chilling effect” for many companies operating in “progressive geographies,” according to Krishnamoorti.

Could this have broader implications outside of the oil and gas industry?

Legal experts and climate activists are closely watching the case because it could set a really broad legal precedent regarding a state’s right to go after companies that cause local harm, Dembicki said.

Because the case is about who can go after global companies for state impacts, it could be used by other industries, including pharmaceutical and chemical manufacturers, Dembicki said.

text:
A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.

Related video: Trump touts G7 plan to release oil and diesel reserves to address high prices

On Monday, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.

The Transportation Department and NHTSA earlier this week lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.

The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles. Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.

Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.

When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: "This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”

Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed Monday's change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.

But environmental organizations decried the changes.

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.

The DOT said Monday that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.

Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the U.S. These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits; scrapping vehicle emissions standards; repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules; and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout.

title: Supreme Court to weigh whether oil companies can be forced to pay for climate damage
description:
The Supreme Court will open its new term Monday by hearing arguments on whether the oil and gas industry may be forced to pay damages for the scorching heat waves, wildfires and droughts that are blamed on climate change.
These are referred to as “common law” claims that are long-standing and traditional but do not rely on a measure approved by the Legislature.
Legal experts say the industry’s claim to be shielded by federal law is weak.
The outcome in the Supreme Court remains in doubt.
Trump administration lawyers filed emergency appeals at the Supreme Court to set aside Murphy’s orders.
text:
The Supreme Court will open its new term Monday by hearing arguments on whether the oil and gas industry may be forced to pay damages for the scorching heat waves, wildfires and droughts that are blamed on climate change.

It’s a momentous question the justices have put off deciding for nearly a decade — and may do so again.

California joined more than two dozen blue states and municipalities in 2023 when it sued the five largest oil companies, alleging “decades of deception” over the danger of a warming climate.

They have “privately known the truth for decades but have fed us lies and mistruths to further their record-breaking profits at the expense of our environment,” California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said.

Such climate-change lawsuits were patterned after the mass claims against the tobacco and opioid industries. Both were accused of concealing the dangers of their very profitable products.

But the climate suits have stalled. Judges have been divided over whether these potentially huge claims should be decided in federal or state court, and if so, under what law.

Last year, Boulder County, Colo., won a 5-2 ruling in the state Supreme Court that allowed its 2018 suit to proceed as a claim of a public nuisance, an unjust enrichment or a civil conspiracy. These are referred to as “common law” claims that are long-standing and traditional but do not rely on a measure approved by the Legislature.

The Colorado judges also said the climate-change suits are not “preempted” or blocked by federal anti-pollution laws because the suit for damages did not regulate greenhouse gas emissions.

The dissenters said the state court was giving Boulder a “green light to act as its own republic” to punish the Exxon Mobil Corp. for the impact of “global climate change.”

Appealing to the Supreme Court, the oil companies sounded the same theme.

“Boulder, Colorado cannot make energy policy for the entire country,” they said. A ruling for the county would “authorize all 50 states and tens of thousands of municipalities” to ask their local juries to “impose ruinous liability” on the fossil fuel industry, they told the court.

The Trump administration joined in support of the industry’s appeal.

“Our federal system would disintegrate if each state could tackle inherently national or international problems by forcing its regulatory prescriptions on the other 49,” the administration’s lawyers wrote.

In February, the justices voted to hear the case and decide whether federal law blocks state law claims for the “effects of interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions.”

The court scheduled the case of Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil vs. Boulder County as the first of the new term.

Legal experts say the industry’s claim to be shielded by federal law is weak.

UCLA law professor Alejandro Camacho described the “preemption arguments as the latest and perhaps most ambitious effort to weaponize federal law to prevent polluters and fraudsters from paying for the harms they cause.”

Neither the Constitution nor the Clean Air Act provides such a shield, he said.

Legal experts on the other side question the notion that a public nuisance can be defined so broadly to include both the sale of a legal product and the impact on carbon pollution, much of it coming from China and India.

The outcome in the Supreme Court remains in doubt.

Last week, Justice Samuel A. Alito, a reliable conservative, announced he was withdrawing from the case. He did not say why, but he owns stock in other oil companies that could be affected by the court’s decision.

A broad ruling for Boulder would send a shock through the fossil-fuel industry and clear the wave of climate-change suits to proceed in state courts.

The industry may turn to Congress. Republicans in the House and Senate have introduced bills that would shield energy companies from such liability claims.

Similarly, a broad ruling shielding the oil companies probably would block all of the climate change suits, including California’s.

The justices may opt out of ruling, however.

When they granted review of the case, they asked the lawyers on both sides to weigh in on whether the high court had “jurisdiction” to decide the Boulder case.

Usually the U.S. Supreme Court reviews only final judgments handed down by state courts, and the Boulder case did not result in a final ruling.

And without Alito, the court could split 4 to 4.

A decision based on a tie vote would affirm Boulder’s early stage victory but would not set a precedent that would govern other cases.

In its new term, the court also will hear major cases on immigration and guns.

Two of the cases test the Trump administration’s strict deportation policies. One denies bond hearings to people who entered the country illegally and may be deported.

In the past, the government usually offered bond hearings to those who could be held for months or even years while their claims were pending, so long as they could show they were not a flight risk or danger to the public.

But the Trump administration said it plans to detain tens of thousands of such persons indefinitely, even if they have no criminal record and pose no risk.

Government lawyers pointed to a provision of the 1996 immigration law that said people who entered the country illegally “shall be detained.” Previous administrations applied the mandatory-detention rule only to migrants who entered the U.S. illegally and were arrested near the border.

On Thursday, the court announced it will hear arguments on the mandatory detention policy, likely to be scheduled for January.

The other case involves so-called “third-country removals.”

The administration is determined to deport immigrants who have “final orders of removal,” many of whom have criminal records. But in some cases, they may not be sent back to their country of origin.

The policy of sending them to a third country has been condemned as harsh and cruel. Thousands of these people have been flown to impoverished countries that are dangerous and where they may be subjected to abuse.

The administration says it seeks assurances from those countries that the deported persons will not be not be abused or persecuted, but it refuses hearings for individuals.

U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy in Boston has ruled these deportees are entitled to a “meaningful notice” of where they are being sent and “meaningful opportunity” to contest this if they have a reasonable fear they will face persecution and torture.

Trump administration lawyers filed emergency appeals at the Supreme Court to set aside Murphy’s orders. They argued that the judge had gone beyond his authority, and the court’s conservatives agreed.

In December, however, the court will hear arguments from both sides on what the law calls for in such deportation cases.

Meanwhile, on Dec. 2, the court will hear a potential landmark on gun rights and and decide whether states may prohibit possession and sale of semiautomatic AR-15 rifles.

California and 11 other blue states have adopted such laws, often in response to mass shootings.

Gun rights advocates say these rapid-fire rifles are among the most popular weapons nationwide and should be protected as lawful under the 2nd Amendment’s right “to keep and bear arms.”

title: The Supreme Court Is Considering the Future of Climate Change Lawsuits
description:
The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments Monday in a case that could block one of the last remaining legal paths for holding fossil fuel companies responsible for damage from climate change.
Other legal avenues for holding fossil fuel companies accountable have already been foreclosed, including by a 2011 Supreme Court decision that effectively left no future for similar cases in federal court.
The Colorado Supreme Court ruled that federal law doesn’t stand in the way of the claims moving forward in state court.
In an unusual move, the Supreme Court agreed to review the issue before the case has gone to trial and before a state court has made a final judgement.
But this week, the conservative justice reversed course, recusing himself with a one-sentence announcement from the Supreme Court clerk.
text:
The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments Monday in a case that could block one of the last remaining legal paths for holding fossil fuel companies responsible for damage from climate change.

The case, Suncor Energy vs. Boulder County, centers on a procedural question of whether the companies must face lawsuits in state courts, or if federal law precludes those.

The answer could shape the future of claims from dozens of states, counties and cities seeking to use state laws to recoup billions of dollars for the costs associated with climate disasters such as fires and floods.

Other legal avenues for holding fossil fuel companies accountable have already been foreclosed, including by a 2011 Supreme Court decision that effectively left no future for similar cases in federal court.

Trending

“So if this one is closed, too, then seeking court remedies is going to be largely off the table,” said Jonathan Adler, a professor at William & Mary Law School who filed a brief in the case.

The city and county of Boulder, Colorado, filed a state lawsuit that aims to hold Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil responsible for costs associated with climate disasters, arguing under a state law that the companies deceived the public about the danger of their products.

The Colorado Supreme Court ruled that federal law doesn’t stand in the way of the claims moving forward in state court. Similar claims have been filed across the country, including Vermont, Minnesota and Hawaii, and courts have been split on the question of whether federal law preempts the lawsuits.

Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil told the Supreme Court in a filing in the case that the justices have a chance to address whether the climate change litigation can proceed before “the energy industry is threatened with potentially enormous judgments.”

“There are few, if any, more consequential questions pending in the lower courts concerning the relationship between state and federal law,” the companies wrote in their petition for the court to hear the case.

In an unusual move, the Supreme Court agreed to review the issue before the case has gone to trial and before a state court has made a final judgement. So the justices also will decide whether they have jurisdiction over the case at this early stage, a question that could give them a way to avoid a major decision at this time.

The Trump administration has unsuccessfully attempted to block several state law cases, suing states that are suing fossil fuel companies. Congress is also trying to weigh in: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) introduced a bill that would expressly foreclose state claims against fossil fuel companies.

The Supreme Court has declined to look at the same question previously, last year on a lawsuit from the city and county of Honolulu, and in 2023 on the same Suncor v. Boulder case. At least four justices must agree to grant a petition.

In both of those instances, Justice Samuel Alito recused himself early in the process, leaving the other eight justices to decide whether the court should take up the case. Alito owns stock ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, companies implicated in related cases.

This time around, Alito did not recuse himself early on, and the court decided to take up the case. But this week, the conservative justice reversed course, recusing himself with a one-sentence announcement from the Supreme Court clerk.

Across the country, climate-related cases against fossil fuel companies vary in terms of their legal claims and the remedies they’re asking the court to provide. But the basic facts are the same, said Corey Riday-White, the legal director of the Center for Climate Integrity.

“They knew, they lied, they should be held accountable,” he said.

Riday-White likened Boulder’s case to those involving tobacco companies, opioid manufacturers and Meta. “You have companies that promote and sell a harmful product without warning the public about those harms, and the courts are the proper venue to go to to get compensated for those harms,” he said.

Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil argue Boulder’s lawsuit amounts to an attempt to regulate its emissions across the country and the globe — a role only federal law can take.

The companies, in their brief, called the variety of claims against fossil fuel firms “complete chaos,” and said using state law to address climate change “represents a serious threat to one of our Nation’s most critical sectors.”

Saikrishna Prakash, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, argues in a brief filed in the case that Boulder is attempting to regulate fossil fuel production across the United States. Prakash contends that allowing the lawsuit to move forward would create a slippery slope to local governments being allowed to regulate consumers of fossil fuels, such as regular Americans who use gas stoves.

“[Boulder’s] lawsuit reflects a desire to change the world and rests on a long-arm theory of regulatory power, where Colorado may regulate worldwide to stem the effects of greenhouse gas emissions,” Prakash wrote.

Boulder argues in court filings that the federal government is not charged with regulating the “deceptive marketing” of fossil fuels. And it asserts that if the Supreme Court ruled that the Clean Air Act preempted any state laws that indirectly affect emissions, that would negatively affect everything from state gasoline taxes to local energy-efficiency regulations.

Historically, greenhouse gas emissions have been regulated under the Clean Air Act. But this year, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the endangerment finding, which provided the basis for the federal government’s ability to regulate emissions under that law.

EPA officials from Republican and Democratic administrations filed a brief arguing that consumer protection and deceptive advertising lawsuits like Boulder’s are not preempted by the Clean Air Act.

Dozens of other amici briefs have been filed, including from members of Congress, climate economists, city and county governments, manufacturing and transportation trade groups and the Justice Department.

In one, a group of Colorado ranchers explains how climate change has affected their livelihoods. One rancher said she had to sell all the cattle on her third-generation ranch after a wildfire ripped through in 2025. Another said his cattle didn’t have enough drinking water and were unable to graze their usual pastures.

“They fear that if municipal government keeps absorbing the increasing costs imposed by heat, drought, fires, and flooding, it will not be able to provide the services on which they depend to continue ranching,” their brief said.

Deirdre Macnab, a cattle rancher who learned about the case from her local newspaper, said she’s watched climate change take a toll on her neighbors and her own ranch, recalling fires that killed 60 of her neighbor’s cattle and took out miles of fences and transmission lines.

title: New England leaders look to nuclear to ease energy costs — but when? - Hartford Courant
description:

text:
The long-anticipated renaissance of American nuclear power is unlikely to get its start in New England.

Lack of demand from data centers, high costs for labor and materials, unseemly battles with neighbors and — perhaps most importantly — uncertain financial options are all pushing developers of new nuclear technologies elsewhere, particularly to the Deep South and Midwest.

But as leaders across the region face rising demand for electricity and few options for delivering that power on-demand without fossil fuels, many are beginning to turn to nuclear as a possible solution, albeit one that is years or even decades away.

This week, officials from all six New England states gathered at the University of Massachusetts in Lowell for a summit on the revival of nuclear power in the region. The event was hosted the National Governor’s Association and featured scientists, clean-energy advocates and industry representatives, along with state officials.

The summit was born, in part, out of a public letter signed by the governors off all six states in March. The letter called for greater regional collaboration to keep New England’s remaining nuclear stations operational and to identify potential locations for expansion.

The location was symbolic for two reasons. The Merrimack River, which flows through the center of campus, was itself the power source that fueled the region’s early industrial rise. UMass-Lowell is also home to one of the few operating university research reactors located in the United States.

“It’s been a while since there was a new energy and a new opportunity like this,” said Emma Cimino, the acting commissioner of the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection who led a small delegation of state officials at the summit.

“All of our states have had some association with nuclear,” she added. “I think we’re all sort of hoping that leads to a little bit more openness to especially some of these new technologies that may not be these big, hulking, kind of traditional nuclear facilities that maybe conjure fears in people’s minds.”

As recently as 1990, New England was home to eight operating nuclear power plants with a combined output of over 7,000 megawatts of electricity. The cost of maintenance on those aging plants, combined with competition from cheap natural gas, contributed to a succession of closures over the next several decades that whittled the number of plants to two: Millstone Nuclear Power Station in Waterford and Seabrook Station in New Hampshire.

Together, Millstone and Seabrook’s three reactors have an output of nearly 3,300 megawatts, or about one-quarter of all the electricity produced in New England.

Efforts to restart commercial production of nuclear power elsewhere in the country have been repeatedly stalled by technical problems and cost overruns. Only two new reactors have entered service in the U.S. in the last decade, both at Georgia’s Vogtle Electric Generating Plant.

The Vogtle project was completed in 2024 at a total cost of over $30 billion and several years behind schedule.

Strategic challenges

Proponents of nuclear power have pinned much of their hopes on the development of a new generation of small modular reactors that can be built from standardized designs to help lower costs. Dozens of companies are vying to complete designs, and early prototypes are under construction in Tennessee and Wyoming.

For similar projects to get underway in New England, however, developers and state officials say they need to figure out a way to address some of the region’s unique political and economic barriers to nuclear power.

Massachusetts, Maine, Rhode Island and Vermont all have restrictions in place that require voter or legislative approval to construct any new nuclear reactor. In Massachusetts and Maine, that approval is also contingent on the federal government finding a long-term solution to the seemingly intractable problem of storing radioactive nuclear waste.

Connecticut lawmakers partially repealed the state’s own nuclear moratorium in 2022, allowing for the development of a new reactor at the Millstone site. Two years later, the legislature went one step further, allowing any city or town to hold a vote on whether to host “advanced” reactor technology.

So far, no municipality has exercised that option.

Ed Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, dismissed the notion that nuclear power offers a realistic solution to New England’s rising energy needs over the next decade.

In addition to old fears about safety that make it difficult to site nuclear facilities within a densely populated region, Lyman said that much of the current interest in nuclear is being driven by startups and unproven technologies that have yet to show they can be cost-competitive with other sources of power.

“It’s the industry’s own problems in strategic planning and … coming up with ways to realistically finance these things instead of a lot of hot air and hoping that if they generate enough steam or generate enough heat about this that investors will come,” Lyman said. “I think we’re still in that that space where it’s mostly being driven by hype and PR, and not by fundamentals.”

Another hurdle in New England’s quest for new nuclear power is the fact that each of the states, with the exception of Vermont, have adopted deregulated energy markets that generally prohibit public utilities — such as Eversource and United Illuminating — from owning their own power plants while also selling power to customers. All of the region’s existing reactors were built by utilities prior to deregulation.

Dominion Energy, the Virginia-based company that owns Millstone, has focused its development of small modular reactors in states with fully regulated electricity markets, which provide a more direct path to recouping upfront costs from ratepayers.

Dominion is also in the process of being sold to NextEra Energy, which would create one of the world’s largest power utilities. NextEra is the owner of Seabrook Station, raising concerns from some New England officials that the sale would give the combined company a monopoly over nuclear power in the region. Earlier this week, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong filed a formal opposition to the merger with federal regulators.

“Right now, we’re just focused on the continued safe operation of Millstone,” Dominion spokesman Ryan Frazier said in a statement Thursday. “Until the merger closes, Dominion and NextEra will continue to operate independently. Beyond that, no decisions have been made. Both companies are proven, high-quality nuclear operators.”

Neil Nissan, a spokesman for NextEra, said in a statement that the company has a “dedicated team” exploring new nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors, but has not announced any plans for expanding Seabrook Station.

“NextEra Energy continuously evaluates opportunities to meet growing energy demand across the country, including in New England,” Nissan said.

Cimino, of DEEP, said Wednesday that one of her key takeaways from the conference was the need to understand developers’ concerns about New England’s energy markets and develop new financing and risk management structures to help attract investment.

“I think that that’s something that we, individually as states, and collectively need to drill in on as we continue to explore this technology,” Cimino said.

At the federal level, officials and Congress are continuing to search for locations that could serve as interim storage sites for spent nuclear fuel until a permanent repository can be built. Currently, the spent fuel from nuclear power plants, including decommissioned plants, is stored on location in concrete casks. Earlier this year, Department of Energy signed agreements with six states to further explore the development of spent-fuel recycling or disposal facilities. (One of those states, West Virginia, dropped out of consideration in September).

“With renewed investment and support for nuclear power as a clean energy source, there is an opportunity to reuse spent fuel and significantly shrink the volume of material that requires disposal,” U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, said in a statement this week. “There is still much work to be done, but Congressional support is strong to move the spent fuel initiative that has occurred over multiple administrations.”

Raising hands

At Wednesday’s summit, Cimino participated in a panel featuring representatives from the six New England states. Each expressed an interest, to some degree, in either hosting a new nuclear facility or providing financial support to make such an expansion happen.

One area that garnered a lot of interest was the town of Waterford, which has hosted Millstone since the 1970s.

Waterford First Selectman Robert Brule also attended the summit to spread the word that his town is open to new nuclear development. He said he met with three different developers who are seeking potential locations to build advanced reactors. (Brule declined to name the developers, citing the preliminary nature of their discussions).

Part of the reason for his town’s interest, Brule said, is the need to make up for shrinking tax revenues from Millstone, which experienced a decline in property values following deregulation. Prior to deregulation, Millstone made up about 64% of the town’s overall tax revenues, according to The Day of New London. That figure has since fallen to around one-third of revenues.

In order to fill that gap, Brule said, the town had previously explored hosting a large data center that would draw about 300 MW of electricity directly from Millstone. That plan fell apart due to public opposition and difficulty executing a host-fee agreement, and Brule told the Connecticut Mirror on Thursday he had no plans of reviving the data center project as long as he is in office.

“We’d rather produce the energy now than produce a project that sucks up the energy,” Brule said.

Brule said Waterford benefits from having residents who are familiar with the realities — and potential risks — of living next to a nuclear power plant. Town officials also undergo regular emergency preparedness training and are in frequent contact with Dominion, he said. As for other potential locations in Connecticut, Cimino said that DEEP has been “laying the ground work” to engage with local officials and community members about their interest in nuclear development.

The 2024 law that allowed municipalities to volunteer to host a new reactor also set aside $5 million in state bonds to establish “site readiness” funding program. That fund can be used to help pay for things such as preliminary technical or environmental studies, community engagement initiatives or other expenses deemed necessary by DEEP.

“There’s about 40 criteria that you got to go through” to determine if a particular location is suitable for a nuclear power plant, according to Jeff Semancik, the director of DEEP’s radiation division. Those criteria include having an adequate footprint, ground seismology and access to large quantities of water.

“We kind of know if a site had nuclear before that’s probably pretty good,” Semancik added. “We don’t know in some of these other sites if it would fit, and so I think [the fund is] kind of helping to do it.”

Cimino said that funding should be available for grants sometime within the next six months.

Another enthusiastic response at Wednesday’s summit came from Vermont, formerly home to the 650 MW Vermont-Yankee Nuclear Power Plant, which closed in 2014. Workers are in the midst of disassembling the old plant, a process that is expected to be completed next year. At that point, Kerrick Johnson, the commissioner of the Vermont Department of Public Service, said the site will become a “ready-made asset” for new nuclear development, with existing access to transmission lines, rail networks and community that is familiar with living next to a reactor.

“The community agrees, we and our department agree, the state, our governor [Phil Scott] agrees, and the region, initially, agrees,” Johnson said. “The collaborative role we can serve — as Vermont has traditionally served — is to go first.”

Johnson added that he hopes officials in surrounding states are driven by the urgency to tackle region-wide challenges posed by climate change, electrification and rising power costs.

“You start now, you’re talking about 2032, 2035,” before anything is finished, he said. “So you’ve got to start now.”

text:
Ottawa (VNA) –Vietnam and Canada are entering a broader phase of strategic cooperation, with their newly established Strategic Partnership opening opportunities beyond trade and people-to-people exchanges to supply chains, advanced technologies, energy security, defence and maritime security.

The assessment was made by Vina Nadjibulla, Co-Founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft (CSS), in an interview with Vietnam News Agency (VNA) correspondents in Canada following the State visit to Canada by General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam Central Committee and President To Lam.

She said one of the visit’s key outcomes was the initial institutionalisation of the new partnership framework. The two sides agreed to step up regular high-level contacts, including foreign ministerial dialogue, while strengthening existing mechanisms such as the Joint Economic Committee, Defence Policy Dialogue and Maritime Dialogue.

They also established an Agriculture Dialogue and agreed to discuss the establishment of a new Security and Law Enforcement Dialogue mechanism.

The foreign ministers of the two countries were tasked with developing an Action Plan to implement the Strategic Partnership. Nadjibulla said the plan would be crucial to translating high-level political commitments into concrete cooperation programmes and should be completed in a timely manner.

The visit also delivered tangible outcomes in energy and clean energy transition, maritime transport, environmental protection and agricultural standards. Expanded air transport agreements could pave the way for direct passenger and cargo services between the two countries.

Vietnam also decided to establish a Defence Attaché Office in Canada.

According to Nadjibulla, these developments demonstrate a shift in Vietnam-Canada relations from a broad cooperation framework centred largely on trade towards a more strategic partnership. The two countries share an interest in maintaining an open and rules-based trading system at a time when the system is facing increasing pressure. Both economies are deeply integrated into global trade and rely substantially on external markets, giving them a common interest in reducing the risks of economic interdependence being used as a tool of pressure.

Vietnam has become an increasingly important partner for Canada, not only as a major trading and manufacturing economy in Southeast Asia but also as an active ASEAN member and Chair of the CPTPP Commission in 2026.

Vietnam has a strong interest in maintaining an open and stable trading environment while preserving room for cooperation with diverse partners. Canada, meanwhile, brings complementary strengths and networks, particularly in Europe and the Indo-Pacific, as well as expertise and resources in energy, critical minerals, finance and advanced technologies.

Nadjibulla pointed out that Vietnam and Canada have different geopolitical positions, political systems and international relationships. However, cooperation between middle powers does not require identical positions on every issue, she said.

Instead, the partnership can be built around converging interests, including maintaining rules-based trade, diversifying economic relations, strengthening supply-chain resilience, upholding international law and supporting multilateral institutions.

Vietnam is more than an important bilateral market for Canada, according to Nadjibulla. It is also part of a broader network of countries that share an interest in ensuring that the Indo-Pacific is not shaped solely by great-power competition.

Closer Vietnam-Canada cooperation could therefore help both countries diversify their options while preserving space for rules, openness and strategic autonomy in an increasingly competitive international environment.

Looking ahead, Nadjibulla identified three areas for the realisation of the Strategic Partnership.

Investment and supply chains are the first priority. While bilateral economic ties have grown significantly through trade, the next phase will depend increasingly on two-way investment and deeper participation by Canadian companies in Vietnam’s production and supply-chain networks.

The Joint Economic Committee could play a central role in identifying specific projects, removing barriers and matching Canadian strengths with Vietnam’s development needs, she said.

Energy is another area where the visit produced notable results. A new memorandum of understanding covers LNG, hydrogen, renewable energy, carbon management and technologies supporting the energy transition.

The two sides are also discussing potential cooperation in civil nuclear energy. If these commitments are translated into concrete commercial projects, energy could become a major source of substantive economic cooperation under the Strategic Partnership.

Technology and innovation represent a third priority. Cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technology, semiconductors, cybersecurity and digital governance has been outlined at an ambitious level, but the number of concrete bilateral projects remains relatively limited.

Nadjibulla said stronger links among universities, research institutions and businesses, together with talent exchanges and innovation partnerships, would be needed to turn these priorities into practical outcomes.

Ultimately, she said, the key test of the Strategic Partnership will be whether the commitments made during the visit can be translated into regular programmes, concrete projects and durable cooperation mechanisms between Vietnam and Canada./.

title: Ecologically damaging saga of retrospective environmental clearances continues: Congress
description:
"The ecologically damaging saga of retrospective environmental clearances continues," Ramesh said on X.
On May 16, 2025, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court had categorically rejected such clearances, the former environment minister said, adding that this was a bold verdict and 100 per cent right.
"It needs to be told again and again that ignorance of the law has never been the cause for seeking retrospective environmental approvals.
It has always been the standard operating practice to start a project and seek environmental approvals later by presenting a fait accompli - the 'baad mein dekha jayega' approach," Ramesh said.
In any case, ignorance of the law, feigned or otherwise, should never be a cause for exoneration, he added.
text:
The Congress general secretary in-charge communications shared the screenshot of a media report which claimed that the Union Environment Ministry has directed its central and state-level expert bodies to resume processing 'post-facto' environmental clearance (EC) proposals, two months after the Supreme Court permitted it to take such pending, rejected or returned proposals to their logical conclusion in accordance with law.

"The ecologically damaging saga of retrospective environmental clearances continues," Ramesh said on X.

On May 16, 2025, a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court had categorically rejected such clearances, the former environment minister said, adding that this was a bold verdict and 100 per cent right.

However, on November 18, 2025, a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court led by the Chief Justice himself by a 2-1 majority overturned the earlier Supreme Court decision, Ramesh said and stressed that this was, to put it most mildly, just wrong.

Thereafter, on July 29, 2026, another three-judge bench of the Supreme Court headed by the present Chief Justice unanimously struck down the facility for retrospective environmental clearances provided by the Modi government initially on March 14, 2017 and later reaffirmed in an Office Memorandum on July 7, 2021, he pointed out.

This was a most welcome development but the verdict also allowed those cases where such approvals had already been granted to be taken forward, Ramesh said.
