text:
A year ago, walking away from Tesla meant taking a deliberate gamble on early-adopter quirks or niche imports. When we published our 2025 breakdown of Tesla alternatives, the non-Tesla landscape was defined by stylish outliers like the Polestar 2 and Chinese disruptors like the BYD Seal.

Twelve months later, the market math has completely shifted. Tesla’s software lead has eroded, its lineup is aging behind cosmetic refreshes, and legacy Detroit alongside dedicated EV startups have spent billions bringing genuinely superior hardware to market.

Whether you are looking to evade software fatigue, avoid brand baggage, or simply want a vehicle with physical turn signal stalks and predictable build quality, here are the absolute best Tesla alternatives on the market in 2026.

Model 3 Rivals: Drivers and Range Kings

BMW i4: The driver’s luxury sedan

While built on a shared combustion platform rather than a dedicated EV skateboard, the BMW i4 remains the sharpest dynamic threat to the Model 3. Starting at $59,250 for the eDrive40 (333 miles of range) and scaling up to the twin-motor 593-hp i4 M50, the Bavarian sedan offers something Tesla still struggles to deliver: actual build consistency, quiet cabin insulation, and tactile driving feedback. It’s heavier than a Model 3, but the fit, finish, and road manners feel like a proper luxury automobile rather than a rolling tech demo.

Hyundai Ioniq 6: The aerodynamic oddball

If your priority is pure efficiency and rapid charging, Hyundai’s streamlined sedan remains a technical marvel. Built on an 800-volt architecture, the Ioniq 6 SE ($44,545) pulls up to 342 miles of range and recharges from 10% to 80% in under 18 minutes on a DC fast charger. It looks like a polished river stone, which splits aesthetic opinions, but on paper, its thermal management and efficiency outclass almost everything in its price bracket.

Model Y Rivals: The Crossover Battleground

Rivian R2: The cool-factor challenger

The most anticipated mid-size crossover of 2026 has officially landed. Starting at $59,485 for the Performance Launch Edition, the Rivian R2 delivers 656 horsepower, an EPA-estimated 330 miles of range, and dual-motor AWD. Unlike the sterile, minimalist interior of the Model Y, the R2 leans hard into adventure-utility aesthetics with roll-down rear glass, clever storage solutions, and robust hardware. A cheaper $46,485 standard-range model arrives later this summer, making Rivian the premier threat to Tesla’s crossover dominance.

Chevrolet Equinox EV: The mass-market sanity check

Where Tesla continually shifts pricing and trims, General Motors delivered a straightforward value punch with the Chevrolet Equinox EV. Starting at $36,795 with an EPA-rated 319 miles of range in front-wheel drive, the Equinox EV proves that functional, spacious electric transport doesn’t need to cost $50,000. It drives like a normal SUV, skips the gimmickry, and offers one of the best range-per-dollar ratios in the entire industry.

BMW iX3: The long-range German counterpunch

For buyers willing to step up into the premium segment ($63,500), the new BMW iX3 50 xDrive throws down an extraordinary stat: 434 miles of range on a single charge and 463 horsepower. Paired with a 21-minute fast-charging curve, the iX3 completely eliminates range anxiety while offering a plush, refined cabin that puts the Model Y’s utilitarian interior to shame.

Kia EV6 & Hyundai Ioniq 5: The 800-Volt veterans

Both built on Hyundai Group’s E-GMP architecture, these twin crossovers continue to set the benchmark for practical daily driving. The Kia EV6 ($42,745 for the long-range battery) offers 319 miles of range and rally-inspired styling, while the Hyundai Ioniq 5 ($39,400) delivers retro-futuristic hatchback space with a massive interior footprint. Their 260kW peak charging speeds mean you spend significantly less time parked at chargers than Model Y owners.

Cybertruck Rivals: Real Trucks for Real Work

Rivian R1T: The usable adventure pickup

While the Cybertruck continues to divide opinions with its angular stainless-steel shell and divisive proportions, the Rivian R1T ($81,885) has quietly perfected the electric truck formula. Offering up to 1,025 horsepower in Quad-Motor trim, an 11,000-pound towing capacity, and a functional 54-inch bed, the R1T combines genuine off-road capability with luxurious daily usability. It’s a precision tool, not a movie prop.

Chevrolet Silverado EV: The endless-range workhorse

If your definition of a pickup involves raw utility and highway haulage, Chevrolet’s Silverado EV obliterates the Cybertruck’s practical metrics. While entry models start around $58,490, the Extended Range variants ($71,695–$91,795) deliver up to a staggering 478 miles of range on a single charge and a max tow rating of 12,500 lbs. It’s a massive, unapologetic work truck that uses its battery pack to deliver real-world range, even with a trailer attached.

title: CAFE-3 is a progressive roadmap for greener mobility: JSW Motors CEO - Business Line
description:
CAFE-3 provides greater regulatory certainty, which is important for companies like JSW Motors as we build our product and technology roadmap for the coming years.
Each technology addresses a different consumer need and can play a role in India’s transition towards cleaner mobility.
The industry now needs to translate that framework into sustained investment, innovation and greater consumer adoption of cleaner mobility technologies.
This can support cleaner mobility while strengthening India’s energy security and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.
The objective should be to translate the framework into sustained investment, innovation, localisation and greater consumer adoption of cleaner mobility technologies.
text:
In what ways will the CAFE-3 fuel efficiency guidelines help new entrants like JSW Motors plan their product strategy??

CAFE-3 provides greater regulatory certainty, which is important for companies like JSW Motors as we build our product and technology roadmap for the coming years. The 3+2-year compliance block structure gives companies greater flexibility to align their sales and powertrain strategies with the stipulated CAFE targets.

The recognition of multiple electrified powertrains also gives us greater clarity on where to focus investments and technology development. For JSW Motors, this is particularly relevant as we are already working towards launching clean technologies across New Energy Vehicles (NEVs). The framework allows us to plan our products, technologies, investments and localisation efforts with greater clarity.

What specific technologies would you leverage to maximize regulatory benefits under these norms?

Our approach is centred on a portfolio of NEVs, including Range-Extended Electric Vehicles (REEVs) and Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs). Each technology addresses a different consumer need and can play a role in India’s transition towards cleaner mobility. NEVs are particularly suited to consumers with convenient access to charging.

REEVs use electric motors for propulsion while a range-extending engine generates electricity when required, offering an alternative for consumers concerned about charging access and long-distance travel. PHEVs combine external charging and electric driving capability with an internal-combustion engine, providing flexibility for both urban and inter-city use.

We particularly welcome the higher volume derogation factor for NEVs and REEVs, followed by PHEVs and eligible strong hybrids, as this recognises the greater contribution of New Energy Vehicles while allowing different electrified powertrains to contribute to the transition.

What would be your localisation levels for these technologies?

Our objective is to progressively build a more localised new energy vehicle ecosystem in line with the broader goals of Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat. As battery manufacturing scales, greater localisation across the electric mobility value chain can strengthen domestic supply chains and reduce import dependence for critical technologies over time. CAFE-3 further strengthens the case for such investments across the industry.

The government has laid out the path now, so what should original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) do to meet carbon neutrality while keeping affordability for customers in mind?

The next phase of India’s automotive transition will require OEMs to take a broader view of mobility. It will require alignment across vehicle technology, charging infrastructure, battery manufacturing, renewable power and consumer adoption.

For OEMs, the focus should be on bringing cleaner and increasingly efficient technologies to consumers while recognising that different powertrains address different consumer needs. Affordability and adoption will ultimately depend on how effectively the industry can develop and localise these technologies and make them relevant for Indian consumers. CAFE-3 provides the regulatory foundation for this transition.

The industry now needs to translate that framework into sustained investment, innovation and greater consumer adoption of cleaner mobility technologies.

Why is NEV approach important for India’s mobility transition?

A new energy vehicle approach can have an impact well beyond the vehicle itself. Greater adoption of NEV technologies can create demand for domestic battery manufacturing, components, power electronics and associated technologies.

India has already taken steps in this direction through the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cells, which aims to establish large-scale domestic battery manufacturing with increasing domestic value addition. For India, this creates an opportunity to build capabilities across cells, packs, materials and other components, strengthen domestic supply chains and support a more self-reliant mobility ecosystem.

How important is the provision for pooling and trading of CAFE compliance credits?

The provision provides manufacturers with greater flexibility in meeting CAFE targets. A mechanism through which manufacturers can exchange credits can also create an economic incentive for companies investing in cleaner and more efficient technologies. For a company such as JSW Motors, which is investing in NEV technology, this provides another element of flexibility as we build our product and powertrain strategy.

Can CAFE-3 help India reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels?

Reducing petrol and diesel consumption in road transport has implications beyond emissions. Greater electrification of passenger mobility can help reduce exposure to international oil price shocks and reduce the country’s dependence on imported fossil fuels.

The larger opportunity is to build a passenger vehicle ecosystem that is increasingly electrified, technologically advanced and domestically anchored. This can support cleaner mobility while strengthening India’s energy security and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.

What will be critical to making this transition successful?

The transition will require continued collaboration and dialogue between policymakers and auto and technology companies. CAFE-3 provides an important regulatory foundation, but the next phase will require alignment across vehicle technologies, charging infrastructure, battery manufacturing, renewable power and consumer adoption.

The objective should be to translate the framework into sustained investment, innovation, localisation and greater consumer adoption of cleaner mobility technologies.

text:
Should you start plugging in or continue filling up with gasoline? That's the question more and more drivers are considering these days, as more electric vehicles hit the streets, with generous tax credits continuing into 2024 and automakers cutting prices on some EVs.

EVs have come a long way since William Morrison debuted his six-passenger electric wagon in Des Moines back in 1891.

It's been more than a century since then… and plug-in vehicles are now making a big comeback, competing with gas cars in looks, performance, and finally, affordability.

Billy Johnson is among the recent converts to EVs.

We found him charging his Tesla at a charging station outside a Target store and doing a bit of shopping while he waited for it to finish. With no need to pay for gasoline or oil changes, Johnson says, "it saved me a ton of money."

Keith Barry is the senior auto reporter at Consumer Reports. He says EVs are becoming a good option because they're cheaper to fuel and maintain, coupled with recent price cuts at Tesla and some other companies.

Plus, with EVs piling up on some dealership lots, dealers are offering price cuts for the first time.

"There are savings to be found," Barry said. "It really depends upon the vehicle you choose."

"In addition," he said, "they have fewer moving parts, fewer things to go wrong, and they are better for the environment."

Many buyers remain hesitant

According to Pew Research Center, 38% of Americans are considering an EV for their next vehicle purchase. Still, many remain hesitant.

Michael Berube is the deputy assistant secretary for Sustainable Transportation and Fuels at the U.S. Department of Energy. He understands the hesitation.

"It's different than what you might be used to," Berube said. "And that's scary at first."

He says the charging network is growing, with plenty of electricity to fuel the switch.

"It's not mission impossible. The bread and butter of what we do is to make sure that the electric grid of the country is there and working for all people," he said.

Tax incentives make them even better

As for the price, you will find more incentives than ever.

You can get a $7,500 tax incentive for buying or leasing a new EV.

You can also qualify for a $4,000 credit if you buy used.

Courtney Wells loves her Tesla and suggests other buyers seriously consider EVs.

"I highly recommend it," she said. "Do it. It will be your best decision. It will save you money."

That way you don't waste your money.

text:
It’s officially October, people! Time is going by so fast this year, maybe due to the chaos.

And this includes the auto industry. We’ve seen so many crazy changes in the last 10 months, from automakers pivoting from electric plans and canceling upcoming EVs to brands leaving the United States altogether thanks to the Trump Administration’s ongoing war on Chinese EVs. The landscape has been changing so rapidly.

Now that we’re in the third quarter of 2026, Car and Driver has shared which automakers have come out on top in this crazy market (as well as those that have suffered).

Winners of 2026 so far: SUVs

This comes as no surprise, but SUVs are having a moment. I know, I know, you’re shocked. Shaking. Americans love their big, ugly SUVs, and 2026 is no different. Kia saw 236,659 units sold in the third quarter, an 8% year-over-year increase, driven by the Kia Seltos (70% increase), Sorento (21% increase), Telluride (18% increase), and Sportage (8% increase). Hyundai was another big player in the SUV game, with the Tuscon seeing a 23% increase in Q3 to 64,075 units.

But it wasn’t only SUVs that saw some love. Americans were also vibing with the Kia Carnival minivan (thanks to millennial dads), the light-duty Ram 1500 pickup, which saw 76,650 sales (a whopping 73% increase), and the BMW 3-Series, up 46% in Q3. Another surprising winner was the Corvette. While the Mustang is still the best-selling sports car in the U.S., the C8 Corvette has been a major player in the space, with 6,585 sales in the third quarter, a 29% year-over-year increase.

Losers of 2026 so far: EVs

Electric vehicles are the clear losers of 2026, particularly for American brands. Interest in EVs has waned ever since the Trump Administration removed the tax incentive for the pretty expensive vehicle segment. Hybrids are the new focus for many car brands, giving the Toyota Prius plenty of competition. Cadillac’s electric SUVs are struggling, with Lyriq sales 51% down. Its other electric SUVs aren’t doing much better. Chevrolet is another American brand that is struggling to sell EVs. The Equinox EV was down 92% in Q3, selling just 1,905 units, and the Blazer EV saw an 84% decline. Yikes. Even the Silverado EV had a 58% decline. But even the smaller Chevy Bolt has been struggling.

Unfortunately for EV fans, we’re not done yet. Ford saw a small decline in the third quarter, but one of the biggest failures has been the Mustang Mach-E. Once a pretty popular choice, the Mach-E saw a 72% decline in Q3, selling just 5,574 units. This is a 59% decline year-over-year. Jeep is another American brand that can’t seem to sell EVs. Most of its vehicles were a bit of a disaster, but the electric Jeep Wagoneer S was the worst: it was down by 96% in Q3. Only 146 units were sold. It’s not a real shocker, but people don’t want an electric Jeep for off-roading.

It should be noted that it’s not just American brands that can’t sell EVs in the U.S. Hyundai and Kia have also seen a pretty rough Q3. The Hyundai Ioniq 5 was down 53%, the Kia EV6 was down 57%, and the Genesis GV60 was down 53%, just to name a few.

text:
The measure increases taxes on commercial wind turbines and creates new taxes on commercial solar and battery systems, natural gas extraction and data centers in unincorporated Solano County. Data centers would pay $5 per square foot annually. Taxes would go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and be adjusted yearly based on inflation. The measure would generate an estimated $353,000 to the general fund annually. Passes with a majority vote.

Yes Argument

This measure strengthens our local economy, protects essential services and maintains infrastructure by ensuring visitors and corporations pay their fair share. Commercial wind farm taxes have not been updated since 1994. While there are no data centers in unincorporated Solano County, this measure ensures they’ll contribute if they do arrive. If so, revenue estimates will be even higher. These funds will stay local to benefit Solano County rather than go to state or federal governments.

No Argument

This measure creates a permanent tax on industries already facing regulation and infrastructure costs. Higher business taxes ultimately raise prices for ordinary families. The proposal will discourage investment in clean-energy projects that create local jobs and revenue and drive technology employers elsewhere. The potential loss of investment outweighs the estimated $353,000 in gains. With no sunset date, ending the tax would require a new ballot initiative.

text:
Solar energy holds the best potential for meeting humanity’s future longterm energy needs while cutting greenhouse gas emissions – but to realize this potential will require increased emphasis on developing lower-cost technologies and more effective deployment policy, says a comprehensive new study on The Future of Solar Energy released today by The MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI).

“Our objective has been to assess solar energy’s current and potential competitive position and to identify changes in US government policies that could more efficiently and effectively support its massive deployment over the long-term, which we view as necessary,” said Robert Armstrong, Director, MITEI.

The study’s chair, Richard Schmalensee, Howard W. Johnson Professor of Economics and Management Emeritus at the MIT Sloan School of Management, added “What the study shows is that our focus needs to shift toward new technologies and policies that have the potential to make solar a compelling economic option.”

The study group is presenting its findings to lawmakers and senior administration officials this week in Washington, D.C.

The Future of Solar Energy reflects on the technical, commercial and policy dimensions of solar energy today and makes recommendations to policymakers regarding more effective federal and state support for research and development, technology demonstration, and solar deployment.

Among its major themes is the need to prepare our electricity systems, both technically and from a regulatory standpoint, for very large-scale deployment of solar generation – which tends to vary unpredictably throughout the day. To this end, the study emphasizes the need for federal research and development support to advance low-cost, large-scale electricity storage technologies.

The analysis finds that today’s federal and state subsidy programs designed to encourage investment in solar systems should be reconsidered, to increase their cost-effectiveness, with greater emphasis on rewarding production of solar energy.

The group also recommends that state renewable portfolio standards, which are designed to increase generation of electricity from renewable resources, be brought under a unified national program that would reduce the cost of meeting set mandates by allowing unrestricted interstate trading of credits.

The study concludes by pointing to the urgent need for an ambitious and innovative approach to technology development, with federal research and development investment focused on new technologies and systems with the potential to deliver transformative system cost reductions. text:
Democrats to restore clean-energy tax credits, pledge wider ESS investment

If Democrats pull off a "blue wave" in the U.S. midterm elections in November by winning both chambers of Congress, sectors such as renewable energy, secondary batteries and energy storage systems, or ESS, could benefit in South Korea's stock market, according to brokerage analysis.

Park Hye-ran, an analyst at Samsung Securities, wrote on October 4 that a Democratic victory would add another driver for energy demand. Republican-led policies that have curtailed renewable-energy subsidies and ended investment tax credits could be partly revised, she added.

In the November 3 midterms, all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, whose members serve two-year terms, will be contested. In the Senate, 35 of the 100 seats, or about one-third, will be up for election. Gubernatorial elections will also be held in 36 states.

In the House, Republicans currently hold 218 seats and Democrats 214, excluding one independent seat and two vacancies. Given that narrow gap, Democrats would need to gain four seats in this year's midterms to take control.

The Senate is also closely split, with Republicans holding 53 seats and Democrats 47. Democrats would need to gain four seats there as well to secure a majority.

Prediction market platform Polymarket is assigning a 62% probability to a Democratic sweep of both the House and Senate. That is up sharply from 51% in March, before the U.S.-Iran war broke out, as the election draws nearer.

Samsung Securities named renewables and utilities as the sectors likely to see the strongest rebound if a blue wave materializes. Democratic leaders have said they would restore clean-energy tax credits scaled back under the Trump administration and expand investment in ESS.

Park said that if Democrats win at least the House, some Republican-led policies could be revised, lifting expectations for policy support for renewable energy. Control of the House would also strengthen Democrats' leverage in next year's budget and debt-ceiling talks. The party could use that leverage to seek changes to some renewable-energy subsidy requirements, with Republicans likely to accept them.

One of the biggest issues in the midterms is electricity costs, including those related to data-center construction. Republicans are pushing to expand nuclear power generation and gas turbines to meet surging power demand and strengthen fuel supply-chain security.

Democrats, by contrast, are emphasizing wider deployment of renewable energy to ease inflation pressures.

In the U.S., investment tax credits for solar projects were slated for early termination through revisions to the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA, last year. Utility-scale solar projects will receive the credit only if they begin operating by the end of next year. Residential solar credits ended at the close of last year.

For onshore wind, installation could also increase sharply if projects scheduled for 2028 through 2030 resume. Those projects had been put on hold after developers judged them less economical once the production tax credit, or PTC, was set to expire earlier than under the IRA under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or OBBBA, a tax-and-spending law passed in July last year.

South Korea's secondary-battery sector tumbled last year after passage of the OBBBA and President Donald Trump's signing of an executive order. The administration formally scrapped former President Joe Biden's mandate targeting electric vehicles to make up 50% of sales by 2030. Weak U.S. sales, in a key downstream market for battery makers, also weighed on utilization rates at Korean companies.

Jang Jeong-hoon, an analyst at Samsung Securities, said a blue wave would not necessarily make legislation promoting EV consumption more likely during Trump's term. Still, because Democrats have explicitly called for upgrades to aging power grids and transmission networks, the push to expand grid-linked ESS deployment is likely to remain intact.

Meanwhile, the Kospi has historically tended to rise after U.S. midterm elections.

Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said returns in the six and 12 months after past elections were generally positive. Rebounds from the lows were also similar for the Kospi and the S&P 500, at about 10%. In her view, post-election strength is better understood not as Korea-specific excess returns but as a recovery in risk appetite after uncertainty eases.

text:
Remarks by ADB President Masato Kanda at the Science and Technology in Society Forum 2026 plenary session "A World in Transition: Science and Technology for a Sustainable Future," 4 October 2026, Kyoto, Japan.

Chair President Nurse, fellow panelists, distinguished guests:

Our global economy is undergoing a profound shift. For over a century, economic growth was limited by the extraction of carbon. Tomorrow, it will be defined by the mastery of science.

Nations are racing to decarbonize, strengthen energy security, and sustain economic momentum. Achieving these goals in a fragmented world requires more than step-by-step policy adjustments. It requires absolute scientific ambition.

Across Asia and the Pacific, the demand for power is surging. Rising living standards, along with massive energy needs driven by advanced computing and data centers for artificial intelligence, are fueling this growth.

The clean energy transition illustrates this challenge. Thanks to technological innovation, the cost of generating power from solar and wind has fallen by 80 to 90% over the past decade.

However, generation cost is not the only factor in the energy transition, and we must address other bottlenecks to deliver renewable energy to people sustainably.

First, the shift toward renewable energy is highly dependent on critical minerals.

Building solar arrays, wind farms, and electric grids requires vastly more copper, lithium, and rare earths than the fossil systems they replace.

This reality drives intense resource competition and geopolitical tension. That is why the Asian Development Bank, ADB, is supporting critical-minerals-to-manufacturing value chains through an integrated approach that spans exploration, processing, manufacturing, recycling, and circularity.

Second, resources for sustainable power generation are frequently far from the cities where people need them. That is why power grids are crucial in overcoming this bottleneck.

Through our $50 billion Pan-Asia Power Grid Initiative, ADB is integrating regional power systems to move clean energy across borders. In addition to financing large-scale grid infrastructure, policy coordination among countries is equally important. Our initiative is enabling cross-border power projects once considered impossible.

True energy security also requires us to invent new materials and rethink existing systems.

The commercial rollout of sodium-ion batteries shows that science can rewrite the economics of energy. By using materials that are vastly more abundant than lithium, we are replacing resource scarcity with technological abundance.

Yet, even with advanced storage and better grids, securing sustainable baseload power for the late twenty-first century requires us to look further ahead.

This brings us to nuclear fusion energy.

Fusion is rapidly transitioning from a challenge in theoretical physics into an urgent engineering priority. Leading national roadmaps now target commercial use in the 2030s. We must aggressively finance and build the infrastructure required to cross this threshold.

I see the human stakes of this transition every day.

Consider the poorest and most vulnerable populations across the developing world. For them, a zero-carbon society powered by abundant energy means resilient infrastructure and accessible electricity, as well as protection from the harmful price swings of fossil fuel markets.

Reliable clean electricity will also power the AI that gives remote communities and people with disabilities the opportunity to leapfrog entire stages of development and build lasting economic fairness. ADB’s $20 billion Asia-Pacific Digital Highway is expanding AI-ready connectivity and skills.

However, rapidly advancing AI also poses an existential risk for humanity. If we fail to harness the development of AI, people risk becoming slaves to AI or to those who exploit it with evil intent. We must ensure AI remains under human control and serves the well-being of people.

Navigating these massive challenges requires societies to fiercely protect and fund curiosity-driven research.

Breakthroughs of this magnitude rarely occur on demand. The discoveries that will ultimately transform our economies often emerge from fundamental questions. And in many cases, their commercial use is not immediately clear.

To deploy technology at this speed, we must recognize that trust is the most critical component of our scientific infrastructure. Scientists and institutions must engage societies, communicate transparently, and demonstrate absolute integrity.

Ladies and gentlemen, the transitions before us cannot be met with hesitation. They demand our boldest collective resolve. We must unite across governments, academia, industry, and society.

Let us fund the curiosity that unlocks the breakthroughs of tomorrow. Let us build the grids and the digital highways that connect our divided world. And let us summon the ambition to turn frontier science and AI into human progress.

Thank you.

title: US auto industry sees modest gains, lingering uncertainty as suppliers bear the brunt under ...
description:
NEW YORK, Oct 4 — President Donald Trump has claimed a “roaring comeback” in American auto manufacturing following aggressive trade policy, but analysts view the cumulative impact as more of a mixed bag.
“It’s a partial win,” Stephanie Brinley, an automotive analyst at Mobility Global, said of the lift from Trump’s tariffs to the US auto industry.
Auto industry experts view the unsettled nature of Trump’s trade measures as a hindrance to bigger wins.
There has been “a noticeable slowdown” in investment by suppliers due to policy uncertainty, including on tariffs, said Tyler Harp, an industry economist at the Centre for Automotive Research (CAR).
The industry is following a “discipline-over-growth playbook” while shifting more investment to automation and robotics, Deloitte said.
text:
NEW YORK, Oct 4 — President Donald Trump has claimed a “roaring comeback” in American auto manufacturing following aggressive trade policy, but analysts view the cumulative impact as more of a mixed bag.

Since Trump returned to the White House, General Motors, Toyota, Ford and other carmakers have announced plans to expand US plants or shift production from overseas to make use of underutilised factories, as the industry navigated measures such as a 25-per cent levy on imported autos.

But as the president’s allies in the Republican party look ahead to mid-term elections in November, the gains to the US carmaker profile look more incremental than decisive, and are accompanied by a drag in spending in some cases due to trade uncertainty.

“It’s a partial win,” Stephanie Brinley, an automotive analyst at Mobility Global, said of the lift from Trump’s tariffs to the US auto industry.

Auto industry experts view the unsettled nature of Trump’s trade measures as a hindrance to bigger wins. This defect has most recently surfaced in the dust-up between the United States and Canada that has clouded the prospects of the North American trade agreement, known as the USMCA.

In August, a top Honda executive said the company was operating near full capacity at its North American facilities and wanted to build a new plant, but might pivot if the fog around USMCA persists.

Moreover, the disruptions from tariffs and Trump’s reversals of US policies favouring electric vehicles have weighed on the US auto supplier sector, which provides parts and technology and employs some 930,000 people in the United States.

There has been “a noticeable slowdown” in investment by suppliers due to policy uncertainty, including on tariffs, said Tyler Harp, an industry economist at the Centre for Automotive Research (CAR).

Investment by suppliers plunged from more than US$8 billion (RM32.6 billion) in the first quarter of 2025 to around US$600 million in the two subsequent quarters before recovering somewhat, according to CAR data.

“Suppliers are more exposed to tariffs,” Harp said. “They’re not in a position to absorb them as well as automakers.”

Investing in automation

After falling for much of 2025, US auto employment has been on an upswing for most of 2026. In September, the sector had just under 1.8 million workers, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

That’s almost one per cent more than the level in January 2025 when Trump took office, but more than two per cent below the peak level from the last decade, in July 2024 when Joe Biden was president, according to the BLS.

US auto production has also been broadly stable, but isn’t expected to rise until around 2030, when GM’s US$4 billion investments in Michigan, Kansas and Tennessee come into force, along with Toyota’s US$3.6 billion plan to move Tacoma pickup production to Texas from Mexico.

Global Mobility projects that US car production will be 10 million vehicles in 2026, about the same as last year, but rise to around 11.3 million in 2030, according to Brinley.

“There is definitely an increase in there and it is partially related to tariffs,” she said, noting that in some cases automakers are reconfiguring plants or making use of underutilised capacity.

A brand-new plant such as the one floated by Honda must be used for decades.

“Plants aren’t put in the ground with the expectation of lasting a presidential cycle,” Brinley said. “The tariffs have an impact, but it’s just not the only input.”

Suppliers have ranked changes in government trade policy as the industry’s “greatest threat” over the next 12 months, according to surveys from MEMA, the Vehicle Suppliers Association.

In the most recent report, nearly 80 per cent of companies ranked trade policy changes among the four top threats, alongside weakness in the US economy, an external or “black swan” event, and poor vehicle sales.

The industry has recovered only about half of tariff-policy-related costs, a “sustained margin drag that is likely to weigh on supplier financials,” according to a commentary from Deloitte accompanying the survey.

The industry is following a “discipline-over-growth playbook” while shifting more investment to automation and robotics, Deloitte said. — AFP

title: Reader's View: Energy choice is the key to lowering New York's utility bills - Saratogian
description:
While I continue working for those long-term reforms, there are resources available right now for households struggling to keep up with heating costs.
The Home Energy Assistance Program, better known as HEAP, provides assistance to eligible New Yorkers with the cost of heating their homes.
Residents may also want to contact their utility to determine whether they qualify for an Energy Affordability Program or another payment-assistance option.
When winter arrives in Upstate New York, heating a home is not optional.
Reliable energy is not a luxury.
text:
As the temperatures begin to fall across the Capital Region, furnaces will soon be running longer, lights will be on earlier and families will once again be bracing for higher energy bills. For many New Yorkers, however, this is no longer just the normal seasonal increase that comes with colder weather. The cost of keeping a home warm has become another major strain on household budgets already stretched by groceries, housing, taxes and nearly every other basic expense. New Yorkers deserve to understand why.

Since the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, or CLCPA, was enacted in 2019, New York has pursued an aggressive transition of its energy system. The law requires major reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions and a significant shift toward renewable and zero-emission energy. Meeting those goals requires substantial new investments in generation, transmission, energy-efficiency programs and the electric grid. The Public Service Commission has continued authorizing investments designed to advance those objectives, including $1 billion annually for energy-efficiency and beneficial-electrification programs from 2026 through 2030.

Those policies come with costs, and I believe New York has moved too quickly without giving enough consideration to what those costs mean for the families and businesses expected to pay them.

Earlier this year, I joined my colleagues in sounding the alarm about the growing affordability problem. Residential electricity prices in New York had risen 47.1% since 2019, and a NYSERDA analysis raised serious questions about the potential future costs associated with meeting the state’s climate mandates. At the same time, concerns about maintaining enough reliable generation have reinforced the need for a more practical approach to our energy future. That is why I have consistently pushed for energy choice rather than energy mandates.

New York should not shut down reliable sources of power before adequate replacements are ready. We should not artificially limit the fuels and technologies families and businesses are allowed to use. And we should not put ideology ahead of affordability or reliability.

I support an all-of-the-above energy strategy that keeps natural gas, nuclear power, hydroelectricity and emerging technologies on the table alongside wind and solar. Earlier this year, I supported proposals to halt costly energy mandates, encourage additional reliable generation, return available clean-energy funds directly to ratepayers through utility credits and provide direct relief to families struggling with their bills.

The principle is simple: more energy choices and more reliable supply give New York a stronger foundation for keeping costs under control. We can continue pursuing cleaner energy without forcing families into a system they cannot afford. While I continue working for those long-term reforms, there are resources available right now for households struggling to keep up with heating costs.

The Home Energy Assistance Program, better known as HEAP, provides assistance to eligible New Yorkers with the cost of heating their homes. Benefits may be available for households that heat with electricity, natural gas, oil, propane and several other fuels. Emergency assistance may also be available to eligible households facing a utility shutoff, loss of heat or dangerously low fuel supply. I encourage residents who believe they may qualify to contact their local Department of Social Services or visit the New York State Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance website for the latest information on HEAP and the upcoming heating season. Residents may also want to contact their utility to determine whether they qualify for an Energy Affordability Program or another payment-assistance option.

My district office also stands ready to help constituents identify programs and connect with the appropriate state agency or utility. These programs are important, but assistance alone cannot solve the larger problem. We also have to stop creating policies that continually add costs to the system and then ask taxpayers and ratepayers to absorb the consequences.

When winter arrives in Upstate New York, heating a home is not optional. Reliable energy is not a luxury. Families should be able to turn on the heat without worrying whether doing so will force them to cut back on groceries, medicine or another necessity. That is why I will continue advocating for a different direction, one built around affordability, reliability and energy choice. New York can pursue a cleaner future, but we must do it responsibly, at a pace our infrastructure can support and our families can afford.

Assemblywoman Mary Beth Walsh represents the 112th Assembly District, which includes parts of Saratoga, Schenectady and Fulton counties. For more information about Assemblywoman Walsh, please visit her official website.

text:
Platform will identify, develop and deploy battery & long-duration energy-storage technologies, while exploring local assembly and manufacturing opportunities.

DUBAI, UNITED ARAB EMIRATES, October 3, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — ROX Capital Group, a UAE based firm that builds and invests in real assets, today announced the launch of the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform. The platform will identify and bring together energy storage technologies for utility-scale and commercial projects in the UAE and Oman, while evaluating opportunities for regional assembly and manufacturing.

The platform will assess a range of storage technologies, including:

• Battery chemistries such as vanadium redox flow, lithium iron phosphate and sodium-ion batteries.

• Long-duration storage technologies such as CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage, compressed-air energy storage and thermal storage.

ROX plans to establish regional partnerships with a select group of technology leaders in each category. Partners will be selected based on a demonstrated global track record of deploying high capacity, utility-scale energy storage projects; proven capability in long duration storage where relevant; financial and operational capacity to support major projects; and ownership or control of the core intellectual property underpinning their technology.

ROX will prioritize companies with bankable systems, established manufacturing capabilities and the ability to provide long-term technical support, performance assurances and warranties. Together, ROX and its partners will pursue upcoming energy storage tenders and assess local assembly or manufacturing opportunities where the commercial case is compelling.

“The Gulf is building some of the world’s largest solar projects. The next challenge is ensuring that clean power remains available after sunset and during periods of peak demand” said Robin Antony, Founder of ROX Capital Group. “No single technology will meet every requirement. We are building a platform that matches the right technology to the needs of each project and, where viable, supports the development of local manufacturing capability.”

“Lithium-ion batteries have transformed energy storage and will remain an important part of the solution,” Antony added. “However, the Gulf’s climate, load profile and energy-security priorities create a need for a broader portfolio of technologies. High summer temperatures can increase cooling requirements, while solar-heavy systems require storage over longer periods after dark. We see an important role for technologies including vanadium flow batteries, CO₂ batteries, gravity-based storage and thermal storage alongside lithium-ion solutions.”

The platform is connected to ROX’s flagship initiative to retrofit an existing UAE tower as a net-zero skyscraper. ROX intends for the project to demonstrate how building-integrated energy storage can support lower carbon buildings and more resilient urban energy systems in the region.

ROX will contribute local market knowledge, project development capabilities, stakeholder relationships and capital alignment. Technology partners will contribute proven systems, technical expertise and manufacturing know-how. Technology companies interested in joining the ROX Gulf Energy Storage Platform can contact ROX at info@roxcapitalgroup.com
