title: The Collision of State Climate Tort Suits with Federal Deregulation | Yale Law Journal
description:
The Essay will examine whether there is a principled, neutral way of distinguishing between these tort suits against fossil fuel companies and other tort suits with global components, such as cases related to the internet, human trafficking, and chemical manufacturing.
Unlike the test for displacement of federal common law, federal preemption of state law requires much more than the simple presence of an applicable federal statute.
And the Supreme Court, while ruling out federal tort suits in AEP,explicitly reserved the question of whether the Clean Air Act affected state tort suits related to climate change.
Defendants and critics have objected to social media tort suits and climate tort suits on similar grounds, such as by arguing that the cases are barred by the Constitution or that nuisance is only supposed to encompass “local” activities.
The same logic should apply to state tort suits against fossil fuel companies over damages to state natural resources from climate change.
text:
abstract. In its October 2026 term, the Supreme Court will review Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, a tort case with significant implications for the balance of power between federal and state law. Three state supreme courts and one federal circuit court of appeals have now issued conflicting opinions on whether plaintiffs can bring state tort suits against fossil fuel companies over climate harms. The split in their decisions is the product of stark differences in their views about the history of litigation over transboundary environmental pollution and the preemptive effects of the Clean Air Act.

This Essay provides a historical corrective to arguments that state common law has been unavailable for litigation over transboundary environmental threats, detailing how and why the Supreme Court preserved such claims nearly four decades ago. It then assesses the preemption arguments in Suncor given this history, the Trump Administration’s position that the Clean Air Act does not provide the federal government authority to regulate greenhouse gases, and the Supreme Court’s decisions limiting the Environmental Protection Agency’s regulatory authority. It argues that state common law should be available for most, if not all, climate tort claims in light of the Court’s recent statutory interpretation methods, traditional approaches to preemption doctrine, and states’ historic police powers over their natural resources and public health.

Introduction

U.S. progress on climate change is in dire straits. In 2025, the Trump Administration halted even minimal efforts to regulate greenhouse gas pollution at the federal level and ended programs to improve the resilience of state and local infrastructure. The Republican-controlled Congress repealed clean energy grants to states, upending their renewable power goals. And the United States withdrew from international initiatives to address the problem. Together, these steps have hampered the country’s ability to avoid some of the worst health and environmental effects of climate change.

In the midst of setbacks to federal climate policy, the Supreme Court will soon wade into a split among courts on whether cities and states can bring lawsuits against fossil fuel companies under state law. Since 2017, city and state plaintiffs have sued corporations such as Chevron and Exxon Mobil under a variety of state tort theories, such as nuisance, failure to warn, trespass, fraud, false advertising, and unjust enrichment. They are seeking financial compensation to address harms to their natural resources and public health from climate change, which the corporation defendants allegedly exacerbated by selling fossil fuels and spreading misinformation about the risks of their products. The defendants have spent the past decade largely waging procedural battles, attempting to remove the suits to federal court. After these efforts proved unsuccessful, several state supreme courts proceeded to two central questions: can plaintiffs bring tort claims under state law over climate harms, and if so, are these suits preempted by the Federal Clean Air Act? Through diametrically opposed approaches to federalism and preemption that could reverberate far outside climate law, two sets of courts have reached two different answers. Following traditional preemption doctrine, the Colorado and Hawai‘i Supreme Courts have said no, the tort suits are not preempted. In contrast, following an approach first adopted by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit in 2021, the Maryland Supreme Court has said yes: only federal, not state, common law is available for claims involving transboundary environmental harms, and Congress displaced federal common law by enacting a comprehensive regulatory scheme for greenhouse gases through the Clean Air Act.

The U.S. Supreme Court recently granted certiorari on the preemption question in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. The case presents the Justices with a crucial test on the balance of power between federal and state law. While the petitioners and their amici have put forward some unconventional arguments for why the Constitution itself preempts state common law, this Essay will focus on the issues that are likely to have the most purchase with the Justices : whether state law is available for tort claims involving climate change, and if so, whether Congress has preempted state common law through federal legislation. On one hand, conservative judicial and political philosophies have generally favored protecting states from federal overreach, and the Roberts Court has restricted the authority of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) over greenhouse gases in two significant decisions. On the other, fossil fuel companies aiming to limit liability for climate damages argue that federal law prevents states and municipalities from exercising authority through state suits. Regardless of one’s beliefs about climate change or the pros and cons of tort litigation as a means of tackling the problem, how the Justices resolve the case could have broad implications for the ability of cities and states to hold out-of-state corporations liable for injuring their residents and property.

Many states, cities, and environmental organizations hope that the Court will dispose of the case without reaching the preemption issue. When the Justices granted the cert petition, they added a second question regarding the Court’s authority to review the case at this stage, which would seem to provide an avenue for delaying a decision about preemption. That strategy, however, carries its own risk. If left undisturbed, the Second Circuit and Maryland Supreme Court’s approach to preemption threatens the availability of state tort law not only for climate-related claims but a host of other civil lawsuits arising from interstate or international activities, including cases involving toxic chemicals, social media harassment, and human trafficking. This approach also conflicts with Supreme Court precedent on preemption, including precedent addressing whether federal environmental statutes override state tort law when pollution crosses state lines.

As this Essay shows, the Second Circuit and Maryland Supreme Court got their history wrong: for nearly four decades, state common law has been available for transboundary pollution claims. The Supreme Court preserved such actions in 1987 after years of wrestling with the use of federal versus state common law over transboundary pollution and the effect of federal legislation on tort suits. In an opinion attentive to states’ traditional police powers over natural resources, the Court in International Paper Co. v. Ouellette upheld the use of state common law for tort suits over transboundary pollution so long as such cases did not obstruct federal permitting programs. Since then, tort suits involving transboundary environmental issues have proceeded under state law against a variety of companies and polluters.

The Justices should be guided by this history in assessing the preemption arguments in Suncor. As an initial matter, they should clarify that the transboundary nature of an environmental problem does not require plaintiffs to bring a tort claim under federal common law. The Court will then need to grapple with the hardest aspect of the case, which neither the petitioners nor the respondents have sufficiently acknowledged: whether the global nature of climate change warrants a different approach from other transboundary harms. The Essay will examine whether there is a principled, neutral way of distinguishing between these tort suits against fossil fuel companies and other tort suits with global components, such as cases related to the internet, human trafficking, and chemical manufacturing. It will argue that tort suits against fossil fuel companies for producing, selling, and marketing their products are not meaningfully distinct from such cases in terms of the relevant “federal interests.” The Court should therefore refrain from finding that all tort suits related to climate change must be brought under federal common law.

The Essay will then turn to the question of whether state tort law, even if available, is nevertheless preempted by the Clean Air Act. Because there is no express preemption provision in the statute, a determination that the Clean Air Act supersedes state tort law should require two findings. First, the Court would need to determine that the Act provides a comprehensive regulatory framework for addressing the harm that the tort lawsuit is also trying to resolve. And second, the Court would need to find that the state law claims would obstruct the operation of that federal regulatory program. Both of these findings would be difficult to square with the Supreme Court’s recent decisions limiting EPA’s regulatory authority and the Trump Administration’s repeals of climate rules governing motor vehicles and power plants. Moreover, the Supreme Court should require the same degree of clarity in the statute to find that Congress preempted state tort law as it requires to find that Congress provided regulatory authority to EPA. The Clean Air Act evinces the opposite intent, preserving state authority over environmental threats through two savings clauses.

Part I of this Essay provides a brief summary of the two lines of cases that are now colliding in Suncor: disputes about EPA’s regulatory authority over greenhouse gases and disputes about using the tort system to address climate change. Part II describes the different approaches to preemption and the availability of state common law between the Colorado and Hawai‘i Supreme Courts, on one side, and the Maryland Supreme Court and the Second Circuit, on the other side. Part III offers a historical corrective to the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit’s claims about the unavailability of state common law for suits over transboundary pollution, unpacking why the Supreme Court preserved such cases in the 1980s. This Essay then assesses how this history and recent decisions regarding EPA’s regulatory authority should shape the outcome in Suncor, arguing in Part IV that the Clean Air Act does not preempt most, or perhaps any, state climate claims.

I. two lines of supreme court doctrine

With Congress largely sitting on the sidelines, various presidential administrations, states, cities, industry groups, and environmental organizations have engaged in parallel legal disputes over EPA’s ability to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and the use of the tort suits to hold companies accountable for climate harms. These cases have increasingly come into conflict as some members of the business community and Republican Party seek to accomplish twin goals without congressional intervention: prevent any federal regulation of greenhouse gases and prohibit states from imposing liability on industries that have contributed to the problem. This Part details the Supreme Court’s resolution of these lines of cases over the past two decades and how they have set the stage for a showdown over climate regulation and preemption in the second Trump Administration.

A. Battles over EPA’s Climate Authority

Whether the Clean Air Act provides EPA the authority to control greenhouse gas pollution has been a matter of vociferous debate among lawyers, judges, politicians, and legal scholars since the Clinton Administration. First enacted in its modern form in 1970, the Act was meant to provide a federal framework for regulating air pollution from stationary and mobile sources. Questions about the applicability of the Act’s various subparts to greenhouse gas emissions arose in the late 1990s as members of Congress discussed the creation of a cap-and-trade scheme to address climate change. Yet efforts to pass such measures have repeatedly failed.

Over the last several decades, there have been sharp divisions between Republican and Democratic administrations over whether the Act as written grants EPA the authority to reduce greenhouse gases, regardless of whatever benefits new, specific climate legislation might offer. The first case to reach the Supreme Court, Massachusetts v. EPA, held that EPA must regulate greenhouse gases from mobile sources if they endanger public health or the environment. The Justices in the majority found that the reference to “air pollutant” in the section of the Act governing motor vehicles “embraces all airborne compounds of whatever stripe,” including greenhouse gases. Congress’s failure to amend the Act subsequently, as it did with acid rain, did not change the meaning of the terms already there. EPA could only decline to regulate such emissions if it found that they do not endanger public health or the environment, and the statute required the agency’s judgment to be based on scientific evidence about climate change.

But despite Massachusetts’s indication that EPA could thereafter address climate change using the existing provisions of the Act, the Supreme Court has repeatedly cabined EPA’s authority in subsequent challenges to the agency’s greenhouse gas regulations. Seven years later in Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA, the Court limited the agency’s ability to restrict greenhouse gas emissions under a different section of the Act known as the Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) program. The PSD program regulates sources emitting harmful air pollutants above numeric thresholds specified in the statute. EPA had sought to change these limits for its initial regulations of greenhouse gas emissions under the provision since applying the listed thresholds would have required millions of new sources to obtain permits. The Court held that EPA did not have discretion to change the numbers in the law and that the dramatic expansion that would result from applying the PSD program to millions of new sources suggested Congress had not intended this section to cover greenhouse gases. As Justice Scalia wrote, interpreting the Clean Air Act to bring about “an enormous and transformative expansion in EPA’s regulatory authority without clear congressional authorization” suggested the agency’s understanding of the statute was mistaken. That approach to interpreting the Act’s provisions seemed to threaten any climate regulations that did not closely match the text of the law and the agency’s prior approaches to air pollution control.

The Supreme Court’s 2022 opinion in West Virginia v. EPA amplified Justice Scalia’s warning and represented a much more significant curtailment of EPA’s authority to use the Clean Air Act to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In addition to formally introducing the major questions doctrine, the Court struck down EPA’s attempt to lower greenhouse gas emissions from power plants through a “generation shifting” regulation that looked suspiciously like a cap-and-trade program. Writing for the Court, Chief Justice Roberts explained that Congress’s failure to enact a cap-and-trade program, combined with the economic and political significance of EPA’s power plant regulation, indicated that the Act was not intended to provide the agency the authority to pursue such a program —at least not directly.

After West Virginia, the Court has continued to reshape administrative law doctrine with decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which eliminated Chevron deference and elevated the importance of statutory language over agency policymaking discretion. In light of these recent changes in administrative law doctrine, the Trump Administration is now arguing that the Clean Air Act does not, in fact, grant EPA authority to regulate greenhouse gases from power plants or mobile sources, the two largest categories of emitters in the country. The intent of these rollbacks is not only to prevent implementation of climate regulations in the current administration, but to prompt the Supreme Court to overturn Massachusetts and tie the hands of any future president in addressing greenhouse gas emissions without congressional action. While it is unclear whether the Supreme Court will go that far, for now and the foreseeable future, stationary sources and mobile sources are able to emit greenhouse gases without federal restriction.

B. Battles over Climate Tort Suits

As these debates over EPA’s regulatory authority made their way to the Supreme Court, states and environmental organizations began filing lawsuits directly targeting major polluters as well as companies involved in fossil fuel production. The first batch of cases, filed before the Court decided Massachusetts v. EPA in 2007, sought to use federal nuisance law to force utilities to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions or provide compensation to plaintiffs injured by the changing climate. The idea of bringing a federal common law claim over transboundary pollution was not new. Prior to the passage of major federal environmental laws in the 1970s, the Supreme Court had allowed plaintiffs to pursue nuisance claims under federal common law against out-of-state polluters. But a few years after Massachusetts, the Supreme Court unanimously held that the Clean Air Act had displaced federal common law suits over greenhouse gases in the 2011 decision American Electric Power Co. v. Connecticut (AEP). The AEP Court reasoned that since several provisions of the Clean Air Act gave EPA the authority to address these emissions, Congress had displaced the power of the federal judiciary to fashion a separate regime. Put plainly: federal common law was unavailable because the Court believed the Act granted EPA, not judges, the authority to regulate greenhouse gases. In concurrence, Justices Alito and Thomas explicitly acknowledged that this displacement ruling depended on the assumption that Massachusetts had been correctly decided.

The Supreme Court’s subsequent decision to limit EPA’s regulatory authority in West Virginia struck some Justices as inconsistent with AEP since both cases involved Clean Air Act section 111, which gives EPA the authority to regulate air pollution from new and existing stationary sources using the “best system of emissions reduction.” In a sharply worded dissent in West Virginia, Justice Kagan argued that the Supreme Court in AEP had interpreted section 111 as providing EPA the authority to determine both “whether and how” to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. By taking a significant regulatory method such as generation-shifting off the table, the Court was arguably acting inconsistently with its prior ruling. Responding to Kagan, the majority opinion attempted to reconcile the two cases by distinguishing between EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gases (which AEP conceded) and its ability to choose the manner in which to regulate them (which West Virginia limited). In doing so, the majority reiterated the low bar courts normally use for finding displacement: the mere “existence” of a relevant statutory provision was enough to remove suits over greenhouse gas emissions from the hands of federal judges.

Unlike the test for displacement of federal common law, federal preemption of state law requires much more than the simple presence of an applicable federal statute. And the Supreme Court, while ruling out federal tort suits in AEP,explicitly reserved the question of whether the Clean Air Act affected state tort suits related to climate change. The issue of state common law preemption began to percolate through the courts in 2017 as cities and states filed lawsuits not against power plant emitters but against fossil fuel producers. The plaintiffs made a variety of state law claims against companies like Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and BP, seeking damage awards to deal with the harmful effects of climate change.

In an effort to find a friendlier judicial audience, the defendants spent years attempting to remove these lawsuits to federal court. All failed, even after a Supreme Court decision that expanded the grounds on which state courts should consider such removal petitions. Now that several cases have proceeded to the preemption issue in state courts, the Justices—at the urging of the Trump Administration —agreed to weigh in again, this time on the relationship between federal and state authority over climate harms.

II. two starkly different views of preemption doctrine

Three state supreme courts and one federal circuit court of appeals have now issued conflicting decisions on whether states can bring tort suits against petroleum companies over climate harms. The Supreme Courts of Colorado and Hawai‘i found that the Clean Air Act did not bar the suits, while the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit held the opposite. The differences in outcomes, however, are not simply a product of disagreements over how to interpret the language of the Clean Air Act. Instead, the judges in these cases have offered two very different approaches to the common law and federal preemption. The Colorado and Hawai‘i courts followed traditional preemption doctrine: they examined the relevant federal legislation, looking at the Clean Air Act’s text and structure, to determine whether it overrode state authority. The Maryland court and Second Circuit adopted a novel approach to preemption: instead of looking to federal legislation, they found that federal common law preempted state tort suits over climate change. They asserted that transboundary pollution has always been “inherently federal” and complaints over such harms could not be brought under state common law. The Maryland court and Second Circuit’s analysis flips traditional preemption analysis on its head, requiring Congress to authorize state tort suits rather than legislate to preempt them. Moreover, those courts did not confine their reasoning to “global” pollution, instead describing state law as unavailable for any claim involving transboundary effects. These competing approaches to preemption are rooted in different conceptions of federal and state power under the U.S. Constitution as well as the history of interstate tort litigation over environmental harms.

A. The Traditional Approach to Preemption

Under the Constitution, Congress has the right to make laws governing interstate commerce and can preempt state laws in areas where there is concurrent federal and state power. So long as federal legislation is consistent with Congress’s commerce power, the key issue in a preemption analysis is discerning when Congress has in fact exercised that power. The question is not what Congress has the power to do but “what Congress has done,” as states retain their police powers under the Tenth Amendment unless and until Congress preempts them.

Consistent with this longstanding, traditional approach to preemption, the Colorado and Hawai‘i Supreme Courts looked to language in the Clean Air Act to determine whether some or all of the plaintiffs’ state tort claims could proceed. They examined whether explicit language in the Act barred the lawsuit, known as “express preemption,” and found no such text. The courts then assessed whether Congress had implicitly preempted state tort suits, either because federal legislation had completely occupied the relevant field of regulation or because state law would pose a conflict with federal law. Both courts concluded that federal legislation did not completely occupy the field of regulation because provisions of the Act foreclosed field preemption, with Congress opting to include “savings clauses” explicitly preserving state legislative authority as well as state common law over environmental pollution. Further, the courts found that the state tort lawsuits did not reach the high bar of posing an “obstacle” to implementation of the Clean Air Act since the claims did not seek to regulate emissions and primarily concerned deceptive marketing.

This approach rested on several premises. First, the courts accepted the plaintiffs’ framing of the complaint: the cases were products liability suits and not an effort to regulate emissions around the world. As the state justices noted, the defendants in the case are fossil fuel producers, not greenhouse gas emitters. Had the plaintiffs named major utilities or power plants as defendants, presumably the courts would have needed to engage in a different kind of preemption analysis that looked more closely at the specific Clean Air Act provisions that might govern greenhouse gas emissions. But because the defendants were not themselves polluters and their allegedly harmful actions were more properly construed as concerning harm from a product, the tort suit would not conflict with federal regulation.

Second, the courts relied on the 1987 U.S. Supreme Court case International Paper Co. v. Ouellette in which the Justices found that state common law was available for claims over transboundary environmental harms. As the Colorado Supreme Court put it, in that decision, the U.S. Supreme Court had not determined that Congress must authorize state actions concerning pollution. Instead, after engaging in an extensive review of the relevant statutory provisions, the International Paper Co. Court held that state tort suits could proceed against polluters who obtained federal pollution permits so long as those suits were brought under the state common law of the source state. In the present cases, because the defendants’ behavior concerned deceptive marketing practices and failure to warn, it was not necessary to evaluate whether these suits posed an obstacle to greenhouse gas permitting programs under the Clean Air Act in the same way the Justices did in International Paper Co.

B. A Federal Common Law Exception to Traditional Preemption Analysis?

Though claiming they were likewise “[a]pplying the preemption framework adopted by the Supreme Court in International Paper Company v. Ouellette,” the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit’s analysis of a nearly identical set of state tort claims could not have been more different from that in the Colorado and Hawai‘i decisions. Both courts first found that the plaintiffs could only bring their claims under federal common law and then concluded that the Clean Air Act displaced that federal common law.

Unlike the Colorado and Hawai‘i courts, the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit characterized the plaintiffs’ suits as primarily concerning the regulation of emissions around the world. Because the injuries were the result of “global consumption” of fossil fuels, the claims were “necessarily seeking damages for harms attributed to all interstate and international emissions combined—plain and simple.” Once they concluded that the complaints were actually about regulating emissions, not the defendants’ marketing and sale of a product, the courts then asserted that only federal common law was available for tort suits over transboundary pollution. Both courts cited International Paper Co. for this proposition, even though the Maryland opinion noted elsewhere that the International Paper Co. Court had preserved state tort law for transboundary pollution suits so long as the suit was brought under the law of the state where the permitted source was located. Finding that the plaintiffs’ complaints could only be brought under federal common law, and that the U.S. Supreme Court had foreclosed federal common law suits in AEP, the judges dismissed the lawsuits. In this way, the courts avoided undertaking a detailed preemption analysis, instead applying the lower bar for displacement: existence of a relevant federal statute.

The foundational premises underlying the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit decisions are thus quite distinct from those underlying the Colorado and Hawai‘i Supreme Court decisions. Despite the fact that the defendants in the cases were not polluting facilities themselves, the judges described the cases as being, at core, about the regulation of emissions. It did not matter that the particular defendants had not emitted greenhouse gases themselves. Because the release of greenhouse gases was necessary to cause the plaintiffs’ injuries, the judges believed the complaint was properly construed as being about emissions regulation. And because greenhouse gases caused the plaintiffs’ injuries through global processes—global emissions and planetary warming—only federal common law should govern the claims.

As a factual matter, of course, natural resource harms from climate change do require global processes. Both the sale of the product into international commerce and a series of global geophysical processes are necessary to cause such an injury. That is true, though, of many environmental problems, including other kinds of pollution that migrate through the air and water. For instance, environmental contamination from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a group of toxic chemicals, involves dispersal through global atmospheric processes. Litigation against chemical companies that produced PFAS is nevertheless proceeding under state tort law. Global activities also drive other tortious behavior that has nothing to do with pollution, whether related to the internet or human trafficking. The Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit opinions do not discuss why geophysical processes that contribute to climate damages should be treated differently from other activities that have an interstate or international component.

Finally—and notably—both the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit describe the Clean Air Act as a “comprehensive federal law” to address air pollution. They cite decisions like Massachusetts and AEP in finding that EPA has extensive authority over greenhouse gas emissions. In assessing the savings clauses in the Clean Air Act, the Second Circuit simply described them as “leaving a slim reservoir of state common law.” The Maryland Supreme Court did not analyze how those provisions should affect the resolution of the case.

It is not hard to see why defendants and some judges would be attracted to the argument that lawsuits about climate change can only be brought under the federal common law. The cases do involve transboundary issues, and finding state law unavailable allows for easy disposal of the claims regardless of their merits. The problem, though, is that binding Supreme Court precedent preserved state common law over transboundary harms after the passage of federal environmental statutes. An accurate history of this preservation—largely developed by a business-friendly, conservative U.S. Supreme Court Justice —must inform the question of preemption in climate tort suits.

III. the history of state tort suits over transboundary harms

Environmental and public health threats from industrial activities emerged as a matter of U.S. government concern in the late nineteenth century. At that time, pollution was thought to be a local issue, though it was widely understood that factories constructed along state boundaries could cause environmental and public health injuries in multiple jurisdictions. In the absence of federal legislation, federal courts allowed cities to enforce local smoke and refuse ordinances against steamboats operating in interstate waterways. It was during this early moment of industrialization that the U.S. Supreme Court first articulated the availability of federal common law for damages from substances that crossed state lines, providing an avenue for injured states to receive abatement of a nuisance or compensation for the harm caused.

A plethora of changes in the 1960s and 1970s eventually reshaped legal understandings of environmental threats and the role the common law should play in mitigating them. Scientific research demonstrated that hazardous substances could travel regionally and globally. The modern environmental movement led to public support for new federal legislation to create administrative agencies that would regulate pollutants across the country. And dramatic increases in the trade of goods around the world meant that harmful products were much more likely to have been produced and sold far from where they ultimately caused an injury.

These developments forced the U.S. Supreme Court to grapple anew with the role of the common law in addressing damage to natural resources and public health as well as what effect federal statutes might have on tort litigation. By the mid-1980s, the Court had settled on the following general approach: congressional legislation had displaced federal common law for disputes over environmental damage from air and water pollution, but state common law was still available for tort suits even if the harmful activity occurred far from the place of injury. Understanding how the Justices resolved questions over the application of federal versus state common law not only shows that the Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit opinions are incorrect as a historical matter. It also reveals that their method of assessing whether such suits are preempted is inconsistent with longstanding separation-of-powers principles under our Constitution.

A. Tort Suits Before the Rise of Federal Environmental Statutes

In the famous 1938 case Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, the Supreme Court declared that “[t]here is no federal general common law.” Yet before and after this decision, the Court applied federal common law in several nuisance cases involving transboundary pollution between states. Scientists at the time may not have possessed modern understandings about what substances should be defined as pollutants or how pollutants could spread via global atmospheric and hydrological cycles. But the public could see growing clouds of black smoke creep across a rapidly industrializing nation and notice how industries would often locate polluting facilities on a state’s borders to send fumes to their neighbors. When a copper-smelting company in Tennessee located its operations on the Georgia border, Georgia successfully brought a federal nuisance case to force the facility to reduce its emissions. The Supreme Court unanimously allowed that litigation to move forward in the 1907 case Georgia v. Tennessee Copper, explaining:

When the States by their union made the forcible abatement of outside nuisances impossible to each, they did not thereby agree to submit to whatever might be done. They did not renounce the possibility of making reasonable demands on the ground of their still remaining quasi-sovereign interests; and the alternative to force is a suit in this court.

Given this understanding of state sovereign rights over property, the Supreme Court allowed nuisance lawsuits over transboundary pollution to proceed under federal common law prior to passage of our major federal environmental statutes in the 1970s. For instance, in a 1972 lawsuit between Illinois and Milwaukee (Milwaukee I), the Court reiterated that federal common law could be used to bring tort claims over interstate environmental problems. Though federal statutes dealing with transboundary pollution existed at the time, the Justices determined that the operation of federal common law provided remedies outside the scope of those statutes. When the Justices decided Milwaukee I, the modern version of the Clean Water Act had not yet passed, and until “new federal laws and new federal regulations” restricted the activity in question, tort law remained an avenue for states to vindicate their right to protect their natural resources.

The Maryland Supreme Court and Second Circuit would later take a quote from Milwaukee I—”[w]hen we deal with air and water in their ambient or interstate aspects, there is a federal common law” —out of context to mean that only federal common law has ever been available for transboundary nuisance suits. But the question of whether such claims could be brought under state common law was not before the Court then. Instead, the issue was solely whether plaintiffs could bring federal common law claims given the existing federal statutes. Far from ruling out state law, the Court acknowledged in Milwaukee I that “consideration of state standards may be relevant” even where “federal law governs,” and “a State with high water-quality standards may well ask that its strict standards be honored and that it not be compelled to lower itself to the more degrading standards of a neighbor.” Questions about the relationship between federal and state common law would only arrive directly before the Court once Congress enacted more sweeping legislation to deal with environmental problems.

Less than a decade after Milwaukee I, the Supreme Court shut down the use of federal common law for resolving disputes over transboundary environmental threats in another dispute between Illinois and Milwaukee (Milwaukee II). Since Congress had by then passed environmental laws like the Clean Water Act, which represented “the most comprehensive legislation ever developed in its field,” the Court determined that federal common law’s “unusual” grant of judicial power had been “displaced” by federal legislation.

Milwaukee II had two important caveats. First, the Court specifically relied on the presence of a permitting system for the pollution discharges at issue in determining that the Act had displaced federal common law. Second, the majority’s view of displacement was not embraced by all the Justices. In a dissent joined by two of his colleagues, Justice Blackmun objected to the Court’s removal of an avenue for states to vindicate their rights absent federal legislation. The Court had not invented the federal common law for transboundary pollution in 1972, he noted, and when entering the Union, states had maintained their “right to such federal protection” from interference with “its natural environment and resources when the interference stems from another State or its citizens.” As he argued, by asking states to give up their sovereign power to abate such activities by military force, the Constitution had necessarily guaranteed the ability for federal courts to hear such disputes.

If Justice Blackmun’s views didn’t win the day in Milwaukee II, his concerns were nevertheless prescient. Heeding his warning about the need to protect state rights over their property and natural resources, the Supreme Court, despite taking federal common law off the table, ultimately preserved the availability of state common law claims over transboundary pollution.

B. Reconciling Federal Permitting Authority and State Common Law in International Paper Co. v. Ouellette

The passage of federal legislation did not end disputes over environmental and public health threats that crossed state lines, and they reached the Supreme Court again a few years after the decision in Milwaukee II. That case, International Paper Co., involved several claims brought against a paper mill on the New York side of Lake Champlain, which was discharging wastewater that damaged the properties of residents on the Vermont side. By the time the suit reached the Supreme Court, only one cause of action remained: nuisance.

Because the Supreme Court had eliminated the availability of tort suits under federal common law, property owners in Vermont had brought their nuisance claim under Vermont state law. A split had emerged, however, over whether state common law had survived federal environmental legislation, and if so, which state’s law should apply in cases involving activities that occurred in one state but caused an injury in another. Some courts believed the nuisance law of the injured state should apply; others believed that the law of the state where the company was located should apply. Both anchored their analysis on the language of federal statutes, relying on different provisions in determining which nuisance law should govern such disputes. Given this clear split in the lower courts and the need to decide the fate of state common law after the passage of federal legislation, nearly all the Supreme Court Justices voted to grant cert in International Paper Co.

The key concern that emerged from conversations among the Justices and their clerks was what impact the common law of various states might have on facilities that obtained pollution permits under a federal statute. Justice Powell, who ultimately wrote the majority opinion in the case, took a particular interest in the challenges that permittees might face if they had to comply with a variety of state common law nuisance standards related to their discharges. Crucially, however, there was “no disagreement” that federal law “permits some type of state common law action to supplement federal remedies.” The question was solely whether the federal statute—in this case the Clean Water Act—barred state nuisance claims under the law of the affected state.

Importantly, just before International Paper Co. reached the Court, the Justices had decided another case on the national reach of the Clean Water Act’s permitting provisions. That case, United States v. Riverside Bayview Homes, Inc., concerned whether landowners needed to obtain a permit from the federal government before destroying wetlands on their property. For context, the Clean Water Act requires permits of all facilities that discharge substances into the “waters of the United States” but does not define that phrase. In 1975, the federal government promulgated a regulation interpreting “waters of the United States” to encompass not only navigable waters but also smaller tributaries and nonnavigable waters located within a state whose “use or misuse could affect interstate commerce.” In Riverside Bayview, a legal challenge to the government’s interpretation of the Act’s broad coverage, a unanimous Court upheld the government’s interpretation and determined that landowners would need to obtain a permit even if they sought to fill wetlands that did not have a continuous surface water connection to nearby navigable waters. The government’s “ecological judgment about the relationship between waters and their adjacent wetlands” entitled it to deference in defining a broadly written statutory term. Congress had intended to regulate water pollution at the furthest reaches of its commerce power, the Justices reasoned, thus allowing for an expansive definition of the relevant water bodies encompassed by the legislation.

One cannot properly make sense of the outcome in International Paper Co. without understanding the Justices’ broad interpretation of the Clean Water Act’s reach, as reflected in Riverside Bayview. As Justice Powell debated International Paper Co. with his colleagues, he asked his clerk to determine how many bodies of water around the country were governed by the federal statute. The clerk’s answer: “[A]ll of them.” Given the Act’s broad scope and comprehensiveness, Powell and those who signed onto his majority opinion believed Congress could not have intended a chaotic common law supplement to the Act’s permitting provisions. At the same time, however, the existence of several savings clauses in the Act suggested Congress had wanted to preserve state authority generally—and the common law in particular. These savings clauses, like similar provisions in the Clean Air Act, stated that nothing in the Clean Water Act should “restrict any right which any person (or class of persons) may have under any statute or common law,” nor restrict the rights of states or cities to enforce limitations on pollution unless such standards were weaker than federal limits.

Justice Powell therefore maintained the availability of state common law tort suits over transboundary pollution so long as they were brought under the law of the state where the facility was located. In doing so, he examined the text in the Clean Water Act and assessed whether Congress had meant to preserve state common law and, if so, in what way. Courts could not apply the law of the state where the injury occurred, Powell found, because that could disrupt the careful balance Congress had tried to strike in setting up its permitting scheme. He worried about the possibility that a permitted facility might face tort suits under the common law of various states, which could require it to comply with numerous different discharge standards. It would also create the possibility that Clean Water Act permits would cease to have any real force, as a court might impose a different limit than EPA allowed. At the same time, Congress had clearly intended to allow states to achieve environmental standards higher than those of the federal government. Allowing tort suits to be brought under the law of the state where the permitted facility was located, far from obstructing the Act’s purpose, complemented it.

International Paper Co. thus kept a role for state tort law in addressing transboundary environmental issues, in accordance with the Justices’ understandings of proper separations of powers and their specific interpretation of the Clean Water Act. As federal environmental laws failed to completely prevent damage to state natural resources and public health, tort litigation under state law became an essential backstop over the next four decades.

C. Tort Litigation After the International Paper Co. Compromise

The Supreme Court’s preservation of state tort cases for disputes over transboundary environmental and public health threats proved important as scientific studies began to document that most harmful substances do not respect territorial boundaries, and as the economy globalized to permit the production and sale of products around the world. Researchers first started to grasp that even locally emitted substances could have global circulation patterns with the discovery of pesticides in Antarctica in the 1960s. After International Paper Co., plaintiffs began to bring claims under state common law to address pollution beyond the kind that had animated lawsuits like Georgia v. Tennessee Copper at the beginning of the twentieth century, where visible pollution drifted across state boundaries. Courts started to hear state tort suits over the harms from substances that were invisible and traveled longer distances to damage natural resources and public health.

In numerous decisions over the past four decades, courts have found that state common law is available for environmental threats even if the claim involves activities or transport beyond the state’s borders, in accordance with the Supreme Court’s International Paper Co. decision. Judges have applied that decision’s reasoning equally to arguments for preemption under the Clean Air Act, which contains savings clauses similar to those in the Clean Water Act. Numerous federal and state courts have therefore held that state tort suits can proceed against facilities that cause transboundary pollution so long as the court hearing the case applies the law of the source state.

To assert that a “mostly unbroken string of cases has applied federal law” to transboundary pollution disputes—as the Maryland justices and Second Circuit judges did —ignores the past forty years of cases that have relied on state tort law to address environmental and public health harms resulting from air and water pollution. Judges have repeatedly affirmed that state law is available even in cases where pollution and products cross state and international lines.

As one illustrative example, oil companies faced tort liability for damages from a chemical added to gasoline, methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE). Used from the 1980s through the mid-2000s, the substance ended up contaminating groundwater, and numerous states and cities sued over the companies’ failure to warn of the chemical’s risks as well as their negligence with respect to manufacturing and sales of MTBE. The global refinement, transport, and sale of the product did not require the application of federal law, nor did courts find that the Clean Air Act preempted state suits. Other examples include state law cases over water pollution discharges that affect downstream states and air pollution across the U.S. and Canadian border.

The international nature of chemical and oil production has also not persuaded courts that tort suits involving injuries from those substances must be brought under federal common law, nor that they are preempted by other federal legislation like the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act or Oil Pollution Act. Even if defendants are multinational corporations selling their products around the world, courts have allowed tort suits over fraud, misrepresentation, and failure to warn to proceed under state law. They have then engaged in traditional preemption analysis, looking to federal statutes for indications of whether Congress intended to override state common law. Other products liability cases, including those over injuries caused by asbestos, opioids, and social media use, have likewise proceeded under traditional state tort theories.

In particular, suits against social media companies over harms from internet use are analogous to state climate suits, as they involve similar claims like public nuisance and failure to warn along with an invisible, global medium routing the injury from the company to the plaintiff. In social media cases, this medium is the internet; in climate cases, it is the atmosphere. The atmosphere’s existence, and changes to the atmosphere, are necessary to cause the injury, but the increasing concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is no more the core source of the harm than the increasing concentration of website traffic on the internet is in suits against social media companies. It is the defendants’ behavior in manufacturing and selling their products that forms the basis for the suit. Defendants and critics have objected to social media tort suits and climate tort suits on similar grounds, such as by arguing that the cases are barred by the Constitution or that nuisance is only supposed to encompass “local” activities. But several state courts have not found these arguments persuasive in the case of social media tort suits, and some social media cases have proceeded to trial and led to successful verdicts in favor of the plaintiffs. Yet if “worldwide production and allegedly deceptive marketing” requires the application of federal common law for torts involving climate damages, it is unclear why there should be any difference for torts involving the worldwide production and deceptive marketing of social media.

IV. the implications for suncor

If the Supreme Court reaches the issue of federal preemption in the Suncor case, this history of state tort litigation over interstate harms—including environmental damages—should factor into the Justices’ analysis of whether state common law is available for claims involving climate damages and whether such claims are preempted by the Clean Air Act. The Justices will also need to consider the effect of recent decisions in environmental and administrative law on the case, particularly in light of the Trump Administration’s revocation of the Endangerment Finding for greenhouse gas emissions. As this Part argues, the Court should find that state common law is available given the historic use of state tort law to address transboundary harms and the similarities between climate suits and other torts that involve global causation chains. It should then preserve at least some tort actions since there is no clear statement in the Clean Air Act indicating that Congress intended to preempt such suits and no permitting program that applies to the defendants.

A. The Availability of State Tort Law for Climate Claims

The fact that state common law has been available for claims concerning transboundary pollution over the past four decades exposes the flawed reasoning of the Second Circuit and Maryland Supreme Court. The U.S. Supreme Court in Suncor should not follow in those courts’ footsteps. The Justices should reject their ahistorical, inaccurate recounting of precedents like International Paper Co. and reaffirm that state common law is available for tort claims involving transboundary pollution.

That clarification brings us to the first hard question in Suncor: should torts involving climate change require a different approach from other transboundary cases, as a constitutional matter, because there are global aspects to the problem? Before assessing this issue in the context of Suncor, it is important to acknowledge that only federal common law is available if one state seeks to sue another state. Such a dispute would be between two sovereigns and could not be resolved by reference to the injured state’s law. However, the plaintiffs in Suncor sued private companies. Although some states have passed legislation to shield companies from liability for climate harms, their efforts to protect defendants from tort suits under their state’s common law should not be a reason to find all state common law unavailable for suits against fossil fuel companies.

To assess whether only federal common law should be available for climate tort suits against private parties, one must instead consider whether there is something different about an injury requiring the global concentration of a substance in the atmosphere compared to the global circulation of a substance or product. Or, to put it another way: is there something different about the atmosphere compared to the marketplace or the internet that requires the imposition of federal common law in climate suits even when the defendants are private parties? Making such a distinction as a constitutional matter, when the cases are against private parties whose relevant activities are production and sale of a substance, is inconsistent with state judicial authority to decide whether their common law can encompass these types of complex tort claims. Nor is there anything in the text or structure of the Constitution to warrant differentiating between the modes of transportation in a tort injury. If the Justices believe that the existence of a global causation chain in a tort suit calls for the application of federal common law, federal common law should apply regardless of whether the injury is caused by global dispersion of a harmful substance or global dispersion of a harmful product through the economy. They should not carve out a “climate exception” for tort claims, requiring the application of federal common law for such suits but allowing other kinds of tort claims that involve global processes to proceed under state law.

B. A Preemption Analysis Consistent with International Paper Co. and Recent Regulatory Developments

Finding that state common law is available does not resolve the preemption question, however. That requires evaluating the federal statute to assess whether state climate tort suits may pose an obstacle to the Clean Air Act or whether federal law provides such a comprehensive regulatory scheme that it has simply left no room for state tort law. It is here that the Court’s recent decisions in environmental and administrative law should lead the Justices to find the Act does not preempt at least certain state tort suits involving climate change. When considering the particular claims and defendants in Suncor alongside the Trump Administration’s legal position on EPA’s regulatory authority on greenhouse gases, some tort liability must remain unless and until Congress enacts new, comprehensive climate legislation.

1. A Clear Statement Rule for Preemption

In numerous recent decisions about federal environmental and public health regulations, the Court has scaled back deference to executive-branch agencies. While many of these decisions weaken arguments for preemption in Suncor, three are especially detrimental. These are West Virginia v. EPA and Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA, which applied the major questions doctrine to curtail EPA’s ability to address greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, and Sackett v. EPA, which required Congress to enact “exceedingly clear” language when altering the balance between federal and state power over natural resources and scaled back EPA’s ability to control water pollution. These three cases suggest that the Clean Air Act neither provides a “comprehensive” regulatory scheme for greenhouse gas emissions nor contains the exceedingly clear language necessary to override states’ power to impose liability on those who damage their property.

Recall that in International Paper Co., the Court initially evaluated whether the Clean Water Act created a comprehensive regulatory scheme to address the water pollution in the underlying tort suit. The Justices answered this question in the affirmative, then examined the effect state tort suits would have on parties that obtained pollution permits. They noted that the Act covered the same types of defendants and activities as those in the underlying suit, and that it granted neighboring states a process for contesting pollution allowed under the federal permits. This finding was critical to the Justices’ holding that suits brought under the law of the injured state were preempted. In the air pollution context, cases like West Virginia and Utility Air Regulatory Group have made it much harder to claim that the federal law provides a comprehensive scheme addressing the issues in climate tort suits. These cases limited the kinds of regulatory controls EPA can use to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, which cuts against preemption.

One might perhaps still argue the Court should employ a more exacting standard when assessing statutory authority to regulate than when assessing statutory preemption of state law. Setting aside the lack of precedent for this bifurcated approach to statutory interpretation, in both cases, the Justices are ostensibly trying to discern congressional intent. It is of course possible that Congress might wish to provide only limited regulatory authority to an agency while simultaneously preempting state tort suits in a particular area. But if that were the case, one would expect Congress to give some indication of this in the text of the statute. And in fact, the Clean Air Act evinces the opposite intent with its explicit preservation of state common law.

The principle of statutory interpretation introduced in Sackett compounds the Justices’ challenge in reading the Clean Air Act to preempt state tort suits over climate damages. Whereas the Court had once read the Clean Water Act broadly to apply to nearly all bodies of water in the country, a majority of current Justices now read the Act narrowly. In Sackett, they interpreted the statute to cover only a small subset of water bodies not only because of the relevant statutory text and structure of the Act, but because Congress must “enact exceedingly clear language if it wishes to significantly alter the balance between federal and state power.” Because “land and water use lies at the core of traditional state authority” under the Constitution, the Justices required extra clarity before finding federal regulatory power over water pollution. For Justice Alito and the majority in Sackett, it did not matter that water cycles are global, nor that pollutants can move from rainfall through tributaries and streams to eventually reach larger water bodies. Background principles of statutory construction required more from Congress to supersede state sovereignty over their natural resources.

The same logic should apply to state tort suits against fossil fuel companies over damages to state natural resources from climate change. These harms are local and implicate core state police powers over land and water. The Justices should therefore apply the same canon of statutory construction to decide the scope of preemption as they did when deciding the scope of federal law for purposes of regulation: a clear statement is required if Congress wants to alter the balance of power over natural resources. That in Suncor the substantive outcome would protect the environment, whereas Sackett led to significant deregulation, should not affect the Court’s reasoning.

It is possible that the Justices will reject such thinking. EPA does have some authority over climate, at least for the time being: West Virginia did preserve EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under section 111, and there may not be an appetite for overturning Massachusetts. Thus, the Court could opt to consider whether the state tort suits conflict with the agency’s regulatory programs in a manner similar to the analysis in International Paper Co. To find that these lawsuits posed a similar obstacle, however, two things would also need to be true: a permitting program would need to be in place, and the lawsuits would have to obstruct that program. As explained below, neither of these conditions currently exists.

2. The Effect of Federal Climate Rollbacks on Suncor

The most favorable legal landscape for getting climate tort suits dismissed on preemption grounds would require the Trump EPA to implement greenhouse gas permitting schemes for mobile and stationary sources under the Clean Air Act. If those regulations were in place, the defendants in the current climate tort suits could more persuasively argue that large financial damages awards would obstruct implementation of those programs, like in International Paper Co. For example, the Biden Administration’s mobile-source standards were projected to increase hybrid and electric vehicle sales thirty-five to fifty-six percent by 2032. If extremely large financial awards in tort suits against oil companies could decrease the supply of gasoline and push Americans to adopt hybrid and electric vehicles more rapidly, there might be stronger grounds for asserting that the tort suits posed an obstacle to a federal program. Congress expressly preempted states from imposing standards on mobile sources other than those of the federal government, with an exception for California and states that follow it. Empirical support for such claims would be essential, however, in light of prior independent research suggesting tort law has not led to such effects in other similar cases.

Notwithstanding this possibility, there would still be enormous problems with such an argument for preemption. Beyond the statutory interpretation issues discussed in Section IV.B.1, it is always the case that tort lawsuits have some downstream effects on businesses. Obstacle preemption should require something more. International Paper Co. involved a situation where the entity that received a federal permit was being sued, and the Court still preserved a role for tort suits under the Clean Air Act’s savings clauses so long as the claim was brought under the law of the source state. By comparison, the defendants in the climate tort suits are fossil fuel producers, not direct emitters. And some of the claims involve products liability claims like failure to warn, not the singular nuisance cause of action present in International Paper Co. Even in the presence of federal greenhouse gas rules, then, some climate tort suits would not generate the kind of disruption feared by the majority in International Paper Co., as they are not directed toward permitted facilities.

The Trump Administration’s repeal of climate regulations for motor vehicles on the grounds that it has no legal authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act makes preemption arguments even more untenable. A finding of obstacle preemption requires that there be some regulatory program for the state law to disrupt. If the federal government has no legal authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions, then arguments that the climate tort suits disrupt the “careful balance” Congress struck in fashioning federal legislation seem absurd on their face. The disconnect in legal arguments between EPA’s repeal of the Endangerment Finding for greenhouse gas emissions and Suncor has led some Republican activists to criticize the Trump Department of Justice (DOJ) after the most recent briefing in the case, accusing government lawyers of trying to sabotage the President’s deregulatory agenda. It is also likely why DOJ and fossil fuel companies have turned to more attenuated arguments like foreign affairs preemption even though a majority of the Justices do not seem receptive to them.

Conclusion

The Trump Administration’s effort to have it both ways—to deny that EPA has authority to regulate greenhouse gases as it argues the Clean Air Act represents a comprehensive regulatory scheme over these air pollutants—should force the Supreme Court to grapple directly with the balance of federal and state authority over climate tort suits. Bearing in mind the history outlined in this Essay, the Court must clarify that state common law has been available for tort suits over transboundary pollution. Climate tort suits do not warrant different treatment because the harms result from global processes, as the same is true of many injuries in our modern world. And in light of current case law and the current Administration’s position that EPA has no authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions, all state common law causes of action should be available absent new congressional legislation clearly preempting them. To find otherwise would suggest states cannot protect their residents and natural resources against damage from external threats unless the federal government intervenes—a position at odds with our Constitution and basic principles of federalism.

title: Renault to Invest €10B in French EVs if Politics Allow - Briefs Finance
description:
In the past five years, the carmaker poured €13 billion ($14.6 billion) into expanding EV production in France.
Renault is 15% owned by the French state.
Carmakers commit capital years ahead of demand, and politics can redirect it almost overnight.
Trade with China is a pressure point too Provost also pressed for European Union action on the auto trade imbalance with China.
For your wallet, the takeaway is simple: Renault's next wave of EV spending - and the jobs tied to it - depends on calmer French politics and clearer rules on China.
text:
What Renault is committing to

Renault's chief executive Francois Provost said Saturday on France Inter radio that the company will keep backing electric vehicles in its home market, so long as the climate in France allows. In the past five years, the carmaker poured €13 billion ($14.6 billion) into expanding EV production in France. Looking ahead, Provost said, "Over the next five years, if the social and political context in France allows it, we will invest more than €10 billion to continue pushing ahead with electric vehicles and make cars more affordable." Renault is 15% owned by the French state.

Politics and markets are the backdrop

France is heading into an uncertain stretch with about seven months until elections that would close out President Emmanuel Macron's decade in office. The strain is showing in parliament, where an increasingly bitter budget fight has the minority government trying to advance a plan that leans on unpopular spending cuts and higher taxes on large companies to contain a swollen deficit. Recent polls suggest April's vote could end in a second-round faceoff between far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen and far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon. The jitters have spilled into markets, fueling a selloff in French assets and sending sovereign yields this week to their highest since the euro-area debt crisis 15 years ago.

Carmakers commit capital years ahead of demand, and politics can redirect it almost overnight. Market Briefs tracks those bets free every morning.

Why it matters to Renault and its people

Provost called the market swings "worrying" for Renault, noting how tied the company is to France: 20% of its business comes from the country and 40% of its workforce is based there. "We have really bet on France and we will continue to bet on France," he said. "So any scenario of instability in France would have a major impact on Renault, a major impact on our employees and a major impact on our suppliers, so yes, I am worried."

Trade with China is a pressure point too

Provost also pressed for European Union action on the auto trade imbalance with China. "The flow of imports coming from China is currently too rapid and not really under control," he said, adding that "The answer is not a tariff war, but an agreement between China and Europe that says Chinese carmakers are welcome provided they not only manufacture here, but also use European suppliers and bring technology." For your wallet, the takeaway is simple: Renault's next wave of EV spending - and the jobs tied to it - depends on calmer French politics and clearer rules on China. Those forces can sway everything from car prices to local investment.

text:
File photo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Picture credit: PTI)

NEW DELHI: India's role in efforts to find a negotiated end to the Russia-Ukraine war has gained greater prominence, with Kyiv describing an Indian proposal as the most comprehensive among four initiatives currently under discussion and saying New Delhi has, for the first time, indicated its willingness to play an active mediating role. Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha recently said Ukraine was prepared to consider both an energy and agricultural truce in the Black Sea, while also remaining open to an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact. "We have four proposals. The most comprehensive is India's proposal. For the first time, India has signalled its willingness to play a role," Sybiha said during a press briefing, according to RBC Ukraine.

India proposal among four initiatives

According to Sybiha, four proposals are currently being considered in diplomatic efforts surrounding the war. India's proposal was described by the Ukrainian foreign minister as the most comprehensive. Türkiye and Egypt have separately proposed a grain and agricultural truce in the Black Sea, while the United States has put forward an energy truce proposal. The agricultural and maritime component is particularly important for Egypt, which relies on Ukrainian grain for roughly a third of its supply, according to RBC Ukraine. The US proposal on an energy truce was also discussed during a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Kyiv has conveyed its own approach to its partners and wants the energy and Black Sea components to be treated as an interconnected package. Sybiha said the energy component would require a complete halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, including port facilities. Ukraine has also expressed readiness for an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact. Sybiha said such a ceasefire could potentially emerge from a meeting between Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The US is currently working actively on this diplomatic track, according to the Ukrainian foreign minister.

Kyiv backs safe Black Sea shipping

The latest Ukrainian position builds on India's earlier engagement with Kyiv over restoring safe navigation in the Black Sea. During last month's UN General Assembly-related engagements, Zelenskyy said Egypt, India and Türkiye had put forward options for a maritime truce between Russia and Ukraine. "We are waiting for Russia's response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere," Zelenskyy said at the time.Also read: India's proposal under consideration for safe Black Sea shipping, Zelenskyy says India has been engaging with both Moscow and Kyiv while advocating dialogue and diplomacy. External affairs minister S Jaishankar had said India was in continuous contact with both sides and was exploring ideas that could help mitigate and eventually end the conflict. "If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there," Jaishankar said during his visit to Kyiv last month. During that visit, Jaishankar met Zelenskyy and Sybiha, with discussions covering peace efforts, bilateral cooperation, Black Sea navigation and global food security. Sybiha had also said Ukraine valued India's engagement in efforts to restore freedom of navigation in the Black Sea. "Restoring freedom of navigation is critical for global food security. Ukraine is ready to play a constructive role and we value India’s engagement," he said in a post on X.

Russia's position remains key to next steps

While Ukraine has indicated its readiness to consider multiple limited ceasefire arrangements, Russia's response remains central to whether the proposals can move forward. Sybiha's comments come amid differing assessments in Europe over Moscow's willingness to enter substantive peace negotiations. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently said Russia was not currently interested in genuine peace negotiations, while German foreign minister Johann Wadephul has expressed expectations that talks to end the war could begin in the near future.

The Kremlin had previously said there were no prerequisites for moving towards a broader peace negotiating track while maintaining that Russia remained open to talks. "For now, there are no prerequisites for moving on to a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. Ukraine's latest position therefore places several limited ceasefire proposals, covering energy infrastructure, Black Sea shipping and agricultural supplies, alongside the possibility of a broader unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact. India's proposal is being considered alongside those initiatives, with Sybiha describing it as the most comprehensive and saying New Delhi has now signalled its readiness to play a role in the process.
