title: Regulators approve 3,000-acre Amazon data center in Wharton County | Texas
authors: Bethany Blankley, The Center Square contributor
description: (The Center Square) – Wharton County residents continue to express opposition to Amazon building a 3,000-acre data center in the rural farm community located roughly an hour south of Houston.
text:
Server racks in a data center. Photo: Brett Sayles / Pexels

(The Center Square) – Wharton County residents continue to express opposition to Amazon building a 3,000-acre data center in the rural farm community located roughly an hour south of Houston.

Abbott announced his data center ban on Sept. 21. The Coastal Bend Groundwater Conservation District issued water permits to Amazon in May and earlier in September.

The CBGCD permits allow Amazon to tap millions of gallons of groundwater a year and don’t apply to millions of gallons of surface water the complex would need.

Amazon is building a 3,000-acre campus outside of Boling, about 10 miles southeast of Wharton. It says the complex will support at least 300 full-time jobs, with 150 becoming available by mid-2027. Construction will generate thousands of additional jobs.

Between 10-13 data center buildings are being built on the complex. Each is equivalent to the size of a Walmart Superstore.

Scarcity of water in rural farm communities is a key reason why so many rural Texas voters oppose data centers. Under Abbott’s tenure, Texas has surpassed Virginia with the most construction of data centers in the country, the Houston Business Journal reported .

Neighboring county judges have raised the alarm about residents and county governments not having water rights, calling on the legislature to act. Texas water rights and water laws are like “the old west,” Bee County Judge George Morrill has said. County officials have also called on the legislature to grant counties zoning authority to regulate data center growth. Without it, county officials say because of private property rights their hands are tied in preventing data center expansion, The Center Square reported .

In response to public outrage and a lack of data center compliance with state laws and regulations, Abbott issued four directives for data centers, including requiring them to reuse their own water. Amazon was among several dozen companies that said they would comply, The Center Square reported .

In a June directive, Abbott ordered state regulators to audit data center companies prior to approving permits to ensure they “pay for their electric infrastructure instead of shifting costs onto Texas families and small businesses, reuse their own water, reduce the cost of electricity for Texans, do not disrupt residential neighborhoods to preserve Texas’ quality of life, and pay their own way and eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives,” The Center Square reported.

Abbott’s data center ban directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt all permits sought by data centers until the audits are completed. In another directive , he instructed data centers to follow the law related to water use reporting requirements and for the Texas Water Development Board to enforce penalties.

Amazon has said it will comply and is “building responsibly in Wharton County.” It says it’s “been building and operating data centers for nearly two decades. In that time, we've proven that we are not only good neighbors, but committed long-term collaborators in the communities where we operate and our employees live.”

In an online post Amazon created to explain to residents its water usage and other plans, it says, “The 13 buildings planned on the Wharton County campus will not use water for cooling. No groundwater will be used for data center cooling at this site.” It says it’s working with regional and local water authorities to “develop responsible, nonpotable water solutions for any potential cooling needs” to ensure “that our projects do not negatively impact water needs for the surrounding community.”

“Besides cooling, data centers use water for everyday needs like bathrooms, cleaning, and fire suppression systems. For our current plans, potable use is limited to approximately 16,000 gallons per day, equivalent to roughly 54 households or a typical office building with a similar number of employees,” it adds.

It also says it’s returning more water to communities than it uses in its data center operations, “and we're already 75% of the way there.”

Amazon also created a Wharton County Community Fund and is funding a water replenishment project. The project will help local farmers adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying irrigation practices to reduce flood-based irrigation demand “by 25% or more without reducing crop yields – in the lower Colorado River watershed. … This effort is expected to replenish more than 225 million gallons of water per year” over 10 years.

The CBGCD permits allow Amazon to tap into three wells to supply groundwater for the project’s restrooms, construction crew and fire protection. The Houston Chronicle reported this could draw up to 78.2 million gallons of groundwater over two and a half years. If distributed evenly over the three-year-permit period, that could translate to 31.2 million gallons annually, enough to support 285 average U.S.-sized households, it estimates.

It also notes that Amazon received additional permits to draw up to 16.9 million gallons from two other wells by February 2029 although it doesn’t expect to use the full amount.

Amazon says it leads the industry in water efficiency. Its “cooling systems run on outside air alone about 90 percent of the time” and surface water “is only used during the hottest hours of the year.” Since 2021, it says it’s cut its water use per IT load in half and runs more facilities on reclaimed water than any other cloud provider. It also says its “actively pursuing reclaimed water and other alternative source partnerships” with state water authorities.

name: Indiana American Energy
title: WV home energy rebate launch offers savings path as PSC eyes potentially costly rules
description: West Virginians looking for more power over their power bills have a new opportunity to find it – four years in the making and as the state considers a rule framework for electric utilities that community advocates fear will make those bills more burdensome. The West Virginia Office of Energy has launched home energy rebate programming funded by the Inflation Reduction Act, landmark sustainable energy legislation signed into law in August 2022 by President Joe Biden without any congressional Republican support.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announces the launch of Inflation Reduction Act-funded home energy rebate programs in West Virginia at a launch event at the Capitol Complex in Charleston on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026.

This is an Aug. 15, 2024, file photo of the West Virginia Public Service Commission in Charleston.

West Virginians looking for more power over their power bills have a new opportunity to find it — four years in the making and as the state considers a rule framework for electric utilities that community advocates fear will make those bills more burdensome.

The West Virginia Office of Energy this week launched home energy rebate programming funded by the Inflation Reduction Act , landmark sustainable energy legislation signed into law in August 2022 by then-President Joe Biden without any congressional Republican support.

West Virginia was assigned $88 million in 2022 to implement the initiative, which consists of two programs:

HOMES and HEAR have different eligibility requirements, approved measures and rebate structures. A household may participate in both programs if it meets the requirements for each and doesn’t get duplicate federal funding for the same improvement.

HOMES supports qualifying whole-home improvements that reduce energy use. Eligible improvements may include insulation, windows and doors, air sealing, ductwork, heating and cooling equipment, and other measures identified through a home energy assessment.

HEAR upgrades may apply to heating and cooling equipment, water heaters, cooking appliances, electrical upgrades, insulation, air sealing and ventilation, with equipment replacements required to use the same fuel type as the existing equipment.

Energy efficiency has long been hard to come by in West Virginia.

Citing an analysis of U.S. Energy Information Administration data, the U.S. Joint Economic Committee — Minority in November projected West Virginia’s average 2025 household electricity expenses would reach $1,960, more than any bordering state except Maryland despite West Virginia having easily the lowest per capita personal income among those neighbors in 2024, per a Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis analysis.

The West Virginia Housing Development Fund last year published a state housing needs assessment that found there are more than 266,000 energy-burdened households in the state (37% of all households), meaning they pay more than 6% of their household income on electricity and other fuel expenses.

One in every five burdened households were low-income and had among the top quarter of highest energy costs in the state, the report found, noting that those households would reap the most potential benefit from weatherization and other energy efficiency programs.

That’s because households with high energy costs can be a proxy for housing conditions since older homes that are in poor condition tend to cost more to heat and cool, the report noted.

West Virginia ranked 45th among all states in 2025 state energy efficiency scorecard rankings released by the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy, a nonprofit research group that develops policies to cut energy waste and fight climate change. States are judged by utility and public benefits programs and policies, transportation policies, building energy efficiency policies, state-government-led initiatives around energy efficiency, industrial energy efficiency policies, and appliance and equipment standards.

In a long-term energy resource plan they filed with the West Virginia Public Service Commission last year, Mon Power and Potomac Edison, FirstEnergy’s West Virginia-serving subsidiaries, acknowledged they didn’t have an energy efficiency plan or surcharge in effect in West Virginia. They have drawn criticism for not planning to include energy efficiency plans, something the company has attributed to West Virginia not requiring energy efficiency programs for its utility customers.

The $88.2 million in funding is West Virginia’s share of a nearly $9 billion pot provided by the Inflation Reduction Act for states and tribes that was focused on low-income consumers and aimed at electrifying home appliances and energy-efficient retrofits of homes.

After years of administrative delay, West Virginia was fully awarded its home energy funding on Jan. 16, 2025, four days before the Trump administration began, the federal Department of Energy recounted to HD Media in July. West Virginia Office of Energy communications manager Chelsea Morrison told HD Media in May 2025 that the office had received all $88.2 million.

Morrison also said in May 2025 that the office was preparing to launch home energy rebate programs last summer with a full statewide rollout expected in August 2025 for the initiative designed to facilitate lasting upgrades and shrink rising energy bills.

But Morrison said in July that projected implementation timelines were affected while the Trump administration reviewed aspects of the home energy rebate programs and adjusted program requirements with its own energy priorities.

In August, the Office of Energy announced it had opened a pilot phase of the HOMES program for a select group of homes in southern West Virginia in collaboration with Coalfield Community Action Partnership, Southwestern Community Action Council and PRIDE Community Services.

The Governor’s Office said Monday the HOMES and HEAR programs are expected to serve roughly 10,000 West Virginia homes and generate between $3 million and $4.5 million in annual savings for participating households.

The Office of Energy said in a news release Tuesday it worked during the pilot phase to increase the number of qualified professionals available to complete rebate-supported projects. Through an office energy efficiency contractor training program in partnership with North Carolina-based software, program management and workforce development training provider Everblue, contractors and individuals interested in entering the energy-efficiency field may receive paid training and credentials needed to take part in the programs.

“Bringing both programs statewide required careful testing, strong regional partnerships, and intentional investment in West Virginia’s contractor workforce,” Nicholas Preservati, West Virginia Department of Commerce deputy secretary and Office of Energy director, said in the news release.

Gov. Patrick Morrisey hailed the programming launch during a brief speech at the Capitol Complex in Charleston Monday.

“Ultimately, I’m interested in results,” Morrisey said. “What are we doing to actually make life easier for everyday West Virginians? Does it put more money back in people’s pockets? Does it improve their quality of life? We always have to ask that question.”

The Office of Energy said Tuesday more than 115 participants were active in the contractor training program.

“West Virginia contractors understand the needs of the communities they serve, and they’ll play an important role in bringing these programs to households across the state,” Contractors Association of West Virginia CEO Jason Pizatella said in the Office of Energy’s news release.

The Office of Energy has said the home energy rebate programs would operate for a limited period and are subject to available funding. Rebates will be offered until the applicable program deadline of September 2031 or until allocated funds are fully committed, whichever happens first, the office has said.

Renters may qualify for certain rebates with written permission from the property owner, and owners of qualifying multifamily buildings may also be eligible.

Eligibility is based primarily on household income, with rebate amounts varying by income level and the type of home energy improvements being completed.

The office has cautioned that submitting an application doesn’t guarantee approval. Eligibility, project requirements, available funding and program authorization must all be confirmed before a rebate is awarded, the office added.

Eligibility and full program details are available at bit.ly/WVHomeEnergyRebates .

The new opportunities for home energy cost relief come as the West Virginia Public Service Commission considers proposed rulemaking governing electric generating capacity requirements established under House Bill 2014 , legislation requested by Morrisey not only for West Virginia to fast-track data center development but to double down on the nation’s highest reliance on coal-fired power for electricity.

HB 2014 requires the PSC to review each state generating unit’s “consumer economic dispatch” — operating generation facilities to produce electricity at the lowest cost while reliably meeting consumer demand.

But HB 2014 goes further, saying the PSC must require utilities to maintain generating units so as to be able to self-generate power and achieve at least a 69% capacity factor — a measure of how often a plant runs at full capacity.

Energy experts and ratepayer advocates have said a 69% capacity factor target set by the PSC for West Virginia’s coal-fired plants in recent years has encouraged uneconomic use of the plants that cost utility customers.

The PSC has contended that operating at higher capacity factors would lower costs recoverable from customers, encouraging self-generation over paying rising PJM market prices for purchased power.

The PSC followed up on HB 2014 by proposing that plants “are expected to take advantage of” an option under regional electricity grid operator PJM Transmission LLC to run at a fixed level of output regardless of economic dispatch in a process known as “self-scheduling,” potentially operating even when the cost of self-generating power exceeds how much it would cost to buy electricity from PJM’s market.

The PSC even proposed requiring that a utility that chooses not to self-schedule its generation capacity “during any day or portions of a day” explain why it made that decision, including the explanation in a monthly generation dispatch report.

The West Virginia Citizen Action Group, Solar United Neighbors, and Energy Efficient West Virginia, intervening as one party in the case, have predicted that the proposed rules building on HB 2014 would further drive up energy bills for customers by enticing utilities to operate their coal units more often without regard to market price.

The West Virginia-serving utilities for American Electric Power and FirstEnergy have objected even more strongly in case filings — so much so that they recommended meeting or presenting at workshops to explain why the proposed rules would be too cumbersome to implement.

During a public hearing the PSC held to take oral input on the proposed rulemaking at its Charleston headquarters Monday, Randy Feucht, FirstEnergy director of regulated commodity sourcing, called for deletion of language in the proposed rule that would require a utility that chooses not to self-schedule “all or any of its generation capacity during any day or portions of a day” to explain why it made that decision.

“[It should be deleted] because it assumes self-schedul[ing] is the norm and not economic dispatch, which is what we’ve done to lower our cost to our customers,” Feucht said.

Feucht also questioned proposed a rule provision that would require utilities to report actual or estimated impact on coal-fired unit maintenance costs and future equipment replacement attributable to “significant ramping of unit output throughout each 24-hour period.”

“We’re not exactly sure how to do that,” Feucht said. “We have experienced engineers throughout our company, and we’re not exactly sure we can do that.”

West Virginia has by far the nation’s highest reliance on coal-fired electricity, deriving 87% of its electricity generation from coal in 2025, per the EIA. The state’s electric power rates have swelled sharply in recent years, driven by escalating fuel costs to support the state’s aging coal plants and their declining, increasingly uneconomic production.

West Virginia ratepayers faced a 90% climb in average residential electricity retail prices from 2005 to 2020, per U.S. Energy Information Administration data. Only Michigan had a greater increase by percentage.

Energy Innovation LLC, a San Francisco-based climate policy firm, found in a 2023 study that 99% of the existing U.S. coal fleet was more expensive to run than it would be to replace it with new solar or wind.

Wear-and-tear-saddled coal plants have struggled to maintain reliability during weather emergencies and peak demand times as coal itself has become more expensive compared with alternative energy sources.

Between 2010 and 2023, the nation’s average unsubsidized costs of solar and wind electricity fell roughly 85% and 70% respectively, according to the United States Environmental Protection Agency. Renewable electricity surpassed coal for the first time in 2022.

West Virginia’s average monthly residential electric bill of $154.76 in 2024 was higher than all 12 other states in the PJM Interconnection LLC regional electric grid except Maryland, per U.S. Energy Information Administration data — 8.8% higher than the national average of $142.26.

Lani Wean, West Virginia field organizer for Moms Clean Air Force , a national environmental advocacy group, said at the PSC’s public hearing Monday that in the winter of 2025, her electric bill soared from $200-250 to $500 per month for her two-bedroom, centrally heated and cooled apartment.

“For context, I make under $50,000 a year, which should be enough money to live at least relatively comfortably in West Virginia, and I was unable to pay those bills,” Wean said.

The roughly 90-minute hearing featured United Mine Workers of America members who claimed continued coal reliance could control power costs, in addition to many non-UMWA critics of the proposed rule’s capacity factor oversight who urged less dependence on coal for the state’s power supply.

“The commission’s rules should not encourage plants to run when cheaper options are available,” Dani Parent, West Virginia Citizen Action Group executive director, said at the PSC hearing. “No single resource should receive special treatment, especially not if it costs customers more money.”

With a new path to lasting home energy upgrades available through West Virginia’s newly launched rebate programs, paying more for coal-fired electricity throughout the state is poised to last, too.

“The public should not carry unnecessary costs,” Wean said, “even more than we already do.”

Mike Tony covers energy and the environment. He can be reached at mtony@hdmediallc.com or 304-348-1236. Follow @Mike__Tony on X.

text:
Coventry Live readers have heard that revised plans for the former Coventry Airport site have been described as a 'pragmatic decision' to attract a wider range of businesses.

The original vision focused on a huge gigafactory producing batteries, mainly for electric vehicles. But Coventry City Council says the market has changed, with growing interest from smaller advanced manufacturing firms. The council is now preparing a new planning application for GreenPower Park, widening the types of businesses that could operate on the site.

Cllr Kindy Sandhu questioned whether bringing in smaller firms could eventually rule out a large gigafactory. Steve Weir, the council's interim director for economic growth, said the market had changed significantly over the past four or five years.

He said the new approach could allow smaller battery manufacturing operations, battery research and development facilities and other advanced manufacturing businesses to move onto the site, while still leaving the door open to a future gigafactory.

Cllr Lynnette Kelly, Cabinet Member for Jobs, Regeneration and Climate Change, said the council had taken a 'pragmatic decision' rather than leave the land empty while waiting for one large project that may never happen.

The council says the aim is to attract investment and create jobs while making better use of the site. Funding from the West Midlands Investment Zone will also be used to strengthen the power supply needed for industrial development.

The Cabinet has approved £1 million towards a new planning application, with GreenPower Park Ltd providing a further £1 million. The outline application is expected to be submitted in October, with a decision anticipated in May or June 2027.

Coventry City Council owns the 125 hectare site, which is leased to GreenPower Park Ltd, formerly Coventry Airport Ltd. Planning permission for a gigafactory was granted in 2022.

The revised proposals would retain the possibility of a large gigafactory while allowing other advanced manufacturing businesses to operate on the site.

Commenter Dave R suggests: “I know it seems outlandish, but how about using it as an airport? That could attract a wide range of businesses?”

Alan Baxter agrees: “Coventry could end up losing its airfield only to replace it with another Amazon warehouse. Surely there is a better long term use for the site, especially when there is already an opportunity to grow aviation MRO and engineering businesses there, bringing skilled jobs and investment while keeping the city’s aviation heritage alive.”

Mouse111 adds: “This is going to turn into a right fiasco. The decision to close Coventry Airport should never have happened. With the right investment, the airport could have boosted the local economy and created jobs, but instead we were sold fanciful ideas about a battery factory that never materialised.

“Just look at the UK EV market and the growing number of Chinese imports. JLR is struggling with weak sales and ongoing concerns over reliability. The whole situation looks like a complete mess and, frankly, an act of desperation.”

Noel L says: “Coventry City Council, please listen to what local people are saying and reconsider the future of the airport. Bringing back commercial flights with airlines such as TUI and Ryanair could create thousands of jobs, attract investment and put Coventry firmly on the map. It would also make economic sense to explore the airport's potential rather than lose it forever. Please reconsider before it is too late.”

Brian L thinks: “Typical Coventry Council, always seeming to pick the wrong option. A battery gigafactory was never going to happen. Drone technology has huge potential, and Coventry Airport could become a central UK hub for the industry, bringing investment, new businesses and plenty of skilled jobs to the area.”

Lynda P points out: “And all of this has created huge and completely unnecessary costs for the Air Ambulance, which has been forced to relocate as a result. Disgraceful.”

Paul M wonders: “How much council tax money has been wasted on ruining an existing business in the hope of creating something else? Why does Coventry Council always seem to want to get rid of the city’s major facilities? And when everything has been sold off, what will actually be left?”

text:
There's one thing Texans can all agree on: The traffic in the Lone Star State is no joke. As billions of dollars in highway construction projects inundate Central Texas and beyond, more alternative transportation modes are being proposed to relieve traffic congestion — including both high-speed rail and a vacuum tube-esqué underground tunnel system.

Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO turned both the world's richest person and a Texas resident, posted on social media in mid-September that The Boring Company is working to develop a "Hyperloop tunnel" linking Austin and San Antonio, with users traveling approximately 200 miles per hour and arriving at their destination in mere minutes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"Due to traffic congestion, that journey [between Austin and San Antonio] can currently take up to 2.5 hours," Musk wrote. "[The Boring Company] can reduce that to a consistent <30 mins."

Are there actually any Hyperloops in the world?

It's not the first time Musk has proposed a Hyperloop project in Texas or other states. The concept has been floated here in Texas for nearly a decade, with a testing facility constructed at The Boring Company's headquarters in the Austin suburb of Bastrop. To date, no commercial sized, full-scale intercity hyperloops are actively operating; the closest concept operating is the Vegas Loop, where Tesla electric vehicles drive passengers point to point underneath the Las Vegas Strip as opposed to between cities.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In Nashville, the Music City Loop is under construction, with crews continuing tunneling operations beneath Austin's pseudo-sister city, per an August project update. As opposed to linking communities, the Music City Loop is projected to operate as a 10-mile underground route connecting downtown Nashville with the Nashville International Airport.

How is a Hyperloop different than high-speed rail?

Hyperloops are conceptual systems where small passenger vehicles travel inside low-pressure vacuum tubes to various points, allowing those vehicles to reach higher speeds to cut down on travel times.

Meanwhile, high-speed rail is a concept that has been executed time and again in countries like Japan, China and various parts of Europe, featuring trains operating around 150 to 220 miles per hour.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In late 2025, Mexico President Claudia Sheinbaum announced the start of construction of a new passenger line rail from Saltillo, southwest of Monterrey, to Nuevo Laredo. That line is expected to reach between 99 and 124 miles per hour when its completed.

Where does Texas' high-speed rail proposal stand today?

Here in Texas, high-speed rail has been touted for years as a prospective investment that could cut down on travel times and diversify Texas transportation modes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The most prominent example of that is the Texas Central Railway, an approximately 240-mile rail line linking Houston and the Dallas and Fort Worth area. Proposed travel times are estimated at less than 90 minutes per trip, with departures expected every 30 minutes during peak travel periods.

However, in 2025, President Donald Trump's administration rescinded an almost $64 million federal grant for the project, with Amtrak departing from the project. Now, the project is dependent on private investment and handicapped by a lack of federal support.

text:
DETROIT (AP) — A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.

On Monday, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

About a fifth of the world’s oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.

The Transportation Department and NHTSA earlier this week lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.

The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles. Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.

Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.

When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: “This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”

Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed Monday’s change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.

But environmental organizations decried the changes.

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.

The DOT said Monday that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.

Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the U.S. These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits; scrapping vehicle emissions standards; repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules; and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout.

text:
HO CHI MINH CITY, Vietnam -- Danish jewelry company Pandora has opened the world's largest fine-jewelry crafting facility in Vietnam, a $150 million factory powered entirely by renewable electricity and using 100% recycled gold and silver.

The expansion highlights a broader challenge for the jewelry industry: reducing the environmental footprint of precious metals while meeting growing demand for jewelry. Using recycled gold and silver can reduce the need for newly mined metals, but experts say making that shift requires reliable supply chains and greater transparency.

The new facility in Ho Chi Minh City in southern Vietnam will produce up to 60 million pieces of jewelry a year, increasing the company's manufacturing capacity by 50% while cutting its carbon footprint by 17%, CEO Berta de Pablos-Barbier told The Associated Press.

"We are leading the way and we really hope that the rest follow," she said.

Pandora expands in Vietnam as manufacturers seek clean power

After 37 years in Thailand, Pandora wanted to expand its manufacturing base to increase flexibility and strengthen supply-chain resilience, Pablos-Barbier said.

She said that it chose Vietnam for its skilled artisans who can meet Pandora's standards for craftsmanship, its business environment and its strong infrastructure.

Access to renewable energy infrastructure to power factories is increasingly an "important factor" for Pandora and other Danish companies, Lina Gandlose Hansen, Denmark's ambassador to Vietnam, said.

Pandora's Vietnam facility, with 7,000 workers, will be powered entirely by renewable electricity from the sun and wind, with solar panels installed on its rooftops and plans to work with local solar farms, the company said.

It is also across the road from the $1 billion factory that toymaker Lego opened in 2025, where it says it makes toys without adding planet-warming gases to the atmosphere.

Vietnam has rapidly expanded renewable energy and had Southeast Asia's largest installed solar and wind capacity at the end of 2024. But the country still relies heavily on coal to power its fast-growing economy, making it important for manufacturers to shift toward cleaner electricity as Vietnam works toward net-zero emissions by 2050.

Manufacturing makes up a fifth of Vietnam's GDP and consumes half the energy it uses. There are plans to phase out its coal power plants by 2040.

Using recycled gold and silver

Pandora's commitment to using recycled gold and silver was a "big deal," said Saleem H. Ali, who leads the program on critical minerals and inclusive energy transitions at the United Nations University.

He said gold is especially easy to recycle and unlike metals such as copper, it does not break down or rust. Silver can also be recycled, although it can tarnish and needs to be cleaned.

"That is why it is so valuable. We still have gold from the ancient Egyptians, in pretty good shape," he said.

The Danish company switched to using 100% recycled silver and gold for new jewelry in August 2024.

Its factories receive small grains of refined metal from recyclers in Europe and Asia, sourced from items ranging from medical equipment to old cutlery, said Pandora's chief sustainability officer Mads Twomey-Madsen.

It also means finding suppliers, smelters or refiners that use only recycled material. There's also a risk that some could add newly mined material into the mix, Ali said. "That involves a lot of auditing."

Pandora began changing its wider supply chain five years ago by adopting standards set by the Responsible Jewellery Council, an industry group that promotes responsible practices including on human rights, workers' rights and environmental impacts, Twomey-Madsen said. The company uses independent auditors, he said.

He said the ultimate goal is for the entire supply chain, including the energy-intensive process of heating and separating metals from other materials to remove impurities, to be powered by clean energy.

Other challenges include urban mining and tracing gold

Recovering valuable metals from discarded products and other waste is a challenge, Twomey-Madsen said.

The world is producing more e-waste than ever -- 62 million metric tons in 2022, projected to grow to 82 million metric tons by 2030, according to a report by the United Nations' International Telecommunications Union and research arm UNITAR. Much of this is processed informally, where workers can be exposed to toxic substances while recovering valuable metals such as gold and silver.

More than 1,000 harmful substances have been found in e-waste or produced when it is improperly recycled, including lead, mercury, cadmium and other toxic chemicals, according to the World Health Organization.

Ali, the critical minerals expert, said that artisanal gold mining -- when individuals or small groups extract gold using simple tools -- was now the largest cause of mercury pollution worldwide. Miners in poor countries may use the toxic metal to separate gold from other materials, harming people and the environment.

He said there have been efforts to improve gold sourcing, but tracing gold remains difficult. South Asia, in particular, has high demand for gold and jewelry sellers often don't ask where their gold comes from.

"Once it gets melted, it's very hard to track it," he said.

Twomey-Madsen said that the company hopes its commitment to buying recycled metals will show suppliers that there is a growing market for the materials. He added that Pandora initially paid a premium for recycled gold and silver, absorbing the higher cost and investing with suppliers to build a more reliable supply chain for the materials.

Making jewelry is far less emissions-intensive than sectors such as aviation or cement. But he said a switch by the entire industry switching to recycled gold and silver could prevent about 58 million metric tons (63.9 million U.S. tons) of carbon dioxide from entering the atmosphere each year.

"That is comparable to the entire emissions of New York City," he said.

title: The Supreme Court will hear a major climate change case involving a devastating Colorado wildfire
authors: LINDSAY WHITEHURST, BRITTANY PETERSON, Associated Press

text:
LOUISVILLE, Colo. (AP) — Less than an hour after the first warning that a wildfire was headed for her suburban street, Tawnya Somauroo’s Colorado home was in ashes.

She has worked tirelessly for nearly five years to rebuild her house and help ensure her neighborhood can withstand the next blaze. But as climate change contributes to more frequent wildfires, she worries that the careful landscaping, metal fencing and flame-resistant siding are not enough.

“We lost our homes and they left us to figure out for ourselves how to make our neighborhoods safe again,” Somauroo said. “At the end of the day, it comes out of our pockets, you know? And it does feel like maybe the oil and gas industry should have a part in this.”

She lives in Boulder County, one of dozens of jurisdictions across the United States suing oil and gas companies to help pay for damage from disasters linked to climate change.

The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation across the country and the world, with billions of dollars at stake. On Monday, the first day of the Supreme Court’s new term, the justices will hear the Boulder case that could decide the fate of others like it.

The city and county of Boulder first sued two oil companies in 2018, years before the fire. They argued that Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil had violated state law by deceiving the public about their contributions to climate change and sought unspecified damages to help cover the cost of worsening disasters.

The companies say that a flood of lawsuits in state courts is not the way to deal with the global issue.

“The problem is that climate change is caused by pretty much everybody living on earth,” said Phil Goldberg, special counsel for the Manufacturers’ Accountability Project, an industry group. “We need to figure out how to address that. We need to address it in a very meaningful way. This litigation doesn’t do that.”

The companies have the backing of the Trump administration. Federal government attorneys say the lawsuits are a backdoor way to regulate heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions and amount to an unconstitutional power grab.

“No one state can superimpose its own regulatory preferences on the rest — least of all to address a global problem that exists almost entirely outside its borders and affects the world at large,” they wrote.

The Clean Air Act, they say, allows the federal government, rather than states, to regulate emissions. The Republican administration has largely used that power to roll back environmental regulations.

Last month, the Environmental Protection Agency ceded some of its climate authority by repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The move could complicate its argument.

Boulder says it is not trying to regulate emissions beyond its borders, only holding companies accountable for local costs.

“Boulder County and city aren’t trying to change what’s happening in Texas or New York, they’re trying to get compensation for things happening now in Colorado,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice, which filed an amicus brief in the case.

Climate change was considered a factor in the 2021 Marshall Fire that destroyed Somauroo’s home, after the county’s suit was originally filed. The total damage was estimated at $2 billion. It was the costliest wildfire in Colorado history.

“Local county municipal governments play a very important role in helping front line communities adapt to climate change. This case could very well set a precedent,” said Chris Winter, executive director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center, an environmental research group in Colorado.

The case will come before a conservative-majority Supreme Court where environmental regulations have not always fared well, including a 2022 decision that limited the EPA’s authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions from power plants.

Only eight of the nine justices will be on the bench, though. Justice Samuel Alito recused himself just a week before arguments after facing calls to step aside because he owns stock in oil companies.

That creates the possibility of a tie vote in the case, though it’s unclear how likely that might be. The court is also weighing a question that experts say is a potential “off-ramp”: whether the justices have jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage.

Whitehurst reported from Washington.

title: How Democrats Can Rein in the High Cost of Energy | Opinion - Newsweek
description:
It should start with embracing an all-of-the-above energy strategy that pairs natural gas and renewables to reduce monthly utility bills.
Read More on Opinion For far too long, Democrats have treated natural gas and renewables as competitors, not partners.
Natural gas remains essential to a reliable and affordable grid, especially as demand keeps rising.
Voters care most about lower energy costs and dependable service, and they reward practical leaders who take a pragmatic path instead of an ideological fight over energy sources.
We know from experience how an all‑of‑the‑above energy policy can benefit our economy.
text:
Every time conflict flares in the Middle East, families in the Commonwealth and across the nation feel it within days. Oil markets swing and pump prices climb. That’s especially true in Virginia, where a recent report found that families have paid $573 more for gas since the start of the war with Iran in February. While Democrats can’t control what happens in the Strait of Hormuz or the president’s chaotic approach to foreign policy, we can champion steps—particularly at the state level—to lower the cost of energy bills.

In states like New York and Virginia, leaders in the General Assembly and the governor’s mansion modeled an approach that Democrats everywhere should embrace, focusing intently on lowering the cost of living and making it easier for families to get by. But there’s much more work to do. It should start with embracing an all-of-the-above energy strategy that pairs natural gas and renewables to reduce monthly utility bills.

Read More on Opinion

For far too long, Democrats have treated natural gas and renewables as competitors, not partners. This positioning has hampered our electoral prospects and failed to lower electricity costs. But if we marry these energy sources together—and take concrete steps to change state-level policies that encourage the union—we can seize tremendous political and economic upsides. Natural gas remains essential to a reliable and affordable grid, especially as demand keeps rising. Renewables provide a long‑term hedge against volatility and are indispensable to building a cleaner energy future. Together, they give communities something neither can deliver alone: affordability, reliability, and stability.

This approach is widely popular. Recent polling around the country shows that strong majorities of voters support an all-of-the-above energy strategy that combines renewables with natural gas when the focus is on affordability and reliability. Voters care most about lower energy costs and dependable service, and they reward practical leaders who take a pragmatic path instead of an ideological fight over energy sources.

This blend of good policy and even better politics can benefit Democrats handsomely in November and beyond. Candidates who can look voters in the eye and say, “I have a plan to lower your bills and keep your power on—and it uses every tool we’ve got,” will meet people’s needs. They’ll also draw a clear contrast with Republicans, who talk a big game about energy dominance, but often implement fragmented policies that increase prices. Voters aren’t asking for perfection; they’re asking for a plan that feels real, lowers their monthly bills, and uses abundant American energy to keep costs down.

We know from experience how an all‑of‑the‑above energy policy can benefit our economy. During his time in Congress, Ryan was a staunch advocate for balanced energy initiatives, helping to establish major energy projects, including two natural gas power plants, the North American Electric Vehicle Hub, and the Ultima Battery Plant.

During her 18 years in the Senate, Landrieu, chaired the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, taking an inclusive approach to energy policy that ranged from expanding domestic energy production to advancing coastal restoration legislation. I fought hard for the priorities of my constituents and for the policies that would drive long-term economic growth in my state. That same practical approach can help Democratic governors, state legislators, and candidates running for U.S. House and Senate seats across the country win big on Election Day.

We can achieve this balancing act by pairing clean energy investments, efficiency and weatherization upgrades, and our nation’s unparalleled natural gas infrastructure to help families see real savings at the end of every month. And while we’re at it, we should put affordability and reliability at the center of our message, showing voters that we hear them and have a way forward.

Let’s show voters that we can shield them from the high prices stemming from the president’s ill-advised forays overseas and embrace an all‑of‑the‑above energy strategy to help lower costs. If Democrats lead with this approach, we can win the day.

Tim Ryan represented Ohio in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2003 to 2023. He currently co-chairs Natural Allies for a Clean Energy Future.

Mary Landrieu served as a Democratic senator from Louisiana from 1997 to 2015. She currently co-chairs Natural Allies for a Clean Energy Future.

The views expressed in this article are the writers' own.

title: Jobs, tax benefits and backlash: Report sheds light on data centers in Illinois
authors: Maggie Dougherty and Ben Szalinski, Capitol News Illinois
description:
Data centers and property taxes There are already more than 240 planned or active data centers in Illinois, or 19 per 1 million residents.
One of the report's recommendations was to ban local property tax breaks so data centers help reduce local tax burdens by a greater amount.
The report also found data centers would create 41,751 consumer-demand-induced jobs over the next decade throughout the economy.
Elmo questioned whether the growth of data centers will continue to be robust given the public backlash and likelihood they will face more regulations.
Read more: Data centers emerging as key issue in Illinois governor's race | POWER Act: Lawmakers seek to regulate new data centers' power, water usage The report also proposed limiting the incentives the state gives to data center developers.
text:
A new study predicts data centers expected to be built in Illinois over the next decade would create thousands of jobs and millions of dollars in new property tax revenue.

But many are skeptical the touted benefits will live up to their promises or outweigh the environmental and energy burdens.

The study by the Illinois Economic Policy Institute projected that $57 billion worth of new data center investments through 2035 will create 121,000 jobs. Most of those would be temporary construction and other jobs throughout the economy, with just 2,800 of them direct, permanent positions.

After lawmakers failed to pass data center regulations in the spring session and Gov. JB Pritzker paused the state's data center tax incentive program, a comprehensive study was needed to help guide policymakers on how to address residents' concerns, according to Frank Manzo, an economist at ILEPI, a labor-backed research organization that "promotes thoughtful economic growth for businesses and working families."

"There's currently a trust deficit amongst the public, and Illinois can ensure responsible development of data centers to address that deficit, and we've come up with possible ways to do that," Manzo said.

Recognizing the growing public distrust of data centers and concerns over their heavy water and energy consumption, the report put forth 10 policy proposals that it says could protect residents while preserving the state's competitive position to attract data center development. Many were in line with a policy plan that stalled in Springfield in the spring, aiming to put guardrails on an industry while still promoting economic development.

"A moratorium sends investment to neighboring states," Manzo said, adding that clear standards and guardrails "give developers certainty and can protect ratepayers."

The Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity estimated that, as of 2025, data centers received an estimated tax break value that exceeded $660 million.

Data centers and property taxes

There are already more than 240 planned or active data centers in Illinois, or 19 per 1 million residents.

The report found that data centers would also supply nearly $300 million in annual property tax revenue once operational, allowing local governments to reduce property taxes for residents by 3-10% if no tax abatements are offered.

Manzo said the impact of a data center on local property taxes would depend on its size, with larger ones eating more of the bill. He said the impact could also be especially strong in more rural and small counties, such as DeKalb.

The report shows that in 2024 while the tech company Meta paid $31 million in property taxes on their new data center in the county, average property taxes in DeKalb County increased by about 2% compared to 6% on average across the state.

"Every local community has to have their own voice and their own will expressed in these," Robert Bruno, a University of Illinois professor who coauthored the report with ILEPI, said in an interview. "But as a possible source of revenue that could achieve a lot of good, it's sizeable and it is a pretty reliable collective source of revenue for schools."

But the city also reduced the property taxes paid on the sprawling Meta data center, lessening what the impact could have been for homeowners, according to Kristan Wong Karinen, a researcher at Good Jobs First, a national policy organization that advocates against corporate subsidies.

"Abating the taxes doesn't help you at all," she said, pointing to Illinois' law limiting how much local governments can raise property taxes in a single year. "It just hurts any kind of gain you could have had from it."

One of the report's recommendations was to ban local property tax breaks so data centers help reduce local tax burdens by a greater amount.

Jobs created would be mostly temporary

Most data centers don't employ many people after they are built. With 2,800 permanent positions expected to be created by the total $57 billion investment, data center developers are collectively spending $20.2 million per permanent job.

"If this were completely private money, it would be a different story," Anthony Elmo, another Good Jobs First researcher, said. "These taxpayer dollars need to actually incentivize good long-term jobs and they're not."

Illinois Economic Policy Institute researchers said many of the jobs created by the data center projects pay well, including six-figure construction jobs. Thirteen projects in 2020 and 2021 created 8,000 construction jobs with wages over $100,000, according to the report.

The report also found data centers would create 41,751 consumer-demand-induced jobs over the next decade throughout the economy. These are jobs that range from local restaurant workers to factory jobs at places that manufacture construction materials.

Elmo questioned whether the growth of data centers will continue to be robust given the public backlash and likelihood they will face more regulations.

But Manzo said the counter argument is that these jobs could go to a different state - something Elmo said could happen anyway as technology progresses.

"As they are able to build their technology and build their ability to run data centers remotely and without permanent positions, how many of those permanent position will go away?" Elmo said.

Energy implications

The report acknowledges that a tradeoff for those job and property tax benefits is the increasing cost of energy driven by power-hungry, always-on data centers. The authors estimate the impact to average residential bills would be around an extra $12 per month, or $150 a year.

The report's estimate was based on what researchers called a mid-level scenario, in which new data centers would add 6.5 gigawatts of energy demand to Illinois' grid by 2035 - enough to power millions of homes.

That scenario, researchers said, would increase electric system costs overall by almost 10%. Other projections estimate the impact will be much higher.

Data from PJM, the regional transmission organization that manages energy flows in northeastern Illinois, forecasts that electricity demand from data centers will grow by 10.7 GW by 2035 in ComEd's territory alone, though all projects are not guaranteed to come online.

The rest of the state is on the MISO grid, which is expected to see peak demand increase by 35% by 2035 across the 15 states in its territory, driven largely by data center development in states like Illinois, Indiana and Michigan.

Analysis conducted by the National Resource Defense Council last year predicted that average families in the PJM territory would see prices increase by as much as $70 per month by 2028.

Rising electricity costs don't just affect residential bills but can also hurt businesses, Citizens Utility Board spokesperson Jim Chilsen said, as consumers have less disposable income.

"One thing that's horrible for the economy is high electric bills, because when consumers are pouring all their money into escalating electric bills, they don't have money to use to spark the economy in other places," he said.

Policy recommendations

Many of the proposed policy recommendations are in line with the POWER Act, a bill that would have made data centers secure their own renewable energy supply and required water-use permits and transparency reporting, among other provisions.

The report also recommended a statewide ban on nondisclosure agreements with developers because they harm trust with the public, who are often left asking questions about data center projects that can't be answered because of the agreements. The POWER Act would also ban such agreements.

Lawmakers didn't pass the POWER Act in the spring legislative session, but advocates are optimistic the bill will advance during the fall veto session. Pritzker, who advocates criticized for a lack of engagement on the issue last spring, called on lawmakers to act last week.

Read more: Data centers emerging as key issue in Illinois governor's race | POWER Act: Lawmakers seek to regulate new data centers' power, water usage

The report also proposed limiting the incentives the state gives to data center developers. Researchers suggested raising the investment threshold and number of jobs that a data center creates to qualify for a state tax break, while also reducing the number of years the incentive lasts.

Christine Nannicelli oversees renewable energy policy at the Sierra Club of Illinois, which has advocated for stronger data center regulations. She said Illinois needs to prioritize rigorous standards, not just incentives for companies that choose to bring their own renewable energy and create jobs.

"The rubber hits the road when we talk about, are we incentivizing good behavior or are we going to require good behavior?" Nannicelli said. "This isn't about offering fluffy tax incentives to do the right thing. We need to really raise the bar for this industry as a whole."

text:
The Trump administration has officially dismantled years of Biden-era clean energy policy, gutting 2031 fuel economy targets from 50 mpg down to 35 mpg. By killing EV incentives and state emissions rules to bail out legacy Detroit automakers, regulators are locking American drivers into burning expensive gas while rendering the domestic auto industry globally obsolete.

Instead of competing with the rest of the world, Detroit just bought itself a political bailout. In a single sweeping move, the Trump administration systematically dismantled years of Biden-era climate and industrial policy, gutting federal fuel economy standards to ensure legacy automakers never have to catch up to global EV benchmarks.

According to reporting from the Associated Press, regulators took the Biden administration’s projected 2031 fleetwide efficiency target of 50.4 miles per gallon and aggressively hacked it down to 34.9 mpg—slashing standards below requirements set a full decade ago.

It completes a total scorched-earth campaign against clean transportation, stacking directly on top of Trump’s repeal of $7,500 consumer EV tax credits, the elimination of non-compliance fines for car manufacturers, and the revocation of California’s historic legal waiver to enforce its own tailpipe emissions rules.

The $4.47 per gallon bailout

The Department of Transportation tried to package this regulatory surrender as a gift to American consumers, claiming lower manufacturing hurdles will shave $1,300 off the average sticker price of a new car. That spin collapses the second you pull up to a gas pump.

The administration finalized the rollback on the exact day national gasoline prices spiked to $4.47 a gallon, driven by escalating military conflict in the Middle East and threats to the Strait of Hormuz.

While Biden’s fuel efficiency rules were projected to save American drivers 14 billion gallons of gas by 2050—easily offsetting initial vehicle costs through lifetime fuel savings—Trump’s rules actively lock consumers into burning expensive fuel in dirtier cars.

Environmental groups estimate this rollback will pump an additional 22,000 tons of carbon dioxide, nearly 5,000 tons of smog-forming compounds, and 90 tons of deadly soot into the air every single year by 2035.

Decades of hard-won public health and climate progress were wiped out overnight so Detroit can protect its short-term profit margins on gas-guzzling trucks.

The protectionist suicide pact

Predictably, Big Auto couldn’t celebrate fast enough. Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis—speaking through the Alliance for Automotive Innovation—praised the Trump administration for aligning federal rules with “market realities” and preserving consumer choice.

As an analysis from InsideEVs points out, that “market reality” is a pure fiction crafted behind protective walls.

In China, relentless domestic competition and rapid battery iteration have pushed New Energy Vehicles to a staggering 60% of all passenger car sales. In Europe, pure battery-electric cars now comfortably outsell traditional gas and diesel models. The rest of the world has already moved on.

While foreign automakers refine high-efficiency electric platforms for global dominance, American manufacturers are using Trump’s regulatory bailout to retool factories for heavy V-8 SUVs.

Shielded by 100% import tariffs that keep cheap, high-tech foreign EVs out of domestic dealerships, U.S. legacy brands are trading their long-term survival for immediate cash flow. Detroit didn’t just lose the electric vehicle race—it lobbied Washington to dynamite the track.

name: American Energy
title: An 850-megawatt battery on the site of a demolished coal plant is now cleared to run flat out ...
description:
Waratah’s a different animal from your average grid battery.
New South Wales runs its big transmission lines harder than they could safely run on their own, because this battery sits ready beside them.
The state government says the battery can carry up to 340,000 New South Wales homes at peak demand at maximum output.
Akaysha’s thank-you list ran five companies deep: Consolidated Power Projects Australia, Hitachi Energy, Wilson Transformer Company, REPT Battero, and EVE Energy.
The New South Wales government ordered the project up, and Akaysha built it, owns it, and runs it.
text:
You might remember this one if you’re into powerful, big batteries. Back in mid-September, we covered an 850-megawatt battery in Australia running its first full-power tests, holding 700 megawatts on the grid in New South Wales for two straight hours and then pulling nearly 850 megawatts back out. At the time, the tests hadn’t been verified yet, so the full contract couldn’t start.

Well, the tests apparently passed. On September 28th, Akaysha Energy declared the Waratah Super Battery at final commercial operations, and the state’s energy minister confirmed the same day that the Australian Energy Market Operator had cleared it to run at full capacity.

That’s 850 megawatts of output and 1,680 megawatt-hours in storage, built where a demolished coal plant used to stand north of Sydney, now fully on the clock 11 months and 10 days after a transformer failure cut its guaranteed service in half. This thing was supposed to be doing its job by late 2025. But there’s no time to dwell on that delay: Australia’s biggest battery is done practicing.

So what actually changed on September 28?

It took surprisingly less than you’d assume to get to this point. The hardware already proved itself during those September tests, and the battery had been running in a reduced state since August 2025.

What’s actually changed is the paperwork. AEMO signed off on full-capacity operation, and “final commercial operations” is corporate-speak for “the whole machine now counts.” I call it corporate speak for “we just wasted a year.” But again, I digress…

After the year this project’s had, I’d argue that’s the only milestone that matters. One of its three high-voltage transformers failed catastrophically in October 2025, a second came down damaged next to it, and the replacement had to be rebuilt from scratch. We went through that saga in the September piece, so I won’t drag you back through it.

Akaysha CEO Nick Carter called it “a landmark moment for Akaysha Energy, our project partners and most importantly, for NSW.” Which is standard CEO phrasing, but I’ll forgive the man during this little moment of celebration.

So why does a grid need a shock absorber?

Waratah’s a different animal from your average grid battery. It doesn’t mainly buy cheap solar at noon and sell it back at dinner. New South Wales runs its big transmission lines harder than they could safely run on their own, because this battery sits ready beside them. When a line drops out, the control system dumps the battery’s output into the network while paired generators wind down, so the stressed wires never see the surge.

Hitachi Energy, which supplied the project’s 288 power conversion systems and the two plant controllers running the show, says the setup detects a grid disturbance within milliseconds and tells the battery to respond. Hitachi’s Australian boss, Bernard Norton, calls the whole arrangement “a giant digital shock absorber,” and honestly, I can’t improve on that. Hitachi also signed on to service and monitor the electronics for 20 years, so someone’s going to be watching this battery’s vitals into the 2040s.

The state government says the battery can carry up to 340,000 New South Wales homes at peak demand at maximum output. But this differs from Akaysha’s own math from September, which boasted 970,000 homes for a single hour. These figures don’t exactly line up, although it’s tough to really make sense of it since they are using different time measurements. Treat both as a ballpark, I guess. The undisputed number here is the megawatts.

A billion dollars and 170 people at the peak

Akaysha says the project attracted more than $1 billion in private investment. That’s in Australian dollars, which is about $700 million for those of us in the U.S. And that’s still a serious check for a field of containers on an old coal site.

About 1,000 people worked across design and construction, with 170 on site at the peak of the build. Akaysha’s thank-you list ran five companies deep: Consolidated Power Projects Australia, Hitachi Energy, Wilson Transformer Company, REPT Battero, and EVE Energy. The New South Wales government ordered the project up, and Akaysha built it, owns it, and runs it.

Does a clear battery change anything for you if you live in Phoenix or Houston? Eh, not directly. But the trick it pulls off here, renting a fast battery so existing wires can run closer to their limits instead of waiting a decade for new transmission, is one that US grid operators are going to keep borrowing. Australia keeps building the test cases, like the pumped hydro cavern it’s digging half a mile inside a mountain, and the rest of us get to watch what works.

Akaysha dated the final commercial operations on September 28, 2026, and Hitachi’s monitoring contract on the site runs for the next 20 years.

title: Pennsylvania is building more EV chargers. Will drivers come? - Mon Valley Independent
description:

Even in Pennsylvania, where EV adoption is lagging, as the state ranks just 29th in electric vehicle ownership per capita.

That’s closing in on the 10-per-day mark that Brown says is a typical break-even point for a charging station.
