Martin’s company has tried to adapt by seeking work in the aerospace and defense sectors.

“If you let that manufacturing go away … it’s going to be really hard to build the momentum and start that back up again,” he said.

Attorney General Charity Clark today joined a coalition of 25 states, counties, and cities suing the Trump administration for dismantling federal greenhouse gas pollution limits for many of the nation’s largest power plants. In September, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) repealed the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, safeguards that required coal- and gas-fired power plants to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. The repeal clears the way for a significant increase in pollution that will worsen extreme heat, deadly storms, flooding, and wildfire smoke. Attorney General Clark and the coalition filed a petition for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, asking the court to strike down the repeal and restore these protections. The coalition is also notifying EPA of its intent to sue over the agency’s continued failure to fully regulate pollution from existing natural gas power plants.

"The Trump Administration’s continued attempts to dismantle environmental protections are an affront to the State we call home,” said Attorney General Clark. “We will continue to advocate for these critical protections to mitigate the dangerous and irreversible damage that happens when we fail to regulate and enforce pollution limits.”

Power plants are among the largest drivers of the climate crisis, producing roughly one-quarter of the nation’s carbon dioxide emissions. Rather than address this pollution, the federal administration erased federal pollution limits for most gas- and coal-fired power plants and introduced a proposal to eliminate power plant emission regulation entirely.

Eliminating limits on these emissions threatens communities across the country. More climate pollution contributes to more frequent and intense heat waves that put children, older adults, and workers at risk. It also contributes to stronger storms and heavier flooding that damage homes, businesses, and transit systems, as well as more wildfire smoke that makes air dangerous to breathe. Increased pollution from fossil fuel power plants can worsen asthma, heart disease, and other serious respiratory illnesses, especially in low-income and other overburdened communities. These changes also increase the financial burden on local and state governments that must respond to increasingly extreme weather.

In addition, Attorney General Clark and the coalition today filed a notice of intent to sue EPA over the agency’s continued failure to regulate greenhouse gas pollution from many existing gas-fired power plants. Those facilities, including “peaker” plants that often operate during periods of high electricity demand, are frequently located in low-income communities and communities of color that already bear a disproportionate share of pollution. Despite issuing standards for new gas plants over a decade ago, EPA has never fulfilled its legal obligation to limit pollution from existing gas plants. By delaying these protections for years, EPA has left many frontline communities without the safeguards required by the Clean Air Act.

Joining Attorney General Clark in filing today’s lawsuit are the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the Governor of Pennsylvania, the Mayors of New York City and Chicago, and the City and County of Denver.

text:
Oct. 2, 2026 (DENVER) – Attorney General Phil Weiser today joined a coalition of 27 states, counties, and cities in filing a lawsuit against the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration challenging its final rule weakening corporate average fuel economy standards for new passenger cars and light trucks.

Historically, NHTSA’s standards have reduced consumer costs by improving fuel efficiency for vehicles, placed downward pressure on gas prices by reducing fuel consumption, protected the U.S. economy from global oil shocks, and reduced pollution from tailpipes and refineries. However, the final rule significantly weakens fuel economy standards and hurts consumers and the environment. In the lawsuit filed today in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, the coalition alleges that the new rule is contrary to law and that NHTSA is violating its mandate from Congress to set fuel-economy standards at their “maximum feasible” level.

“The federal government’s backsliding on standards for the next five years requires less fuel economy than what the U.S. fleet of new cars and trucks achieved in 2021. Rolling back fuel efficiency standards will cost Coloradans even more at the gas pump, harm public health, and undermine our nation’s position in the EV market. These clean car rules are part of our clean energy future and that’s why we are challenging this illegal action,” said Attorney General Weiser.

In 1975, Congress enacted the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which requires NHTSA to establish “maximum feasible” fuel economy standards for new vehicles that reflect technological feasibility, economic practicability, the effect of other motor vehicle standards of the government, and the need to conserve energy. In past rulemakings, including during the first Trump administration, NHTSA started from a baseline fleet that included the millions of electric vehicles that already existed on our nation’s highways and roads and based fuel-economy standards on how additional technological improvements to gas-fueled cars could make that fleet more efficient. NHTSA never based fuel-economy standards on mandating automakers to produce more electric vehicles or requiring consumers to buy them.

The final rule ignores the presence of millions of electric vehicles in the nation’s existing fleet, leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the maximum feasible fuel economy level that the auto industry can achieve. NHTSA’s novel reinterpretation of the law essentially renders the federal fuel-economy program toothless, unable to protect consumers against rising gas prices or ongoing global oil market shocks.

NHTSA has also utilized defective analyses of vehicle affordability and sales, fleet turnover, fuel savings, and vehicle safety to make a harmful and destructive rule look net-beneficial to society. For example, NHTSA tries to paper over nearly $220 billion in lost fuel savings — money that drivers would have saved at the pump under the previous fuel economy standards. It also refuses to consider hundreds of billions of dollars in future damages from climate change-driven disasters, disregarding the best science and research and effectively setting these costs at zero. Defying a longstanding and repeatedly affirmed congressional mandate, NHTSA claims that the U.S. does not need to conserve energy after all. Finally, NHTSA’s rule will end the CAFE credit trading program in 2028, which will significantly harm electric vehicle industries that employ Americans and support the economy.

In today’s lawsuit, the coalition alleges that NHTSA’s final rule is arbitrary and capricious and violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Energy Policy and Conservation Act.

In filing this lawsuit, Attorney General Weiser joins the attorneys general of California, Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai‘i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the City of Chicago, the City and County of Denver, the City of New York, and the City and County of San Francisco.

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Reps. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) and Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), and Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), member of the Environment and Public Works Committee, today announced the reintroduction of the Fossil Free Finance Act. The legislation would require banks to adopt emission transition plans to reduce financial sector emissions and deforestation risks.

Under this legislation, large bank holding companies would be required to implement plans to reduce financial sector emissions 50 percent by 2035 and reach zero financial sector emissions by 2050. Additionally, it would require banks to discontinue financing for new or expanded fossil fuel projects within 60 days of enactment, immediately discontinue thermal coal financing and facilitation, and eliminate facilitation of deforestation risk commodities. Despite climate-driven wildfires, floods, and other disasters continuing to devastate regions across the country, banks continue to invest in contributing fossil fuel projects. Plans created from this legislation will help the financial sector align with science-based projections for emissions.

“Our financial institutions and banks are funding the pollution of our air and water that make us sicker. They choose to invest billions of dollars in dirty fossil fuel projects,” said Rep. Tlaib. “Instead of acting to protect us, the Federal Reserve allowed these banks to finance the destruction of our planet and our health. I’m taking action with Senator Markey and Congresswoman Pressley to require the Federal Reserve to finally do something and address the dangers of our climate crisis.”

“Our economy and global financial systems have a codependent relationship with the fossil fuel industry. We cannot wait for big banks to address the very climate crisis they are financing if we are serious about reducing greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation. It’s like giving an arsonist a hose for one hand while they hold a gas can in the other,” said Senator Markey. “The Fossil Free Finance Act would require our financial institutions, including banks, to protect Americans’ savings, investments, and our economy by addressing the threats posed by climate change. We need to put the planet over profit and get fossil fuels out of our finances.”

“We should be using every tool available to protect our planet, our people, and our economy, and one way we can do that is by stopping giant banks from financing fossil fuel projects,” said Rep. Pressley. “Our Fossil Free Finance Act would help confront the climate crisis by stopping financial institutions, including our nation’s largest banks, from providing trillions in fossil fuel financing and deepening the health inequities and harms that already plague our communities. I’m grateful to Senator Markey and Congresswoman Tlaib for their ongoing partnership on this bill to take urgent action to help prevent a massive, climate-induced economic collapse.”

“Major US banks’ ongoing finance for fossil fuel expansion is driving worsening climate change and putting the entire financial system and public at risk,” said Alex Martin, Climate Finance Policy Director at Americans for Financial Reform. “The Fossil Free Finance Act would recognize the role that fossil fuel finance plays in driving climate-related financial risk, and require banks to develop climate action plans that address those risks, creating a critical safeguard for the public and the financial system.”

“While financial policymakers around the world actively work to decarbonize their economies, U.S. policymakers have fallen behind, leaving our financial system exposed to the impacts of climate change,” said David Arkush, Director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program. “Financial institutions continue to finance, invest, and underwrite unnecessary projects—creating systemic risks that can reverberate across the economy. Rather than continuing to create risks for the financial system, large and systemically important financial institutions should be required to reduce their financed and facilitated emissions in line with science-driven targets. Neither Congress nor the Federal Reserve should wait for a financial crisis to address climate-related financial risk.”

The Fossil Free Finance Act of 2026 would address climate-related threats to financial stability and help align the financial sector with science-based emissions targets by redefining financial sector emissions, mandating bank holding companies with at least $50 billion in assets to align with science-based emissions targets, and requiring the Federal Reserve to report to Congress on financial sector emissions, commitments by covered institutions, progress toward emissions targets, regulatory gaps, data challenges, and equitable transition needs.

The Fossil Free Finance Act of 2026 is cosponsored by Senators Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).

The legislation is endorsed by Public Citizen and Americans for Financial Reform.

Senator Markey, and Reps. Tlaib, Pressley, and former Rep. Mondaire Jones (NY-17) first introduced the Fossil Free Finance Act during the 117th Congress in September 2021. Senator Markey first reintroduced the legislation with Senator Merkley in March 2023.

text:
DETROIT — A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.

On Monday, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.

The Transportation Department and NHTSA earlier this week lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.

The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles. Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.

Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.

When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: "This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”

Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed Monday's change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.

But environmental organizations decried the changes.

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.

The DOT said Monday that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.

Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the U.S. These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits; scrapping vehicle emissions standards; repealing the fines for automakers who don't meet mileage rules; and attempting to block the nation's EV charging buildout.

text:
Alibaba Group Holding has held preliminary talks with Spanish clean-energy company Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente about supplying power for a data center in Spain, according to Bloomberg.

The Solaria installation being considered sits in Puertollano, a city approximately 240 kilometers from Madrid, Bloomberg reported, citing people who declined to be identified. These conversations remain less advanced than the data center commitments Alibaba has publicly disclosed in other European countries, and Alibaba has also approached additional energy providers about the project. Spokespeople for both Alibaba and Solaria declined to comment.

The talks are part of a broader push by Alibaba into European digital infrastructure. Last week, Alibaba announced plans to establish its first cloud regions in Finland and the Netherlands within 12 months, while also expanding its data center presence in Germany and France. The moves put Alibaba in more direct competition with cloud providers including Amazon $AMZN and Microsoft $MSFT.

Alibaba has been investing heavily in artificial intelligence infrastructure. In 2025, the company committed to a three-year, $53 billion AI spending program. Capital expenditures reached 67.68 billion yuan ($9.98 billion) in its most recent fiscal quarter, a 75% increase from the same period a year earlier.

The possible Spanish arrangement is taking shape as Madrid works on a regulatory package that would limit data center operations to E.U.-headquartered firms and tie any incremental power consumption by such facilities to an equivalent addition of new renewable generation, Bloomberg reported. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez aims to issue those rules by the end of the year.

Bloomberg noted that Chinese capital has increasingly flowed into Spain over recent years, touching industries such as electric vehicles, battery manufacturing, clean energy, and freight. Earlier this year Sánchez traveled to Beijing and concluded multiple deals intended to draw Chinese capital to Spain; he has distinguished himself among European heads of government by pursuing warmer relations with China instead of pushing for higher trade barriers.

DETROIT (AP) — A group of environmental organizations sued the Trump administration on Friday over its recent relaxation of key vehicle fuel economy rules, a decision that the group says will make vehicles less efficient, contribute to more pollution and increase gas consumption.

On Monday, the Trump administration lowered Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards that set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The announcement was made as the Trump administration negotiated with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

About a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait on a typical day, and the fight over its control has sent energy prices soaring across the globe.

The environmental groups filed the petition for review Friday in the U.S. Court of Appeals against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Jonathan Morrison, the administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which sets the rules.

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” Katherine Garcia, director of Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All program, said in a statement. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars, forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air.”

The Center for Biological Diversity, the Conservation Law Foundation, the Environmental Defense Fund and Public Citizen, along with the Sierra Club, filed the suit.

The Transportation Department and NHTSA earlier this week lowered the standards to an industry fleetwide average of roughly 34.9 miles per gallon for passenger cars and light trucks in the 2031 model year, down from a projected 50.4 miles per gallon under rules set by the Biden administration.

The administration said the change would provide Americans more vehicle choice and encourage consumers to buy newer, safer vehicles. Experts say reducing fuel economy requirements in vehicles does not necessarily lower their cost, nor would it automatically translate to new vehicle sales.

Duffy said the new rule also cuts the “illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

There has never been a mandate that manufacturers sell EVs or Americans buy them; the rules and other cleaner vehicle standards incentivized automakers to sell a mix of electric, hybrid electric and increasingly-efficient gasoline-powered vehicles.

When reached for comment, a DOT spokesperson referred to statements made by Duffy: "This administration understands the freedom of every American family starts with affordable cars. That’s why our new standards will make that dream more achievable by letting auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families’ needs at a lower price.”

Auto companies and industry groups broadly welcomed Monday's change, saying the rules under the Biden administration were too stringent and did not benefit consumers.

But environmental organizations decried the changes.

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute, said in a statement. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

Gas prices have hovered around $4.50 and diesel has hit unprecedented heights in recent weeks, according to AAA.

The DOT said Monday that the rule would cut yearly oil consumption in 2050 by about 1.3 billion barrels as compared with yearly oil consumption in 2024, but NHTSA had estimated the 2024 standards would have saved 14 billion gallons of gasoline from being burned by that year.

Fuel economy requirements have been in place since the 1970s energy crisis, and over time, have led to improved average efficiency in vehicles.

President Donald Trump has made a number of moves to undercut cleaner vehicles in the U.S. These include eliminating electric vehicle tax credits; scrapping vehicle emissions standards; repealing the fines for automakers who don’t meet mileage rules; and attempting to block the nation’s EV charging buildout.

text:
Entergy will receive $13.7 million in federal funding from the U.S. Energy Department to deploy advanced transmission technology to strengthen grid performance and unlock additional transmission capacity.

The funding, made available through the DOEʻs SPARK program, will help the company improve the power delivery to customers across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

“Installing this new technology is intended to help us deliver more reliable, affordable electricity to customers by reducing congestion, improving system readiness for large loads, and potentially avoiding capital costs for other transmission upgrades,” John Hudson, chief external affairs officer for Entergy, said. “With this federal funding, we’ll be able to deploy advanced dynamic line rating technology across more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, boosting the amount of power we can safely move using the infrastructure we already have. We appreciate the Department of Energy’s partnership and its commitment to strengthening energy resilience in our region.”

With this funding, Entergy and its electric companies in Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana will implement dynamic line rating technology, targeted geographic surveys, substation and terminal upgrades and hardware integration across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines. These upgrades will help the company better manage its energy infrastructure in areas experiencing load growth driven by new industrial development, manufacturing and data center expansion.

This work is designed to unlock at least a 25 percent increase in transfer capability on selected transmission corridors by using real-time line ratings and operational enhancements. Early modeling has shown the potential for a 29 percent to 61 percent increase in available power capacity across the project area.

By expanding the capability of existing transmission corridors, Entergy will be better positioned to support new and expanding industries across the region.

Entergy generates, transmits and distributes electricity to power life for more than 3 million customers through its operating companies in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas.

text:
C2ES is encouraged by the introduction of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, one of the most significant bipartisan energy proposals in decades. Durable, bipartisan progress on permitting reform is essential to delivering the affordable, reliable, and increasingly clean energy system the country needs. For too long, the status quo has delayed all types of energy projects, leading to inaction and higher costs for consumers. This bill would reform how the country builds energy infrastructure, with provisions addressing transmission planning and siting, permit certainty, federal environmental review, and other critical permitting processes. C2ES will release a section-by-section summary in the coming days detailing the bill’s major provisions and why they matter.

The bill arrives at a critical moment. America is in a period of rising energy demand and extraordinary economic opportunity. Meeting that demand, while keeping energy affordable, reliable, and clean, will require building at a scale the country has not seen in decades. Our permitting system must allow America to turn investment into infrastructure.

Nowhere is that challenge more apparent than on the electric grid. The United States needs stronger transmission connections between regions so electricity can move from where it is abundant to where it is needed most. A more interconnected grid provides consumers greater access to lower-cost power, allow regions to support one another during periods of stress, including severe weather, and connect areas rich in energy resources with growing centers of demand.

Building new transmission lines, however, is only part of the answer. We also need to make better use of the grid we already have. Advanced transmission technologies can increase the amount of electricity existing lines can carry, adding capacity more quickly and efficiently while larger, longer-term greenfield projects move forward.

At the same time, companies investing in America need greater certainty. Energy infrastructure requires substantial capital, often committed years before a project begins operating. Developers and investors need confidence that if they follow the rules and secure the necessary permits, those approvals will endure. A predictable, technology-neutral process can provide that confidence, helping unlock investment in generation, transmission, manufacturing, and other critical infrastructure, including the clean energy projects needed to reduce emissions.

Faster permitting should not come at the expense of meaningful environmental review. It should make that review work better. Federal environmental laws serve important purposes: identifying project impacts, protecting communities and natural resources, and ensuring agencies make informed decisions. A better permitting system should also use accessible and transparent tools for public engagement like those proposed in the bill, making it easier for communities to understand proposed projects and participate in the process. Those goals are entirely compatible with a process that is better coordinated, focused on the impacts that matter most, and governed by transparency and clear, predictable timelines.

America already has the resources, technology, and capital to meet this moment. What it also needs is a permitting system capable of putting them to work. Getting that system right will be critical to keeping energy affordable and reliable, strengthening American competitiveness, reducing emissions, and building the clean energy economy.

text:
Time to consider nuclear: Assembly Bill 2647 requires the California Energy Commission to prepare an assessment of the potential role for advanced nuclear technologies in the state by January 1, 2028, including whether new nuclear power plants in California could help the state achieve its goal of transitioning fully to renewable and zero-carbon electricity by 2045.

As enacted, the bill instructs the commission to make a comprehensive assessment considering cost, reliability, workforce benefits, emission impact, fuel cycle, public health, and potential siting for new nuclear power. According to the governor’s press release, the assessment will be conducted with public input.

The California legislature established a moratorium on new nuclear power plants in 1976. When first introduced in February, A.B. 2647 proposed amendments to clarify that the state’s moratorium does not include advanced nuclear reactors.

According to an assembly floor analysis from August, Assemblymember Lisa Calderon, the bill’s author, said this bill marks a historic step by mandating that California consider nuclear energy’s role in filling statewide electricity needs.

“Advanced nuclear technology could help meet California’s long-term electricity needs,” said Calderon. “Fifty years ago, California made a choice based on the technologies and needs of that era. Today, we face an entirely different reality. Our grid needs firm, clean power. Our families and businesses need affordable electricity. A.B. 2647 gives us the information to make a new choice, based on the technologies and needs of our century.”

A framework for fusion energy: Newsom signed Senate Bill 925, which requires the State Energy Resources Conservation and Development Commission to develop a strategic plan for the development of fusion energy in California to be submitted by December 31, 2029.

Specifically, the plan should develop a strategy for the expansion and development of fusion research, development, and commercialization in California; develop a regulatory framework for fusion energy; and assess how fusion energy at scale could support the state’s long-term goals.

Existing law authorizes the commission to certify certain sites as environmental leadership development projects, offering streamlining benefits. S.B. 925 expands the types of facilities eligible for this certification to include “a discretionary project, as described, for the manufacture, production, or assembly of specialized products, components, or systems that are integral to fusion energy.”

Fusion is a priority sector under the 2025 California Jobs First Economic Blueprint, and the state has a resolution to support fusion energy with the goal of siting a fusion pilot plant by the 2040s, though S.B. 925 specifies that it “does not create a technology set-aside, mandatory minimum, or mandate procurement of fusion energy by load-serving entities.”

“California has made substantial progress toward its climate goals. But fusion energy has the potential to provide nearly limitless clean, safe, and reliable power, while creating an economic ecosystem that will rival Silicon Valley,” said California state Sen. Jerry McNerney, who introduced the bill. “S.B. 925 lays the groundwork for widespread adoption of fusion energy in the state and will help ensure that California is a fusion technology leader in the coming decades.”

text:
A new analysis from a nonpartisan San Francisco think tank says the energy policies enacted by the Trump administration will lead to higher energy prices, lost jobs and worsening air pollution.

Published Thursday, the Energy Innovation report estimates U.S. households will pay about $6,500 more for energy from 2026 to 2040 due to the effects of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year and congressional and Trump administration energy policies that have been put in place during his second term.

The analysis expects gasoline prices to increase 54 cents per gallon in 2035 and 93 cents per gallon in 2040 because of policies that promote fossil fuels and reduce innovations in efficiency. Federal cuts to innovation and domestic manufacturing, along with policies in the OBBBA, will cost the country an average of 390,000 jobs per year, the analysis found, while slowing electrification and the manufacturing of domestic energy will cost state economies $1.3 trillion.

The Energy Innovation analysis comes as many Americans are already struggling with higher prices. Gas prices were about $3.10 per gallon when Trump began his second term; they now average $4.40, according to AAA. The bipartisan Joint Economic Committee said last month that American families have spent an additional $4,200 on goods and services since Trump took office in 2025, including $833 more on housing, $216 more on electricity and at least $310 more for groceries.

“Lowering electricity prices remains a top priority for President Trump, and he is aggressively unleashing reliable energy sources like coal and natural gas to reverse the catastrophic damage that Joe Biden and the Democrats did to our power grid,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Spectrum News.

She blamed President Joe Biden for creating a “grid crisis” that she said Trump is now fixing.

The White House priorities page says it is focused on unleashing domestic energy production to ensure affordable, reliable energy for American families and businesses. It says executive actions this year have sped up approval timelines to expand oil, natural gas, coal and nuclear capacity to lower utility bills and create high-paying energy jobs.

Trump has frequently derided solar and wind renewable energy as part of a “green new scam” implemented by the Biden administration.

Rogers cited data from the conservative Institute for Energy Research that found 86% of states that voted for the Democratic nominee for president in 2020 and 2024 have electricity prices above the national average largely because of renewable energy mandates and restrictions on natural gas power production.

She took issue with Energy Innovation’s description as a nonpartisan think tank, saying its founder is a Democratic donor and its CEO worked as a special assistant to Biden.

The Energy Innovation analysis said its estimates are based on seven sets of policy changes that have taken place during Trump’s second term. In addition to the OBBBA, which eliminated solar, wind and electric vehicle tax credits, the analysis considered the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of Clean Air Act greenhouse gas standards, mercury and air toxics standards and Clean Water Act limits on untreated liquid waste for electric power plants.

The Energy Innovation analysis also factored in the EPA’s repeal earlier this year of its 2009 Endangerment Finding, which scientifically determined that six greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare.

Other changes the report’s analysts considered were the Trump administration’s repeal of federal and state tailpipe emissions standards, limitations on solar and wind energy development, and the Energy Department’s cancellation of $7 billion in funding for regional clean hydrogen hubs announced during the Biden administration and approved through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021.

Energy Innovation said states may be able to counteract some of the Trump administration’s actions with their own policies, such as reducing red tape for businesses and households to install solar panels and other clean energy systems; offering incentives for the electrification of buildings and factories; and bolstering the market for electric vehicles and charging infrastructure.

text:
While the risks and opportunities for the battery space echo the challenges of other industries, opportunities and demand are likely to be anything but common — and in fact will likely be exceptional.

Risks and opportunities in battery manufacturing

That’s the perspective of Jason Schenker, president of Prestige Economics, chairman of The Futurist Institute, and keynote speaker at Informa’s Battery Show North America in Detroit from Oct. 12-15.

Schenker’s presentation, “The Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks and Opportunities in the Age of AI and Cold War Two,” will spotlight how US economic mobilization for a wartime-ready economy is supporting domestic battery manufacturing. “At the same time, AI power needs are also supporting domestic manufacturing, industrial investment and power infrastructure buildouts that are both on-grid and behind the meter,” Schenker asserted.

The challenges facing this new paradigm of manufacturing are all too familiar, he added: a tight labor force and high labor costs, supply chain disruption risks, and Cold War Two geopolitical challenges. That said, “rising power demand, industrial-scale power storage needs and high petroleum fuel prices are all likely to support battery demand.”

The role of industrial-scale batteries in energy storage

Industrial-scale batteries “can help ensure consistent dispatch, smoothing out load serving during on-peak periods by storing off-peak renewable wind power generation and supporting consistent baseload reliability and general grid reliability,” he explained. “Reshoring and the reindustrialization of the United States represent significant pent-up demand for batteries. Meanwhile, U.S. critical materials needs are likely to be reflected in policies that support mineral extraction and processing, as well as financial market dynamics that incentivize battery recycling.

At present, global battery manufacturing capacity is high, he added, but more capacity is planned.

“The bigger questions are where that capacity is located, how much will eventually come online, and whether there will be sufficient minerals and materials in secure supply chains to support future battery demand. Battery demand is likely to rise significantly over the next 10 years. Meeting that demand will require not only additional battery throughput, but also significant investment across the entire battery supply chain.”

As reported often in Battery Technology, the global nature of energy storage production and competition for raw materials and investment dollars is a moving target subject to geopolitical shifts and domestic imperatives. Schenker sees a battery manufacturing environment in which “the global supply chain for dual-use goods is bifurcating.

The technological iron curtain

“A Technological Iron Curtain is falling, with the US and its allies on one side and China and its allies on the other side. It would not surprise me if there were a medium-term objective established to ensure, or at least strengthen, US battery self-sufficiency. This is likely to drive greater domestic capacity as well as more secure battery materials supply chains for the United States and US allies.”

So what’s Schenker’s best-case version for how battery manufacturing evolves in a manner that ensures sufficient and secure supplies of the minerals and materials the United States and U.S. allies will need?

title: G7 to release 100M barrels of fuel amid high prices - The Hill
description:
Major economies will release fuel, including diesel, from their stockpiles as prices have skyrocketed in recent weeks.
This is expected to include a “frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners” the group said.
Trump administration officials had called on Europe to release diesel stocks.
Reuters reported this week that the administration had threatened to stop exporting diesel to France and Germany if they did not release fuel from their stocks.
Some rural-area Republicans have called for a ban on U.S. diesel exports across the board.
text:
Major economies will release fuel, including diesel, from their stockpiles as prices have skyrocketed in recent weeks.

The Group of Seven (G7), which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S., said in a statement Friday that it would “begin immediately” releasing 100 million barrels of fuel over the next four months.

This is expected to include a “frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners” the group said.

In addition, the countries said they will “coordinate maintenance schedules” of their refineries that process oil into fuels including gasoline and diesel, to “prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible.”

“We also encourage engagement with countries holding significant refining capacities to boost global production of refined products, particularly diesel, in light of ongoing market pressures in this segment,” the countries said.

Their statement did not specify which countries the releases would come form.

However, the news comes after significant U.S. pressure on the issue. President Trump on Friday touted the announcement, saying in a post on Truth Social “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”

A White House official told The Hill that Trump spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron late Thursday and with leaders of the G7 Friday morning to negotiate the release.

Trump administration officials had called on Europe to release diesel stocks.

Reuters reported this week that the administration had threatened to stop exporting diesel to France and Germany if they did not release fuel from their stocks.

Macron said in a post on X that as part of the new agreement, the countries agreed to “take no measures to restrict the exchange of energy and petroleum products between partner countries.”

The announcement comes as high diesel prices have hurt U.S. farmers in particular and have shaken up U.S. politics as the midterm elections approach. Some rural-area Republicans have called for a ban on U.S. diesel exports across the board.

As of Friday, diesel was averaging $6.37 per gallon, according to AAA, a very high price for this fuel.

Global conflicts, including the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, are factors in the high prices.

At the start of the conflict in Iran earlier this year, a large coalition of countries agreed to release a total of 400 million barrels of oil to offset the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping waterway off Iran’s coast.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a press release earlier this week that the U.S. and Japan were “delivering on their commitments” from March while “several European member countries have released only a fraction of the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged.”

Two diplomats suggested to Politico that Friday’s announcement may just be a reiteration of the previous pledge.

The 100 million barrels is about on par with one day’s worth of total global oil consumption.

text:
(The Center Square) - Arizona is considering a preventative step to block a per-mileage tax.

In November, Arizona voters will decide on Proposition 141, a constitutional amendment that would prevent state and local governments from instituting a per-mileage tax or fee based on the number of miles a vehicle travels.

The proposition also prohibits these entities from creating laws that monitor or restrict vehicle miles traveled without a person’s approval.

Proposition 141 would not apply to state or local government-owned vehicles or commercial vehicles operating in more than one state.

Jay Beeber, the chief policy officer for the National Motorist Association, said the association, which defends motorists' rights, supports Proposition 141.

Beeber told The Center Square it's a good idea for states like Arizona to “be proactive” and ensure they don't implement a per-mileage tax. The tax “would be an additional cost of driving,” he explained.

Four states currently have a per-mileage tax: Hawaii, Oregon, Utah and Virginia.

He said several states, such as Massachusetts, Michigan and California, have considered implementing a mileage tax.

At the federal level, in 2021, as part of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, the Department of Transportation ran a per-mileage tax pilot program to see whether the tax could help sustain the Federal Highway Trust Fund.

As technology continues to improve, Beeber said he can see more states considering implementing a per-mileage tax.

“Government is always looking for a way to bolster [its] revenues,” he said.

Governments talk about replacing the gas tax, but Beeber said it is “not very often that government gives up a way of taxing people.”

Senate Minority Leader Priya Sundareshan, D-Tucson, said she opposed Proposition 141, calling it “bad policy for transportation.”

She said the proposition is “counterproductive to efforts to provide a secure funding source” for Arizona’s roads.

Sundareshan told The Center Square the proposition would allow “electric vehicles to continue not contributing towards road funding.” She called the proposition a “gift to the electric vehicle industry.”

“Road funding is a complicated matter, and I do think there does need to be a more inclusive and updated approach to our transportation funding,” she said.

If the Legislature ever proposed a per-mileage tax, Sundareshan said Democrats “would look into” the matter.

Sundareshan said a per-mileage tax is not “her preferred method,” adding that she would consider a tax based on the weight of a car.

“A weight-based mechanism might be the most equitable and just approach to ensuring that the wear and tear on the roads is paid for by those who are causing” the damage on Arizona’s roads, she explained.

Sundareshan said there is “bipartisan recognition” that the state’s “road transportation funding mechanism is woefully inadequate and behind the times.” A 2026 report from the Tax Foundation found that 56.2% of road-related user revenues go toward highway spending, which ranked 27th nationwide.

"The gas tax is the only thing that funds Arizona’s road construction, and it hasn't been updated since the 1990s,” the Senate minority leader told The Center Square. Arizona’s current gas tax is 18 cents per gallon.

Eric Fowler, chair of the Maricopa County Libertarian Party, said the government needs to examine how it spends its money on fixing roads. “Another tax scheme is not how you build the roads."

“There’s too much waste, fraud, and abuse in the government to ask for yet another tax for these roads,” he told The Center Square.

Fowler said the proposition is attempting to constrain “the government before it does something terribly bad.” He added that getting ahead of issues like this is much easier than playing defense after the government has already implemented the policy.

Spencer Kamps, vice president of legislative affairs at the Home Builders Association of Central Arizona, said the association supports Proposition 141, noting that any potential per-mileage tax would “significantly impact [its] workers and their ability to travel around the Valley to various job sites.”

The association’s workers' No. 1 challenge is “accessibility to the job site and workspaces” across the Phoenix Valley, he told The Center Square.

In the future, the association doesn’t want to see any policy that makes it harder for people to enter the construction workforce or access a job site, Kamps said.

“Labor is an issue in Arizona," he noted. "We want [fewer] barriers to people working in the state, not more."

text:
After a decade of hoping and planning, Camp JORI in South Kingstown finally dedicated its new solar array, which promises tens of thousands of dollars in savings each year, as well as a major reduction in the camp’s environmental footprint.

The reduction in greenhouse gas output looks to be substantial. Each year, JORI’s new system is expected to prevent 103.4 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, equivalent to the amount produced by burning 11,630 gallons of gasoline. According to the EPA, it takes nearly 1,700 tree seedlings growing for 10 years to clean that much of the pollutant from the air.

The project began in 2016, when the camp’s board voted to explore using solar energy to power its facilities, which span 30 buildings across 72 acres. Engineering began, but the project hit a roadblock when the initial outlay of more than half a million dollars proved to be too expensive.

“It just wasn't economically feasible,” the camp’s Treasurer and President Emeritus Mike Schuster said. “The best we could do was get some small grants and then finance the balance. For the camp to take on the kind of debt that would have been required just wasn't fiscally responsible.”

That changed in 2024, starting with an email from Nina Stack, of the Champlin Foundations, alerting Schuster to the possibility of a grant from the Rhode Island Infrastructure Bank. The camp applied for it — and was awarded $382,425. That led to more success: The Commerce Corporation of Rhode Island provided an additional $57,000 in the form of a rebate. The camp received another $50,000 when it became one of the eight organizations to receive funding from the 2024 Jewish Solar Challenge.

The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act made the camp eligible for a $188,681 tax credit. Previously, nonprofit organizations were ineligible for the credit.

The 384-panel system, which began production in 2024 and completed in 2025, is expected to generate just under 146,000 kilowatt hours, most of the camp’s electrical needs. Each year, Camp JORI uses about 200,000 kWh, 40% of which is consumed in July, when campers are on site.

“We won't know for sure until we get through the first year, but we're estimating around $30,000, between $25,000 and $30,000 annually,” Schuster said.

During months when the camp doesn’t use the full amount of power generated, the excess electricity will be fed into the electrical grid for use elsewhere through a partnership with Knollwood Energy. The camp will receive $37.50 per 1,000 kWh, generating roughly $7,500 yearly in revenues.

Schuster said saving that money was a motivating factor, because “we would certainly be able to plow that money back into scholarships and programming at the camp.”

The solar panels were installed in an area of the camp away from campers and the road and are consequently not visible. Keeping to the aim of minimal environmental disruption, all trees that needed to be removed to make way for the panels were replanted elsewhere in the camp.

Across the country, few summer camps are powered by solar electricity.

“This is very unique,” Schuster said.

text:
Joins broad coalition of 26 states, counties, and cities in filing lawsuit against new NHTSA rule that weakens fuel-economy standards for new cars and light trucks, hurts consumers, economy, and the environment

NHTSA’s novel reinterpretation of the law renders the federal fuel-economy program toothless, unable to protect consumers against rising gas prices or the ongoing global oil shock from President Trump’s war

October 2, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison today joined a coalition of 26 states, counties, and cities in filing a lawsuit against the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), challenging its final rule that weakens corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards for new passenger cars and light trucks. Historically, NHTSA’s standards have reduced consumer costs by improving fuel efficiency for vehicles, placed downward pressure on gas prices by reducing fuel consumption, protected the U.S. economy from global oil shocks, and reduced pollution from tailpipes and refineries. However, the final rule significantly weakens fuel economy standards and hurts consumers and the environment.

In the lawsuit filed today in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition allege that NHTSA’s final rule is arbitrary and capricious and violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. They further allege that NHTSA has contravene its mandate from Congress to set fuel-economy standards at their “maximum feasible” level. Far from “maximum feasible,” NHTSA’s backsliding standards for the next five years require less efficiency than the U.S. fleet actually achieved in 2021.

“Trump’s war on our economy and our environment continues,” Attorney General Ellison said. “For five decades, federal fuel-economy standards have made our environment cleaner and our economy stronger and have saved consumers astronomical sums of money. No matter, though: if hurting consumers, the environment, and the economy benefits Big Oil and lines billionaires’ pockets, Trump will do it, illegality be damned. So once again, I’m standing with my fellow attorneys general to protect Minnesotans’ clean air and bank accounts and stand up for the rule of law.”

In 1975, Congress enacted the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which requires NHTSA to establish “maximum feasible” fuel economy standards for new vehicles that reflect technological feasibility, economic practicability, the effect of other motor vehicle standards of the government, and the need to conserve energy. To set fuel economy standards, NHTSA first models the current fleet’s performance and then considers what, if any, additional actions manufacturers could take to improve their fuel economy in future model years above that. In past rulemaking, including during the first Trump Administration, NHTSA started from a realistic baseline fleet that included the millions of electric vehicles that already existed on our nation’s highways and roads and based fuel-economy standards on how additional technological improvements to gas-fueled cars could make that fleet more efficient. NHTSA never based fuel-economy standards on “mandating” automakers to produce more electric vehicles or requiring consumers to buy them.

The final rule misinterprets NHTSA’s statutory authority and improperly forces the agency to ignore the presence of millions of electric vehicles in the nation’s existing fleet, leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the “maximum feasible” fuel economy level that the auto industry can achieve. Essentially, NHTSA’s novel reinterpretation of the law renders the federal fuel-economy program toothless, unable to protect consumers against rising gas prices or the ongoing global oil shock from President Trump’s war.

NHTSA has also utilized defective analyses of vehicle affordability and sales, fleet turnover, fuel savings, and vehicle safety to make a profoundly harmful and destructive rule look net-beneficial to society. For example, NHTSA tries to paper over nearly $220 billion in lost fuel savings — money that drivers would have saved at the pump under the previous fuel economy standards, which will instead benefit Big Oil. It also refuses to consider hundreds of billions of dollars in future damages from climate change-driven disasters, flouting the best science and research and effectively setting these costs at zero. Defying a longstanding and repeatedly affirmed Congressional mandate, NHTSA asserts that the United States does not need to conserve energy after all — treating the high gasoline prices and the instability of global oil markets as an acceptable trade for fossil fuel companies’ profits. Finally, NHTSA’s rule will end the CAFE credit trading program in 2028, which will significantly harm electric vehicle industries that employ Americans and support the economy.

In filing this lawsuit, Attorney General Ellison joins the attorneys general of California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai‘i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the City of Chicago, the City and County of Denver, the City of New York, and the City and County of San Francisco.

text:
A new analysis from a nonpartisan San Francisco think tank says the energy policies enacted by the Trump administration will lead to higher energy prices, lost jobs and worsening air pollution.

Published Thursday, the Energy Innovation report estimates U.S. households will pay about $6,500 more for energy from 2026 to 2040 due to the effects of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year and congressional and Trump administration energy policies that have been put in place during his second term.

The analysis expects gasoline prices to increase 54 cents per gallon in 2035 and 93 cents per gallon in 2040 because of policies that promote fossil fuels and reduce innovations in efficiency. Federal cuts to innovation and domestic manufacturing, along with policies in the OBBBA, will cost the country an average of 390,000 jobs per year, the analysis found, while slowing electrification and the manufacturing of domestic energy will cost state economies $1.3 trillion.

The Energy Innovation analysis comes as many Americans are already struggling with higher prices. Gas prices were about $3.10 per gallon when Trump began his second term; they now average $4.40, according to AAA. The bipartisan Joint Economic Committee said last month that American families have spent an additional $4,200 on goods and services since Trump took office in 2025, including $833 more on housing, $216 more on electricity and at least $310 more for groceries.

“Lowering electricity prices remains a top priority for President Trump, and he is aggressively unleashing reliable energy sources like coal and natural gas to reverse the catastrophic damage that Joe Biden and the Democrats did to our power grid,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Spectrum News.

She blamed President Joe Biden for creating a “grid crisis” that she said Trump is now fixing.

The White House priorities page says it is focused on unleashing domestic energy production to ensure affordable, reliable energy for American families and businesses. It says executive actions this year have sped up approval timelines to expand oil, natural gas, coal and nuclear capacity to lower utility bills and create high-paying energy jobs.

Trump has frequently derided solar and wind renewable energy as part of a “green new scam” implemented by the Biden administration.

Rogers cited data from the conservative Institute for Energy Research that found 86% of states that voted for the Democratic nominee for president in 2020 and 2024 have electricity prices above the national average largely because of renewable energy mandates and restrictions on natural gas power production.

She took issue with Energy Innovation’s description as a nonpartisan think tank, saying its founder is a Democratic donor and its CEO worked as a special assistant to Biden.

The Energy Innovation analysis said its estimates are based on seven sets of policy changes that have taken place during Trump’s second term. In addition to the OBBBA, which eliminated solar, wind and electric vehicle tax credits, the analysis considered the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of Clean Air Act greenhouse gas standards, mercury and air toxics standards and Clean Water Act limits on untreated liquid waste for electric power plants.

The Energy Innovation analysis also factored in the EPA’s repeal earlier this year of its 2009 Endangerment Finding, which scientifically determined that six greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare.

Other changes the report’s analysts considered were the Trump administration’s repeal of federal and state tailpipe emissions standards, limitations on solar and wind energy development, and the Energy Department’s cancellation of $7 billion in funding for regional clean hydrogen hubs announced during the Biden administration and approved through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021.

Energy Innovation said states may be able to counteract some of the Trump administration’s actions with their own policies, such as reducing red tape for businesses and households to install solar panels and other clean energy systems; offering incentives for the electrification of buildings and factories; and bolstering the market for electric vehicles and charging infrastructure.

text:
October 2, 2026

SMITHFIELD, Va. – During an event at the Windsor Castle Park in Smithfield, Virginia, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi was joined by U.S. Representative Jen Kiggans (R-VA-02) and others to announce more than $90 million for the Chesapeake Bay watershed. EPA is awarding $37 million with an additional $53 million in funding coming from other agencies to implement 83 new projects that will support critical restoration and provide long-term water quality improvements.

“Through these grants, EPA is working collaboratively with our local partners to deliver practical restoration solutions that improve water quality, restore habitat, and support the vital Chesapeake Bay watershed. These improvements will have a significant impact of the more than 1,800 local communities that depend on the watershed to support their economies,” said EPA Deputy Administrator Fotouhi. “This type of funding has a proven track record of delivering tangible environmental results and is a shining example of taxpayer dollars being put to accomplishing EPA’s core mission.”

“Preserving the health of the Chesapeake Bay is critical to the communities and native species who call Coastal Virginia home,” said Representative Kiggans. “I’m grateful to the EPA, NFWF, and James River Association for supporting commonsense conservation efforts that protect our waterways and strengthen our coastal communities. I want to thank Deputy Administrator Fotouhi for joining us in Virginia’s Second District to celebrate this investment, and I look forward to continuing to work with the Deputy Administrator and the EPA to advance practical solutions that preserve the Chesapeake Bay for generations to come.”

The projects being supported today emphasize the Trump EPA's cooperative federalism approach to engaging local communities in the planning, design, and implementation of community-level clean water projects that will improve soil quality, install physical barriers, and restore habitats. Since 1999, EPA has partnered with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) to award over $800 million across more than 2,000 grants, resulting in the reduction of nitrogen pollution by more than 40 million pounds, the restoration of over 3,000 miles of streamside forests and 9,500 acres of wetlands, and the treatment of stormwater runoff from over 23,000 acres of impervious surfaces.

The Trump EPA is committed to safeguarding the Chesapeake Bay to both protect human health and the environment and grow the booming economies that come from it. Having clean and accessible water is essential to everyday life. This $90 million will benefit communities from farmers to homeowners, churches, businesses, and municipalities with improvements to local water quality that will also help restore the Chesapeake Bay. This investment bolsters the robust economies of the more than 1,800 communities that the Chesapeake Bay watershed supports and ensures that the families and nearly 18 million people living in the watershed continue to prosper.

text:
In the final hours of the 2026 California legislative season, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a suite of closely watched legislation on energy and the environment.

Among them are laws that will reshape how California pays for and operates its energy system — including limiting utility profit and making greater use of clean energy at home — and how the state protects itself against environmental challenges from the federal government.

Senate Bill 913 from Sen. Josh Becker (D-Menlo Park) will advance the use of virtual power plants — networks of customer-owned home batteries, solar panels, electric vehicle chargers and smart thermostats — that can be linked together to relieve the state’s electric grid during times of peak demand.

Specifically, the law directs the California Public Utilities Commission to create a pathway for these separate devices to be aggregated to export electricity by June 30, 2027. Existing rules limited how much people can be paid for the electricity these appliances provide for the grid.

“Instead of simply building more expensive infrastructure and passing those costs on to ratepayers, SB 913 helps us get more out of the resources Californians have already paid for,” Becker said in a statement. “That means more competition, a cleaner and more reliable grid, and an opportunity to lower costs for everyone.”

A related bill from Becker, SB 905, will require the CPUC to consider lowering utilities’ profit on lower-risk investments, such as undergrounding power lines. Utilities often see a return of 9% or 10% on new transmission projects.

It will also require utilities to identify where the existing grid has room for more electricity — and be more transparent about unused capacity — so they can make better use of batteries and other resources.

Taken together, the laws “are the legislative session’s clearest attempt to hold down electricity bills by using equipment installed at homes and businesses rather than expanding utility expenditures which are passed on to customers,” according to the California Solar and Storage Assn., the state’s largest clean-energy business group.

But two of the state’s largest utilities, Pacific Gas & Electric and Southern California Edison, opposed SB 905, with SCE spokesperson David Eisenhauer stating that “keeping electricity affordable for customers requires policies that both reduce costs and support continued investment in the reliable and resilient energy system Californians depend on.”

PG&E spokeswoman Lynsey Paulo said similarly that the utility is concerned the law will discourage the investments needed to accommodate rising electricity demand and stabilize rates and affordability.

Both said they were neutral on the virtual power plant law, with Paulo noting that PG&E “supports efforts to better recognize the value distributed energy resources can provide to the grid.”

Becker’s bills were seen as companions to a new law from Sen. Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco) that allows Californians to use small plug-in solar systems — sometimes called “balcony solar” — without going through the normal rooftop solar permitting process. It’s seen as particularly beneficial for apartment dwellers and renters.

“Together, these three common sense clean energy bills will allow California to continue advancing toward a cleaner, healthier future, in which we rely more on abundant renewable resources including rooftop solar to power our lives,” said Laura Deehan, state director at the nonprofit Environment California.

And although energy affordability and reliability were key issues in Sacramento this year, the governor on Wednesday also signed important legislation to address efforts by the Trump administration to advance the sale and production of fossil fuels in and around California.

They include a bill from Assemblymember Mia Bonta (D-Alameda) that will require a new environmental impact report before any major bulk coal facility is approved, giving the state more control over such projects. The bill was largely a response to President Trump’s $75-million investment in a new coal export terminal in Oakland, which would receive more than 13 million tons of coal each year from interior states to be shipped overseas.

California no longer burns or buys electricity generated by coal. Opponents of the project, who have long been concerned about increased pollution in the surrounding area, celebrated the bill’s passage.

“Today California is standing up for public health, the environment, and our climate. We will not sacrifice our communities to prop up the failing coal industry,” said Ada Waelder, senior state legislative representative with the nonprofit Earthjustice.

This week, Newsom also signed a bill that will make it illegal for oil producers to use oil rigs, pipelines and other equipment in state waters to support any new federal offshore oil leases. It was largely a response to Trump’s plan to open up California’s entire coastline to offshore oil and gas drilling for the first time in more than 40 years.

The legislative session also brought some disappointments for some community groups, such as Newsom’s decision to veto SB 954. It would have closed a loophole that makes it easier for advanced manufacturing facilities to be sited in vulnerable neighborhoods without environmental review. He also vetoed an effort to overhaul the state’s struggling community-solar program.

But Newsom did highlight the environment in his final bill signing of the session, which he announced at the top of the Golden Gate Bridge on Wednesday.

The bill, SB 895 by Sen. Wiener, will put a $7.5-billion science and health research bond before voters in March 2028, “supporting research at California universities and institutions in medicine, public health, climate, wildfire prevention, agriculture and other fields,” according to the governor’s office.

It was the last of 1,160 bills acted on during this legislative session, and 7,803 bills since the start of Newsom’s administration in 2019.

text:
Rollback would cost drivers nearly $220 billion at the pump

Attorney General Dan Rayfield is taking action to stop a new Trump Administration rule that would roll back fuel efficiency standards and let automakers sell less fuel-efficient cars and trucks, a move that means Oregonians will pay more at the pump.

“When gas prices are at an all-time high, it’s astonishing that the Trump Administration would want to roll back fuel efficiency standards,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “The administration’s actions would cost families and small businesses billions of dollars, increase air pollution, and lead to even hotter summers.”

For nearly 50 years, federal fuel economy standards have done something simple: they’ve required new cars to go farther on a gallon of gas. That’s saved families money, helped keep gas prices in check, made the country less vulnerable to oil price spikes overseas, and cut down on pollution. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has now weakened those standards so much that, for the next five years, new cars would be held to a lower bar than the cars Americans were already driving in 2021.

text:
Rivian Automotive Inc. (NASDAQ:RIVN) on Friday reported a sharp increase in third-quarter vehicle production and deliveries while reaffirming its full-year delivery outlook.

The electric vehicle maker produced 19,751 vehicles at its Normal, Illinois, plant during the quarter ended Sept. 30. It delivered 19,248 vehicles during the period. Rivian said both figures were in line with its outlook.

CNBC reported that deliveries came in above Wall Street’s expectation of 18,000 vehicles, based on the average of estimates compiled by FactSet.

Deliveries Jump From Second Quarter

Third-quarter deliveries rose about 58% from 12,194 vehicles in the second quarter. Production increased about 57% from 12,613 vehicles.

The latest results also marked a strong improvement from a year earlier. Rivian delivered 13,201 vehicles and produced 10,720 vehicles in the third quarter of 2025. That means deliveries increased about 46% year over year, while production jumped roughly 84%.

Reuters attributed the growth to the production ramp-up of Rivian’s R2 SUV, which launched in June as a smaller, lower-priced alternative to its flagship R1 SUV.

Analysts see the R2 as key to Rivian’s growth strategy as the EV industry faces a tougher U.S. policy backdrop, including the end of federal EV tax credits, tariffs and softer industrywide demand, Reuters reported.

Maintains 2026 Delivery Outlook

Rivian reaffirmed its full-year 2026 delivery guidance of 65,000 to 70,000 vehicles. The company had raised that range in July from its previous forecast of 62,000 to 67,000 vehicles after second-quarter deliveries exceeded its outlook.

The company said at the time that stronger quarter-over-quarter growth in its electric delivery vans and R1 vehicles, along with the introduction of R2 deliveries, helped drive the second-quarter performance.

Rivian Stock Falls

Rivian shares were trading lower despite stronger-than-expected third-quarter deliveries. Reuters reported that investors appeared disappointed after management maintained its full-year guidance rather than raising it.

“The market is reacting to management maintaining full-year guidance,” Morningstar senior equity analyst Seth Goldstein told Reuters. He said investors were likely looking for an increase after the strong third-quarter results.

Goldstein added that the results suggest Rivian’s R2 production ramp remains on track. Higher volumes over the coming quarters could help the company meet its full-year delivery target, he said.

Rivian confirmed it will report its third-quarter financial results after the market closes on Oct. 29.
