text:
Petition for Review

TRENTON – Attorney General Jennifer Davenport today joined a coalition of 26 states, counties, and cities in filing a lawsuit against the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), challenging its final rule that weakens Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards for new passenger cars and light trucks. Strong fuel economy regulations help consumers save money at the pump, and this federal rollback would cost drivers even more under today’s high gas prices.

Historically, NHTSA’s standards have reduced consumer costs by improving vehicle fuel efficiency, placed downward pressure on gas prices by reducing fuel consumption, protected the U.S. economy from global oil shocks, and reduced pollution from tailpipes and refineries. However, the final rule significantly weakens fuel economy standards, harming both consumers and the planet at the exact moment when global gasoline prices are soaring.

In the lawsuit filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, the coalition alleges that NHTSA’s new rule is contrary to law and contravenes its mandate from Congress to set fuel-economy standards at their “maximum feasible” level. Far from achieving this “maximum feasible” requirement, NHTSA’s backsliding standards for the next five years require less efficiency than what the U.S. fleet actually achieved in 2021.

“Every mile driven impacts our children’s future,” said Attorney General Davenport. “When we set high fuel efficiency standards, we cut the carbon emissions that contribute to climate change while saving families money at the pump—proof that protecting the environment and consumers go hand in hand.”

In 1975, Congress enacted the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which requires NHTSA to establish “maximum feasible” fuel economy standards for new vehicles that reflect technological feasibility, economic practicability, the effect of other motor vehicle standards, and the need to conserve energy. When setting fuel economy standards, NHTSA first models the current fleet’s performance and then considers what, if any, additional actions manufacturers could take to improve their fuel economy in future model years above that.

In past rulemakings, NHTSA started from a realistic baseline fleet that included the millions of electric vehicles that already existed on our nation’s highways and roads, and based fuel-economy standards on how additional technological improvements to gas-fueled cars could make that fleet more efficient.

The final rule misinterprets NHTSA’s statutory authority and improperly forces the agency to ignore the presence of millions of electric vehicles in the nation’s existing fleet, leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the “maximum feasible” fuel economy level that the auto industry can achieve. Essentially, NHTSA’s novel reinterpretation of the law renders the federal fuel-economy program toothless and, if allowed to take effect, would exacerbate the affordability challenges consumers are already facing due to rising gas prices.

NHTSA’s rule relies on defective analyses of vehicle affordability and sales, fleet turnover, fuel savings, and vehicle safety to make a profoundly harmful and destructive rule look net-beneficial to society. For example, NHTSA attempts to paper over nearly $220 billion in lost fuel savings—money that drivers would have saved at the pump under the previous fuel economy standards, which will instead benefit Big Oil. It also ignores the hundreds of billions of dollars in future damages from climate change-driven disasters—spurred by increased fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions—effectively setting these costs at zero, contrary to scientific evidence.

Defying a longstanding and repeatedly affirmed Congressional mandate, NHTSA asserts that the United States does not need to conserve energy after all, continuing the Trump Administration’s pattern of benefiting the fossil fuel industry at the expense of American consumers. Finally, NHTSA’s rule will end the CAFE credit trading program in 2028, which will significantly harm electric vehicle industries that employ Americans and support the economy.

In today’s lawsuit, the coalition alleges that NHTSA’s final rule is arbitrary and capricious and violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Energy Policy and Conservation Act.

In filing this lawsuit, Attorney General Davenport joins the attorneys general of California, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai‘i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the City of Chicago, the City and County of Denver, the City of New York, and the City and County of San Francisco.

NextEra Energy Resources is partnering with Related Companies, a privately owned real-estate development firm, and Lewis Energy Group to develop a more than $22 billion natural gas-powered energy campus in Encinal, Texas, a project that the companies say will generate 6.47 gigawatts (GW) of electricity and support a planned data center campus.

The U.S. Department of Commerce and the Republic of Korea selected the group to develop Project Star, which is expected to be built in phases. Initial power generation could come online as early as 2029, subject to permitting and other approvals, the companies said in a joint Sept. 30 statement.

“Project Star demonstrates how energy infrastructure and economic growth can advance together,” said John Ketchum, chairman and CEO of NextEra Energy. “By bringing new generation online to serve new demand, we’re helping strengthen reliability, support investment and jobs, and protect electricity customers.”

NextEra Energy Resources and Related Companies plan to develop, build, and operate the natural gas generation facilities. Lewis Energy Group will provide associated infrastructure, including natural gas.

At full scale, the project is expected to provide power for a privately funded 5-GW data center campus that Related Digital is developing on an adjacent site. The energy project is also expected to send excess electricity to the Texas power grid.

The project also will create thousands of construction jobs over several years, including an estimated 8,400 jobs during peak construction, the companies said.

Once the power campus is operating, the companies said it will support about 170 permanent jobs. The adjacent data center is expected to create hundreds of additional permanent jobs.

For NextEra, Project Star adds to a significant existing presence in Texas. The company says it has invested more than $20 billion in the state and operates more than 9 GW of electricity generation there.

“We look forward to working with the administration, the State of Texas, Related Digital, and Lewis Energy Group to responsibly develop this project while building on our long-standing investment in Texas and its communities,” Ketchum added.

The project is being announced as part of the implementation of a U.S.-Korea trade agreement announced in July 2025 and a strategic investment memorandum signed in November 2025. Those efforts aim to enhance cooperation between Korea and the U.S. in strategic industrial sectors such as energy and artificial intelligence.

Under the planned structure, the energy campus will be jointly owned by the United States and South Korea and built and operated by the Related/NextEra Energy Resources joint venture team.

The companies said that Project Star is consistent with Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s directive that data centers provide their own electricity generation.

Lewis Energy Group will provide the project with land, produced water, and natural gas. The company has operated in La Salle County for decades.

“I am excited to be working with two world class companies in Related Digital and NextEra Energy to develop Project Star,” said Rod Lewis, founder and CEO of Lewis Energy Group. “This project will bring much needed jobs to south Texas, add new power generation to be available to the state of Texas, and ensure the natural gas produced in the south Texas region provides direct economic benefits to our local communities.”

Related Companies Chairman Jeff Blau said the project is intended to provide its own electricity for the data center while also sending excess power to the grid.

“Related Digital was founded on a commitment to responsible infrastructure development, and we are proud to partner on this historic project, which will advance our nation’s energy independence, power American innovation, and strengthen not just the Texas economy, but relations between the United States and Korea,” Blau said.

NextEra and its partners said they plan to work with state and local officials and communities as the project moves through the permitting and approval process.

Governor visits brand new $200 million Sheboygan Falls facility that will generate 44 high-paying jobs

SHEBOYGAN FALLS — Gov. Tony Evers today joined Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC) Secretary and CEO John W. Miller and leaders of EMD Electronics to celebrate the opening of a new 38,000-square-foot research and development facility at the company’s Sheboygan Falls site. The new facility is part of a multi-year, $200 million investment in Wisconsin by EMD Electronics, the North American electronics business of Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, to expand the company’s ability to develop and scale advanced materials for next-generation semiconductor manufacturing. When completed, the project is expected to create 44 new high-paying, family-supporting jobs.

“Over the last nearly eight years, my administration has been proud to celebrate major business investments with our partners at WEDC, and today’s announcement further adds to those efforts,” said Gov. Evers. “Thanks to these critical partnerships, we’re building the 21st-century jobs and infrastructure we need to support a 21st-century economy. Together with EMD Electronics, we’re expanding Wisconsin’s manufacturing capabilities and increasing economic opportunity for folks in Sheboygan Falls and throughout the region.”

This new research and development facility aims to invest in critical manufacturing sectors, such as the semiconductor industry, which is increasingly advancing toward complex architectures, underscoring the need for materials innovation as it is becoming increasingly critical to chip performance and scalability. The new Sheboygan Falls facility provides dedicated capabilities for synthesis, scale-up, and technology transfer, helping EMD Electronics work more closely with customers to accelerate new materials from early-stage development through final products.

“The semiconductor industry is entering a period where integrated workflow solutions play a defining role in enabling the next generation of devices, particularly as AI drives increasing complexity and performance requirements,” said Dr. Bing Han, executive vice president and head of Thin Films at EMD Electronics. “Materials innovation remains at the core of that transformation, but success increasingly depends on combining materials discovery, process expertise, and scale-up capabilities. This new facility brings together the capabilities needed to work alongside our customers on their most complex materials challenges and accelerate innovation from the lab to commercial production.”

WEDC is supporting the expansion with up to $4.5 million in performance-based tax credits. The amount of credits the company receives depends on the amount of capital invested and the number of jobs created.

“EMD Electronics’ continued investment in Sheboygan Falls demonstrates the important role Wisconsin’s skilled workforce and strong manufacturing foundation can play in the future of the semiconductor industry,” said Secretary and CEO Miller. “This R&D facility brings advanced research and development capabilities to our state, creates opportunities for highly skilled jobs, and strengthens Wisconsin’s position as a place where global companies can develop and scale the technologies of the future.”

The new facility introduces eight purpose-built laboratories supporting the product development lifecycle, including discovery, development, qualification, analytical development, purification, packaging, and hazard testing to EMD Electronics’ global footprint. By bringing research and development, scale-up, and technology transfer capabilities together at the Sheboygan Falls site, EMD Electronics can collaborate more closely with customers and respond more quickly to evolving technology roadmaps and local customer requirements.

The facility was also designed to expand EMD Electronics’ research capabilities while reducing its environmental footprint and is among its pioneering laboratories powered by renewable energy. The company aims to meet LEED Gold certification with this new facility and is among the pioneering EMD Electronics laboratories powered by renewable energy. Geothermal energy provides 100 percent of the building’s cooling and approximately 50 percent of its heating requirements, complemented by heat pumps, energy recovery systems, LED lighting, and low-water-use fixtures.

The new facility is part of EMD Electronics’ multi-year investment in its U.S. footprint. The company has announced $200 million in investments supporting its U.S. semiconductor capabilities, including a further investment in Sheboygan Falls to be completed in 2027, as well as recent expansions in Carlsbad, California, and Catoosa, Oklahoma. The investment is part of the company’s $1 billion, five-year investment program to strengthen its innovation and manufacturing capabilities in the U.S.

text:
DETROIT, MI — The U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s Free Enterprise Express and Opportunity Tour continues with a stop in Detroit, where Neil Bradley, Executive Vice President and Chief Policy Officer at the Chamber, will unveil a groundbreaking new study alongside the Detroit Regional Chamber that reveals that small businesses are using artificial intelligence (AI) to grow their businesses.

The report, led by the U.S. Chamber’s Technology Engagement Center (C_TEC), finds that four times as many small businesses report that AI is right now creating permanent jobs in their firm (25%) than those that report it is allowing them to reduce headcount (6%). Further, small businesses that use AI are 10% more likely to have added headcount in the past year compared to their peers that are not using AI.

These findings run directly counter to the prevailing narrative about AI — and it helps explain why the United States is seeing record numbers of new businesses formed.

The data comes from the Chamber’s fifth annual Empowering Small Business report, which tracks the role of technology and AI in the small business economy. AI adoption among small businesses has surged from just 23% in 2023 to 66% today — nearly tripling in three years — as owners deploy the technology for marketing, customer service, and daily workflow management.

“The four-to-one advantage in job creation over job reductions turns the conventional wisdom about AI on its head,” said Neil Bradley, Executive Vice President and Chief Policy Officer at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. “For small businesses, AI is creating opportunity and it’s exactly the kind of real-world progress the Free Enterprise Express Opportunity Tour is highlighting across the country. Policymakers should take this evidence seriously and avoid restricting the tools that are helping Main Street businesses hire, compete, and grow.”

The report’s findings have implications for millions of Americans, since half of private sector workers work for an employer with fewer than 250 employees. For these employees, this report is an early and concrete signal that AI is contributing to job growth at the firms where most of the country earns a living.

The report also identifies risks that come with constraints on AI. Seventy-eight percent of small businesses expressed that limiting their access to AI tools would inhibit their ability to grow—with a majority identifying complexities in the regulatory environment as a concern.

"This data defies the headlines: AI is adding jobs, growing the economy, and creating more opportunities than ever for working Americans,” said Jordan Crenshaw, senior vice president of the U.S. Chamber’s Technology Engagement Center. “Entrepreneurs who use AI are outperforming their peers who are not in hiring, sales, and profits. This report should reshape how we think about this technology and its role in American prosperity. Getting AI policy right means building a national framework that supports continued growth for those businesses while giving workers and the public the accountability they deserve."

Earlier this week, the Chamber’s Q3 2026 Small Business Index, sponsored by Justworks, found that seven in ten small businesses reported good business health. Overall, the Index improved to 70.5, though small business owners remain cautious due to inflation and cost concerns. That makes AI adoption even more crucial as small businesses seek to become more efficient and grow.

To view the full findings and methodology of the Empowering Small Business report, please visit the report here.

The national Free Enterprise Express Opportunity Tour is a six-week trip through 20 states and more than 50 events to make the case for free enterprise in communities across America and push back against growing support for government-directed economic policies that threaten economic freedom, opportunity, innovation, and growth.

The Opportunity Tour is a part of the U.S. Chamber’s New Fight for Free Enterprise initiative, a multi-year strategic effort to defend, protect, and promote free enterprise.

To boost its profitability, BMW plans a product lineup more tailored around regional preferences. It’s also turning its focus toward higher-margin models that can offer the greatest value for customers over the long term in each of its global markets.

The Neue Klasse platform will also merge software and AI to deliver improved customer experiences. BMW says the focus of Neue Klasse platform vehicles will no longer be on updating individual functions, but on the intuitive interaction of the entire vehicle across all vehicle domains, such as advanced driver assistance systems, infotainment and comfort functions.

BMW also plans to further adopt AI technologies to speed up vehicle development timelines, including to boost efficiency across its manufacturing operations. BMW is implementing a standardized IT and data model, using intelligent systems at nearly every stage of production, the company said.

These AI-powered technologies include virtual factories, digital twins and AI-supported quality inspections. In the future, BMW plans to deploy digital AI agents to perform challenging tasks autonomously and deploy self-learning robots in its factories for more flexible and efficient vehicle production.

In the near future, BMW plans to use specialized digital agents and existing IT systems that the automaker has built up over decades. That will allow BMW to analyze complex information more rapidly in order to automate routine tasks to boost efficiently, per the release.

BMW is currently working with AI company Mistral on crash simulations. The testing combines BMW’s engineering datasets with Mistral AI’s training capabilities to create an AI model that enhances the quality and speed of vehicle development. BMW says it’s relying on next-generation AI-powered large industry models trained on specific engineering and simulation data to make the process more scalable.

“Consistent use of agentic AI applications across all areas of the company will be a game-changer for more agile and efficient development, leaner structures and faster decision-making,” said Walter Mertl, member of the Board of Management of BMW, in a statement.

BMW is also harnessing AI to develop more advanced autonomous driving technologies. This includes a new L2++ system developed in partnership with Momenta that will be offered in China on the new BMW iX3.

In Europe, BMW is working with its partner Qualcomm to offer a navigation-guided driver assistance system in Germany that can operate autonomously on highways, secondary roads and urban streets. BMW intends to roll out this same technology in the U.S in stages. In 2027, BMW said it will launch its more advanced L2++ driver assist systems in China, the EU and the U.S.

Neue Klasse platform vehicles will be able to download new functions via over-the-air software updates, per the release. By the end of the year, BMW said that its Highway Assistant hands-free driving systems will be available on vehicles in 21 countries. However, for the new iX3 and future New Klasse platform vehicles, Highway Assistant is being upgraded to BMW’s new Symbiotic Drive Level 2 driver assist technology, offering hands-free highway driving at speeds up to 85 mph.

BMW also announced in a separate press release that it’s investing 2 billion euros in vehicle production and battery manufacturing to prepare its plants in Germany to produce the next-generation BMW 3-Series built on its Neue Klasse platform, which is one of its top-selling models globally. These plans included a new battery factory to produce cells for the electric versions of the 3-Series sedan. Series production of cells for the BMW i3 began this week at the new plant.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — A coalition of environmental and consumer protection organizations filed a lawsuit today challenging the Trump administration’s final rule rolling back federal Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, a move that will make new vehicles less fuel efficient, increase gasoline consumption, and drive up costs for American drivers already facing high gas prices.

The lawsuit challenges the administration’s attempt to weaken longstanding fuel economy requirements that have helped reduce gasoline consumption and save drivers money at the pump. The rollback comes as families are already struggling with record-high gas prices, with transportation ranking as the second-largest household expense after housing, accounting for roughly 17% of average household spending.

The existing fuel economy standards, which the Trump administration has weakened, would have saved 64 billion gallons of gas. Even before the current rise in gas prices, they were set to deliver $35 billion in savings to consumers over the lifetimes of the vehicles covered. However, today’s final rule weakens those standards, allowing manufacturers to produce a fleet of vehicles in model year 2031 that are less efficient than the model year 2024 vehicle fleet that is already on our roads.

The administration’s own projections show that Americans will be forced to spend over $1,600 more on fuel over the life of these life-efficient vehicles, and NHTSA estimates this final rule will result in an increase of over 121 billion gallons of fuel consumption through 2050.

“The Trump administration’s rollback will mean wasted gas, more air pollution, and higher costs for Americans who are already struggling with high fuel prices,” said Andy Su, Senior Transportation Attorney at Environmental Defense Fund. “We’re going to court to oppose this dangerous U-turn away from decades of successful work to make our cars more efficient and less expensive to drive.”

“We’re taking the Trump administration to court for this reckless rollback that prioritizes Big Oil and automaker profits over American families,” said Katherine Garcia, Sierra Club’s Clean Transportation for All Director. “It is unlawful for Trump to turn back the clock on fuel-efficient cars forcing drivers to waste more money on gas and communities to breathe toxic air. The Sierra Club is proud to stand with our coalition partners in defending our right to cleaner, more affordable vehicles.”

“The Trump administration is steering us toward cars that burn more gas to travel the same miles, draining family budgets along the way,” said James Crowley, senior attorney at Conservation Law Foundation. “As the needle drops toward empty, more grocery and rent money goes into the tank, while more pollution fills the air we breathe. We’re taking this administration to court because families can’t afford to be steered backward.”

“With gas prices at historic highs, Trump picked the worst possible time to roll back federal mileage standards,” said David Pettit, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity’s Climate Law Institute. “Oil companies will profit from less efficient cars, but drivers will take a hit to their wallets and our kids will breathe dirtier air. We’ll all pay the price for more tailpipe pollutants spewing everywhere from playgrounds to wild places. We’re asking the courts to put a stop to this callous giveaway to Big Oil and Big Auto.”

text:
An electric utility serving Western Kentucky counties is telling the state regulator it anticipates keeping its existing coal-fired and natural gas-fired power plants open beyond 2050, a projection amid state and federal efforts seeking to boost fossil fuel-fired power.

On Tuesday, Owensboro-based Big Rivers Electric Corporation filed a new integrated resource plan before the Kentucky Public Service Commission, detailing the utility’s future plans for power plants, electricity transmission infrastructure and the direction of its future electricity demand.

Such plans are required to be filed by Kentucky electric utilities before the commission every few years, detailing how the utility will provide an “adequate and reliable” supply of electricity to meet future consumer and industrial demands at the “lowest possible cost” generally at least over a 15-year outlook.

Big Rivers Electric Corporation’s newest plan projects a future where, instead of retiring and replacing its existing fossil fuel-fired fleet, it instead makes “reliability” investments into its 40-year-old coal-fired D.B. Wilson Generating Station in Ohio County and its natural gas-fired turbines at its Robert D. Green Generating Station in Webster County.

The utility wrote that “preserving and improving the existing dispatchable fleet produces lower-cost portfolios and stronger reliability and resilience than retirement and replacement strategies.”

The utility, which also receives solar power and hydropower through contracts, said it would add additional renewables as it was “economically justified.”

Energy sea changes

The plans also provide a window into the decision-making process of utilities amid a sea change of federal regulation of coal-fired and natural gas-fired power plants. The Biden administration had sought to force such plants, particularly coal-fired power plants, to cut down on pollution including nearly all of climate-warning greenhouse gas emissions.

The Trump administration within the past two years has now moved to reverse the Biden-era power plant rules including weakening rules on toxic air pollution and repealing limits on greenhouse gas emissions. The administration has praised the rollbacks as steps to stop past Democratic-led efforts to “destroy” coal and natural gas. The New York Times reported last month an industry group for coal-fired power plants pitched the idea of using emergency powers to keep coal-fired power plants operating to the Trump administration.

An attorney with the environmental legal group Kentucky Resources Council who is familiar with Big Rivers Electric Corporation’s past utility plans told the Kentucky Lantern he’s heard from utilities in the past that the uncertainty, from administration to administration, of what fossil fuel and energy regulation will look like in the future is costly.

“Uncertainty drives costs up. They can’t plan for a future where they don’t know what they’re going to have to do,” Gary said, who’s been critical of Trump-era regulatory rollbacks.

In an emailed statement Wednesday afternoon, Big Rivers Electric Corporation spokesperson Stephanie McCombs said the utility doesn’t comment on active cases before the PSC. The state regulator will eventually issue a report that analyzes and critiques Big Rivers’ plan.

While not the preferred outlook chosen by the utility, Big Rivers did model a scenario under which “increasingly stringent carbon regulations drive significant reductions in U.S. power sector emissions.” Under that scenario, the Wilson plant would be retired in 2032 and the utility would invest in 800 megawatts of wind power, 400 megawatts of natural gas-fired power and 200 megawatts of battery storage.

The utility wrote that given Trump administration repeals of greenhouse gas emission rules are being litigated, the “long-term regulatory outlook remains uncertain” and “future carbon regulation remains a plausible risk”.

But the utility also highlighted the role that laws passed by the GOP-controlled state legislature play in making it significantly harder for utilities to retire fossil fuel-fired power plants.

Gary, whose group has also been critical of the state laws, said it limits utilities’ ability to choose a “least-cost option” for ratepayers while meeting electricity grid reliability requirements. State lawmakers have defended the laws as ensuring state energy policy is “driven by facts, reliability, and long-term competitiveness.”

“How do you plan for an uncertain future where you also know that you have a limited choice of options due to state law makes it very difficult, I can imagine, for planners?” Gary said.

The utility also noted in its plans that there’s been significant interest from prospective data center developers seeking power and electricity infrastructure. The utility has received 31 inquiries from data center customers, but only five of those inquiries have advanced beyond “initial stages.”

Two of those five projects are a planned hyperscale data center at a former aluminum mill in Hancock County and a planned hyperscale data center at the federally-owned Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant in McCracken County. Three other projects are “confidential development prospects” that “have not progressed beyond preliminary evaluation.”

text:
WASHINGTON — California, Michigan and two dozen other states, cities and counties on Friday, Oct. 2 sued the U.S. Transportation Department over its decision this week to finalize sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards in a win for gas-powered vehicles.

The revised standards from President Donald Trump's administration seek to reverse former President Joe Biden's push toward greater fuel efficiency and electric vehicles. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the new rules violate requirements that the standards be set at the maximum feasible level. A separate lawsuit was filed challenging the new rules by a coalition of environmental and consumer groups.

The new standards will cut the cost of new vehicles but increase fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions for decades, according to the department's estimates.

The states — which also include Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York and Washington — as well as the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and Denver and several environmental groups, filed suits in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

The Transportation Department finalized rules on Monday, Sept. 28 requiring a fleetwide average of 34.9 miles per ⁠gallon by 2031, down from 52.5 miles per gallon under Biden. Environmental groups said the 2031 vehicles would be less efficient than the current fleet.

The states said the Trump administration is ignoring the presence of millions of EVs, "leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the 'maximum feasible' fuel economy level."

U.S. drivers have paid sharply higher fuel prices since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran at the end ​of February.

The states said the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration "tries to paper over nearly $220 billion in lost fuel savings — money that drivers would have saved at the pump under the previous fuel economy standards, which will instead benefit Big Oil."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy defended the rule, saying the agency would let "auto manufacturers produce the cars that fit families' needs at a lower price."

The Transportation Department said the ​regulation reduces manufacturers' average cost per vehicle to comply by $1,289 but increases fuel costs by more than $1,600 over the ​life of the vehicles. The department said the rule would increase U.S. gasoline consumption through 2050 by 4.6% — about 121 billion gallons — compared to the Biden rules but also boost new car sales.

In 2024, the Biden administration finalized rules to push automakers to build more EVs to meet ​rising fuel-efficiency standards.

The rules will also end credit trading among automakers in 2028, ‌which ⁠previously was a significant source of income for EV manufacturers Tesla Inc. and Rivian Automotive Inc.

Trump has mounted a multipronged effort to make it easier to sell gasoline-powered vehicles and last year scrapped a $7,500 new EV tax credit.

The latest standards also adjust the auto sector's primary gas mileage regulation in ways that could cause shockwaves through the industry. The new rules make it harder for automakers to classify vehicles as trucks — which have ballooned to about 70% of the U.S. new vehicle market — and phase out the buying and selling of credits to achieve compliance. Most automakers lobbied against both of those changes.

Detroit News Washington Correspondent Grant Schwab contributed.

text:

AUSTIN, Texas — The Texas Public Utility Commission (PUC) ruled today that Southwestern Public Service Company (SPS) can proceed with closing its Tolk coal plant near Lubbock and constructing renewable energy and battery storage to provide reliable, clean electricity to Southwest Power Pool customers. While also approving two new gas peaker plants in Texas – with strict cost caps – the PUC’s decision paves the way for significant water savings and enough renewable energy to power about 375,000 homes in Texas and New Mexico, including 1,100 megawatts of wind, 322 MW of battery storage, and 189 MW of solar. (Note: Commissioners take up this item at 4:10 in the video, and discuss Chairman Gleason’s cost cap recommendation.)

STATEMENTS FROM SIERRA CLUB

“Contrary to what the people in power want us to think, there is a common-sense path in Texas to transition away from expensive, dirty, thirsty coal,” said Josh Smith, a Sierra Club Environmental Law Program attorney who has worked on the Tolk plant for years. “Texas doesn’t need coal anymore – even as it prepares for increased demand – and today’s decision clearly shows that. When Tolk closes, it will save abundant water in a drought-prone region, millions of ratepayer dollars, and eliminate millions of tons of harmful pollution every year, making rural West Texas a healthier place to live.”

“These solar, wind, and battery storage projects are clearly the most cost-effective and efficient means of replacing the aging and increasingly expensive Tolk coal plant while also maintaining system reliability, saving scarce groundwater resources, utilizing existing transmission rights, and reducing harmful pollution,” said Cyrus Reed, the Legislative and Conservation Director of the Lone Star Chapter of Sierra Club.

BACKGROUND

SPS (owned by Xcel Energy) first said it would retire Tolk no later than 2032 due to a 2020 agreement with Sierra Club and agreed to study an even earlier retirement based on the plant’s costliness and declining levels of the Ogallala Aquifer, which the plant depends on to operate. SPS then proposed retiring the plant in December 2028, and this summer’s decisions from New Mexico and the Texas PUC confirm a retirement just a few months later, in early 2029. Retiring Tolk has long made sense considering how much water it withdraws from the rapidly depleting Ogallala Aquifer to cool its coal-burning boilers. According to Sierra Club’s new analysis Watts Wasting Texas Water, in 2024, Tolk used 1.2 billion gallons of groundwater. As recently as 2015, the plant consumed 3.3 billion gallons of water in a single year. Renewables use negligible water resources.

The Tolk coal plant is in Sudan, about one hour northwest of Lubbock. Tolk is regulated by both Texas and New Mexico’s utility oversight agencies because it provides power to both states. Earlier this summer, the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission permitted SPS to proceed with construction of the renewable energy and gas plants, while also ruling that it couldn’t receive an early exemption from New Mexico’s renewable energy requirements. It also declined to rule on the company’s request to treat new gas-fired power plants as zero-carbon resources (SPS claimed it would be helping to electrify the oil and gas industry in the Permian) under the state’s Energy Transition Act. For their part, Texas regulators placed capital cost caps on the gas plants, and production expectations on the wind contract.

text:
As the federal government weakens standards, CR data shows that fuel economy is still a major priority as people shop for a new or used vehicle

Survey finds consumers’ concerns about electric vehicles easing, but limited first-hand experience and other barriers to purchase interest remain

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Consumer Reports (CR) today released new survey data showing that fuel economy remains vitally important to prospective buyers of new and used vehicles, even as the federal government finalizes revised, substantially weaker standards for auto manufacturers.

Chris Harto, Manager, Energy Impact at Consumer Reports, said, “Consumers have long told us that fuel economy was important to them, so it comes as no surprise that hybrids are flying off dealer lots as automakers—encouraged by strong fuel economy standards over the past few years—finally start delivering more hybrid options. What is unknown is if automakers continue to respond to strong consumer demand for efficient hybrids, or if momentum slows in the face of weak and toothless efficiency standards.”

The new data comes from a July 2026 Consumer Reports nationally representative survey of 2,124 U.S. adults, which found that fuel economy remains a major priority for Americans shopping for their next vehicle. According to the survey, 94% of people who expect to buy or lease another vehicle say fuel economy is at least somewhat important; about two-thirds (68%) say it is very or extremely important—on par with the results of other nationally representative CR surveys of drivers in 2022 and 2024.

CR’s survey also asked about electric vehicles, and while CR found a modest easing in Americans’ concerns about EVs compared to previous research, this shift has not yet translated into increased consumer interest in purchasing an EV.

On the one hand, there has been a statistically significant decrease in all of the top 5 barriers to EV adoption since a previous nationally representative survey in 2023. Among Americans who are not definite EV buyers, the most common barriers remain charging logistics (57%), range anxiety (51%), and purchase/ownership costs (45%). Also, since 2023, the shares of people who have seen an EV, know someone who owns an EV, or have ridden in an EV have noticeably increased.

On the other hand, the share of those who reported having driven an EV in the past year has improved only slightly since 2023. Specifically, just 11% of Americans reported having driven an electric-only vehicle in the past year. Overall, a quarter of Americans (25%) said they would definitely buy or seriously seriously consider buying an EV if they were to get a vehicle today, but this varies depending on whether they have already driven one. Of those 11% who reported having driven an EV in the past year, 68% say they would definitely buy or seriously consider buying an EV today. Among those who have not driven one, only 20% say the same.

A 2024 CR nationally representative survey of 2,146 US adults found that half of consumers would be interested in test-driving a battery electric vehicle while car shopping, even if they were not ready to buy one, indicating an opportunity for dealers to potentially capitalize on.

“Time behind the wheel doesn’t guarantee that someone will become interested in an EV, but it’s a necessary step for them to realistically consider purchasing one,” Harto added. “People can’t reasonably be expected to adopt a new technology that they have very limited hands-on experience with, especially something as important to their daily lives as their car.”

Because most shoppers’ hands-on experience with battery electric vehicles remains limited, and concerns around charging, range, and cost remain significant, Consumer Reports advises that fuel-efficient hybrids can be good options for many drivers. The growing availability of hybrid models can provide a practical stepping stone for car buyers and lessees, allowing consumers to enjoy savings at the pump with lower barriers to entry.

text:
Are we starting to see a transition from small-scale pilots of electric trucks to serious volume orders? Tesla has been booking some sizable orders for its Semi, and Harbinger recently announced a 2,000-truck order from FedEx.

The latest news comes from Workhorse—a company that has weathered the ups and downs of the commercial EV industry for a decade.

Gateway Fleets, a California-based provider of turnkey electric vehicle and charging solutions for commercial delivery operators, has placed a follow-on purchase order for 200 of Workhorse’s W56 electric step vans.

Gateway will purchase the vehicles through Kingsburg Truck Center, a California truck dealer, and plans to lease them to its customers, most of whom are independent last-mile package delivery providers. Deliveries are expected to begin in the second half of 2027, and to continue through 2028.

Gateway bundles purpose-built electric trucks with charging infrastructure, fleet support and depot access through flexible financing arrangements designed to enable operators to acquire EVs without large upfront capital expenditures. Gateway currently operates depots in Southern California.

“Gateway’s innovative model will help unlock wider adoption of electric trucks through its bundled pricing that eliminates the two biggest barriers to widespread adoption: the higher upfront cost of the vehicle and the added capital required to build out the charging infrastructure,” said Scott Griffith, CEO at Workhorse.

The W56 step vans available through Gateway are Standard Wheelbase (178-inch) configurations with a 210 kWh battery, 1,000 cubic feet of cargo space, a payload of 10,000 lbs and a range of 150 miles. The van features a purpose-built composite body, an ergonomic driver environment, and a platform optimized for last-mile delivery.

All W56 models are produced at Workhorse’s manufacturing facility in Union City, Indiana, which is capable of producing up to 5,000 vehicles per year on a standard shift. To date, Workhorse has delivered more than 1,100 vehicles.

“Getting the truck on the road is only the beginning. Keeping operators moving takes the right combination of infrastructure, service, and support,” said Jamie Miller, Chief Revenue Officer of Gateway Fleets. “Workhorse has brought us an innovative vehicle, while Kingsburg provides the service expertise and support our customers need in the field. Gateway brings those pieces together with the charging infrastructure and capital to make electrification work for operators.”

title: A new solar park brings more clean energy to Michigan
description:
Now, that commitment is helping bring more clean energy to Michigan.
This Thursday, DTE, Ford, and community leaders celebrated the new Cold Creek Solar Park, the first solar park made possible through Ford’s participation in MIGreenPower.
Cold Creek Solar can produce 100 megawatts (MW) of clean energy, which is the equivalent of powering more than 27,000 homes.
“Through our voluntary MIGreenPower program, this project is bringing more clean, renewable energy to Michigan’s electric grid,” said Ryan Thomas, director, Renewable Energy Development, DTE Energy.
Projects like Cold Creek Solar Park will help Michigan reach its goal of getting 60% of its energy from renewable sources by 2035.
text:
In 2022, Ford Motor Company joined DTE’s MIGreenPower program and agreed to the largest renewable energy purchase in the United States. Now, that commitment is helping bring more clean energy to Michigan.

This Thursday, DTE, Ford, and community leaders celebrated the new Cold Creek Solar Park, the first solar park made possible through Ford’s participation in MIGreenPower.

Cold Creek Solar can produce 100 megawatts (MW) of clean energy, which is the equivalent of powering more than 27,000 homes. This is an important step toward Ford’s goal of using 100% carbon-free electricity by 2035. It also helps DTE move closer to its goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions.

“Through our voluntary MIGreenPower program, this project is bringing more clean, renewable energy to Michigan’s electric grid,” said Ryan Thomas, director, Renewable Energy Development, DTE Energy. “It strengthens our diverse generation portfolio, supports the local community through jobs and tax revenue, and helps participating customers, like Ford, meet their own sustainability and clean energy goals. Most importantly, it shows what is possible when strong partners work together.”

Programs like MIGreenPower help speed up the development of renewable energy projects across the state. These projects bring more clean energy to the power grid while also creating local jobs and generating tax revenue for communities.

“Cold Creek Solar Park is now delivering on the promise we made when we broke ground on this project — clean, reliable energy for our Michigan operations and for the communities where we build our vehicles,” said Amir Mirshahi, director, Energy Infrastructure & Engineering, Ford Motor Company. “Projects like this strengthen the resiliency of the grid that our plants, our employees and our neighbors all depend on. Investments like Cold Creek are about more than meeting our own sustainability goals — they’re about being a good neighbor and a strong partner to the communities that support us.”

Today, DTE operates 20 wind parks and 36 solar parks across Michigan. Together, these facilities generate enough clean energy to power nearly 1 million homes; but there is still more work ahead. Projects like Cold Creek Solar Park will help Michigan reach its goal of getting 60% of its energy from renewable sources by 2035.

As DTE celebrates the new Cold Creek Solar Park and the addition of 100 MW of renewable energy to the grid, the company looks forward to building even more clean energy projects in the future.

title: A six-acre field of solar panels hanging 3.6 feet over an Oregon pasture grew 38 percent ...
description:
Oregon State University measured it at a solar array on its own land in Corvallis, and the pasture under the panels grew 38 percent less forage than open ground next door.
The trial ran in spring 2019 and spring 2020, and the results came out in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems on April 29, 2021.
The authors, for what it’s worth, believed nobody had run a livestock trial under solar panels before theirs.
Roughly half of each solar paddock sat in full shade under the glass, and the other half sat in the partly shaded alleys between the rows.
Add it all up across the study, and the solar pastures produced 38 percent less forage than the open ones.
text:
Solar farms have a bit of a bad reputation in farm country. Often, it boils down to one objection you’ll hear at pretty much every county land-use meeting: the panels kill the grass, and land that grows panels stops growing food.

Hearing that, yeah, it sounds bad. The first half of that objection is true, which probably adds to the feeling of concern if you’re on the outside. Oregon State University measured it at a solar array on its own land in Corvallis, and the pasture under the panels grew 38 percent less forage than open ground next door.

However, it’s the second half that falls apart. The university also ran lambs on both pastures for two springs, weighed them on the way in and on the way out, and found that the lambs on the thinner grass gained pretty much the same weight. The trial ran in spring 2019 and spring 2020, and the results came out in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems on April 29, 2021.

Sure, it’s years ago, but I’m dragging it back into the light because the argument it speaks to is still being had in county meeting rooms all over the US. And from the looks of things, hardly anyone in those rooms has read it. The authors, for what it’s worth, believed nobody had run a livestock trial under solar panels before theirs.

So what do the panels actually do to the grass?

The array sits on about six acres west of the Corvallis campus. OSU’s facilities people call it the 35th Street array, while the researchers call it the Rabbit Hills solar farm. No matter what you wanna call it, it’s a real 1.4-megawatt power plant, with 5.4-foot-wide panels tilted 18 degrees toward the south, rows nearly 20 feet apart, and the low edge of the glass hanging 3.6 feet off the ground.

That layout splits the ground into stripes. Roughly half of each solar paddock sat in full shade under the glass, and the other half sat in the partly shaded alleys between the rows. The alley grass kept up with the open pasture reasonably well. The grass directly under the panels came in thin and patchy, and the lambs made it worse by crowding into the shade and trampling whatever grew there. Add it all up across the study, and the solar pastures produced 38 percent less forage than the open ones.

So the county-meeting crowd is right about the grass, I’ll give them that. But are the animals that eat the grass noticing the difference? That’s exactly what this trial was built to answer.

The lambs came out even anyway

The test animals were weaned Polypay lambs, a workaday American breed, about two and a half months old at turnout. Each side got a core group of nine lambs every spring, plus spare animals the team shuttled in and out to keep grazing pressure matched to the rate at which the grass was growing. (Grazing researchers call that put-and-take, and it’s the standard way to keep a pasture trial honest.)

Man, what I’d give to be paid for a test where I get to eat all day…

In spring 2019, the solar-side lambs gained 0.265 pounds a day against 0.262 pounds in the open, and in 2020 it was 0.196 against 0.203. Neither gap comes close to being statistically significant. The team even ran a heavier stocking rate on the solar side in late spring 2019, and the gains still held.

How do you get the same lamb out of a third less grass?

According to researchers, the shaded forage was measurably richer. Grass growing in shade stays leafier and greener for longer, and the lab work showed higher crude protein in the solar pastures both years. Less salad, but more of the good stuff in every bite, so the smaller supply fed the lambs just as well. That’s the authors’ interpretation of their own data, and I’d add the obvious hedge: it held on this grass, in this climate, with these animals. Nobody should promise a ranch in a Texas summer the same arithmetic.

The lambs spent their downtime parked under the panels

The behavior logs are, frankly, my favorite part of the paper, as someone who wants to picture lambs frolicking and eating in a field. When the lambs were loafing or chewing their cud, they were under the glass more than 96 percent of the time. When they were actually grazing, they split their day about evenly between the shade and the alleys. In short, the flock treated the panels as furniture.

There’s a water angle too, though it’s easy to oversell. In the hot back half of spring 2019, lambs in the open field drank about a fifth of a gallon more per head per day than the ones with shade. In spring 2020, the difference didn’t show up at all. So shade saved water in one of the four measured periods. It’s a modest effect, but it’s still an effect.

The grazing pays the array back in kind. Sheep working the rows keep vegetation down in strips a mower can’t reach, and around hardware a mower shouldn’t touch, the same logic that has a Virginia outfit breeding a 1,000-pound cow specifically to fit a solar farm. Under panels, the animal is the maintenance plan.

The whole thing is still a working power plant

It’s interesting to see innovations leave the paperwork behind and do some real-world implementation. The 35th Street array is the largest of five ground-mounted arrays that have been feeding OSU’s buildings since 2013, and the university doesn’t even own the hardware. Tesla installed, owns, and operates it, and OSU buys the electricity under a power purchase agreement at a rate below what the local utility charges.

The money side of the grazing came out nearly flat. The researchers put the return from spring grazing at about $423 an acre per year in open pasture and $416 under the panels ($1,046 versus $1,029 per hectare in the study’s own figures), a 1.6 percent haircut before you count a single kilowatt-hour. Study co-author Serkan Ates, an animal scientist at OSU, argued in the university’s announcement that a setup designed for production “would likely get even better numbers.” By the team’s land-use math, running sheep and power off the same six acres roughly doubled what the land produced compared with doing either alone.

Germany has started writing that kind of measurement into its rulebook, with a yield threshold farmland has to keep hitting after the panels go up. The US mostly hasn’t, which is why a two-season trial with actual scales remains one of the better data points an American county has to argue from.

What I can’t tell you is whether a flock is out there this fall. OSU hasn’t published follow-up lamb numbers from this site, and the 2021 announcement said lead author Alyssa Andrew was moving on to test three different pasture mixes under the panels. So treat the animal side as a completed experiment rather than a running operation.

title: Electrification momentum growing amid Hormuz crisis, and more top energy stories
description:
Top energy news: Electricity’s ‘increasingly central role’; Latin America’s critical minerals potential; How the energy transition has become a four-part challenge.
For more on the World Economic Forum’s work in the energy space, visit the Centre for Energy and Materials.

But in increasingly digitalized and interconnected energy systems, that separation is beginning to look like the problem itself.

text:
This round-up brings you key stories from the energy and materials sectors over recent weeks.

Top energy news: Electricity’s ‘increasingly central role’; Latin America’s critical minerals potential; How the energy transition has become a four-part challenge.

For more on the World Economic Forum’s work in the energy space, visit the Centre for Energy and Materials.

1. IEA: Electricity ‘taking centre stage amid Hormuz shock’

Electricity is taking an “increasingly central role” in economies across the globe, creating new opportunities for nations to strengthen energy security, boost competitiveness and cut emissions, a new report from the International Energy Agency (IEA) says.

The analysis – prepared at the request of COP31 President Turkey to inform energy transition discussions at the recent United Nations General Assembly in New York – examines the speed of electrification across different regions as countries consider adopting a global electrification target of 35% of final energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% today.

It finds that faster deployment of available technologies could cost-effectively meet 33% of the world’s final energy consumption by 2035, bringing the 35% goal within “striking distance”.

Meanwhile, energy prices at current levels amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis would make even more of the world’s energy consumption economical to electrify. Many countries are exploring how they can leverage electrification to further reduce dependence on imported fuels while lowering emissions.

The report's authors find “substantial potential” in all regions to increase electrification rates above today’s levels cost-effectively. Realizing this potential will require scaling up investment in generation and grids and implementing smarter, more flexible power systems.

Clean power technologies have rapidly scaled over the past two decades, led by solar PV – deployment of which approached 600 gigawatts in 2025 alone, more than 10 times the annual level a decade earlier.

But as noted in the latest Energy Transition Index from the World Economic Forum (WEF), meeting demand will require a “much closer alignment between the speed of electrification and the capacity of systems to absorb it”.

2. World Economic Forum report: Greater collaboration is key to advancing Latin America’s minerals potential

Latin America has the potential to become a leading supplier of the minerals needed for batteries, power grids and digital technology, a new Forum report finds. But catalyzing greater value calls for stronger collaboration across the region.

In production terms, the continent accounts for about 40% of mined copper production and around 30% of mined lithium production globally.

But according to Advancing Latin America’s Critical Minerals Potential, a white paper created in collaboration with McKinsey & Company, the region has the opportunity to better convert its “exceptional geological endowment” into sustainable growth, quality jobs and shared value.

Currently, 62% of critical minerals exported from Latin America and the Caribbean are raw materials, while only 38% are processed goods. This gap highlights an opportunity for countries to generate greater industrial and economic value where competitive advantages exist in refining, processing and downstream manufacturing, the report says.

Factors such as rising geopolitical competition and growing demand for resilient supply chains are driving interest in diversified sources of critical minerals, creating an opportunity for Latin America to strengthen its position in the sector and attract long-term investment.

For some countries, this may mean strengthening upstream productivity. For others, it may mean moving into processing, technology and manufacturing – and doing so will likely require advances in technology and cluster-based ecosystems that connect resources, infrastructure, talent and investment.

With the scale of investment and capabilities needed to build end-to-end critical minerals ecosystems often too large for individual countries to meet, regional collaboration is increasingly important, the report says.

Loading...

3. News in brief: More energy stories from around the world

Takeaways from the 1st Energy Forum held at the World Economic Forum: Leaders from across the global energy ecosystem met in Geneva this month to explore the forces reshaping the future of energy and work on pathways to create growth, strengthen resilience and accelerate innovation.

With attendees from 35 nations with strong representation from Europe, North America, China and additional representation from India, MENA and ASEAN, discussions focused on how to meet rapidly growing energy demand; build secure, sustainable and affordable energy systems against a backdrop of global uncertainty; and how countries and companies can stay innovative and competitive in this fast-evolving energy landscape.

Key takeaways included the energy transition’s four interconnected challenges of security, sustainability, affordability and competitiveness; the importance of regional and public-private cooperation in driving innovation and resilience; and the critical role of grids and flexibility in determining the pace of energy-system growth.

The overall message was clear: The next phase of the energy transformation is less about identifying individual technologies and more about integrating infrastructure, markets, and policy through collaboration so that innovation can be deployed at scale.

US energy storage record: The United States installed a new quarterly record of 18.9 gigawatt-hours of battery energy storage systems in the second quarter of 2026, according to figures from the American Clean Power Association and Wood Mackenzie.

Italy approves nuclear power law: Italy’s parliament gave final approval to a government plan to restart nuclear power generation in the country, almost 40 years after a referendum led to the closure of its reactors. Italy wants to deploy advanced modular reactors to help decarbonize industry and strengthen energy security.

Germany plans fossil fuel exit: Germany’s cabinet has greenlit a roadmap to phase out coal, oil and gas by 2045. Electric vehicles and heat pumps will form a key part of the transition. France and the Netherlands have recently adopted similar national roadmaps.

South Korea seeks to diversify supply: South Korea is aiming to cut its reliance on crude oil from the Middle East to 50% by 2035, from 70% today, as it moves to diversify energy supplies amid disruption caused by the Iran war. Under its 10-year natural resources security plan, the country adjusted its stockpiling plan for crude oil, targeting an expansion of about 20 million barrels by 2030.

US proposes Gulf energy investment: The US has proposed investing $5 billion in a new fund to help countries in the Middle East rebuild energy infrastructure that has been hit by the Iran war and reduce their reliance on the Strait of Hormuz to transport oil and gas, the Wall Street Journal reports. Countries including Saudi Arabia and the UAE are among the nations discussing the plans.

Construction begins on major Kenyan oil refinery: Ground has been broken on a $16 billion oil refinery in Kenya aimed at lowering East Africa's fuel costs and creating energy self-sufficiency across the region by replacing imports of refined products. East Africa has been hit hard by rising fuel prices amid the Iran war.

4. More on energy from Forum Stories

Energy Nexus Playbook: Energy systems are deeply interconnected with economies, nature and agriculture, but these connections are often misunderstood or managed poorly. To identify approaches to bridge the gap, the WEF’s Global Future Council on Energy Nexus convened experts from across regions and sectors. The Energy Nexus Playbook collates insights from the council through a 'systems lens' on five priority sectors facing imminent vulnerabilities across their value chains: clean energy; food and agriculture; artificial intelligence and data centres; shipping and ports; and fresh and used water. Read more.

Rethinking resilience: For most of the past decade, energy companies have treated cyberattacks, physical sabotage, extreme weather and geopolitical disruption as distinct problems. But in increasingly digitalized and interconnected energy systems, that separation is beginning to look like the problem itself. Energy resilience has to be built in by design across public and private actors – not added on after something has already gone wrong, argues Prajeev Rasiah, SVP and Regional Director, Northern Europe, Energy Systems, DNV.

To learn more about the work of the Centre for Energy and Materials, contact Ella Yutong Lin: ellayutong.lin@weforum.org

text:
DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1m fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.

The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.

Floodlight sent technical data about the generators – obtained through public records requests – to a Rutgers professor and a former EPA air division chief.

“Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers department of environmental sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data.

NOx are a dangerous group of smog-producing gases linked to asthma, heart attacks and even premature death. It was “the most important air pollutant in the US that affects most people”, Jin said.

Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounded like an airplane in the back of her house.

“What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said.

The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit – a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit.

Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution” and the fleet’s potential emissions are “well over the regulatory threshold for a new major source”, said Buckheit.

New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source”. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods – all before construction can even begin.

That didn’t happen at DataOne, despite the operation being capable of emitting more than half the NOx put out by New Jersey’s entire power sector.

“That is basically offsetting some of the air quality improvements [regulators] have achieved for decades,” Jin said.

DataOne did not respond to Floodlight’s emissions analysis. Instead, its spokesperson sent the same statement as they did in response to NJDEP’s decision to fine them, saying the company was “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution and have the necessary approvals in place for this solution”.

The company disagrees with NJDEP’s determination and had argued the generators did not require permits – but plans to apply for them now.

A Microsoft spokesperson wrote that “we expect our suppliers and partners to meet all applicable legal and regulatory obligations” and the company was working with DataOne “to support their completion of the facility’s transition to its permanent long-term power solution”.

In press releases, New Jersey regulators said the tractor-trailer-sized generators were detected during a 29 July 2026, site inspection but not during an earlier visit in December. However, the fleet was there to find, according to a letter DataOne later sent NJDEP.

The letter, obtained by Floodlight through a public records request, notes the generators first began to arrive in July 2025. Sixteen generators started operating in October 2025, with another 16 brought online in early February. By June, all 62 had been fired up.

By the time state inspectors noticed them, the unpermitted fleet had collectively run for more than 46,000 hours in total, according to the letter.

“How did 62 generators get installed and operated and nobody did anything until now? That blows me away,” Leone-Vespa said. “Clearly somebody wasn’t doing their job.”

A spokesperson for NJDEP declined to comment.

For many Vineland residents, confirmation that DataOne’s generators have been running for nearly a year is a bittersweet vindication. Locals have reported strange noises emanating from the facility for months, with more than 100 noise complaints submitted to the Cumberland county department of health since March, according to records obtained by Floodlight. Many of the complaints list generators as the suspected source.

“They’re just running these monster generators. And they think, by right, they have every ability to do so at the expense of anyone else,” said local flower farmer Michael Atkinson.

Atkinson’s family has been farming a patch of land beside the datacenter for more than 70 years. He said DataOne was “one of the richest and worst neighbors that I have ever had to deal with in my entire life”.

During a Vineland town hall meeting in late January, DataOne’s chief executive, Charles Beyney, told residents that his datacenter would be “polluting less than a farm”.

“I’m too French to just kill my lungs, the lungs of your kids and all the community around us,” he told the crowd.

Beyney confirmed during that speech that DataOne was running generators, and he said NJDEP was aware – the agency had been at the site that same morning and was “on us big time”.

While the generators may have evaded state regulators for almost a year, local officials knew about them for much longer.

A City of Vineland inspection activity report noted that “phase 1 generators are online” in early February. And in May, a Cumberland county health department inspector responding to a noise complaint visited the site and reported that the source of the noise appeared to be two generators, “possibly more”.

The inspector noted that the noise “exceeded night-time violation”.

As part of the record fine levied against DataOne, the state is mandating the company apply for and obtain the required permits or cease operations, but is allowing them 45 days to do so, according to a NJDEP spokesperson.

During that time, regulators are allowing the facility to continue running the generators – which are capable of emitting more than four tons of NOx in nearby neighborhoods each day.

“I just don’t understand how this is being allowed,” Leone-Vespa said. She hopes independent air monitoring can help protect her community in the future. Until then, she has little faith in New Jersey regulators to watch out for them.

“It’s like they don’t care about the residents.

text:
This piece is part of a series of articles examining where 2026 Southeastern candidates for state and federal offices stand on key energy and climate issues, like data centers and energy costs.

Note: The Southern Alliance for Clean Energy does not support or oppose candidates or political parties. Links to reports, candidate websites, and outside sources are provided as citizen education tools.

In this blog post, we examine the policies and positions of Byron Donalds, the Republican Party candidate running for Governor of Florida. Also in this series, we profile Democratic candidate David Jolly. Election Day is November 3.

Byron Donalds is a former U.S. Congressman who represented Florida’s 19th Congressional District. Prior to serving in Congress, he served in the Florida House of Representatives from the 80th district. He graduated from Florida State University with a Bachelor’s Degree in finance and marketing.

Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency

In an article published in the Fort Myers News-Press in 2023, Byron Donalds writes, “Many ‘green energy’ promoters fixate on an energy grid centered around wind and solar to ‘reduce fossil fuel consumption’—but such an energy future is a dishonest fantasy.” He goes on to say, “Today, the United States theoretically has enough wind and solar capacity to power an electric grid, and sufficient battery technology to store power for when the wind isn’t blowing and when the sun isn’t shining. Yet, there are many considerations that complicate this wishful energy opportunity and must be explored further in green alternative energy discussions.” He concludes by saying, “In sum, I’m not opposed to wind turbines and solar panels, but if we seriously want an affordable, reliable, secure ‘green energy’ grid, we cannot rely on the dishonest fantasy of utilizing spiky intermittent energy sources like wind and solar. Instead, we must embrace nuclear power and include nuclear in future green alternative energy discussions.”

Regarding energy efficiency, in 2024, Donalds voted for H.R.6192, the Hands Off Our Home Appliances Act, which would effectively block the Department of Energy from setting appliance efficiency standards that reduce energy use.

Climate Change

Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) has consistently dismissed the connection between climate change and human actions as well as between climate change and extreme weather. In the summer of 2023, during broiling heat waves, Donalds was asked by reporters if he believed in the underlying correlation between the ongoing heat waves and climate change; he replied, “No, I don’t.”

During a hearing before the House Committee on Financial Services, titled “Protecting Investor Interests: Examining Environmental and Social Policy in Financial Regulation,” on July 12, 2023, Donalds stated, “I know a comment was made about belief in anthropologic global warming as it used to be called, or climate change, or whatever you want to say it is. No, I actually don’t agree with that statement. I don’t think that ‘science’ is settled. I think it’s interesting in 2023 that people talk about settled science unless you’re talking about physics and the laws of gravity and other things that are tried and true over many, many decades. But no, the science is not settled on that.”

Donalds has introduced legislation to allow Wall Street firms to exclude environmental, social, or political (ESG) shareholder proposals. And in 2021, he voted against the “Climate Risk Disclosure Act” that would require companies to disclose risks from climate change as part of a suite of corporate transparency bills, calling the legislation “liberal fascism.”

According to the Center for American Progress, which tracks fossil fuel contributions to Congress members, Donalds received $150,071 from anti-climate money during his tenure in Congress.

Electric Transportation

Donalds has criticized policies to transition the federal postal fleet to electric vehicles, arguing they “make no sense at all”.

Energy Justice

Donalds has engaged in localized, consumer-focused relief. He partnered with Florida Democrats on a bipartisan initiative to demand that Florida receive its fair share of Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) funding to assist at-risk seniors and low-income families facing high utility costs.

Energy Affordability

State regulators set a permitted return on equity (RoE) for the biggest utility companies, which is a guaranteed profit they are allowed to earn from ratepayers. Utilities make money building new infrastructure because that guaranteed profit is baked into new building costs. To address accountability and affordability, David Jolly, Donald’s opponent, has proposed a cap on RoE. On the campaign trail at a press conference in Tampa, Donalds dismissed the idea, saying, “One thing we know about when a government decides to institute caps, what you actually end up getting is worse service, because what ends up happening is you don’t have the capital that goes into invest into the future of your electric grid. So, a cap might sound good politically, but it’s a terrible solution.”

Tracking from the nonprofit group CLEO Institute found that Donalds has received $1.79 million in campaign contributions from Florida’s major power utilities while in office. He is the state’s second-highest recipient.

High-Risk Energy: Nuclear, Coal, Methane Gas

Byron Donald’s congressional record makes him one of the most pro-nuclear advocates in Congress, and he promotes nuclear energy as the primary driver for lowering utility bills, ensuring baseload reliability, and strengthening national security.

In September 2025, Donalds voted in favor of the Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable (GRID) Power Act. The bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to prioritize dispatchable power projects (fossil fuel projects) over intermittent power projects (renewable energy projects).

Data Centers

Donalds has received $5 million dollars in support from data center developers and is making the case that Florida needs AI and data center infrastructure to stay competitive and power economic growth. He has also stated that these facilities need to be in Florida, and has advocated for “small modular nuclear reactors and micronuclear reactors” and “closed-loop water filtration systems” as part of the builds. He was recently quoted as saying, “There ain’t no bans coming” in reference to opponents who want to stop AI data centers.
