text:
Ahead of the midterm elections, Congress is scrambling to show that it understands voter concerns about AI data centers and their potential impact on electricity rates. But answering the question of how much of those costs will be shouldered by residential utility customers is surprisingly difficult to answer.

That uncertainty is at the heart of a growing fight on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers advance competing proposals aimed at protecting ratepayers in a debate that often belies the complexity of the underlying economics.

On Capitol Hill this week, Republicans have been trying to push through the Ratepayer Protection Act, sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. The bill would have state utilities consider holding "large-load" customers responsible for the increased costs.

Husted is in a heated reelection campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2024. Brown has made Husted's past support of data centers in Ohio a major campaign issue. The bill easily passed the House in September with strong bipartisan support.

Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer opposes the measure, saying its protections for ratepayers are voluntary. Instead, Schumer is promoting the GRID Savings Act, a similar bill authored by New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich, which he says has more teeth.

Several other data center and AI-related bills are at various stages in the legislative process.

The cost of AI is showing up in customers' bills

The question of how much of the energy and grid costs are being borne by ratepayers is a complicated one and has no universal answer, experts tell NPR. They say it varies by utility and state, but that in the end residential electricity customers will pay for a share of the AI buildout.

By one estimate, Maryland customers, for example, pay somewhere around $168 to $216 more per year on their electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom.

"We're talking tens to hundreds of millions of dollars [of infrastructure] that are being built by these local utilities," says Connor Waldoch, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Grid Status, which focuses on making electricity-market data easier to access and understand. "In many cases, it is just ultimately going to end up in customers' bills."

Tracking the impact of data center growth on residential bills isn't easy, however. How much of the increase is passed on to residential customers and when, depends on utilities' power-purchasing contracts, retail rates and regulatory decisions about who pays, according to Lucy Qiu, a professor at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland.

PJM is a regional transmission organization that coordinates the electricity grid and wholesale power market across 13 states and the District of Columbia. It supplies power to Northern Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world. PJM's Independent Market Monitor estimates that data centers have cost their 67 million ratepayers about $29 billion over roughly the past two years.

"Everyone pays those costs," says Ari Peskoe, director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative. "They're spread across the region to every business and resident that has an electricity meter."

How to determine who the grid infrastructure benefits?

Data center growth can push up wholesale costs of energy by increasing demand. This determines how much generating capacity utilities and regional grid operators need to secure, Qiu says. There are also costs with building new power lines, substations and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the grid. Determining how much of that exclusively serves data centers — and how much also benefits other customers — is part of the difficulty in determining who gets the bill, she says.

"It really depends on the scale of the upgrade and also how utilities are doing the accounting of that different share, whether it's being used solely by the data centers or also being shared by other customers," Qiu says.

No "single, clean number"

Even so, "a single, clean number" that applies nationwide is just not possible, Harvard's Peskoe says, because "a lot of the data about how much particular data centers are paying is hidden behind non-disclosure agreements."

Those NDAs have become a major sore spot on the local level, as residents opposed to new data centers call out local officials for the secrecy that has surrounded many deals. A study last year by the University of Mary Washington found that NDAs had been signed in 80% of Virginia localities where there were existing, approved or proposed data centers.

In an email to NPR, Jeremy L. Slayton, a spokesman for Dominion Energy, which serves Loudoun County, Va., home to about 250 data centers, said, "We recover costs for distribution and transmission infrastructure from customers."

"These assets are core to the reliable electric service we provide our customers. All costs we recover from customers are reviewed and approved by the Virginia State Corporation Commission," he said, referring to the independent state agency that regulates public utilities.

Added costs of building out in a hurry

There is still another factor at play, University of Maryland's Qiu says. The data center industry is in a hurry and waiting for new power-generation technologies doesn't seem to be in the cards. As a result, to meet the demand, utility companies will likely need to opt for less efficient power plants and those costs will be passed onto consumers over time, as well.

One other consideration is optics, Waldoch of Grid Status says. Big customers like AI data centers pay less per kilowatt hour for power than residential customers do. Think of it as a volume discount. In the current environment where 70% of Americans are worried that data centers will increase their electricity bills, Waldoch says, "If you're saying, hey, this data center is actually paying a lot less for electricity than you are, even though it matters much less to them ... it's not like that's palatable for a lot of people at this point."

Benefits of the AI buildout

But not all price increases in recent years are linked to data centers, Qiu says.

"The fuel cost ... is a very important factor," she says and some of those new substations and power lines were going to need to be replaced anyway due to things like extreme weather events.

Qiu also notes that the U.S. power grid needs upgrades to accommodate higher demand for things like electric vehicles. The AI boom "can accelerate the upgrade of the grid infrastructure," she says.

text:
The electric sedan is finally getting vehicle-to-load (V2L) functionality, but you'll need to move out of the country to get one.

Tesla has updated the Model 3 EV overseas.

The electric four-door sedan now finally comes with vehicle-to-load (V2L) functionality via an adapter.

The infotainment screen is also larger, and the headliner color has been switched to black.

The Tesla Model 3 is getting a few improvements, but American customers will have to wait a little longer, as the company has decided to start the rollout outside of the U.S.

Model 3s delivered starting in the fourth quarter of this year will finally be capable of exporting energy from their high-voltage batteries through a feature called vehicle-to-load (V2L). It's something that EVs from other automakers have been equipped with for years, and now Tesla has added it to the Model 3.

The feature will only be available on cars sold in China, Australia, New Zealand, and South Korea, but other countries are expected to get in on the action in the following months. By using an adapter that plugs into the vehicle's charging port, owners can power tools, appliances, or camping equipment with a combined power draw of up to 2.2 kilowatts.

What's more, all Model Y versions sold in these countries are also getting V2L functionality. In the United States, the only Tesla vehicles that come with V2L out of the box are the Cybertruck, Model Y Premium, Model Y L, and Model Y Performance. The entry-level Model Y is left out, but that's probably going to change after Tesla ramps up the distribution of the updated hardware that enables bidirectional charging.

The Tesla Outlet Adapter for cars with a Type 2 charging port.Photo by: Tesla

In the U.S., all Model Y EVs that can export power need an adapter that plugs into the mobile charger. With it, the car can deliver up to 2.4 kW through a pair of outlets.

Getting back to the Model 3, its central infotainment screen is also getting a minor update, with a 16-inch touchscreen with an improved pixel density replacing the 15.4-inch display of the outgoing model. Tesla didn't say it out loud, but it's probably the same 16-inch screen that made its way into the Model Y earlier this year.

Other changes include a black headliner, a new Zen Grey seat color, and 19-inch Dark Nova wheels.

It's worth noting that retrofitting V2L to an older Model Y or Model 3 is not possible, as the hardware that enables the function differs. That may change in the future, but for now, it's a no-go. What's more, owners won't be able to power an entire house off the V2L adapter, as its power output is quite limited, but it should be enough to power a fridge and some essential gear during an outage.

description:

IRS Notice 2026-15 does not require full supply chain tracing where a manufacturer has no reason to doubt its suppliers’ certifications.

text:
MACR compliance is often framed as a sourcing problem: identify inputs linked to prohibited foreign entities, find alternative suppliers, and restructure procurement accordingly. The evidence from current supply chains suggests this framing understates the difficulty. The constraints that bind are not simply about where materials come from. They extend through the regulatory frameworks that govern how compliance is measured, the capital and trade dynamics that limit how quickly alternatives can scale, and the technology dependencies that persist even after physical sourcing has been redirected. These constraints interact and compound in ways that make the compliance challenge considerably harder to resolve than geography alone would suggest.

4.1. Regulatory and Traceability Constraints

Even when manufacturers can identify PFE-linked inputs, translating that knowledge into MACR compliance is far from straightforward. The framework creates friction in three dimensions: attributing costs to their PFE or non-PFE origin, tracing constituent materials through supply chains where transparency is limited, and unwinding contractual arrangements that were lawful but now trigger PFE exposure. Together, these constraints complicate compliance in ways that go beyond conventional supply chain restructuring.

4.1.1. Cost Attribution

Manufacturers must now assign precise cost percentages to each constituent material and trace those costs to their PFE or non-PFE origin. For LFP battery cells, this is harder than it sounds. Many of the highest-risk inputs, particularly graphite and cathode active material, are sourced from suppliers that are vertically integrated across multiple processing stages (IEA 2025a). Consider a Chinese supplier that mines and processes graphite before selling it to a US cell manufacturer. The MACR rules require the manufacturer to determine what share of that input’s cost is PFE-attributable, and when the entire processing chain sits within a single PFE-linked entity, the answer is, effectively, the whole thing.

Now consider the cell manufacturing level. Here, the manufacturing equipment and process know-how represent a significant share of production costs, and much of that equipment is sourced from PFE-linked suppliers (MarketsandMarkets 2024). Unlike physical materials, equipment costs are not direct material costs under the Section 45X Eligible Component MACR calculation, which excludes labor and capital. However, if that equipment is supplied under agreements that grant the supplier effective control over production parameters, it can trigger PFE status for the manufacturer itself, which shifts the compliance problem from the MACR numerator to the entity-level PFE definition.

4.1.2. Traceability

Battery-grade graphite, one of the highest-risk inputs, is mined, purified, refined, and coated before it enters a cell. At each stage, the material may change hands, cross borders, or be blended with material from other sources (IEA 2025a). The MACR framework requires that constituent materials be traced to the entity that mined, produced, or manufactured them; under the Certification Safe Harbor rules, that tracing is performed link by link, with each supplier certifying to its customer. For graphite, however, the processing chain is rarely transparent even to its participants, so certifications may rest on claims about the material’s origin no one in the chain can verify. And because graphite processing is overwhelmingly Chinese, a cell manufacturer presented with a clean certification for graphite of uncertain origin may have precisely the “reason to know” that makes reliance on it a potential violation (Benchmark Minerals 2026).

The same challenge applies to electrolyte and separator production, where Chinese firms dominate not just supply but also the intermediate chemical inputs. A US manufacturer purchasing electrolyte from a nominally non-PFE distributor may still be exposed if the underlying lithium salts or solvents were processed by a PFE, and the Certification Safe Harbor provides limited relief if the manufacturer has reason to know the certification is inaccurate. IRS Notice 2026-15 does not require full supply chain tracing where a manufacturer has no reason to doubt its suppliers’ certifications. However, because Chinese firms dominate processing, any given input is likely to have passed through PFE hands somewhere upstream, and a manufacturer can rarely confirm that it did not.

4.2. Trade Exposure and the Limits of Substitution

To assess trade exposure, this section examines how the United States can find new sources for LFP inputs, who controls the supply flows that reach US manufacturers, and whether exposure to PFE supplies is narrowing or widening over time. The relevance of these questions to MACR compliance is direct. Because the MACR measures the share of an input’s direct material cost that is not attributable to a PFE, and attributes that cost to the entity that produced the material rather than the country where it was mined, the structure of trade flows determines how each input enters the compliance calculation (Bellile et. al 2026; RSM US 2026).

4.2.1. Feasibility of Substitution

Substitution feasibility is deeply uneven across the supply chain, and the variation maps onto cost share in a way that compounds compliance risk.

US manufacturers obtain raw lithium predominantly from Chile and Argentina, both non-PFE jurisdictions, and this pattern has been stable since at least 2015 (USGS 2025b). Here, trade exposure aligns naturally with MACR requirements because the dominant suppliers are not prohibited foreign entities.

For processed lithium, the picture is more complex. China is the world’s leading exporter of lithium hydroxide. It processes Australian and South American raw material into battery-grade compounds for export to the United States, Japan, and South Korea (Statista/WITS 2024). Even when the raw material source is non-PFE, then, the refining stage creates PFE exposure, since the direct cost of the refined input carries Chinese attribution.

Graphite and LFP cathode active materials are the least tractable—and also the inputs where substitution would most improve the material assistance cost ratio. China accounts for 68–92 percent of US battery-grade graphite imports and more than 98 percent of global LFP cathode material production (IEA 2025a). One case illustrates this clearly. BTR New Material Group, a Chinese company headquartered in Shenzhen, is the world’s largest producer of battery-grade graphite anode materials. It planned to produce graphite from factories in Indonesia and Morocco, which US firms saw as viable non-PFE sources (Taulli and Busby 2025). However, in January 2025, the US Department of Energy designated BTR as a PFE and extended that ruling to its overseas subsidiaries (Taulli and Busby 2025), meaning the location of production does not matter if the company itself remains under Chinese government control (Shihua 2024). Since the MACR attributes material to the producing entity rather than the country of manufacture, third-country production by a PFE-controlled firm yields no compliance benefit (Miller and Chevalier 2026).

4.2.2. Ownership Stakes and Control of Supplies

Geographic origin statistics consistently understate China’s effective control, and the gap falls precisely where the MACR is most sensitive. Because China imports raw lithium carbonate from Chile and Australia (as well as using some material extracted domestically), refines it into battery-grade lithium hydroxide, and exports the processed product, US manufacturers may appear to import from non-PFE sources in the upstream while remaining PFE-exposed at the midstream. China exported $6.22 billion of lithium hydroxide in 2023, with Chile a distant second (Statista/WITS 2024). Ownership compounds the processing concentration, since Chinese firms have acquired roughly $5.6 billion in lithium mining assets across Chile, Canada, and Australia, and China controls more than 60 percent of global lithium refining capacity (WEF 2023). For cathode material and graphite, this control extends across both production and the specialized processing steps. That places a cell’s highest-cost inputs and its most PFE-concentrated inputs in the same position.

4.2.3. Dynamic Trends in Input Sourcing

China produces 77 percent of the world’s graphite, the United States imports 42 percent of its requirement from China, and domestic production in the United States is negligible (S&P Global Mobility 2024). At battery grade, the concentration is higher still, since China accounts for 97 percent of global anode output, and US imports of active anode material from China reached approximately $374 million in 2023, roughly 67 percent of all such imports (USITC 2024). China controls about 75 percent of natural graphite production and dominates spheronization and purification downstream, so relocating extraction does not relieve the processing bottleneck (Crux Investor 2025). The extension of IRA credit eligibility for EVs containing Chinese graphite through the end of 2026 was itself an acknowledgment that no alternative supply exists at scale (Park et al. 2025).

The policy response to this concentration illustrates the limits of trade measures as a substitute for diversification. In early 2026, the Department of Commerce finalized antidumping and countervailing duties on Chinese active anode material that, combined with prior tariffs, brought the effective rate to roughly 160 percent, raising the landed cost of Chinese anode material from about $3,700 to $9,300 per tonne, against domestically produced material at roughly $5,400 per tonne before the Section 45X production credit (Benchmark 2025a). These measures improve the relative cost position of non-PFE producers, but they do not create qualifying supply where none exists at scale, and in the interim they raise input costs for US cell manufacturers that have no alternative source. The same dynamic appears in China’s use of export controls as leverage. In October 2025, China announced licensing requirements on a range of graphite and lithium products effective that November, then partially suspended stricter verification measures for graphite shipments to the United States through late 2026, a sequence that eased immediate friction while leaving the structural dependence and the threat of renewed restriction intact (Crux Investor 2025; Fastmarkets 2025).

Lithium runs in the opposite direction. Chile and Argentina supply roughly 94 percent of US raw lithium imports, with China below 3 percent across the period (USGS 2024). The advantage is partial, since a major share of Australian and Chilean ore is still refined in China before reaching US manufacturers, triggering PFE attribution at the midstream even though the mine itself is non-PFE (WEF 2023).

4.2.4. Trade Exposure Takeaways

The evidence across those three dimensions points to a single conclusion: trade exposure in the LFP supply chain is not uniform but concentrated, and it is concentrated in the hardest places to change. Inputs that can be re-sourced through existing trade relationships, most notably raw lithium, are also the inputs that already contribute little PFE exposure, so diversifying them does little to raise the overall material assistance cost ratio. In contrast, the inputs that would move the ratio most, particularly graphite and cathode active material, currently lack viable alternative suppliers at scale, limiting the feasibility of friendshoring strategies. Critically, even processed lithium carries significant hidden PFE exposure because China dominates global refining. Trade policy has so far been unable to close this gap, since tariffs have raised the cost of Chinese material without creating qualifying supply. Export controls are a further concern related to dependence on China. Friendshoring can reduce MACR risk at the raw material margin, but the binding constraints lie in the middle of the supply chain—where substitution so far is structurally limited and where these inputs also carry the greatest cost weight. Substantial new non-PFE investment will be needed to increase substitution possibilities.

4.3. Capital and Scale Feasibility Constraints

Capital and scale feasibility is here defined as the ability to mobilize finance to develop an MACR-compliant LFP battery supply chain. Mobilizing capital is a primary indicator for mineral capacity development, especially in supply chain bottleneck sectors.

4.3.1. Upstream

The United States primarily imports lithium and copper from countries that have signed a free trade agreement (FTA), mainly Australia and Peru, but less than 15 percent of graphite—critical for LFP batteries—comes from FTA countries (OEC 2026). Replacing the current PFE-dominated supply chain will be challenging for some time to come. China has the world’s largest reserves of natural graphite, at 1 million metric tons, followed by Brazil, at 740,000 metric tons (see also Statista 2026b). China is also the largest producer of graphite in the world. Although investment in critical minerals as a whole is required for a resilient supply chain, investments in bottleneck areas like graphite are especially needed to reduce PFE dependence.

Recent US commitments have moved in that direction. Federal agencies have used a mix of Department of Energy loans, Development Finance Corporation equity, and Export-Import Bank financing to support upstream capacity, both domestically and in allied jurisdictions, with graphite a recurring target; Table 6 compiles the major commitments. The Graphinex and Syrah projects illustrate a pattern of particular relevance to the MACR: each pairs a mine outside the United States with anode or processing capacity intended to serve the US market, so the compliance question is about the ownership and structure of the integrated chain rather than the location of the mine alone.

Allied producers are expanding as well. Canada and Australia have both increased public investment in mineral capacity in recent years, with a growing share directed toward projects that combine extraction with processing and manufacturing rather than mining alone; other FTA partners, including Peru, have announced large projects (Leary et al. 2025; Radwin 2026). The direction is toward greater capital mobilization across FTA partners.

Upstream investment is expanding, but MACR compliance also depends on reducing cost exposure to PFEs. Continued reliance on PFE-dominated minerals such as graphite means that even increased upstream investment may not be sufficient to meet MACR thresholds.

4.3.2. Midstream

Midstream processing remains a major bottleneck in the supply chain, and dependence on PFE-linked processing capacity directly lowers the material assistance cost ratio. Even when upstream minerals are sourced from allied countries, continued reliance on PFE-dominated refining and processing infrastructure can prevent manufacturers from meeting the required thresholds. Developing non-PFE-linked processing capacity will require significant investments. One estimate suggests that the cost of additional lithium processing in the United States just to cover demand for EV manufacturing could be up to $25 billion, depending on the EV adoption scenario (Whitlock et al. 2025). That in turn is only a fraction of the future total US demand for processed lithium.

Processing capacity outside China continues to lag. Like graphite processing, lithium processing in the United States is constrained (Cai and Nakano 2026). However, many processing projects that would increase capacity are planned. There has also been an uptick in support for upstream projects combined with midstream processing. Syrah’s graphite processing facility in Louisiana is one such integrated supply chain strategy. Though indicative of movement toward integrating processing with mining, these efforts remain limited in scale relative to global demand.

Several spherical and synthetic graphite facilities are under development in the United States, including projects by Graphite One (Alaska), Westwater (Alabama), and Syrah Resources (Louisiana), with planned capacities ranging from roughly 7,500 to more than 45,000 t/yr. Synthetic graphite production is also scaling up, with NOVONIX and Anovion expanding capacity, though total output remains modest relative to projected demand. Anovion’s planned Georgia facility targets 40,000 tonnes, and Novonix’s Chattanooga plant targets 20,000 tonnes (Syrah Resources n.d.; Anovion Technologies 2023; Novonix Limited 2026; US DOE 2022b). In lithium, the Silver Peak (brine) facility remains the only operating site, but multiple projects are under development, including Piedmont Lithium (hardrock spodumene), Thacker Pass (clay), and Tonopah Flats (clay), with planned production reaching up to 40,000 tonnes per year in initial phases. More planned projects are listed in Table 6.

Canada and Australia are similarly advancing investments, particularly in refining and processing capacity linked to upstream resource bases. In Canada, Metals Australia is planning a large-scale graphite refinery in Quebec, and Rock Tech Lithium is developing lithium conversion capacity in Ontario (Metals Australia 2026); Rock Tech Lithium 2026). Additional initiatives, including projects by Focus Graphite, are focused on advancing graphite processing and materials development in Canada.

Outside China, South Korean producers represent the most credible near-term source of LFP cathode active material. However, commercial-scale LFP production remains limited and is only beginning to emerge. L&F, a South Korean company, is expected to become the first company to mass-produce LFP cathodes outside China. POSCO Future M, another South Korean company, is developing additional capacity through a joint venture with China’s CNGR (L&F Plus 2026; POSCO Future M 2025). Because POSCO’s production relies on a Chinese partnership, it remains uncertain whether its output will qualify as non-PFE under MACR rules. Meanwhile, most other Korean cathode manufacturers, including LG Chem, remain focused on nickel-based chemistries rather than LFP (LG Chem 2025). Consequently, despite growing investment, non-Chinese LFP cathode active material production is likely to remain constrained in the near term, limiting manufacturers’ ability to source qualifying cathode materials. This challenge is compounded by a broader shortage of domestic cathode production capacity in the United States, where projected demand is expected to significantly outpace supply by 2030 (Reinsch et al. 2024).

4.3.3. Downstream

As of 2026, the United States had 12 operating battery manufacturing plants and 23 under development (Plante et al. 2026). In addition, since 2019, 180 primary component facilities have been planned for development (Cai and Nakano 2026). Based on production data from 29 US-based facilities, current and planned capacity stood at 210 GWh in 2024 and was expected to reach approximately 820 GWh by 2032 (Bui and Slowik 2025). However, since early 2025, many U.S. battery manufacturing investments and projects have been cancelled (Cai and Nakano 2026). As of early 2026, at least $22 billion USD in battery manufacturing investments have been cancelled (Gearino 2026).

Forge Nano and Group14 Technologies have announced a collaboration to produce lithium-ion battery cells in the United States using a predominantly domestic supply chain, combining advanced materials with US-based manufacturing infrastructure (Forge Nano 2026). Innovation in manufacturing processes is also supporting industry scale-up. Major automakers, such as Toyota Motor North America, continue to invest in production capacity (Pulsenics 2026). However, battery facilities have faced delays or closures. For example, GM and its partner, Samsung SDI, indefinitely paused construction on their planned EV battery plant in New Carlisle, Indiana (Barta 2026).

Farther downstream of manufacturing, the EV adoption market is an important piece of the supply chain. A slowdown in the EV market has been driven in part by rollbacks in tax incentives and subsidies, combined with uncertain outlook on policy stability. Despite the slower EV market, recent developments in EV deployment and related technologies reflect continued expansion in end-use demand alongside emerging new applications. New Flyer of America secured additional orders from the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority for hybrid and battery-electric buses (NFI Group 2026).

At the same time, battery applications are expanding beyond traditional transportation. SK On is exploring supply agreements with a US defense contractor for batteries in AI-powered unmanned submarines, though large-scale deployment is not expected before 2028 (Korea Bizwire 2026). There are also some efforts to strengthen capacity in battery recycling. Aqua Metals and American Battery Factory have announced plans to evaluate colocating a lithium-ion battery recycling facility alongside battery manufacturing operations in Arizona (Aqua Metals 2026).

Downstream manufacturing has seen increasing investment, but further growth will require sustained support and it remains dependent on upstream and midstream inputs that shape overall cost structures. Because MACR compliance is determined by the composition of material inputs, downstream expansion alone cannot ensure compliance if earlier stages of the supply chain remain exposed to PFE-linked sources.

4.3.4. Capital and Scale Feasibility Takeaways

US LFP supply chain capacity development projects reflect a mismatch between current investment patterns and the requirements of the MACR framework. Table 6 lists recent supply chain capacity investments. Although investments are being made across the supply chain, the downstream and upstream segments are comparatively well funded, but the midstream is comparatively underfunded. Midstream investment will be critical if downstream projects are to succeed in the MACR framework. Moreover, if upstream projects are well funded but midstream capacity remains underdeveloped, mining projects might have to ship ore out to be processed internationally, complicating MACR compliance. Projects that link upstream and midstream capacity development can help breach such supply chain gaps.

Many of the projects were only recently announced, and the ecosystem is in flux. Achieving a resilient and fully compliant LFP supply chain will require not only expanded mining investment but also sustained long-term financing, coordinated industrial policy, and targeted support for processing and refining capacity in the United States and allied countries. Investment transparency would help support research and analysis for effective investments and policymaking.

text:
Meta is expanding its Richland Parish artificial intelligence (AI) data center to a planned 5 gigawatts of computing capacity, while questions involving new power generation, utility regulation, water use, environmental permitting, tax incentives and public disclosure have all made headlines. Tulane Law’s Haley Gentry, Assistant Director of the Institute for Water Resources Law & Policy, looks at what these centers mean for communities and the state. Gentry is an environmental lawyer who focuses on water resource management and public decision-making processes.

AI data centers are arriving in Louisiana on a scale we haven’t seen before. What makes Louisiana attractive for these projects, and what does a facility of this size actually mean for the state’s economy, energy, water and other infrastructure?

Through recent legislative measures and statewide economic incentives, Louisiana’s government has signaled that data centers are a priority sector for economic growth. There are multiple major proposed data center projects in Louisiana – Meta’s Hyperion facility in Richland Parish, multiple Amazon Web Services data center campuses in the Shreveport/Bossier City area, Anthropic in West Feliciana Parish, and a recently announced large data center project in Rapides Parish.

Many factors contribute to the current economic development trends across the state. For one, Louisiana has promoted large tracts of industrial and agricultural land across the state already zoned for development. In 2024, Louisiana lawmakers passed generous sales and use tax exemptions related to data center equipment. Entergy’s interest in expanding its power generation capacity in connection with data centers played a crucial role in early negotiations with Meta. Most recently, utility regulators are using an expedited process to review utility applications for new generation to serve large load customers.

Louisiana is likely considered an ideal region because of its access to energy infrastructure and transit corridors, like the Mississippi River. Plus, there is a historical abundance of water resources, making Louisiana attractive from a development standpoint, as water shortages are constraining economic activity, especially in Western states. However, there is much more to the water question, which we can get to in a moment.

AI data centers pose risks to the grid due to the amount of power they require. They also can create localized water issues. It is difficult to encompass the wide range of potential impacts (primarily related to water usage, but also from a water quality perspective) because the type of cooling system employed, energy source, surface versus groundwater sourcing, and whether facilities rely on municipal water services, or are using on-site private water wells, can alter the inquiry. Even more, it is critical to acknowledge tradeoffs in various types of cooling technologies. Evaporative cooling is the most water-intensive type of cooling process and poses the biggest risk to local water supplies. Air cooling uses a minimal amount of water but much more energy. So, if coal, gas, or nuclear generation is used to power a hyperscale data center, water is still being consumed, just in a different location.

Some data centers are tapping into municipal water services. While it certainly would be easier to get a sense of water usage if going through a public entity, this raises a set of related concerns. First, the physical infrastructure needed to deliver larger volumes of water (and the effluent water that would be treated after it’s used for cooling) strains aging drinking water infrastructure. Moreover, there is something to be said about using pretreated municipal potable water for cooling rather than domestic use.

What are the biggest legal and regulatory issues surrounding the development of AI data centers — and where does authority lie among federal, state, and local governments?

There are many critical questions about the regulation of artificial intelligence technology itself and what role governments should play in the actual oversight and use of the large language models as they are integrated into all facets of society and what protections workers/creators will have into the future. Yet in terms of governance, a key legal issue is the widespread use of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) between officials and developers. In Louisiana, even elected officials, members of the cabinet, and the governor himself signed NDAs with Meta. That means that there has been little public input or comprehensive review across agencies or between jurisdictions.

There is not much by way of federal regulatory oversight for data centers. Most of the land-use and water resource decisions fall primarily to state agencies, and various federal review processes that come into play for components of data centers (pipelines and transmission lines through waters and wetlands) have been expedited in response to several of President Trump’s executive orders.

A key legal issue is the protection and management of water resources. Water for public use is the highest priority under both state law and U.S. Supreme Court jurisprudence. However, Louisiana currently does not have the frameworks in place to comprehensively manage water resources and prevent conflicts. For example, a company relying on groundwater can drill wells on their site, register the wells and estimated withdrawal rates with Louisiana’s Department of Conservation & Energy (LDCE), but from then on does not have to monitor, report or restrict usage absent a formal emergency declaration for that region or aquifer. However, LDCE is currently taking steps toward groundwater oversight through an ongoing rulemaking, but more robust authority will likely be needed to ensure local water supplies are not compromised.

Local government authorities are primarily focused on zoning and land use decisions. Most municipal entities have the authority to designate what kinds of economic and commercial activities are compatible with existing land uses. For example, the New Orleans City Council passed a temporary moratorium on data centers to give regulators time to understand what controls and oversight might be needed.

Power may be the biggest issue. Data centers can require enormous amounts of electricity and significant new generation and transmission infrastructure. Legally, how do regulators determine who should pay for that expansion, and what protections exist to keep those costs from being shifted to ordinary ratepayers?

Regulation of utilities is unique from other industries. In Louisiana, this authority lies with the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC), a constitutionally created body. In Orleans Parish, that authority lies with the New Orleans City Council. Three new gas plants in connection with the Meta facility were approved in August 2025. Last fall, the Governor signed Executive Order 25-102, aimed at expediting project development for large load users. In response, the LPSC adopted an expedited review process called the “Lightning Amendment” which it is now using to review Entergy’s application to build seven additional gas plants in connection with the Meta project.

While LPSC’s decisions often have major implications for natural resources and the environment, they are not robustly considered in the LPSC’s review process, which is primarily focused on ensuring the utility is acting prudently and that future costs will not negatively impact customers. Environmental considerations come up through integrated resource planning, but resource planning does not dictate whether LPSC will approve or deny a proposal. Rather, it functions as a periodic planning and disclosure mechanism.

There have been efforts to address concerns about protections built in for ratepayers, but they are not absolute. Meta has agreed to finance the initial energy infrastructure at around $2.6 billion under a 20-year contract, but the life cycle of these facilities can be upwards of 30 years. Despite another executive order from the governor in the summer of 2026 seeking to alleviate concerns about ratepayer protection, local communities and affordable energy advocates on the whole do not feel that key concerns surrounding this unprecedented buildout have been addressed. The Lightning Amendment does not require Entergy to prove this proposal is the “least cost option” to meet Meta’s power demands, which is typically part of the review process.

What environmental questions should Louisiana be considering as data centers expand, from water use and air emissions to the construction of new natural-gas generation? Are existing environmental laws and permitting processes equipped to handle projects of this scale?

There are real concerns that there are not sufficient environmental safeguards in the approval process for facilities and associated energy infrastructure. Hyperscale AI data centers differ from previous kinds of data centers and cloud services. Because there is little federal oversight of data centers themselves, classic environmental statutes, like the National Environmental Policy Act, do not apply to the whole project, reducing understanding of the potential impacts and limiting opportunities for public input. Further, because most of the air pollution impacts, especially for data centers relying on fossil fuels, are offsite, they are not fully encompassed when studying the data center itself.

These gaps in regulatory oversight are very important to address, as Louisiana does not have more protective environmental standards beyond minimum federal requirements. States have primary oversight over water supply and allocation. Most states have assumed authority from the EPA to administer water pollutant discharge permits under the Clean Water Act. Louisiana’s Department of Environmental Quality is responsible for issuing water pollution discharge permits and any air permits associated with new power plants. In addition, gaps in water information regarding data centers and power generation should be studied. LDCE has authority over data collection for water resources. Currently, there is not a regulatory framework for surface and groundwater withdrawals, but users must register groundwater wells with LDCE and estimate daily water use. It is only in specially designated areas that groundwater use might be monitored or restricted.

The governor recently signed Executive Order 26-078 in an attempt to further expedite environmental review and permitting. Though the extent of this executive order and what the governor and state regulators can actually accomplish toward that goal without accompanying legislation or additional federal rollbacks is unknown, it indicates a lack of concern for public health and ecological needs amid emerging industrial developments.

Environmental and health impacts from the dramatic increase in pollution burdens associated with natural gas power generation cannot be overlooked. The LPSC has already approved three new gas plants for Meta’s project, and in December, it will decide on approval of seven additional gas plants. It certainly raises questions on the status of renewable energy goals and efforts to diversify the grid to improve energy security.

Louisiana is offering significant incentives to attract data centers, with the promise of local investment and jobs. From a legal and public-policy standpoint, what should the state require in return, and how should we measure whether these projects ultimately benefit Louisiana communities?

Louisiana lawmakers could consider measures that improve transparency surrounding water use and disclosure mechanisms. Initial investments in energy and water infrastructure upgrades by these companies are certainly welcome, but little is known about the long-term costs that could be pushed onto local ratepayers. Other states have slowly begun adopting measures requiring companies to disclose water and energy demand for proposed facilities and subsequent reporting measures once operational. Moreover, policymakers need to consider decommissioning. What happens if some of these projects are scrapped mid-construction? What happens when a data center reaches the end of its life cycle? Without additional standards or rules in place, this could create real problems for local governments and adjacent communities.

To ensure economic development incentives align with sustainable natural resource management, legislators and policymakers could consider a robust interagency review or consultation process, as well as limiting what information can be protected under NDAs as confidential business information, like water use for cooling. These kinds of measures would provide more access to information for decision-making, as well as help restore public trust between officials and their constituents. There is also a conversation to be had about who can sign NDAs and how expansive they can be, particularly when it comes to elected officials at state and local level.

Lastly, and though unrelated to environmental measures, legislators could consider strengthening the enforceability of commitments on data center companies to hire locally to help to ensure that project benefits flow to local Louisiana communities rather than remote or out-of-state workers.

This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Amazon has signed a 20-year power purchase agreement with Constellation Energy to expand and improve Maryland’s sole nuclear plant, which is also the state’s largest source of clean energy, the companies announced Wednesday.

The tech giant and the energy producer said the agreement will allow for over $3 billion in Maryland infrastructure, including renovations at the 1,790-megawatt Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center. The deal will also enable around 190 MW of new generating capacity, expected to come online between 2030 and 2032.

Constellation — the largest producer of clean energy and largest nuclear energy company in the United States — said in the Sept. 30 release that the investment and revenue certainty from the PPA will allow it to relicense the nuclear plant for another two decades. The company said the extension will allow for the development of new clean energy power plants at the site and enhance Maryland’s supply of carbon-free energy.

Dive Insight:

Through the agreement, Amazon will receive 690 MW of power from the nuclear plant, including the 190 MW uprate.

The tech and e-commerce company has also entered a separate retail supply agreement with Constellation to support its operations in the 13-state PJM market, according to the release. PJM is the largest power grid operator in the U.S. and centrally dispatches generation and oversees the movement of wholesale electricity in all or parts of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia and the District of Columbia.

All the electricity generated by the Maryland nuclear plant will flow to the PJM regional grid as usual, Constellation said. The deal demonstrates “how large energy users can support investments in new, reliable generation while strengthening the broader electric system,” the energy company added.

The companies said the agreement will help Amazon manage its energy costs for facilities located in the region.

“Amazon is committed to investing in carbon-free energy to strengthen the grid and benefit the communities where we operate,” Kerry Person, Amazon Web Services vice president of global operations and data center delivery, said in the release. “This long-term agreement with Constellation sustains the continued operation and expansion of Maryland’s largest source of carbon-free energy, supports hundreds of jobs, and brings significant new generation to the regional grid.”

The Calvert Cliffs plant generates roughly 80% of Maryland’s clean energy, producing enough electricity to power approximately 1.3 million homes, according to the release.

Constellation has recently inked deals with several companies that are increasingly turning to nuclear energy to power their operations and make progress on their sustainability goals.

Earlier this year, retail giant Walmart entered a long-term PPA with Constellation that will provide the retailer with nuclear energy, environmental attributes and energy capacity to support its Illinois operations.

title: Pingree Presses Zeldin for Action as EPA Leaves Farmers in Limbo on PFAS-Contaminated Sludge
description:
An extensive state investigation found contamination on more than 50 farms linked to sewage sludge application.
“Without additional action by EPA, farmers across the country will continue to be at heightened risk from PFAS exposure from land application of biosolids,” Pingree wrote.
Please respond to these questions by November 16, 2026: Does EPA intend to finalize the Draft Sewage Sludge Risk Assessment for Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctane Sulfonic Acid (PFOS)?
What are EPA’s next steps to propose enforceable regulatory limits on land application of sewage sludge?
Without additional action by EPA, farmers across the country will continue to be at heightened risk from PFAS exposure from land application of biosolids.
text:
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies, is pressing Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin to stop delaying meaningful federal action on per-and polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) in sewage sludge. In a letter to Zeldin, Pingree warns that EPA’s latest draft guidance fails to provide a clear path toward enforceable protections for farmers, rural communities, and the nation’s food supply. The guidance was issued instead of finalizing EPA’s January 2025 draft risk assessment—which would have been an important step toward restricting the application of PFAS-contaminated sewage sludge, also known as biosolids, on farmland.

“As you and I have discussed at length, PFAS chemicals have been linked to serious health effects, including cancer, reproductive and developmental harms, and weakened immune systems. Maine farmers have had their livelihoods disrupted due to PFAS contamination, which originated in sewage sludge that was spread as fertilizer by farmers who were told by the government that it was safe to use,”Pingree wrote. “Unfortunately, this sewage sludge contained PFAS, leading to contamination of agricultural land, products, and water.”

Maine has been at the forefront of testing, cleanup, and research into PFAS contamination of farmland. An extensive state investigation found contamination on more than 50 farms linked to sewage sludge application. Farmers have lost income, faced threats to their livelihoods, and experienced health problems after unknowingly spreading contaminated sludge that government authorities had said was safe. Yet instead of completing its risk assessment and tightening protections for farmers and rural communities, Trump’s EPA released draft guidance this summer that leaves its regulatory plans unresolved.

“[...] Rather than finalizing this risk assessment, the Agency’s release of Draft Guidance for Reducing Risk from PFOA and PFOS in Biosolids leaves regulatory next steps unclear and farmers in limbo,” Pingree said.

With the public comment period on the guidance scheduled to close October 5, Pingree is calling on Zeldin to explain:

Whether EPA intends to finalize its draft sewage sludge risk assessment for PFOA and PFOS;

What scientific review supports a decision not to finalize it;

How EPA will prevent further contamination and protect farmers from the unique exposure risks created by land application of sewage sludge;

When EPA will propose enforceable limits on land application;

Whether EPA will address PFAS chemicals beyond PFOA and PFOS; and

How EPA is working with the Department of Agriculture to help farmers, ranchers, and rural communities manage PFAS contamination.

“Without additional action by EPA, farmers across the country will continue to be at heightened risk from PFAS exposure from land application of biosolids,” Pingree wrote. “It is critical that EPA takes additional steps to protect our rural communities and food supply.”

The full letter is available here and is copied below.

+++

Dear Administrator Zeldin,

I write to you regarding the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) efforts to reduce risk from per-and polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) in sewage sludge, also known as biosolids. As you and I have discussed at length, PFAS chemicals have been linked to serious health effects, including cancer, reproductive and developmental harms, and weakened immune systems. Maine farmers have had their livelihoods disrupted due to PFAS contamination, which originated in sewage sludge that was spread as fertilizer by farmers who were told by the government that it was safe to use. Unfortunately, this sewage sludge contained PFAS, leading to contamination of agricultural land, products, and water.

Maine is far from the only state in this situation, but we have been on the front lines on testing, cleanup, and research. An extensive state investigation found contamination found on over 50 farms because of sewage sludge. These farmers have had their livelihoods lost or threatened and experienced health problems. This is an issue across the country whether states are taking action or not, and it is imperative the federal government, and EPA specifically, continues to advance research and remediation efforts to protect our food supply and rural economies, including by actively preventing additional contamination.

EPA’s Draft Sewage Sludge Risk Assessment for Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctane Sulfonic Acid (PFOS), released in January 2025, was an important step towards eventual restrictions on applying contaminated sludge to farmland, but rather than finalizing this risk assessment, the Agency’s release of Draft Guidance for Reducing Risk from PFOA and PFOS in Biosolids leaves regulatory next steps unclear and farmers in limbo.

Please respond to these questions by November 16, 2026:

Does EPA intend to finalize the Draft Sewage Sludge Risk Assessment for Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctane Sulfonic Acid (PFOS)?

If not, how is that decision documented, and what scientific review supported that conclusion?

If not, how does EPA intend to prevent additional land contamination and protect farmers specifically from the additional, unique exposure pathways they face from land application of sewage sludge?

What are EPA’s next steps to propose enforceable regulatory limits on land application of sewage sludge?

Does EPA plan to expand its focus beyond PFOA and PFOS to other types of PFAS contamination?

How is EPA working with USDA to help farmers, ranchers, and rural communities manage PFAS impacts in agricultural settings?

Without additional action by EPA, farmers across the country will continue to be at heightened risk from PFAS exposure from land application of biosolids. It is critical that EPA takes additional steps to protect our rural communities and food supply. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,

text:
Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state.

LUBBOCK — A new water tower in Turkey: $3 million. Upgrades for a museum in Stamford: $400,000. A first responders appreciation barbecue in Medina County: $10,000.

These are just some of the public investments data center companies have paid for across rural Texas in the past year.

According to Texas Tribune analysis, data center companies have donated or invested more than $343 million across the Lone Star state for various community needs, including school programs, infrastructure repairs and emergency services. Much of that money has gone to the very communities that have fought against data center development and are seemingly an effort to win over public support through their bottomless bank accounts.

The Texas Tribune reviewed news releases, public meeting agendas and interviewed local officials to understand how data centers are using their money in Texas. Because not every donation is made public, the total — the first of its kind compiled in Texas — is likely an undercount.

Google donated millions of dollars to the Haskell area for its hospital, pregnancy center and other causes. Rowan Digital Infrastructure is giving $38 million to Temple for its water infrastructure, along with more money for STEM Centers at schools in nearby small towns.

Data centers also created community action grants, which are used for recurring investments in the communities they’re building in. Others, such as Google’s Texas Water Impact Fund, provide funds to restore resources that cause concern for Texans or provide direct lump sum donations to both community and state funds.

As data centers move into the state at a rapid pace, Texas communities in mostly rural areas face a fiscal cliff from property tax cuts, inflation and overall economic uncertainty. Over the last year, data center companies have stepped in as a white knight of community investment.

“There is no question that these data centers are an opportunity for rural communities that are living in the margin,” said Suzanne Bellsnyder, an editor and publisher of two Panhandle newspapers and a Substack focused on rural issues. “Most infrastructure resources are paid with tax dollars, and there’s not a ton there.”

It’s not a new strategy. Major corporations regularly invest in communities and make charitable gifts big and small. Oil and gas companies in West Texas, for example, have donated to fire and police stations and hosted back-to-school backpack drives to weave themselves into communities.

Data centers have also capitalized on tax breaks from both state and local governments. A Texas Tribune analysis earlier this year found the state will forgo at least $3 billion in sales tax revenue over the next two years due to the exemption for the state’s booming data center industry.

Because of the negative public perception toward data centers, however, they still have some ways to go. In an August poll from The Texas Politics Project, a nonpartisan research hub focused on Texas government and politics, 57% of respondents said they would oppose the construction of a data center in their communities.

“I hope their intentions are good, and they’re not just trying to buy these communities off,” Bellsnyder said.

Tied into the community

It’s been two years since a tornado struck Temple, a city of just over 96,000 people that lies 70 miles north of Austin. The city was devastated. Hundreds of homes and businesses were severely damaged or destroyed. One of the buildings lost was the beloved Sammons Community Center, where senior citizens could come together for bingo, swimming and meals.

The price tag for the city’s recovery was high — $7.7 million.

Then, Rowan Digital Infrastructure stepped in. The company is developing a $4.2 billion data center campus with six facilities planned in East Temple.

Earlier this month, Rowan announced a $38 million investment in Temple’s public infrastructure, including $25 million to the South Temple Water Infrastructure Capital Program and $10 million for an aquifer storage and recovery program.

As for the Sammons Community Center, city leaders have proposed a $15 million bond to rebuild it. If voters approve the measure, Rowan has promised to put $3 million to help the project. It’s one of many actions that has made Rowan stand out to Tim Davis, Temple’s mayor, particularly since the company is not making money from the town yet.

“To go ahead and invest dollars into the community for a current need is very generous of them,” Davis said. “That tells me they want to work hard to have a positive impact, and they’ve chosen to help the city.”

Gaining public support is an important tactic for data center companies coming to Texas, and one that can’t be ignored. Over the last year, communities all over the state have voiced opposition to data centers coming to their areas — their main concerns being rising electric bills, losing water and housing issues. Some cities have prevented developments from moving forward. For example, a project in East Texas was pulled after community backlash and Lubbock leaders passed a 90-day moratorium on large-scale projects following a citizen-led petition.

Nathaniel Brown, director of public relations for Rowan, admits that integrating into a community hasn’t been an easy task. Brown said Rowan began hosting neighbor dinners every month for residents to talk with the construction team and ask them questions. The company has also held public hearings, open houses and have Facebook pages dedicated to its project updates.

“This development doesn’t happen in a vacuum. It needs to be able to fit into the community’s vision for their area,” Brown said.

Google has used a similar strategy. On top of community meetings, the tech company hosted a dinner in August to announce $6 million for nonprofits in Haskell, Stamford and Rule.

Suzie Shin, manager of data center sustainability programs for Google, said some of their investments are the company’s way of saying they are listening to the public’s concerns. The company has given millions toward major water infrastructure projects, as well as supporting local school programs. Most recently, the company announced a $4.5 million commitment to help Vernon, a town with less than 10,000 residents, fix a leaking pipeline.

Shin said she feels strongly about investing in modernizing water and wastewater infrastructure for the broader community, not just their data centers.

“I think there’s a win-win for communities,” Shin said. “Again, we have employees who live and work there. We are part of the community. It’s a great way to show the value and help improve outcomes, not only for the watershed but for the water users there.”

Bellsnyder, the newspaper publisher and resident in Spearman, said she’s spoken with some of the data center executives who visit the Texas Panhandle. She does think their intentions are to partner with the communities and make them better.

However, she’s still wary because of the boom-and-bust industrial patterns that have become all too familiar for rural Texas. Spearman was built by an oil and gas service company, Bellsnyder said, and when the business left, there wasn’t a long-term plan for the town.

“I don’t want our entire identities to be built around what one company can provide to us,” Bellsnyder said. “We still need to figure out ways to take care of our own business. Nobody likes taxes, but taxpayers will have to be invested in the community.”

Pros vs. cons

When the water tower went out in Turkey, a small Panhandle town of about 275 residents, people were without water for weeks and had to find places in other towns to live temporarily. Lynette Findley, the city manager, said everyone’s known for years that the tower would fail. However, with an annual budget of $500,000, the city had no way to pay for it to be fixed.

After weeks of no water, QTS Data Centers, one of the data center companies in the county, said it would replace it for the city. The cost for the company, which is a major global data center developer, is estimated to be between $3 million to $5 million.

“It was right before major conversations were starting on how QTS could help with our infrastructure,” Findley said. “I joke about it failing at the exact right time.”

For cities and towns facing a budget crunch, data centers are hard to turn away, especially as the Legislature continues to cut their resources. Kevin Hodges, the city manager for Childress, said the more restrictions on cities, the less money they have to put into the city’s needs.

Childress is facing a similar problem as Turkey. The small town of just over 5,834 people has been under a boil-water notice for a month, and the town issued a disaster declaration because of the problems. Local leaders have handed out bottled water to residents the last few weeks, and employees from IREN, one of the two data centers in town, stepped in to help.

“We’ve had some of our employees help distribute water, particularly to folks who might be challenged to get it, or to the health services, and the elderly,” said David Shaw, COO of IREN. “We’ve been in Childress for around four years now, so it was important to us to establish that connection with the community.”

Hodges, the city manager, blames the ongoing drought on their water issues because Greenbelt Lake levels dropped. While people in town blame the town’s water shortage problems on IREN and Lancium, another data center company in town, Hodges says they are helping.

“The fact of the matter is Lancium does not get any water from Greenbelt Lake,” Hodges said. “They get zero, but they’re willing to give us water from their own water wells.”

While Lancium does not take water from the lake, the company does have wells to take water from the nearby Blaine Aquifer. Hodges said Lancium is running a 16-mile pipeline from its campus to the Greenbelt storage tank, and the company will treat and provide the city with 1 million gallons of water a day — all with no cost to the town, Hodges said.

“They’re not taking,” Hodges said. “They’re providing.”

Hodges said the Legislature will look into more property tax cuts and other measures that could cause cities to lose money. That will hurt small towns, Hodges said, but data centers could give municipalities the money they wouldn’t normally get.

Davis, Temple’s mayor, agrees. He said municipalities are also impacted by inflation, and delivering essential services is expensive. However, the tax revenue generated by a data center will allow a city to set its own path financially, Davis said.

“If the ability to raise money is hampered, then those dollars have to come from somewhere,” Davis said. “Or, a community simply delivers less services to its residents. And I don’t think that’s acceptable to them.”

Still, Davis said leaders have to weigh the city’s capabilities and guard against any damage that could happen from a data center moving in.

Findley, the city manager in Turkey, said QTS and Lancium have promised to help with other needs too by providing funds for emergency services and the schools. She said all the contracts are with Hall County — not the city — and they are trying to navigate what has been put in their backyard.

“Data centers get a ton of negative publicity, so I’m sure it is a little self-serving on their end,” Findley said. “But to be honest, I don’t know what we would have done without their assistance.”

Alejandra Martinez contributed to this reporting.

title: Investing in a cleaner, more resilient Southeast Texas - Entergy
description:

Since 2021, Entergy Texas has contributed more than $1 million through our Environmental Initiatives Fund to support environmental projects across Texas.
The Trinity River project is one example of how the Environmental Initiatives Fund is supporting locally driven solutions across Southeast Texas.
These investments build on years of Environmental Initiatives Fund partnerships in Texas.

text:
From restoring wetlands and strengthening coastal resilience to improving energy efficiency and planting more trees in Southeast Texas communities, Entergy Texas is investing in projects that help protect the environment and strengthen the places our customers call home.

Since 2021, Entergy Texas has contributed more than $1 million through our Environmental Initiatives Fund to support environmental projects across Texas. The shareholder-funded EIF, created in 2001, partners with local organizations on projects designed to deliver meaningful environmental and community benefits.

One of those partnerships came to life this spring along the Trinity River in Liberty County.

Entergy Texas provided $20,000 to the Liberty County Office of Emergency Management to support efforts to restore and reclaim wetlands and help manage community cleanup efforts. In April, Entergy Texas employees joined Liberty County officials, first responders and community volunteers for a cleanup along the Trinity River and surrounding riverbank.

Together, volunteers removed nearly two tons of debris, helping beautify the area and protect a waterway that plays an important role in the region.

“Protecting the environment and strengthening our communities go hand in hand,” said Abby Weaver, vice president of business operations and strategy for Entergy Texas. “The Environmental Initiatives Fund gives us an opportunity to work alongside organizations that understand the unique needs of the communities we serve. These partnerships are creating benefits that will last well beyond any single project.”

Pictured: Entergy Texas employees Abby Weaver and Karen Do pick up debris near Trinity River.

The Trinity River project is one example of how the Environmental Initiatives Fund is supporting locally driven solutions across Southeast Texas.

In 2025, the Environmental Initiatives Fund also provided $80,000 to the Montgomery County Food Bank to modernize its HVAC system. The improvements will help the organization use energy more efficiently while continuing its mission of providing food to families throughout Montgomery County.

Another $125,000 investment supported the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation’s Texas Resilience Project. The funding helps leverage federal and private investments to advance nature-based solutions in eastern Texas that can reduce risks from coastal hazards while improving habitat for fish and wildlife.

Entergy Corp. also continued its partnership with the Arbor Day Foundation through the Energy-Saving Trees program. The systemwide initiative helps residential customers plant the right trees in the right places, providing 1,000 customers with free trees while supporting environmental benefits that can grow for years to come.

These investments build on years of Environmental Initiatives Fund partnerships in Texas. In just the last five years, Entergy Texas, through the Environmental Initiatives Fund, has supported projects including coastal and wildlife habitat restoration with the Houston Audubon Society, longleaf pine habitat and resilience work with The Nature Conservancy, monarch and pollinator habitat projects, LED lighting upgrades, electrification projects and an electric transit bus.

While the projects vary in size, they share a common goal: working with organizations that know their communities to create lasting environmental benefits.

Through the Environmental Initiatives Fund, Entergy Texas will continue working alongside local partners to support cleaner, stronger and more resilient communities across Southeast Texas.
