text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) defied political expectations on Wednesday and signed into law a slate of energy-affordability legislation aimed at containing the utility spending that is driving up electricity costs in the Golden State.

Among the bills he signed are two that will boost the use of virtual power plants — aggregations of rooftop solar–charged batteries, EV chargers, smart thermostats, and other controllable devices — as an alternative to costly grid investments and gas-fired power plants.

Newsom’s move drew praise from consumer advocates, clean energy trade groups, and environmental organizations. ​“I’d say we saw today a lot of evidence that Gov. Newsom has really prioritized affordability and accountability to an increased extent,” said Mark Toney, executive director of The Utility Reform Network, a ratepayer advocacy group that sponsored seven bills this legislative session, all of which were passed into law.

That outcome was far from assured. California’s big utilities have opposed legislation that would reduce how much they’re able to spend on capital investments for which they earn regulated profits and recover via the rates they charge customers. The Newsom administration has focused on smaller-bore energy-cost-containment policies in previous legislative sessions, even as critics have argued for more sweeping reform.

Clean energy advocates did not get everything they wanted from this legislative session. Newsom vetoed a bill that would have ordered state agencies to revamp a moribund market for community solar-battery systems — a form of clean energy that many other states have used far more effectively than California has.

Still, the outgoing governor’s choices this year largely align with the public’s increasing frustration over the soaring cost of electricity. Average residential rates charged by the state’s three major investor-owned utilities have risen to roughly twice the U.S. average in the past decade, even as those utilities have reported record profits.

“Governor Newsom is delivering on his promise to bring down electricity costs and clean up climate pollution,” Kat Lockwood, CEO of The Climate Center, a nonprofit think tank, said in a Wednesday statement.

Virtual power plants score big wins

Two bills in particular — Senate Bill 905 and Senate Bill 913, both authored by state Sen. Josh Becker (D) — will create new opportunities for virtual power plants to reduce utility costs.

As Becker explained it in a Wednesday statement, the goal is to take advantage of the ​“millions of batteries, electric vehicles, smart thermostats, and other technologies” that Californians have already bought. Controlling those devices en masse can shift hundreds of megawatts of power demand away from the grid during moments of maximum stress — usually hot summer evenings — that drive an outsize portion of the grid costs that utilities pass on to customers.

SB 913 takes aim at the cost of keeping aging gas-fired power plants online for use during a handful of hours per year. For decades, utilities have been paying customers to turn off air conditioners and other appliances to reduce the need for those ​“peaker” plants.

California has lagged behind other states in making use of these customer-owned resources to achieve this goal. SB 913 instructs the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) and the California Independent System Operator, which manages the state’s transmission grid, to better measure and reward the grid value of these devices.

SB 905 targets another category of costs: the money that utilities invest in their grids to deliver power during those peak hours. All utilities overbuild their grids to meet those peaks, which means much of that capacity is underused most of the time. If they could rely on customers to reduce power use during such moments — or store power in batteries to ride through them — they could avoid some overbuilding.

But utilities need to better assess how efficiently they’re using their existing grids to know what’s possible. SB 905 instructs the CPUC to start requiring utilities to measure and report this data. That’s a first step toward discovering where VPPs or other technologies could improve utilization at a lower cost, and how regulators could reward utilities for using the tech rather than paying for traditional grid upgrades.

Newsom hasn’t been friendly to VPPs in recent years. He vetoed three VPP bills last year, and his administration has demanded successive funding cuts to the state’s premier VPP program, which may leave it unable to keep operating next year unless the legislature and the next governor can quickly agree on a way to fund it.

“We’re kind of shocked that he signed both bills,” Becker said in a Wednesday interview. But ​“as we build out these distributed energy resources, and have them in more and more people’s homes, it just makes sense to help them out to help the grid” by paying them for the services their devices can provide. ​“And if they can’t deliver in a cheaper fashion, they won’t be used.”

Brad Heavner, executive director of the trade group California Solar and Storage Association, agreed that Newsom’s approval of these VPP bills is a step forward. But he also cautioned in a Wednesday statement, ​“Implementation of the bill at the CPUC under the next governor will determine whether customers see lower bills.”

Going wide on checking rising utility costs

SB 905 isn’t just a VPP bill. It also contains a host of utility cost-containment measures, many of them building on SB 205, another Becker bill enacted last year.

Both pieces of legislation look to rein in the return on equity, or the amount of profits that utilities can collect, on one of their biggest costs: their massive investments in wildfire prevention and mitigation. They also order utilities to borrow more money to pay for a larger share of their grid investments, which can offset a portion of their profit-earning capital expenditures.

Becker said California’s big utilities were ​“very opposed” to these provisions. But with public anger over energy costs on the rise, ​“it’s a huge sign to the public that we can get something done that works on fundamental utility economics and get it signed by the governor.”

Last year’s SB 205 also ordered state agencies to create a ​“transmission accelerator” program that could use state-backed bonds to pay for a portion of utility transmission grid projects. Last month, Newsom signed Assembly Bill 192, which officially funds that effort with $325 million collected from a $10 million climate bond package passed by voters in 2024.

California’s utilities have tens of billions of dollars of transmission grid expansions underway, but many of them are running behind schedule. Another bill that Newsom signed on Wednesday, AB 2493, orders the CPUC to monitor progress on those buildouts and take ​“remedial action” if they don’t stay on schedule.

Last, SB 1098, also signed by Newsom on Wednesday, will slice away at the cumulative costs that utilities pass on in rates. The new law will limit utilities’ use of balancing and memorandum accounts, which were created so utilities could manage hard-to-forecast costs but have become overused and hard for regulators to police, The Utility Reform Network’s Toney said. The common goal of this bill and of SB 905 is ​“making sure that utilities don’t overspend,” he said.

text:
Published on October 01, 2026

The City and County of Denver today joined the State of Colorado and a coalition of 24 other states, counties and cities in suing the Trump administration for dismantling federal greenhouse gas pollution limits for many of the nation’s largest power plants. In September, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) repealed safeguards that required coal- and gas-fired power plants to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, clearing the way for a significant increase in pollution that will worsen extreme heat, deadly storms, flooding, and wildfire smoke. Denver and the coalition are filing a petition for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, asking the court to strike down the repeal and restore these protections. The coalition is also notifying EPA of its intent to sue over the agency’s continued failure to fully regulate pollution from existing natural gas power plants.

“Denverites are sick of breathing wildfire smoke and enduring record-breaking heat,” said Mayor Mike Johnston. “The president’s actions won’t unleash American energy, but they will lead to record profits for polluters- all while our air gets dirtier and our bills stay just as high. The cost of these rollbacks is our health, and we look forward to fighting this in court and seeing these commonsense regulations restored.”

Denver and the coalition are challenging EPA’s repeal of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, which required many of the country's largest power plants to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Power plants are among the largest drivers of climate change, producing roughly one-quarter of the nation’s carbon dioxide emissions. Rather than hold those polluters accountable, the federal administration erased federal pollution limits for most gas- and coal-fired power plants and introduced a proposal to eliminate power plant emission regulation entirely.

Eliminating limits on these emissions threatens communities across the country. More climate pollution contributes to more frequent and more intense heat waves that put children, older adults, and workers at risk. It also contributes to stronger storms and heavier flooding that damage homes, businesses, and transit systems, as well as more wildfire smoke that makes air dangerous to breathe. Increased pollution from fossil fuel power plants can worsen asthma, heart disease, and other serious respiratory illnesses, especially in low-income and other overburdened communities. These changes also increase the financial burden on local and state governments that must spend billions of dollars recovering from increasingly extreme weather.

In their lawsuit, the coalition will argue that EPA unlawfully abandoned these pollution limits without properly considering reasonable alternatives or the enormous health and climate costs of allowing more pollution into the atmosphere. They will assert that the rescission was arbitrary and capricious because EPA did not properly calculate the cost of repealing the rule. The coalition is asking the court to strike down this unlawful rollback of environmental protections and ensure the United States can keep limiting pollution from many of the nation’s biggest polluters.

In addition, Denver and the coalition today filed a notice of intent to sue EPA over the agency’s continued failure to regulate greenhouse gas pollution from many existing gas-fired power plants. Those facilities, including “peaker” plants that often operate during periods of high electricity demand, are frequently located in low-income communities and communities of color that already bear a disproportionate share of pollution. Despite issuing standards for new gas plants over a decade ago, EPA has never fulfilled its legal obligation to limit pollution from existing gas plants. By delaying these protections for years, EPA has left many frontline communities without the safeguards required by the Clean Air Act.

Joining Mayor Mike Johnston and Attorney General Phil Weiser in filing today’s lawsuit, which was led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, are the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, as well as the Governor of Pennsylvania, the Mayors of New York City and Chicago.

Denver has filed six lawsuits and five amicus briefs challenging actions by the Trump Administration. Those cases seek to protect Congressionally-appropriated funding, push back against National Guard and ICE deployments in cities, prevent ICE from stationing at polling places, defend reproductive rights, and preserve Denver’s values around equity, diversity, and immigration.

text:
A coalition of more than 20 Democratic attorneys general sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on Thursday, alleging the agency’s rescission of Biden-era power plant emissions rules last month was illegal. The complaint says the rules repealing greenhouse gas emissions controls from coal, oil and gas-fired power plants violate the Clean Air Act.

“The Trump administration is pushing for catastrophic rollbacks of federal limits on greenhouse gas pollution,” New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X on Thursday. The state of New York and the mayor of New York City are both plaintiffs in the lawsuit.

“I’m suing to stop this administration from giving the nation’s biggest polluters a free pass to set our country back decades in the fight against climate change,” she said.

An EPA spokesperson told Spectrum News it does not comment on pending litigation.

Last month, the agency finalized its repeal of 2024 power plant regulations, saying they adversely impacted the nation’s energy systems. The EPA estimated the rule rollback would save $310 billion, mostly in costs power companies would no longer need to pay to reduce emissions.

“The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement when he announced the final rule. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices.”

Environmental groups immediately decried the rules rescission as part of a larger Trump administration effort to dismantle federal climate regulations and bolster the fossil fuel industry.

In 2022, the EPA estimated that U.S. electric power plants accounted for 24% of total domestic carbon dioxide emissions released during the combustion of coal, oil and natural gas — second only to transportation, which accounts for 29% of greenhouse gas emissions.

In 2023, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said about 60% of U.S. electricity generation came from fossil fuels, compared with 19% from nuclear and 21% from renewables.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said failing to control the emissions from electricity generation would increase heat waves, wildfires, severe storms, flooding, disease, air pollution and harm to regional ecosystems.

The EPA rules repeal “significantly undermines efforts to address climate change and exposes communities to greater environmental harm by undoing climate regulations on power plants,” the lawsuit contends.

California and its Air Resources Board were part of a coalition of states, counties and cities that filed the lawsuit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Thursday.

In addition to California and New York, the attorneys general for Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia are part of the lawsuit, along with the governor of Pennsylvania, the mayors of Chicago and New York City and the City and County of Denver.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to restore the EPA’s greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants.

text:
WBEZ’s Curious City answers questions from listeners about Chicago and the region. We include the public in our storytelling, making journalism more transparent and interconnected.

Chris Gerben grew up in the metro Detroit area in the 1980s and ’90s, and even as a child, he noticed a lot of major shifts in the city.

“We were a steel mill town, and in the mid ’80s is when a lot of this kind of emptying-out of the city was happening,” Gerben said.

He remembers going to at least three different elementary schools because teachers kept getting laid off.

From the peak of Detroit’s auto industry until Gerben was born, roughly three decades, the city lost over 200,000 jobs — more than during the Great Depression. It also lost more than half a million people.

Gerben now lives with his family in Chicago, and he wonders if what happened in Detroit happened across the Midwest in the same way. How did deindustrialization hit Milwaukee? And why was Chicago seemingly spared?

“If you don’t know any better … it would seem like, ‘Oh, [Chicago] is privileged in some way,’” Gerben said.

Deindustrialization shaped the Midwest in ways seen and unseen. We look back at how things differed across cities when it came to the industries that built them up and how each city dealt with the fall out of losing so much.

The Motor City

More than a century ago, the “Big Three” automakers — General Motors, Ford and Chrysler — made a home in Detroit, which led to more cars being built in the Motor City than anywhere in the world.

These factory jobs attracted the first wave of the Great Migration — African Americans leaving the rural South for the urban North, starting in the 1910s — as well as immigrant workers. Marsha Battle-Fillpot said her dad, Joe Von Battle, was one of those early workers coming up from Georgia.

“The auto industry here allowed for a relative prosperity that was unprecedented,” Battle-Fillpot says. “It’s sort of not viewed like that, with all the bells and whistles of, say, a New York, but this place is no joke.”

Von Battle was laid off from the auto plant when white workers returned to the factory after World War II. This gave rise to the axiom “last hired, first fired” with regard to Black workers.

“He was so despondent about [facing] a reversal like that, he vowed at that point he would never work for another man,” Battle-Fillpot said.

With the prosperity of the auto industry lifting all boats, Von Battle decided to start his own business. In 1945, he opened Joe’s Record Shop in the city’s historic Black Bottom neighborhood. It was an instant hit: In the first two years, he had over $100,000 worth of records in stock.

But in the ’50s, the Big Three started pulling out of the city, moving to the suburbs for cheaper land.

This began well before the “Rebellion of ’67,” five days of racial unrest in late July 1967 during which 43 people died, hundreds reported injuries and police arrested more than 7,000 people.

“There’s a whole narrative that says that, well, Detroit was basically doing okay until 1967 and all the whites left, and then Detroit fell into decline,” Battle-Fillpot said. “That’s just so wrong-headed. There’s no statistics that bear that out.”

In over 20 years since opening, Joe’s Record Shop became a symbol of Black art and opportunity that defined the time. During the Rebellion, it was looted.

“When my father walked back into that store … and he saw the destruction, I really say that my dad really died then,” Battle-Fillpot said. “He tried to reopen after that, even, but he was just unable to gather it back altogether.”

Today, headquarters for the Big Three automakers are still in metro Detroit, but jobs in the city never bounced back.

‘The Machine Shop of the World’

The story of industry and its demise echoed in Milwaukee, the home of beer and brewing, heavy manufacturing, and iron and steel, also called ‘The Machine Shop of the World’. There, industry here was more diverse than Detroit, which went all-in on the auto industry. With a bustling port and growing rail system, Milwaukee was critical to the economy of the Wisconsin region.

“‘Blue-collar’ in Milwaukee meant middle class,” says Adam Carr, a public historian and artist in the city. “That’s entwined with the history of socialism here, that the worker was not a chump in Milwaukee.”

An image that, for Carr, exemplifies the city’s indigenous roots, its peak in industry and the decline is Three Bridges Park — an old brownfield turned into a sprawling park, filled with walking paths built over a freeway that cut through the city.

The loss of jobs and wealth in Milwaukee, specifically Black and Latino Milwaukee, went down just like in Detroit. Urban renewal brought in freeways but also displaced families in lower income neighborhoods. Redlining discriminatorily shut people out of certain neighborhoods. This stunted generational wealth, a history the city is still dealing with. Like Detroit, industry jobs never bounced back.

“I heard someone say, ‘Pie in the sky in Milwaukee was the factory job,’” Carr remembers. “We thought the gravy train would never end. And I think we haven’t found exactly who we are after industry yet.”

The Second City

In Chicago’s West Loop neighborhood, built on a graveyard of old industry, you’ll find the University of Illinois Chicago’s Cuppa Hall and the Great Cities Institute.

Associate director Matt Wilson studies the long shadow of deindustrialization in Chicago. He says historically, the city had a lot of the same advantages as Milwaukee and Detroit: natural resources, a bustling port. What separated Chicago was the rail system — and as the country pushed west, Chicago became a major hub.

“Chicago still has that identity of the crossroads. A lot of goods flow through here,” Wilson says. “It’s really easy, when you go on the river, to see barge traffic, and when you go to any of the ports that are around the city, you see the large-scale movement of goods.”

Industry varied in Chicago. The famous Union Stock Yards was considered the meatpacking center of the world. Then, in the 1980s, the city pivoted.

“Chicago needs to compete with other cities to attract jobs in corporate headquarters,” Wilson says. “It needs to bring in tourism and make sure all the hotels are filled and that there’s a nightlife.”

Tax incentives and tax dollars were funneled to rebuild Downtown, though not other parts of the city.

“The neighborhood of South Chicago, on the southeast side of the city, it feels like [it’s] from the historical archives I’ve read, that the center of gravity was the steel plant,” Wilson says.

Until the early 2000s, that included Pressed Steel, Republic Steel, Wisconsin Steel and the big one, U.S. Steel. These plants were the source of middle-class employment, which stabilized the housing market and both retail and commercial businesses.

“Both my grandfathers worked [in the plants]. My dad worked there and I worked there,” says Michael Lisecki, who grew up in South Chicago. “It was like everybody worked in one of the mills, whether it was U.S., Wisconsin. It was devastating when we all got laid off.”

Lisecki started working in the mills in 1978 when he was 18, making better money than he ever dreamed possible. Three years later, he was laid off and the neighborhood was never the same.

Chicago pivoted to a post-industry chapter earlier than Detroit and Milwaukee. But no matter the city, deindustrialization left a hole, and it’s clear the bones of the past are still with us.

text:
Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LA Metro) has approved an order for 220 battery-electric buses from US manufacturer ENC, with all vehicles to be built in Jurupa Valley, California.

The award covers 40-foot AXESS EVO-BE battery-electric buses. According to ENC, it is the largest base award of 40-foot battery-electric buses made by a US transit agency.

The order comes as Los Angeles prepares to host the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, while LA Metro continues work to transition its bus fleet towards zero-emission vehicles.

The 220 buses will be manufactured at ENC’s 227,000-square-foot facility in Jurupa Valley. More than 300 people work at the site, which carries out production activities including frame welding, painting, final assembly and vehicle testing.

The award is also expected to support jobs within ENC’s wider supplier network, which includes companies employing workers across Los Angeles County and Southern California.

John Obert, ENC’s vice president of transit sales said:

An award of this scale is built on trust, and we intend to keep earning it every day. Our California team will build these buses close to the communities they serve, with the quality and reliability Metro riders count on. We are proud of the good jobs this work represents for hundreds of Californians, and of the role these buses will play in how Los Angeles County moves.

The AXESS EVO-BE is ENC’s battery-electric heavy-duty transit bus. The model uses BAE Systems’ Gen3 electric drive system and can be equipped with up to 738 kWh of energy storage.

The buses are built on a 304-grade stainless steel structure and have undergone Altoona testing. The AXESS EVO-BE is available in 33-, 35- and 40-foot configurations, with ADA-compliant designs and configurable interior layouts.

LA Metro currently operates around 2,000 low-emission buses alongside six rail lines. The agency records nearly one million weekday boardings and more than 280 million boardings annually across its network.

text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — A record electric rate went into effect Thursday in Puerto Rico as outages persist and the U.S. territory’s power grid continues to crumble.

A residential customer that consumes 800 kilowatt-hours a month will see the monthly bill rise about 18%, from $229 to $271, according to Puerto Rico’s Energy Bureau, which approved the increase.

The new rate will remain in effect until at least Dec. 31 and is expected to drive up an already high cost of living on the island of 3.2 million people, where more than 40% of residents live in poverty.

The new rate of 33.86 cents per kWh far surpasses the average rate of 18.3 cents per kWh for residential customers in the U.S. mainland, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Luma Energy, which oversees the transmission and distribution of power in Puerto Rico, had requested an increase of more than six cents per kWh and stressed that it would not generate additional revenue for the company, but rather cover an increase in costs.

“The difference is driven by higher energy consumption due to high summer temperatures, rising global oil prices resulting from the conflict in the Middle East — which has constrained fuel transportation and increased costs — greater use of customer batteries, and the need to rely on more expensive fuel when power plants do not generate enough electricity,” Luma said in a statement.

The increase comes as outages persist nearly a decade after Puerto Rico’s power grid was razed by Hurricane Maria when it struck the island in 2017 as a powerful Category 4 storm, although the grid was already weak given a lack of maintenance and investment for decades.

Last week, a large fire that erupted at a substation left more than 200,000 customers without power in the latest outage to hit the island.

The Energy Bureau said in a statement late Wednesday that it approved an increase of 5.28 cents per kWh to reduce the financial burden on customers.

It noted that it did not pass along the cost of $17.6 million associated with what it called alleged failures by New Fortress Energy to supply fuel from June to August.

“Fuel costs must not be automatically passed on to the consumer simply because they were incurred or billed,” the Energy Bureau said.

New Fortress Energy supplies natural gas to power generation plants on Puerto Rico’s north coast. Currently, those plants are using diesel — driving up costs — because a vessel laden with a delivery of natural gas has been blocked from entering the San Juan Bay for two weeks given its size. The case remains mired in court.

The Energy Bureau said it also is investigating some $19 million that Luma said was paid for gas quantities that officials say exceeded what Genera PR “ultimately needed or could receive.” Genera PR oversees the generation of power in Puerto Rico.

The increase comes as the administration of Puerto Rico Gov. Jenniffer González pushes to cancel the contract with Luma, with the case currently tied up in court with ongoing lawsuits.

Luma and Genera PR were awarded contracts as Puerto Rico’s state-owned Electric Power Authority struggles to restructure its more than $9 billion debt load.

In 2024, petroleum represented 63% of the island’s overall energy use; natural gas accounted for 31%, coal 5% and renewables 1%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

text:
October 1, 2026

DALLAS, TEXAS (Oct. 1, 2026) – U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed air permits to allow for construction on the Blue Marlin Offshore Port in the Gulf of America off the coast of Cameron Parish, Louisiana. If finalized as proposed, EPA’s actions will enable Blue Marlin to export around 80,000 barrels of crude oil per hour resulting in around 605 million barrels per year. The Trump EPA is committed to unleashing American energy and strengthening supply to lower costs for Americans across the nation.

“This project is not just about expanding infrastructure, it is about providing good-paying energy jobs and lowering prices at the pump by unleashing the full potential of American energy. If finalized as proposed, the Blue Marlin Deepwater Port will bring prosperity to not only the Gulf of America states but to Americans across the nation,” said EPARegional Administrator Scott Mason. “American families win when we encourage innovations in engineering technology that allow home-grown energy dominance to flourish while maintaining high environmental standards.”

“There has been no greater champion for the energy industry than President Trump and his Administration. The Blue Marlin Offshore Port project demonstrates that there has been no better home for energy dominance than Louisiana,” said Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry. “I’m grateful to President Trump and Administrator Zeldin for working with us to make this project a reality. This is a win for Louisiana and the nation!”

"Louisiana leads the world in advanced energy production, and Cameron Parish is certainly at the forefront of American energy dominance. When finalized, EPA’s proposal will build on that strength while creating excellent jobs for Louisiana families,” said Representative Clay Higgins (R-LA-03). “My office has fought for deepwater projects, and Blue Marlin reflects the Trump administration's aim to expand American energy policy worldwide. I look forward to seeing Blue Marlin at 100% production.”

After thorough review, EPA is proposing two draft permits: a Prevention of Significant Deterioration preconstruction permit and a title V federal operating permit. In order to maintain strong air quality protection throughout construction and operation, the project will use vapor-capture technology to prevent the release of volatile organic compounds as crude oil is transferred onto the carriers to protect air quality. A dedicated vapor collection system and vapor combustion units at the port will also ensure an expected 99 percent vapor-capture efficiency, preventing excess emissions from the transfer and loading process. This ensures that increasing crude oil exports can occur while maintaining air quality standards in the area.

EPA’s review and issuance of air permits is just one part of the overall permitting process for the Blue Marlin Deepwater Port. EPA will accept public comments for 30 days following publication of the proposal. For more information, please visit: https://www.epa.gov/caa-permitting/public-comment-and-hearing-opportunity-blue-marlin-offshore-port-llc-bmop-deepwater.

text:
Renewables supply less than a tenth of Caribbean electricity, and the region depends on international fuel markets to generate the rest. Contracts signed in the region itself show that fossil generation is no longer the cheapest way to produce electricity. Many countries have set renewable targets, but not all can be measured. Of those that can be measured, none are on track.

Eleven of the thirteen Caribbean countries analysed in this report produce none of the fuel they burn to generate electricity, and 91% of the region’s power still comes from fossil sources. In four of them, imported fuel for all uses costs more than 7% of GDP – two to three times the world average. When oil prices rise, the cost passes through to household bills or to the public accounts through subsidies.

The region’s fossil dependence persists even though renewables are already contracted at lower prices than fossil power. In the Bahamas, the state utility contracted solar at less than half the price of gas-fired generation in the same contracting round. In June 2026, the Dominican Republic awarded renewables with batteries at a lower price than its distribution companies were paying generators on average the year before.

Yet renewables remain under a tenth of the region’s generation, and countries with verifiable targets had reached less than a fifth of the goal by 2024. The region is buying solar panels far faster than those figures suggest: 1,809 MW of Chinese panels arrived in 2024, five times the 2021 total, and official capacity statistics do not register that pace.

Policies, not costs, are the main barrier to renewable deployment in the Caribbean. This report proposes three policy changes: measurable targets, with regular progress checks that are verified independently; an independent decision-making body to approve generation and grid connections; and tenders designed around what the system needs, with the result published.

Many Caribbean countries are highly dependent on imported fossil fuels to meet their electricity demand. Only two of the thirteen countries in this report burn fuel they produce themselves: Trinidad and Tobago generates its electricity with gas produced on its own territory, and Cuba covers close to 60% of its electricity output with domestic crude and gas. Barbados produces some oil and gas, but none of it is used to generate electricity. In the remaining ten countries, every unit of fuel burned to generate electricity is imported, at a price set outside the region.

Imported fuel for every use – electricity, transport, cooking and the rest – absorbed 9.5% of GDP in Jamaica in 2023, 8.5% in Dominica, 8.0% in Grenada and 7.3% in Barbados, compared to 3.2% worldwide and 2.8% on average for Latin America and the Caribbean. The indicator can be measured in seven of the thirteen countries, and all seven exceed both averages, even the three least exposed – the Dominican Republic, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and the Bahamas – which sit between 4.1% and 4.4%.

That exposure reaches households through the cost of living. Two oil shocks of this century show up in Caribbean inflation: in 2008, Jamaica’s rose from 9.2% to 22.0%, and in 2022 Saint Lucia’s quadrupled. Antigua and Barbuda’s more than tripled in both. The third shock is under way: Brent passed $100 USD in March 2026 after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and its effect will not be measurable until 2027.

1.2 Households pay among the highest power prices in the world

Electricity in much of the Caribbean is among the most expensive in the world. The World Bank puts the regional average at around 25 c/kWh, more than double the United States average, with some countries above 40 c/kWh. In the six eastern Caribbean states that share a common currency – Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines – the International Monetary Fund measured rates of 26-37 c/kWh, three to four times the median price in emerging economies (10 c/kWh) and almost double the 19 c/kWh in advanced economies.

Three factors help explain those prices. The first is the grid: ageing and poorly maintained infrastructure produces transmission and distribution losses of 15-20% in those six eastern Caribbean countries, compared to 6% in advanced economies. The second is that generation is mostly fossil-fired, so every kilowatt-hour carries a fuel purchase – a largely imported, recurring cost that renewable generation does not carry at all. The third is scale: these are small, isolated systems that buy in small volumes, have no neighbouring grid to draw on, and have little bargaining power over what they pay.

In 2024, the average residential tariff was 38.0 c/kWh in Grenada, 36.9 c/kWh in Jamaica and 32.3 c/kWh in Barbados – the three highest of the eighteen Latin American and Caribbean countries in OLACDE’s price series, whose median was 16.9 c/kWh. Trinidad and Tobago, at the other extreme, recorded 6.2 c/kWh: it generates its electricity entirely with its own gas and has had its tariff frozen since 2009.

High electricity prices land on households. In the Bahamas, which generates 99% of its power from imported oil products across grids on separate islands, the average household spends around $4,800 USD a year on energy – five times the Latin American and Caribbean average. Among the poorest fifth of households, electricity alone takes 7.3% of income, compared to 4.4% regionally.

2.1 Solar with batteries now costs less than a new gas plant

Globally, more than 90% of utility-scale renewable projects commissioned in 2025 produce cheaper electricity than the cheapest new fossil plant available in their market. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) puts the global weighted-average levelised cost of onshore wind at 3.3 c/kWh and of solar at 4.4 c/kWh. That same year, gas turbine shortages roughly doubled the investment required for a new combined-cycle plant, pushing its levelised cost towards 10 c/kWh in high gas-price markets. That is already changing what gets built: in 2025, the rise in solar was eighteen times larger than that of gas, the only fossil fuel that grew at all.

For an island system, what matters is the firm cost: generation plus the storage needed to deliver power at any hour. IRENA models this for places with strong and steady sunshine, where less storage is needed to cover the gaps: Bahia State in Brazil, the Thar Desert in India, Southern Queensland in Australia. None of them is an island. It finds that firm solar-plus-battery cost at 95% reliability fell from above 10 c/kWh in 2020 to 6.5-8.2 c/kWh in 2025, and for grid-constrained or islanded systems it treats that figure as a conservative ceiling rather than an expected cost. Both generation and storage got cheaper: the installed cost of a four-hour utility-scale battery fell 95% from 2010 and stood at $140 per kWh of capacity in 2025.

Borrowing costs range from 3-5% to more than 12% depending on the market, and the difference falls hardest on renewables, whose spending comes almost entirely at the start of a project. Renewable and battery costs have fallen far enough to absorb that difference, and the Caribbean already has cases that prove it.

In two recent Caribbean contracts, renewables came in cheaper than the conventional alternative

In Great Exuma, the Bahamas, the state utility Bahamas Power and Light (BPL) contracted 3 MW of solar at 11.5 c/kWh compared to 23.3 c/kWh for generation with liquefied natural gas bought from third parties. Under the same procurement process, solar cost less than half the price of gas per kilowatt-hour. The solar plant contracted in the Bahamas was well above the global utility-scale benchmark, yet it still won against the fossil alternative. The contract did not include batteries, and adding them would have brought solar to 14.8 c/kWh: still a third below the gas price. The difference is almost entirely fuel: the fixed part of the gas contract, 10.5 c/kWh, is almost equal to the full price of solar, and the remaining 12.8 c/kWh is recalculated every month.

Another example from the Caribbean shows the pattern repeat on a much larger scale. In June 2026, the Dominican Republic awarded 326 MW of renewable generation with 50% battery backup at 10.6-10.9 c/kWh, below the 14.9 c/kWh that distribution companies paid their generators on average in 2025, with commercial operation expected from June 2028. The National Energy Commission justified the auction on the same premise as this report: reducing exposure to imported fuel costs.

The way renewable targets are set varies greatly across the Caribbean. Only six express it as a share of electricity generation in an adopted instrument. The Bahamas and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines set theirs on the national energy mix, Barbados on electricity sales, Dominica does not state a basis; and that of the Dominican Republic exists only in an indicative plan.

Every target set on electricity generation is behind

By the end of 2024, none of the six countries whose target is set on electricity generation had reached even a fifth of it. And the lag is not explained by over-ambitious targets: Cuba set the most modest of the six, 26% for 2035, yet stood at 3.7% in 2024; Jamaica, the most advanced, set 50% for 2030 and stood at 8.9% in 2024. For Trinidad and Tobago, with a 30% target for 2030, the statistics record no renewable generation at all. Meeting these commitments would mean multiplying 2024 renewable generation by seven in Cuba, by six in Jamaica, by thirteen in Antigua and Barbuda, and by more than twenty in both Saint Kitts and Nevis and Saint Lucia.

Three of the countries in this report have moved further away from their target since 2020, not closer: the renewable share fell 3.8 points in Jamaica, 0.9 in Cuba and 0.3 in Saint Lucia. The reasons differ: in Saint Lucia nothing new was built and the additional demand was met with oil; in Jamaica hydro and wind generated less while demand grew by a fifth and was met with gas and oil; in Cuba biomass generation (largely bagasse from sugarcane) fell by more than a third and solar generated less despite more capacity. Antigua and Barbuda is the only country that gained ground, by 1.8 points; Saint Kitts and Nevis has not moved at all.

Some targets are not firm promises either. Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia and Trinidad and Tobago make theirs conditional on international finance. Only Cuba committed unconditionally, and Jamaica does not state either way.

The six countries whose commitments are measured as a share of electricity generation account for 56% of the region’s fossil generation. Meeting their renewable targets would cut fossil-fuelled generation by between 23% and 100% in each. At the regional level, this would lift the renewable share from 9.1% in 2024 to 23% in 2030, almost regardless of how much demand grows. If consumption continues to grow at the rate observed between 2018 and 2024, fossil generation would fall 9% in absolute terms. Less than half of those new renewables would be enough to stop it from growing.

Four Caribbean countries weakened or dropped their renewable target between 2021 and 2025

Four countries adjusted the target instead of accelerating delivery. Barbados says so in its own NDC: the 95% it committed to for 2030 in 2021 “is maintained”, but is “now expected to be achieved by 2035”. Saint Kitts and Nevis moved its 100% from 2020, set in its 2014 energy policy, to 2030 in its 2021 NDC. Saint Lucia’s target went from 50% for 2030, set in 2015, to being omitted from its 2021 update, and then reappeared at 40% in 2025 – below the 50% that still stands in its national energy policy. Finally, Haiti removed the 47% it had set in 2015.

Not every country followed that path. Trinidad and Tobago adopted a 30% target for 2030 after missing a 10% for 2021. And the Dominican Republic advanced more than anyone without a target that could be required of it: its law says that the authorities “shall endeavour” that 25% of service needs be covered by renewables in 2025, and its energy plan sets 30% for 2030 on an indicative basis only. Its renewable share of electricity generation rose from 7.6% to 16.6% between 2015 and 2024: solar went from 0.2% to 5.8% and wind from 1.6% to 4.2%, while hydro barely moved.

4.1 Set targets that can be checked, and verify progress

Renewable energy targets that are credible and fully verifiable by design will help to attract private investment. A robust target should rely on existing public datasets while clearly defining its baseline, deadline, and scope – such as whether distributed generation counts. Governance is most effective when there is a designated reporting agency, a fixed reporting schedule and interim milestones. If a milestone is missed, regulations should require a public corrective plan to catch delays early. Finally, figures should be verified by an independent body, as reporting mandates without external verification lose accountability over time.

Current status

Six countries have a target set in a way that can be measured; that is the one requirement widely met. Only one country’s law names who must publish the renewable figure and how often.

Elsewhere, such a requirement is either absent or omits the obligation to report renewable generation data. Dominican law requires its energy commission to report to Congress each year on the execution of its renewable programmes, but not on the share itself. Where no one is named, more than one figure circulates: in Jamaica the energy ministry’s statistics put the renewable share at about 10% for 2024, while the regulator’s annual report gives 12.9% – a figure that carries neither a year nor a source. The regional dataset this report uses, OLACDE-sieLAC, gives 8.9% for the same year. In short, three different figures for one country, and no way for a reader to know which of them is the valid one.

Four countries set an interim renewable share for a date before their final target year, two of them in annexes rather than in the commitment itself. However, none of these instruments specify what happens if a target is missed, with no requirement for a corrective plan, mandatory review or follow-up action.

Finally, in no country is the published figure checked by a body outside the one that produces it. Jamaica shows what that permits: two official figures, more than two points apart, with no process by which either is reconciled.

Where this has worked

No country meets the full recommendation, but Antigua and Barbuda comes closest – at least on paper. Since 2015, its Renewable Energy Act has required what most of the region still has not legislated: renewable targets for electricity generation prescribed by regulation, middle-term as well as long-term, an annual published report on progress towards them, and a quarterly return on connected capacity. Ten years on, the regional centre that compiles Caribbean energy statistics still obtains Antigua and Barbuda’s electricity data by private communication from the utility. The Act requires no action if progress falls short and gives every function to the minister, so there are no outside observers to notice delays. Antigua and Barbuda is at 6.7% of generation against 86% for 2030.

4.2 Stop the utility deciding who competes with it

Two decisions determine whether a new generator can enter the market: who is permitted to generate, and who gets connected to the grid. Both should be taken by a body that neither generates nor sells electricity – not by the incumbent utility, which is precisely who that new generator would compete with. In practice this means two things. First, the generation licence is granted against criteria published in advance. Second, connection to the grid can be refused only on grounds that a body outside the utility can review.

Current status

On paper, the monopoly has all but disappeared. Most of these countries now allow companies other than the incumbent utility to generate and sell electricity. But the monopoly survives by another route. The laws opened up generation, yet left in the incumbent’s hands the decisions that determine whether a competitor can actually enter.

Where the incumbent decides who may generate, the Bahamas is the clearest case and the newest law: under an Electricity Act passed in 2024, BPL decides whether new capacity is needed, then it may meet that need itself on nothing more than a notification to the regulator, or where it opts for a third party it selects the winner. In Trinidad and Tobago, the right to generate is vested in the state utility by statute, which then declares a generator “approved”.

In other countries, the decision on whether a new generator receives a licence rests directly with a minister, with no independent regulator taking part. That is the case in Saint Kitts and Nevis, under its 2011 Electricity Supply Act, and in Barbados, under its Electric Light and Power Act 2013: there, a committee reviews applications, but it is made up of government officials and only issues recommendations; the decision remains the minister’s. There is also a third case: a law that opens the market but is never put into effect. Saint Lucia took renewables out of the monopoly in 2016, but the regulations needed to grant licences were never made. Ten years on, its only renewable plant is still the utility’s own.

The second decision, connection to the grid, is rarely regulated in writing, and that is where the incumbent utility recovers the control the law had taken from it over generation. In Barbados, the utility stopped connecting new solar customers for about two years on the grounds that the grid could take no more; it was a decision it took itself, with no outside review. In Antigua and Barbuda, the law makes the connection of renewable projects depend on the interconnection policy set by the utility itself, the Antigua Public Utilities Authority. Cuba reaches the same outcome by another path: a private producer may own its plant, but is obliged to sell all of its generation to UNE, the state utility, at the price UNE decides.

Where this has worked

Dominica shows what happens when this change is applied. There, both decisions rest with the regulator, not the utility: the regulator grants generation licences and approves the technical rules for connecting to the grid. In addition, the incumbent utility’s licence is non-exclusive, so the regulator was able to grant a second licence to an independent producer. That producer’s 10 MW geothermal plant entered commercial operation in 2026 and in June supplied around 43% of the country’s electricity. Added to the hydropower already in place, two-thirds of Dominica’s electricity that month was renewable.

Grenada already has the legal mechanism, though not yet the result. Its law prohibits any generation licence from being exclusive, and requires the capacity available to connect new projects to be assessed jointly by the network operator and the regulator, rather than the utility alone deciding whether the grid is “full”. Since 2021, 17 small producers have been licensed. But renewable generation is still 1.7%, and the technical rules for connection remain in draft.

4.3 Tender what the system needs, and publish the result

Buying through competition, and saying publicly what it cost, allows the next buyer in the region to start from a real price rather than from a cost model. On an island grid the value of a renewable project is not only how cheaply it generates but whether the system can take the power when it arrives; the tender should therefore be written around what the system needs – generation, storage, network capacity, or a combination – and where it asks for batteries it should say what their function will be, frequency regulation and reserve included, not only how many hours of electricity they can supply. And the award should be published: who bid, what each project’s levelised cost was, and how each tariff is indexed.

Current status

Most generation in the region is contracted bilaterally. Of the five power purchase agreements in force in Trinidad and Tobago, one was awarded by tender and the rest were negotiated directly; all five are confidential, with only general terms disclosed to a parliamentary committee. The electricity statute of Saint Kitts and Nevis says nothing about how generation is to be procured and Cuban law provides for no tender at all – an independent producer negotiates with UNE.

Barbados shows what happens when only generation is bought. Solar was procured project by project, with no storage contracted alongside it, until the grid could take no more. The remedy was a tender for storage on its own – 60 MW and 240 MWh – to clear a backlog of projects already approved.

Trinidad and Tobago shows the same gap from the other side. Its 92 MW Brechin Castle solar plant is the largest in the country and the only one of its five power purchase agreements awarded by tender. It began delivering in July 2025 and came off the grid at the end of January 2026. The minister responsible attributes that to the plant having no batteries: the tender bought solar generation, but the system could not absorb that power when it arrived.

Where this has worked

Jamaica published what its tender resulted in. Twelve bids for 100 MW led to two awards of solar without storage, at 6.5 and 7.0 c/kWh, and the results were published with the bidders, each project’s levelised cost and the indexation of each tariff. The Dominican Republic did the same at scale, for a different product: 32 qualified bidders for 326 MW of renewables with battery storage, awarded at 10.6-10.9 c/kWh for delivery from 2028.

Both results are public, and in both cases what is known is not only the price but exactly what was bought at that price: how much capacity, with or without batteries, with what delivery date, and how the tariff adjusts over time. That is the value of publishing: a price on its own is no reference, but a price alongside the description of what it bought is. Whoever prepares the next tender in the region no longer needs to rely on a global cost model, or accept the price a single bidder proposes. They can start from prices already bid and signed a few hundred kilometres away, in systems of similar size and with similar fuel costs, and use those documents to draft their own terms: how the tariff is indexed, what the storage must do, when the plant must come online. With just two published tenders, the other countries of the Caribbean now have a point of comparison that did not exist before.

In conclusion, none of these three decisions depends on a new technology appearing or on finance arriving. They depend on the decisions of those who have the authority to take them. And the Caribbean reaches that moment with an advantage: its own contracts show that renewables are already the cheaper option, its ports show that the panels are already arriving, and several of its countries show that the right rules produce results. Every percentage point that renewables gain is a point less exposure to a price the region does not control, and a step closer to electricity generated with resources that are its own.

Scope

The report covers thirteen Caribbean countries: Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, Barbados, Cuba, Dominica, Grenada, Haiti, Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Saint Lucia and Trinidad and Tobago. The unit of analysis is electricity generation, not primary energy. Installed capacity appears in one place only: to compare the solar the region has bought with the solar its statistics record.

Electricity generation

Data by country and fuel come from OLACDE-sieLAC for the seven member countries and from IRENA for the remaining six, consulted in August 2026.

For Antigua and Barbuda, The Bahamas, Dominica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Saint Lucia – 5.5% of regional generation – IRENA does not publish 2024, and the 2023 technology mix was used. Growth is measured from 2018, the base year used throughout this report.

Where installed capacity is converted to generation, a 13.5% capacity factor is used: the rate implied by the Dominican Republic’s own 2024 solar generation and its average installed capacity that year, the only country among the thirteen with enough solar to measure it.

Renewable targets

Each target was verified against its primary source – NDCs registered with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, decrees and national plans. Secondary compilations were not used, as they reclassify as installed capacity targets that governments expressed on generation. Figures circulating without an instrument behind them were excluded: 37% for Cuba, 100% for Grenada, 80% for Haiti, and Barbados’s 100%, which covers the whole energy system. Four of the six targets set on electricity generation are conditional on international finance; only Cuba’s is unconditional, and Jamaica does not state either way.

Progress is the 2024 renewable share divided by the target. The reduction in a country’s own fossil generation if it meets its target is 1 − (1 − target) / (1 − 2024 share); the generation projection cancels out, so it needs no demand assumption.

For the region, the six are assumed to meet their targets and the other seven to hold their 2024 share, giving 23% in 2030 – invariant to uniform demand growth, and between 23.2% and 23.8% with divergent rates. The fall in fossil generation does depend on demand: 9% at the 1.25% annual growth observed from 2018 to 2024, and 16% if demand is flat. All four conditional targets are treated as met; excluding Trinidad and Tobago’s would give a 2030 share of 19% and a fossil fall of 4%.

Cuba’s commitment is 26% for 2035; the 2030 projection uses the 24% that its Nationally Determined Contribution states as the 2030 reference point from which that commitment is measured.

Fuel imports as a share of GDP

Fuel imports (% of merchandise imports) / 100 × Merchandise imports (current US$) / GDP (current US$). Only seven of the thirteen countries have all three series available and stable; in the other six the fuel share swings by more than a factor of twenty between adjacent years, or is truncated. The last year with all seven is 2023.

Solar panel imports

Imports: Ember, China Solar PV Export Explorer, commodity type “Panels”, in watts-peak direct current; 2026 covers January to July. Capacity: IRENA, Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026, 16 April 2026 release. No country among the thirteen has a solar capacity figure from an official national source for any year from 2019 to 2024; the first four appear in 2025.

Installations are estimated from imports following Ember’s method: 73% of reported Chinese panel exports are installed, after a six-month lag, applied on calendar years as half the current year plus half the previous one. The two series are compared over the same window, 2021 to 2024, with capacity added measured as the 2024 figure minus the 2020 one. Ember’s adjustments for non-Chinese imports, re-exports and domestic manufacturing are not applied, and no DC-to-AC conversion is made, following Ember. Ember treats 73% as conservative for 2026; in a young and fast-growing market more panels are still in warehouses, so the estimate here is more likely to overstate installations than to understate them. Cuba is reported separately.

Tariffs

The Latin American comparison is against the eighteen countries covered by OLACDE, a sample that does not include Haiti.

Legal and regulatory review

Section 4 rests on a review of each country’s electricity statute, any renewable-specific law, and the instrument setting its renewable target, asking of each: who may authorise an independent generator; who decides connection; whether an interim renewable figure is set before the target year and what follows if it is missed; and whether verification is assigned to any body other than the one reporting. The review distinguishes what a statute provides from what exists – several instruments create powers never brought into effect, such as the licensing regulations under section 64 of Saint Lucia’s Electricity Supply Act – and states where a finding rests on a regional compilation rather than on the instrument itself. The findings on procurement rest on a different evidence base: published tender documents and award announcements, power purchase agreements where their terms are public, and what utilities and ministries have disclosed to parliaments or to the press.

Units and comparability

Electricity prices are in US cents per kilowatt-hour (c/kWh) and battery costs in dollars per kWh of capacity. Five cost metrics circulate in this field and are not interchangeable: end-user tariff, generation cost, contract or award price, average wholesale purchase price, and modelled levelised cost. The report keeps them separate and states which one it is using in each case.

title: AGs sue EPA over repeal of power plant emissions rules - Spectrum News
description:
A coalition of more than 20 Democratic attorneys general sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on Thursday, alleging the agency’s rescission of Biden-era power plant emissions rules last month was illegal.
The complaint says the rules repealing greenhouse gas emissions controls from coal, oil and gas-fired power plants violate the Clean Air Act.
Last month, the agency finalized its repeal of 2024 power plant regulations, saying they adversely impacted the nation’s energy systems.
The EPA rules repeal “significantly undermines efforts to address climate change and exposes communities to greater environmental harm by undoing climate regulations on power plants,” the lawsuit contends.
The plaintiffs are asking the court to restore the EPA’s greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants.
text:
A coalition of more than 20 Democratic attorneys general sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin on Thursday, alleging the agency’s rescission of Biden-era power plant emissions rules last month was illegal. The complaint says the rules repealing greenhouse gas emissions controls from coal, oil and gas-fired power plants violate the Clean Air Act.

“The Trump administration is pushing for catastrophic rollbacks of federal limits on greenhouse gas pollution,” New York Attorney General Letitia James wrote on X on Thursday. The state of New York and the mayor of New York City are both plaintiffs in the lawsuit.

“I’m suing to stop this administration from giving the nation’s biggest polluters a free pass to set our country back decades in the fight against climate change,” she said.

An EPA spokesperson told Spectrum News it does not comment on pending litigation.

Last month, the agency finalized its repeal of 2024 power plant regulations, saying they adversely impacted the nation’s energy systems. The EPA estimated the rule rollback would save $310 billion, mostly in costs power companies would no longer need to pay to reduce emissions.

“The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement when he announced the final rule. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices.”

Environmental groups immediately decried the rules rescission as part of a larger Trump administration effort to dismantle federal climate regulations and bolster the fossil fuel industry.

In 2022, the EPA estimated that U.S. electric power plants accounted for 24% of total domestic carbon dioxide emissions released during the combustion of coal, oil and natural gas — second only to transportation, which accounts for 29% of greenhouse gas emissions.

In 2023, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said about 60% of U.S. electricity generation came from fossil fuels, compared with 19% from nuclear and 21% from renewables.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said failing to control the emissions from electricity generation would increase heat waves, wildfires, severe storms, flooding, disease, air pollution and harm to regional ecosystems.

The EPA rules repeal “significantly undermines efforts to address climate change and exposes communities to greater environmental harm by undoing climate regulations on power plants,” the lawsuit contends.

California and its Air Resources Board were part of a coalition of states, counties and cities that filed the lawsuit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on Thursday.

In addition to California and New York, the attorneys general for Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia are part of the lawsuit, along with the governor of Pennsylvania, the mayors of Chicago and New York City and the City and County of Denver.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to restore the EPA’s greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants.

text:
The U.S. Energy Department has selected Entergy to receive $13.7 million in federal funding to improve power delivery to Entergy’s customers and communities and support economic growth across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

The investment will help the company provide customers with more reliable, affordable electricity by deploying advanced transmission technology to strengthen grid performance and unlock additional transmission capacity.

“Installing this new technology is intended to help us deliver more reliable, affordable electricity to customers by reducing congestion, improving system readiness for large loads, and potentially avoiding capital costs for other transmission upgrades,” said John Hudson, chief external affairs officer for Entergy. “With this federal funding, we’ll be able to deploy advanced dynamic line rating technology across more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines across Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi, boosting the amount of power we can safely move using the infrastructure we already have. We appreciate the Department of Energy’s partnership and its commitment to strengthening energy resilience in our region. This is another example of Entergy doing all we can to modernize the electric grid while reducing the financial impacts of these large projects on our customers and communities.”

Through the DOE’s SPARK program, Entergy and its electric companies in Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana will implement dynamic line rating technology, targeted geographic surveys, substation and terminal upgrades and hardware integration across 1,125 miles of existing transmission lines. These upgrades will help the company more effectively manage its energy infrastructure in areas experiencing load growth driven by new industrial development, manufacturing and data center expansion.

The project is designed to rapidly unlock at least a 25% increase in transfer capability on selected transmission corridors by using real-time line ratings and operational enhancements. Early modeling has shown the potential for 29% to 61% increase in available power capacity across the project area, demonstrating significant opportunities to reduce congestion and use existing assets more efficiently.

Like this news? Make BIC Magazine a Google preferred news source.

By expanding the capability of existing transmission corridors, Entergy will be better positioned to support new and expanding industries across the region, helping communities attract investment and sustain long-term economic growth. By improving visibility into grid conditions, Entergy can better manage congestion, defer capital investments and reduce costs — benefits that can ultimately translate into savings for customers.

Project timeline

The four-year project also establishes a scalable, repeatable model for deploying advanced transmission technologies across multiple operating companies. As constraints shift over time, Entergy will be able to redeploy dynamic line rating sensors to new corridors, extending the value of the investment and accelerating future modernization efforts.

title: Communist China Copies Biden's Homework With Their Own EV Mandate
description:
At the end of last year, new energy vehicles accounted for 54% of all passenger vehicle sales in China.
From 2021 to 2025, China’s vehicle exports increased by about one million units annually.
In the first seven months of this year, China’s vehicle exports reached 6.14 million units, up 66.8% year on year.
In its first-half earnings release, Sinopec noted falling domestic fuel sales, which have been weighing on the company’s earnings for two years.
These sales goals are not far-fetched, as NEV sales in August were 62% of total vehicle sales, and high oil prices due to the Iran conflict helped drive EV adoption.
text:
China released the “Intelligent Connected New Energy Vehicle Industry 15th Five-Year Plan,” a 2026-2030 roadmap, announcing new targets: new energy vehicles (NEVs) should account for 70% of domestic new passenger-car sales and 40% of new commercial-vehicle sales by 2030. China also plans to deploy vehicles equipped with autonomous driving functions at scale, saying that the safety performance of such vehicles should substantially surpass that of human drivers. They say mechanisms will support this by assessing the technology’s maturity and safety. The plan calls for tighter oversight of vehicle and battery capacity, mergers and restructuring, and curbs on improper local investment incentives. It is a top-down approach led by the central government, with strict goals and standards for companies and the buying public.

China’s goal is only sightly different than the mandate proposed by the Biden administration which would have required automakers to have electric vehicles command about 67 percent of their new car sales in 2032. The Biden mandate was later eliminated by the Trump administration.

Besides setting NEV sales shares, the plan calls for average passenger-vehicle fuel consumption to fall to 3.3 liters per 100 kilometers by 2030, while battery electric passenger cars should consume around 11.5 kilowatt-hours per 100 kilometers. Labor productivity per employee across the industry is targeted to rise 15% from 2025 levels. Highly automated driving will be implemented on expressways, urban expressways, and selected urban roads. To advance commercialization, China will conduct demonstrations involving autonomous passenger cars, buses, long-haul logistics and urban delivery, while taking an orderly approach to vehicle approvals and road access. The plan also aims to foster several automakers ranked among the world’s top 10 by sales, along with auto parts companies ranked among the global top 100. China wants its auto industry to join the ranks of the world’s automotive powerhouses.

To implement the plan, China will maintain NEV tax incentives, support vehicle trade-ins, promote NEV adoption in rural areas, and back the replacement of city buses and their batteries. It will also deepen reforms to NEV insurance. It aims to centralize transportation control under the State.

At the end of last year, new energy vehicles accounted for 54% of all passenger vehicle sales in China. Electric vehicles and hybrids accounted for 65% of China’s total passenger car sales in August, according to data by the local Passenger Car Association (PCA). EV targets are expected to continue eroding road fuel demand in China, which has been falling for the second year in a row. This year’s decline is steeper due to higher oil prices stemming from the Iran conflict.

In Southeast Asia, consumers are willing to wait in long lines to buy popular Chinese NEV models. In Europe, five Chinese automakers sold a combined 138,000 vehicles across 31 countries in May, up 64% year on year. For the first time, Chinese automakers surpassed Japanese carmakers in monthly new vehicle registrations in Europe. In South America, Brazil is the largest destination for China’s NEV exports. In July, BYD’s plant in Brazil produced its 100,000th vehicle.

Data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers show that China’s exports rose from 977,300 in 2013 to 7.098 million vehicles in 2025, more than sixfold in 12 years. From 2021 to 2025, China’s vehicle exports increased by about one million units annually. In the first seven months of this year, China’s vehicle exports reached 6.14 million units, up 66.8% year on year. Strong NEV growth has played a major role in propelling China to become the world’s largest automobile exporter.

China’s Sinopec, the world’s top refiner by capacity, expects Chinese oil demand to drop by 8.9%— 600,000 barrels per day — in 2026 from a year earlier, due to demand destruction from higher oil prices and the acceleration of EV adoption. Gasoline demand is expected to decline by 8.7%, while diesel consumption is expected to drop by 11.4%. The only petroleum product used in transportation expected to increase is jet fuel, whose demand is expected to rise by 1.3% this year compared to 2025.

China, the world’s largest oil importer, built a huge oil reserve of around 1.4 billion barrels and banned exports of petroleum products during the spring and early summer of the Iran conflict, which helped the country absorb price increases from the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz by the Iranians. The high oil prices also sped up the adoption of electric vehicles.

With these changes, Sinopec, or China Petroleum & Chemical Corporation as it is officially known, is looking to transform its business. Sinopec will be allocating more capital to new energy and chemicals by the end of the decade to grow revenues and profits amid the lowest domestic fuel sales in China in nearly a decade. The company’s chairman is looking to develop shale oil fields, sustainable aviation fuels, and cut refining costs to make Sinopec more resilient to the declining fuel demand in China. In its first-half earnings release, Sinopec noted falling domestic fuel sales, which have been weighing on the company’s earnings for two years.

Conclusion

China targets NEV shares of 70% for passenger-car sales and 40% for commercial-vehicle sales by 2030 in its 5-year plan. Vehicles equipped with autonomous driving functions are expected to enter large-scale use, with safety performance substantially surpassing that of human drivers. These sales goals are not far-fetched, as NEV sales in August were 62% of total vehicle sales, and high oil prices due to the Iran conflict helped drive EV adoption. China, the world’s largest oil importer, is weathering the closure of the Strait of Hormuz fairly well, as it has reduced its oil imports and banned petroleum exports for much of the conflict in the spring and early summer of 2026.

title: General Motors' EV Sales Are Way Down. But It's Not As Bleak As It Seems - InsideEVs
description:
Q3 EV sales fell by more than a third, only 25,473 electric cars delivered.
EV and hybrid sales are down across the board in the U.S., not just at GM, despite growing consumer interest.
So the Chevy Equinox EV saw the biggest sales fall from last year, at a massive 92.4%.
Interestingly, both EV pickups dropped a similar amount, with the Silverado EV falling 58% and the Sierra EV losing 50.8% of sales.
(The Chevy Bolt might technically have improved in sales but that's only because it wasn't on sale during Q3 2025.)
text:
Last year's Q3 was a big one for GM. It sold 66,501 EVs in Q3 2025, making last year its strongest ever for electric vehicles. This year, things look different. Q3 EV sales fell by more than a third, only 25,473 electric cars delivered. While that drop is massive, it likely has more to do with the loss of federal tax credits and an industry reset than a lack of demand for GM's electric portfolio.

The Trump administration eliminated the federal tax break for $7,500 EV buyers one year ago. Many buyers pulled ahead their purchases, racing to get EVs before the tax credit ended on September 30, 2025. That led to GM's record third quarter last year, which may have over-inflated its sales perceptions.

So this drop off more likely just a recalibration toward normal than it is customers losing interest in electric Chevys and Cadillacs. EV and hybrid sales are down across the board in the U.S., not just at GM, despite growing consumer interest. These vehicles are more expensive than they were last year, and the regulations that incentivized automakers to sell more EVs have been largely dismantled.

Some electric GM models are still selling pretty well, though, even though Cadillac seems to be doing most of the heavy lifting. America's luxury brand had two of GM's three best-selling EVs in Q3. The Cadillac Optiq recorded 4,550 deliveries. The return of the Chevy Bolt took the number two spot, with 3,866 deliveries, and the Cadillac Lyriq was close behind with 3,617. The Cadillac Vistiq did well, too, with 2,587 sales.

Photo by: Jeff Perez / Motor1

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the cheaper models suffered the most. The previous tax incentives benefited affordable car buyers most, as rich folk don't need the extra discount. So the Chevy Equinox EV saw the biggest sales fall from last year, at a massive 92.4%. The Blazer EV dropped 84.4%, too. Interestingly, both EV pickups dropped a similar amount, with the Silverado EV falling 58% and the Sierra EV losing 50.8% of sales. Cadillac Escalade IQ and IQL sales fell only 29.2%. The outlier is the Hummer EV, which saw a massive 72.9% decline. (The Chevy Bolt might technically have improved in sales but that's only because it wasn't on sale during Q3 2025.)

It might seem like doom and gloom, over at GM's electrified lineup, but only if you just look at the sales sheet without context. This year, GM is only down from a record year. If anything, this proves how effective federal tax incentives are for customers to switch over to electric. As demand recovers and gas prices rise, we'll see how long it takes for GM to reach its previous high water mark.
